## 1. Background

Lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is one of the most frequently occurring musculoskeletal injuries in general and athletic populations engaged in recreational and competitive sports [[Citation 1–8](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The precise etiology of LAS is complex [[Citation 9](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and often presents as a mechanical laxity and proprioception deficit [[Citation 5](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Clinically, lateral ankle sprains are categorized into grade I injury as mild, grade II injury as moderate, and grade III injury as severe [[Citation 1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 5](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Although LAS is typically believed to be a one-off injury, the evidence from hospital emergency department records shows that up to 74% of patients with LAS continue to have persistent symptoms [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 11](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Studies reported that LAS patients have the most significant risk of re-injury in all lower-extremity musculoskeletal injuries [[Citation 12](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In specific sports populations, the re-injured population could be as high as 70% [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], and nearly 40% of LAS patients would experience chronic ankle instability within a year of the initial injury due to the re-injury [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 14](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The high rate of re-injury might be brought on by either premature return to sport (RTS) or inadequate rehabilitation [[Citation 15](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 16](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

RTS is considered safe for an injured athlete to return to training or competition [[Citation 17](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This also results from the anticipated evaluation, medical intervention, and rehabilitation procedure [[Citation 17](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] RTS should be viewed as a continuous process rather than finished in a single step. Thus, each stage is seen as a tiny step toward the RTS [[Citation 19](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Ardern et al. [[Citation 20](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] defined the RTS continuum as the three process parts of “return to performance”, “return to sport”, and “return to participation” [[Citation 19](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 22](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. These three processes are influenced by the injury grade, rehabilitation strategies, pre and post RTS foot function tests, the amount of time spent in RTS, psychosocial elements of RTS, emotional values, and self-perceptions [[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 23–25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. All these factors could be combined to assess whether the injured athlete satisfied the criteria for RTS and gauged the performance level after RTS.

Even though the criteria for RTS in patients with LAS have not been clarified in the current literature, the components of RTS decision-making (i.e. pain, ankle perception, including proprioception, ankle injuries, muscle activation, sensorimotor control systems, and motor testing) were previously described in narrative reviews, with consensus among clinical experts [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 26](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Furthermore, it has been shown that the decision-making factors for RTS in patients with LAS consider using quantitative methods, which is a crucial criterion for RTS [[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 28](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Similarly, these quantitative parameters should be incorporated into self-reporting and assessing ability after RTS decision-making in patients with LAS [[Citation 29](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The evidence-based clinical guidelines [[Citation 16](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] recently included exercise-based rehabilitation programs for various treatment options for LAS patients [[Citation 30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In addition, some studies have shown that kinesio taping may facilitate RTS by improving muscle contraction [[Citation 31](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], although this is not without debate[[Citation 32](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This treatment can help LAS to have a good supporting effect during exercise performance, but it may also have a negative impact on the active stability of the lateral muscles [[Citation 33](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In addition, there are many other therapies, such as (acupuncture [[Citation 34](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], laser [[Citation 35](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], manual [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], etc.), which can help LAS to RTS [[Citation 37](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. However, the clinical experience typically dictates how best to treat patients with LAS and when sports activities may be resumed [[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 39](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In such cases, the time of RTS is used to measure and quantify the rehabilitation success [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 40](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. However, the isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive, as evidenced by the significant recurrent rate of LAS injuries. Therefore, it’s essential to build a methodical decision-making process for patients with LAS regarding RTS, considering various factors.

The process of RTS from LAS is multifactorial, and there has yet to be a published systematic review that evaluates this complex process over time. Therefore, this systematic review aims to investigate the process factors of RTS for LAS, including the timing of RTS for LAS, the rehabilitation program, the outcome indicators, and the assessment of the performance recovery after decision-making, to provide further guidance and clinical implications for LAS patients to develop RTS program.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1. Protocol registration

The PRISMA 2020 Guidelines Reporting Items checklist [[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] was strictly followed to conduct the current systematic review, with protocol in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluations (PRISMA) statement. The study protocol was registered on the International Register of Prospective Systematic Evaluations (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024522798).

### 2.2. Search strategy

Four online electronic literature databases, including Web of Science, MEDLINE (_via_ PubMed), Scopus, and ScienceDirect, were searched up to March 1, 2024. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) developed the search strategy, filtered by term-level search, to identify possible studies. Two sets of terms combined with the Boolean indicator “AND” were used, including Lateral Ankle Sprain (e.g. “Lateral Ankle Coper”, “Lateral Ankle Injury”) and Return To Sport (e.g. “Return To Play”). The terms used were either MESH or non-MESH terms, and the Boolean indicator separated the words in each term, “OR”. This technique was restricted to the use of the English language. All screened documents were imported into reference management software (Endnote®version X9, Thomson Reuters, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and duplicate references were removed. A third researcher (Q.M.) would be referred to discuss solutions if any discrepancies were found during the search.

### 2.3. Eligibility criteria

This study covered prospective studies, surveys, and randomized controlled trials (RCT) published in peer-reviewed scientific articles written in English before March 1, 2024. Firstly, the titles and abstracts were screened by two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) using a glossary of terms. Then, the full text was reviewed using the following inclusion and exclusion criteria: the third researcher (Q.M.) was referred to decide the eligibility of the final study if an agreement could not be reached during the screening process. Finally, we conducted a manual search after completing the full-text search to find any studies that had been overlooked the first time.

#### 2.3.1. Inclusion criteria

These articles were included in this review if, (1) the subjects are human and were not restricted by sex or race; (2) RTS is the article’s primary outcome; (3) the article should report the biomechanical parameters covering the lower extremity kinematics, kinetics, muscle activity, joint range of motion, functional assessment, or dynamic postural control; (4) the articles should concentrate solely on LAS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment at least 50% were included in this review [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

#### 2.3.2. Exclusion criteria

The following criteria were followed to exclude articles, (1) conferences, dissertations, reviews, abstracts, and meta-analyses; (2) study subjects were non-human; (3) LAS requires ligament reconstruction surgery; (4) the results of the article were not relevant to RTS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment less than 50% were excluded in this review [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

#### 2.3.3. Outcome of RTS

The result indicators in the article should be pertinent to RTS. We concluded that due to the multifactorial nature of the RTS process, the following outcome indicators should be used to screen articles, the evaluation of LAS, the duration from the time of the sprain until RTS, rehabilitation measures, decision-making indicators (pre- and post-functional tests, pre- and post-pain tests, self-perceptions, mood determinations, and quantitative parameters) and post-decision-making tests (ratings of athleticism and observations of athletic performance).

### 2.4. Quality assessment and risk of bias assessment

The quality and risk of bias of the included articles were assessed using an improved quality indicator checklist [[Citation 28](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 44](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Fourteen (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22) out of the 27 items on the list were used in the previous review study on chronic ankle instability and LAS [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 46](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This prior research could assign multiple quality labels according to quality scores. Consequently, 14 items from the list were adopted in this study to examine the confounding bias, reporting, external validity, and internal validity of all the papers. Half of the 14 item types in the list were assessments of data descriptions. According to the purpose of this study, studies with a score of > 50% were included in this review; otherwise, they were excluded. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently scored each article in this review, yielding a maximum quality score of 15.

### 2.5. Data extraction and manager

Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently employed standardized and pre-programmed data modules for extraction tables. For each article that met the requirements of this review, modules were selected and data removed according to the study: (1) authors, (2) publication year, (3) country, (4) sample size (gender and age), (5) duration (time from intervention initiation), (6) frequency of interventions (number and intervals), (7) level of LAS, (8) treatment (measures of rehabilitation interventions), (9) outcome variables (10) main result, (12) evaluator, (13) research type, (14) criteria for RTS, (15) RTS time, and (16) RTS tests.

### 2.6. Statistical analyses

Due to the large number of direct variables and lack of indirect comparative variables in the randomized controlled trials (RCT) and prospective studies included in this study, the present work failed to satisfy the meta-analysis standards. Therefore, the resultant data was presented in the Tables of this study.

## 3. Result

### 3.1. Search results

In the beginning, 1081 records were found. After removing all duplicates, 690 records were retained. Three hundred eighteen records were included based on title and abstract screening for a full-text review of inclusion and exclusion criteria. A total of 18 articles satisfied the inclusion criteria. After another manual search for studies missed during the initial search, two articles fulfilled the inclusion criteria. In the end, all 20 articles achieved more than 50% scores of quality. Of the scores recorded, 11 articles scored >70%, and 19 articles scored > 60%. The Modified Quality Index checklist papers had the most methodological constraints regarding external validity (⑧, ⑨) and internal validity (⑬, ⑭). ### 3.4. Process factors of RTS in patients with LAS

All 20 studies included in this systematic review described criteria for RTS in patients with LAS and analyzed process factors from LAS to post-RTS.

#### 3.4.1. Rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS

Rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS were summarized in the 12 [[Citation 9](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 62–68](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] included studies. Eight [[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 64–66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] of these studies were on rehabilitation measures for grade 1, 2 LAS sprains, two [[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] were on rehabilitation measures for grade 2 LAS sprains, and two [[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 68](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] were on rehabilitation measures for grade 1,2,3 LAS sprains. Included were eleven [[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 62–66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 68](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] with a set control group and one [[Citation 69](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] with an intervention group only. Most of the interventions for LAS were delivered within the 48-hour post-trauma acute period; only one [[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] was given within three weeks of trauma, and one [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] did not mention the time of intervention initiation. For the rehabilitation measures in treating 941 patients with LAS, the mean age was 27 years (age was not mentioned in two [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] studies). In the studies where the gender ratio was mentioned, women accounted for about 44% and men for about 56%, according to Table 2.

#### 3.4.2. Classification of outcome indicators

The outcome indicators of the included rehabilitation treatments were classified according to the PAASS guidelines [[Citation 70](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] as: (1) pain severity: [numerical rating scale (NRS) for pain, visual analog scale (VAS), pain after/during 20 m walk]; (2) ankle impairments: [isometric strength, range of motion, total ankle mobility, lateral differences in total mobility]; (3) athlete perception: [Brunel mood scale BRUMS, psychological preparation for return to sport (Psychological Preparation for RTS Scale I-PRRS)]; (4) sensorimotor control: [assessment of static balance (BESS), dynamic balance (SEBT), sense of joint repositioning, measures of postural control, self-report (Walking Disability Scale)]; (5) sport/functional performance: [gait running and jumping analysis]; (6) other (not part of the PAASS classification): adherence to rehabilitation [Rehabilitation Adherence Scale (RAdMAT)], foot and ankle function tests [Karlson Ankle Function Scale (KAFS), Foot and Ankle Ability Test (FAAM)], Impairment [Foot and Ankle Disability Index (FADI), overall assessment of ankle impairment (5-point categorical scale)], patient satisfaction with treatment (10-point flat scale), time to return to pain-free and disability-free exercise, number of recurrent ankle sprains, the effectiveness of assigned treatment, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT), activities of daily living (ADL), and numeric pain rating scale (ALT).

#### 3.4.3. Classification of intervention treatments

##### 3.4.3.1. Electrotherapy

Electrotherapy could release high amplitude/density currents based on electrode positioning [[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Acute [[Citation 66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] or chronic [[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] injuries were treated by selectively stimulating A, δ, and c nerve fibers. Since the electrode positions and the current frequency were different, the effectiveness and principles of treatment vary. Mendel et al. [[Citation 35](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] used high-voltage pulsed present, based on inhibiting edema, to treat patients with grade 1 and 2 LAS within 48 h of the injury. It was found that HVPC did not influence the healing process for moderate (grade 2) ankle sprains and prolonged recovery from grade 1 LAS by approximately one day.

This method had no clinical significance for recovery after LAS and was only used as an adjunctive treatment. Also, using electrotherapy in patients with grade 1 and 2 LAS within 48 h, Razzano et al. [[Citation 66](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] found that the use of noninvasive interactive nerve stimulation, an electrotherapy that works by targeting areas of the skin with low impedance, improved the short-term prognosis of athletes with grade I or II LAS and may accelerate the return to physical activity by half the time.

##### 3.4.3.2. Balanced intervention approach

Injured athletes were provided with a sense of autonomy by creating variability in rehabilitation to increase their perceived control [[Citation 63](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Arvinen-Barrow et al. [[Citation 71](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] used active video gaming (AVG) as a balancing intervention for individuals suffering from grade 2 LAS. This approach provided more flexibility for both static and dynamic postural control exercises and responded to the perceived readiness for RTS and the emotional state of patients with LAS (M ± SD = 26.75 ± 19.03).

##### 3.4.3.3. Joint injection

Pharmacological injections that would change the intra-articular matrix and fill in skin gaps could reduce pain and stiffness [[Citation 72](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Petrella et al. [[Citation 73](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and Petersen et al. [[Citation 64](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] used hyaluronic acid to treat patients with grade 1 and 2 LAS. HA is a naturally occurring biological substance that is a significant component of the ultrastructure of ligaments, cartilage, and synovium. In the short and long term, this method demonstrated outstanding outcomes in treating LAS [[Citation 49](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and allowed the patients to RTS 6 days earlier.

##### 3.4.3.4. Functional movement approach

Patients treated with functional movement therapy return faster to sport or work [[Citation 64](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This approach not only consistently reduces swelling but also improves mobility [[Citation 64](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Mailuhu et al. [[Citation 56](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] developed a standardized 8-week neuromuscular training program using APP for patients with grade 2 LAS. It has been demonstrated that this program affects well for athletes and may be a useful immediate treatment option for acute LAS in general. Similarly, Punt et al. [[Citation 74](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and Tennler et al. [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] designed a 6-week training intervention program, and both results recognized that exercise therapy can improve ankle function in patients with LAS by 8–9 points.

##### 3.4.3.5. Ligament fixation Protection method

O’Connora et al. [[Citation 75](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and Wells et al. [[Citation 76](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] used ligament immobilization protection for patients with lateral ankle sprains. This is a conservative therapy approach, which is the main objective of ligament preservation [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. They protect the injured ligament from excessive tension by immobilization in a bandage or cast for 4–12 weeks to achieve moderate healing. For complete recovery, almost a year is needed [[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 65](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

##### 3.4.3.6. Combination of approaches

Athletes, particularly in contact sports (such as basketball and football), may often suffer multiple ankle injuries with typical joint instability, thus requiring a safe and rapid approach to help sports rehabilitation [[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Therefore, various methods were successfully merged to shorten the period and RTS. Ammendolia et al. [[Citation 77](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. used a combined process of ultrasound therapy and cold therapy in patients with grade 1 and 2 LAS, which was effective in relieving the pain intensity and speeding up the time of RTS. However, it was difficult to identify the role of cold therapy and ultrasound therapy separately. In contrast, Toyoshima et al. [[Citation 78](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] employed a combined Electrical Muscle Stimulation method using isometric exercise during immobilization, which not only increased total ankle mobility and shortened the time to reach RTS but also optimized single-factor rehabilitation measures by being able to separately identify the roles and benefits of ligament immobilization and protection.

#### 3.4.4. Criteria for RTS in patients with LAS

Criteria for RTS in LAS patients were listed in four of the included studies [[Citation 1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 70](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Three of these investigations specifically interviewed 347 doctors, 20 athletes, and 103 physical therapists using questionnaires, with 99 doctors with over 15 years of clinical experience [[Citation 30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 70](ht

This is a systematic review published in *Annals of Medicine* (2025, Volume 57, Issue 1) by Jiang et al. from Ningbo University, University of Auckland, and University of Essex, titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The review investigates the factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries in athletic populations. Up to 74% of patients have persistent symptoms, and re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports, with nearly 40% developing chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may be due to premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024522798). Quality assessment used the Downs and Black checklist. Inclusion criteria required human subjects, RTS as a primary outcome, biomechanical parameters, and quality scores ≥50%.

**Results:** Twenty papers were included (mean quality score 75.36±10.40%; 11 RCTs, 7 prospective studies, 3 questionnaires). Studies were divided into four categories: (1) rehabilitation measures, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and RTS time.

**Rehabilitation interventions identified:** Electrotherapy (high-voltage pulsed current, noninvasive interactive nerve stimulation), balanced intervention approach (active video gaming), joint injection (hyaluronic acid), functional movement approach (neuromuscular training, exercise therapy), ligament fixation/protection (immobilization 4-12 weeks), and combination approaches (ultrasound + cold therapy, electrical muscle stimulation + isometric exercise).

**Key findings:** The RTS process is multifactorial, influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. No standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation currently exists. The review identified that RTS should be viewed as a continuous process (not a single event), with the RTS continuum comprising "return to participation," "return to sport," and "return to performance." Outcome indicators were classified according to PAASS guidelines: pain severity, ankle impairments, athlete perception, sensorimotor control, and sport/functional performance.

**Conclusion:** The study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS, providing theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance. The authors emphasize that isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive given the high recurrence rate, and a methodical decision-making process considering multiple factors is essential.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Abstract

### Background

Returning to sport (RTS) from lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is multifaceted and interdisciplinary. This systematic review aimed to investigate the factors involved in RTS and further establish a standard paradigm of RTS to treat and rehabilitate the LAS.

### Methods

Four electronic databases, including PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, Science Direct, and Scopus, were searched until March 1, 2024. The literature was identified, screened, evaluated, managed and data was extracted by developing inclusion criteria based on the PICO model for systematic reviews. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Downs and Black checklist and the measurement parameters were summarised.

### Results

This systematic review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Participant’s information, research content, purpose, methods, and interventions were extracted and summarized. The included articles were divided into four categories for further discussion, including (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS of LAS, (3) performance assessment after RTS of LAS, and (4) the relationship between criteria and time of RTS for LAS.

### Conclusion

RTS for LAS is a continuous process, which is influenced by complex factors, such as the injury extent, injury causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The standard paradigms of RTS rehabilitation for LAS is still lacking in the literature. Current study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS. Findings may provide theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance for the RTS of LAS patients.

**Keywords:**Ankle Sprain, clinical treatment, Foot and ankle, return to play, sport rehabilitation

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Background

1.
Lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is one of the most frequently occurring musculoskeletal injuries in general and athletic populations engaged in recreational and competitive sports [[1–8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0001)]. The precise etiology of LAS is complex [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0009)] and often presents as a mechanical laxity and proprioception deficit [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0005)]. Clinically, lateral ankle sprains are categorized into grade I injury as mild, grade II injury as moderate, and grade III injury as severe [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0001),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0005)]. Although LAS is typically believed to be a one-off injury, the evidence from hospital emergency department records shows that up to 74% of patients with LAS continue to have persistent symptoms [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0010),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0011)]. Studies reported that LAS patients have the most significant risk of re-injury in all lower-extremity musculoskeletal injuries [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0012)]. In specific sports populations, the re-injured population could be as high as 70% [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0013)], and nearly 40% of LAS patients would experience chronic ankle instability within a year of the initial injury due to the re-injury [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0013),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0014)]. The high rate of re-injury might be brought on by either premature return to sport (RTS) or inadequate rehabilitation [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0015),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0016)].

RTS is considered safe for an injured athlete to return to training or competition [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0017)]. This also results from the anticipated evaluation, medical intervention, and rehabilitation procedure [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0017),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0018)] RTS should be viewed as a continuous process rather than finished in a single step. Thus, each stage is seen as a tiny step toward the RTS [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0019)]. Ardern et al. [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0020),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021)] defined the RTS continuum as the three process parts of “return to performance”, “return to sport”, and “return to participation” [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0019),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0022)]. These three processes are influenced by the injury grade, rehabilitation strategies, pre and post RTS foot function tests, the amount of time spent in RTS, psychosocial elements of RTS, emotional values, and self-perceptions [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021),[23–25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0023)]. All these factors could be combined to assess whether the injured athlete satisfied the criteria for RTS and gauged the performance level after RTS.

Even though the criteria for RTS in patients with LAS have not been clarified in the current literature, the components of RTS decision-making (i.e. pain, ankle perception, including proprioception, ankle injuries, muscle activation, sensorimotor control systems, and motor testing) were previously described in narrative reviews, with consensus among clinical experts [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0010),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0026),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0027)]. Furthermore, it has been shown that the decision-making factors for RTS in patients with LAS consider using quantitative methods, which is a crucial criterion for RTS [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0028)]. Similarly, these quantitative parameters should be incorporated into self-reporting and assessing ability after RTS decision-making in patients with LAS [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0029)]. The evidence-based clinical guidelines [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0016),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0025),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0027)] recently included exercise-based rehabilitation programs for various treatment options for LAS patients [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0030)]. In addition, some studies have shown that kinesio taping may facilitate RTS by improving muscle contraction [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0031)], although this is not without debate[[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0032)]. This treatment can help LAS to have a good supporting effect during exercise performance, but it may also have a negative impact on the active stability of the lateral muscles [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0033)]. In addition, there are many other therapies, such as (acupuncture [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0034)], laser [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0035)], manual [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0036)], etc.), which can help LAS to RTS [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0037)]. However, the clinical experience typically dictates how best to treat patients with LAS and when sports activities may be resumed [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0038),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0039)]. In such cases, the time of RTS is used to measure and quantify the rehabilitation success [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0018),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0040)]. However, the isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive, as evidenced by the significant recurrent rate of LAS injuries. Therefore, it’s essential to build a methodical decision-making process for patients with LAS regarding RTS, considering various factors.

The process of RTS from LAS is multifactorial, and there has yet to be a published systematic review that evaluates this complex process over time. Therefore, this systematic review aims to investigate the process factors of RTS for LAS, including the timing of RTS for LAS, the rehabilitation program, the outcome indicators, and the assessment of the performance recovery after decision-making, to provide further guidance and clinical implications for LAS patients to develop RTS program.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Methods

2.
### Protocol registration

2.1.
The PRISMA 2020 Guidelines Reporting Items checklist [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0041)] was strictly followed to conduct the current systematic review, with protocol in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluations (PRISMA) statement. The study protocol was registered on the International Register of Prospective Systematic Evaluations (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024522798).

### Search strategy

2.2.
Four online electronic literature databases, including Web of Science, MEDLINE (_via_ PubMed), Scopus, and ScienceDirect, were searched up to March 1, 2024. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) developed the search strategy, filtered by term-level search, to identify possible studies. Two sets of terms combined with the Boolean indicator “AND” were used, including Lateral Ankle Sprain (e.g. “Lateral Ankle Coper”, “Lateral Ankle Injury”) and Return To Sport (e.g. “Return To Play”). The terms used were either MESH or non-MESH terms, and the Boolean indicator separated the words in each term, “OR”. This technique was restricted to the use of the English language. All screened documents were imported into reference management software (Endnote®version X9, Thomson Reuters, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and duplicate references were removed. A third researcher (Q.M.) would be referred to discuss solutions if any discrepancies were found during the search.

### Eligibility criteria

2.3.
This study covered prospective studies, surveys, and randomized controlled trials (RCT) published in peer-reviewed scientific articles written in English before March 1, 2024. Firstly, the titles and abstracts were screened by two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) using a glossary of terms. Then, the full text was reviewed using the following inclusion and exclusion criteria: the third researcher (Q.M.) was referred to decide the eligibility of the final study if an agreement could not be reached during the screening process. Finally, we conducted a manual search after completing the full-text search to find any studies that had been overlooked the first time.

#### Inclusion criteria

2.3.1.
These articles were included in this review if, (1) the subjects are human and were not restricted by sex or race; (2) RTS is the article’s primary outcome; (3) the article should report the biomechanical parameters covering the lower extremity kinematics, kinetics, muscle activity, joint range of motion, functional assessment, or dynamic postural control; (4) the articles should concentrate solely on LAS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment at least 50% were included in this review [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042)].

#### Exclusion criteria

2.3.2.
The following criteria were followed to exclude articles, (1) conferences, dissertations, reviews, abstracts, and meta-analyses; (2) study subjects were non-human; (3) LAS requires ligament reconstruction surgery; (4) the results of the article were not relevant to RTS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment less than 50% were excluded in this review [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042)].

#### Outcome of RTS

2.3.3.
The result indicators in the article should be pertinent to RTS. We concluded that due to the multifactorial nature of the RTS process, the following outcome indicators should be used to screen articles, the evaluation of LAS, the duration from the time of the sprain until RTS, rehabilitation measures, decision-making indicators (pre- and post-functional tests, pre- and post-pain tests, self-perceptions, mood determinations, and quantitative parameters) and post-decision-making tests (ratings of athleticism and observations of athletic performance).

### Quality assessment and risk of bias assessment

2.4.
The quality and risk of bias of the included articles were assessed using an improved quality indicator checklist [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0028),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0043),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0044)]. Fourteen (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22) out of the 27 items on the list were used in the previous review study on chronic ankle instability and LAS [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0045),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0046)]. This prior research could assign multiple quality labels according to quality scores. Consequently, 14 items from the list were adopted in this study to examine the confounding bias, reporting, external validity, and internal validity of all the papers. Half of the 14 item types in the list were assessments of data descriptions. According to the purpose of this study, studies with a score of > 50% were included in this review; otherwise, they were excluded. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently scored each article in this review, yielding a maximum quality score of 15.

### Data extraction and manager

2.5.
Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently employed standardized and pre-programmed data modules for extraction tables. For each article that met the requirements of this review, modules were selected and data removed according to the study: (1) authors, (2) publication year, (3) country, (4) sample size (gender and age), (5) duration (time from intervention initiation), (6) frequency of interventions (number and intervals), (7) level of LAS, (8) treatment (measures of rehabilitation interventions), (9) outcome variables (10) main result, (12) evaluator, (13) research type, (14) criteria for RTS, (15) RTS time, and (16) RTS tests.

### Statistical analyses

2.6.
Due to the large number of direct variables and lack of indirect comparative variables in the randomized controlled trials (RCT) and prospective studies included in this study, the present work failed to satisfy the meta-analysis standards. Therefore, the resultant data was presented in the Tables of this study.

### Search results

3.1.
In the beginning, 1081 records were found. After removing all duplicates, 690 records were retained. Three hundred eighteen records were included based on title and abstract screening for a full-text review of inclusion and exclusion criteria. A total of 18 articles satisfied the inclusion criteria. After another manual search for studies missed during the initial search, two articles fulfilled the inclusion criteria. In the end, all 20 articles achieved more than 50% scores of quality. ### Characteristics of the included studies

3.3.
This review divided the 20 studies into four categories based on the topic and content of the included studies, which were the rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#t0002)), the criteria for RTS in LAS patients ([Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#t0003)), the performance assessment after RTS in LAS patients ([Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#t0004)), and the relationship between test assessment and time of RTS in LAS patients ([Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#t0005)). Each table provided a comprehensive summary of all the variables related to the RTS procedure. The 20 studies included three questionnaires [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0015),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0047),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0048)], 11 randomized controlled trials [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0005),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0006),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0026),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0034),[49–55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0049)], 7 prospective studies [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0036),[56–60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0056)], and 1 prospective study that qualified as a randomized controlled trial [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0061)].

### Process factors of RTS in patients with LAS

3.4.
All 20 studies included in this systematic review described criteria for RTS in patients with LAS and analyzed process factors from LAS to post-RTS.

#### Rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS

3.4.1.
Rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS were summarized in the 12 [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0009),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0049),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0051),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0054),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0057),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0060),[62–68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0062)] included studies. Eight [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0049),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0051),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0054),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0057),[64–66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0064)] of these studies were on rehabilitation measures for grade 1, 2 LAS sprains, two [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0049),[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0062)] were on rehabilitation measures for grade 2 LAS sprains, and two [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0060),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0068)] were on rehabilitation measures for grade 1,2,3 LAS sprains. Included were eleven [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0049),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0051),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0054),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0057),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0060),[62–66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0062),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0068)] with a set control group and one [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0069)] with an intervention group only. Most of the interventions for LAS were delivered within the 48-hour post-trauma acute period; only one [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0062)] was given within three weeks of trauma, and one [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0051)] did not mention the time of intervention initiation. args.summary:
This is a systematic review published in Annals of Medicine (2025) titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review" by Jiang, Mei, Wang, Yang, Liew, Fernandez, and Gu from Ningbo University, University of Auckland, and University of Essex. The review investigates factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Scopus) were searched up to March 1, 2024. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024522798). Quality assessment used the Downs and Black checklist (14 items).

**Results:** 20 papers were included with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. The studies were categorized into four areas: (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and time of RTS. The 20 studies included 3 questionnaires, 11 randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective studies, and 1 study that qualified as both.

**Key Findings:**
- LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries; up to 74% of patients have persistent symptoms, and re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports populations
- Nearly 40% of LAS patients develop chronic ankle instability within a year
- RTS should be viewed as a continuous process with three stages: "return to participation," "return to sport," and "return to performance"
- Rehabilitation measures included cryo-ultrasound, neuromuscular training, balance exercises, electrical stimulation, bracing, hyaluronic acid injections, and various therapeutic modalities
- RTS criteria included pain, swelling, range of motion, muscle strength, proprioception, functional stability, and functional tests
- Standard paradigms for RTS rehabilitation for LAS are still lacking in the literature

**Conclusion:** RTS for LAS is a continuous process influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The findings provide theoretical basis and clinical guidance for RTS decision-making in LAS patients.

# Return to Sport After Anatomic Lateral Ankle Stabilization Surgery for Chronic Ankle Instability

## A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

* Yanzhang Li
* Tong Su
* Yuelin Hu
* Chen Jiao
* Qinwei Guo
* Yanfang Jiang
* Dong Jiang

American Journal of Sports Medicine [52(2):p 555-566, February 2024.](https://www.ovid.com/journals/ajsm/toc/2024/52020) | DOI: 10.1177/03635465231170699

### Background:

Chronic lateral ankle instability that develops after ankle sprains has a severe, negative influence on the patient’s lower extremity function. Anatomic repair or reconstruction of the lateral ankle ligament is an effective treatment for people with chronic lateral ankle instability who want to regain their preinjury levels of work and sport.

### Purpose:

To determine the rate of return to sport (RTS) and related factors after anatomic lateral ankle stabilization (ALAS) surgery.

### Study Design:

Systematic review and meta-analysis; Level of evidence, 4.

### Methods:

Electronic databases including Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and EBSCO Rehabilitation & Sports Medicine Source were searched from the earliest feasible entrance until August 2021. Articles reporting the number of patients who returned to sport after ALAS surgery and analyzing the relevant factors were included. The results were combined using proportion meta-analyses.

### Results:

A total of 25 publications were reviewed, with a total of 1384 participants. Results showed that 95% of patients (95% CI, 91%-99%) returned to any sport, 83% (95% CI, 73%-91%) returned to their preinjury level of sport, and 87% (95% CI, 71%-98%) returned to competitive sport after surgery. The mean time to RTS was 12.45 weeks (95% CI, 10.8-14.1 weeks). Each decade of age increased the likelihood of RTS failure by 6%, and increases in body mass index (BMI) of 5 kg/m2 raised the risk of RTS failure by 4%. The rate of RTS was higher in professional and competitive athletes (93%; 95% CI, 73%-100%) than in recreational athletes (83%; 95% CI, 76%-89%). Analysis showed no differences for arthroscopy versus open surgery, repair versus reconstruction, and early versus late weightbearing.

### Conclusion:

In most cases, patients may return to some kind of sport after ALAS surgery, and some patients RTS at their preinjury level. The relative risk of RTS failure increases according to the magnitude of the increase in age and BMI. Elite athletes are more likely to return compared with nonelite athletes.

## Abstract

Ankle injuries, particularly sprains, are among the most prevalent musculoskeletal injuries in the physically active population, with substantial risk of developing chronic ankle instability and long-term complications such as posttraumatic osteoarthritis. Despite their frequency and potential severity, ankle sprains are often perceived as minor, with many patients delaying or avoiding clinical intervention. This chapter explores the principles and practices of rehabilitating ankle injuries and achieving a safe return to sports. Evidence supports functional management approaches, such as early weight-bearing and bracing, combined with therapeutic exercise, as effective for reducing recurrence risk and enhancing recovery outcomes. Key rehabilitation strategies include protecting injured tissue during acute phases, progressive loading to enhance ligament strength, and addressing impairments in pain, swelling, mobility, strength, and sensorimotor control. Exercises are tailored to mimic sport-specific demands, with an emphasis on restoring the ankle’s dynamic and multiplanar functionality. The chapter also addresses psychological aspects, including athletes’ confidence and readiness to return to sport. Emphasizing periodic assessment throughout recovery, it is discussed the return to sports frameworks that integrate physical, psychological, and performance-based criteria, supplemented by evidence on the utility of external supports like bracing or taping. The integration of evidence-based rehabilitation strategies is critical for preventing reinjury and optimizing athletic performance.

args.summary: This is a living reference work entry from the Springer publication "Orthopaedic Sports Medicine" (2025) by Chris M. Bleakley (Ulster University, UK), focusing on rehabilitation and return to sports following ankle injuries. The abstract highlights that ankle sprains are among the most prevalent musculoskeletal injuries in physically active populations, with substantial risk of developing chronic ankle instability and posttraumatic osteoarthritis. Despite their frequency, ankle sprains are often perceived as minor, leading many patients to delay or avoid clinical intervention. The chapter supports functional management approaches such as early weight-bearing and bracing combined with therapeutic exercise, which are effective for reducing recurrence risk and enhancing recovery outcomes. Key rehabilitation strategies include protecting injured tissue during acute phases, progressive loading to enhance ligament strength, and addressing impairments in pain, swelling, mobility, strength, and sensorimotor control. Exercises should be tailored to mimic sport-specific demands, restoring the ankle's dynamic and multiplanar functionality. The chapter also addresses psychological aspects including athletes' confidence and readiness to return to sport, and discusses return-to-sport frameworks that integrate physical, psychological, and performance-based criteria, supplemented by evidence on external supports like bracing or taping. The entry was first published online on June 11, 2025, and includes 79 references covering topics from diagnosis, functional treatment, rehabilitation exercise parameters, chronic ankle instability, and return-to-sport decision-making frameworks.

# Lack of Consensus on Return-to-Sport Criteria Following Lateral Ankle Sprain: A Systematic Review of Expert Opinions

Click name to view affiliation

***Context**:* Lateral ankle sprains (LAS) have one of the highest recurrence rates of all musculoskeletal injuries. An emphasis on rapid return to sport (RTS) following LAS likely increases reinjury risk. Unfortunately, no set of objective RTS criteria exist for LAS, forcing practitioners to rely on their own opinion of when a patient is ready to RTS. ***Purpose**:* To determine if there was consensus among published expert opinions that could help inform an initial set of RTS criteria for LAS that could be investigated in future research. ***Evidence Acquisition**:* PubMed, CINHL, and SPORTDiscus databases were searched from inception until October 2018 using a combination of keywords. Studies were included if they listed specific RTS criteria for LAS. No assessment of methodological quality was conducted because all included papers were expert opinion papers (level 5 evidence). Extracted data included the recommended domains (eg, range of motion, balance, sport-specific movement, etc) to be assessed, specific assessments for each listed domain, and thresholds (eg, 80% of the uninjured limb) to be used to determine RTS. Consensus and partial agreement were defined, a priori, as ≥75% and 50% to 75% agreement, respectively. ***Evidence Synthesis**:* Eight domains were identified within 11 included studies. Consensus was reached regarding the need to assess sport-specific movement (n = 9, 90.9%). Partial agreement was reached for the need to assess static balance (n = 7, 63.6%). The domains of pain and swelling, patient reported outcomes, range of motion, and strength were also partially agreed on (n = 6, 54.5%). No agreement was reached on specific assessments of cutoff thresholds. ***Conclusions**:* Given consensus and partial agreement results, RTS decisions following LAS should be based on sport-specific movement, static balance, patient reported outcomes, range of motion, and strength. Future research needs to determine assessments and cutoff thresholds within these domains to minimize recurrent LAS risk.

Lateral ankle sprains (LAS) are the most common injuries in sport[1](#r1)–[4](#r4) and the military[5](#r5),[6](#r6) and are extremely common among the general public.[7](#r7) In 2010, LAS resulted in excess of $1.1 billion in health care charges from emergency departments in the United States alone.[7](#r7) Despite this volume and cost of LAS, these injuries are erroneously considered as innocuous. However, the recurrence rate of LAS is one of the highest of all musculoskeletal injuries.[1](#r1),[8](#r8)–[11](#r11) Prospective evidence also indicates that at least 40% of individuals who sustain a first time ankle sprain develop residual symptoms, often defined as chronic ankle instability (CAI).[12](#r12) The condition of CAI is associated with a variety of perceptual, sensorimotor, and structural deficiencies and alterations[13](#r13)–[15](#r15) that are hypothesized to contribute to an increased risk of reinjury and to the development of ankle posttraumatic osteoarthritis.[16](#r16) Effective intervention strategies for acute LAS exist[17](#r17) but many individuals who sustain a LAS, regardless of population (eg, sport, general public), fail to seek medical care[18](#r18) or complete recommended rehabilitation.[19](#r19) This clinical phenomenon is likely because LAS are perceived as an innocuous injury but failure to complete supervised rehabilitation likely increases the risk of reinjury and facilitates development of long-term residual symptoms.

Within sporting populations, LAS patients often receive care but an emphasis on rapid return to sport (RTS) exists. For example, among intercollegiate athletes seen by a health care provider for LAS, 44.4% RTS in less than 24 hours (ie, a nontime loss injury).[20](#r20) Similarly, among interscholastic athletes seen by a health care provider, the average RTS time was 3 days for a new LAS and less than 24 hours for recurrent sprains.[21](#r21) Further, the average number of treatment sessions for time-loss LAS among interscholastic athletes was 10 days.[22](#r22) These treatment timelines and volumes are lower than the treatment durations and volumes shown to be effective for LAS.[17](#r17)

Such rapid timelines to RTS likely fail to provide adequate healing time. These rapid timelines are also likely inadequate to fully address the impairments associated with LAS.[13](#r13)–[15](#r15) Thus, rapid RTS could serve as a possible mechanism for the increased injury risk and long-term sequelae within sporting populations. Recent evidence supports this hypothesis as a mix of interscholastic and intercollegiate LAS patients had increased ligamentous laxity, limitations in self-reported function, limited dorsiflexion range of motion, and impaired dynamic postural control on their involved limb, relative to their uninvolved limb, when they were cleared to RTS. The RTS clearance occurred on average 12.7 ± 10.0 days following the LAS.[23](#r23) Given the rapid RTS timelines and residual deficits still present, sporting LAS patients appear to be cleared for RTS too soon. RTS decisions for LAS, and musculoskeletal injuries more broadly, are derived from anecdotal evidence and practitioner experience. RTS decisions can also be influenced by stakeholders (eg, patients, parents, and coaches) pushing RTS expediency. Thus, unique practitioner experiences and job setting environments facilitate inconsistent RTS decisions for LAS. The development of evidence-based criteria that could guide the RTS decision-making process for LAS would help providers quell external pressures and reduce risk of recurrent injury.

Such criteria should assess domains that are based on risk of reinjury (eg, range of motion, balance, etc); use techniques that are quantifiable and scalable (eg, the Star Excursion Balance Test); and gauge RTS readiness against specific measurable thresholds (eg, 80% of the uninvolved limb). Such RTS decision paradigms exist for lower-extremity musculoskeletal injuries[24](#r24),[25](#r25) but such efforts have not been undertaken for LAS despite the high volume of index and recurrent LAS. However, there are numerous published expert opinion papers on RTS within the literature. Establishing agreement among such opinions could help to further clinical practice and research into this important area.

## Objective

To determine if there was consensus among published expert opinions that could help inform an initial set of RTS criteria for LAS that could be investigated in future research. We hypothesized that minimal consensus would be reached regarding the domains (eg, postural control, range of motion, strength, etc) that should be assessed. We further hypothesized that little to no agreement would be noted on assessment techniques or thresholds that should be used to gauge athlete RTS readiness among the published expert opinion papers.

## Evidence Acquisition

### Search Strategy

To assess the published literature, we searched the PubMed, CINHL, and SPORTDiscus databases from the earliest available date until March 2019. Each search used the following combination of keywords: (1) return to sport OR return to play OR return to participation OR return to work OR return to duty and (2) ankle sprain OR lateral ankle sprain OR acute ankle sprain OR acute lateral ankle sprain. Reference lists of all retrieved full-text papers were manually searched for additional potentially eligible papers, but we failed to identify any additional articles for this systematic review.

### Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Included opinion pieces/papers/articles for this systematic review were required to list RTS criteria for LAS. For this investigation, an a priori decision was made to accept both broad (eg, strength) and specific (eg, complete a single-limb balance test for 10 s) RTS criteria given the dearth of available information on the topic. The search was limited to English language, full-text, and original peer-reviewed journal articles. Two authors (C.M. and E.A.W.) independently assessed all full-text records to determine eligibility. Initial agreement between the raters was 92%. Differences among the raters were discussed until a consensus was reached.

### Assessment of Methodological Quality

No assessment of methodological quality was conducted for this investigation. All included papers were expert opinion pieces (Evidence Level 5) with no methodology that could be assessed.

### Data Extraction and Synthesis

To determine if consensus exists among the published expert opinions on LAS RTS criteria, 2 authors (C.M. and E.A.W.) independently reviewed the included papers and extracted the relevant data when possible. Extracted data included the background/credentials of the authorship team; a definition of RTS; domains (eg, range of motion, balance, sport-specific movement, etc) that recommended to be assessed; specific assessments for each listed domain; and specific thresholds (eg, 80% of the uninjured limb) to be used when determining if an athlete is ready for RTS. Domains were created qualitatively by the research team based on our review of the data extracted from the included papers. Expert consensus was defined, a priori, as ≥75% agreement. Partial agreement was defined, a priori, as 50% to 75% agreement. Lack of consistency/no consistency was defined, a priori as <50%.[26](#r26)

## Evidence Synthesis

### Study Selection

Figure [1](#f1) is a display of the flowchart summarizing the result of the systematic search, which identified a total of 194 records while an additional record was identified through another source. After removing duplicates (n = 91), having screened records by title, abstract, and ineligible articles, 11 papers were identified and included in this systematic review (Table [1](#tab01)).[27](#r27)–[37](#r37) All of the 11 identified papers focused on RTS with no identified papers making recommendations for report to work or return to duty.

### Author Background and RTS Definition

Of the 11 papers included, 9 were from health care providers based in the United States.[27](#r27)–[30](#r30),[32](#r32)–[36](#r36) Two papers were written by single authors,[31](#r31),[34](#r34) whereas 8 papers were authored or coauthored by physicians.[27](#r27)–[33](#r33),[36](#r36) Three papers were coauthors by physical/physio therapists,[30](#r30),[32](#r32),[37](#r37) 1 paper was authored by a nurse,[34](#r34) 1 paper was authored by doctors of podiatric medicine,[35](#r35) 1 paper was coauthored by a doctor of osteopathy,[29](#r29) and 1 paper was coauthored by athletic trainers.[32](#r32) Of the 11 papers included, only 2 were written by interdisciplinary teams.[30](#r30),[32](#r32)

Only 4 papers included a definition of when RTS should occur.[27](#r27),[29](#r29),[31](#r31),[35](#r35) Three of these definitions focused on safety (ie, when it is safe to participate in the desire sport).[29](#r29),[31](#r31),[35](#r35) Of these 3, one also specifically indicated that RTS should happen when recurrent injury will not occur and an athlete’s performance is equal to their preinjury performance.[31](#r31) The fourth paper indicated that RTS should occur when the athlete’s specific rehabilitation goals are met.[27](#r27)

### RTS Criteria

Within the 11 included articles, 8 different domains were identified (Table [2](#tab02)). Consensus was reached regarding the need to assess sport-specific movement (n = 10, 90.9%).[27](#r27)–[33](#r33),[35](#r35)–[37](#r37) Partial agreement was reached regarding the use of a hop test (n = 6, 54.5%),[28](#r28),[29](#r29),[31](#r31),[32](#r32),[35](#r35),[36](#r36) but there was little consistency as to which hop test should be used. Only 2 papers provided a threshold (ie, the injured leg should perform at ≥80% of the uninjured leg) from which an objective decision could be made for RTS.[32](#r32),[35](#r35) Partial agreement was also reached for the need to assess static balance (n = 7, 63.6%).[27](#r27),[29](#r29),[31](#r31),[34](#r34)–[37](#r37) The use of a single-leg balance test (n = 4, 36.4%) was the most recommended.[29](#r29),[34](#r34),[36](#r36),[37](#r37) While some objective thresholds were provided, no consistency was noted among the included papers.

Abbreviation: SEBT, Star Excursion Balance Test.

A total of 6 studies (54.5%, partial agreement) recommended pain and swelling as a domain that should be tested during an athlete’s RTS assessment.[27](#r27)–[29](#r29),[31](#r31),[34](#r34),[37](#r37) While specific assessments and thresholds were provided, there was no consistency. Six studies reviewed (54.5%, partial agreement) also recommended that subjective assessments (ie, patient reported outcomes),[29](#r29)–[32](#r32),[35](#r35),[37](#r37) range of motion,[29](#r29)–[31](#r31),[33](#r33),[35](#r35),[37](#r37) and strength[27](#r27),[29](#r29)–[31](#r31),[33](#r33),[37](#r37) also be assessed to determine RTS. However, there was no consistency among the recommended tests or among the included thresholds. A minority of papers recommended dynamic balance (n = 5, 45.5%)[29](#r29),[30](#r30),[32](#r32),[35](#r35),[37](#r37) and running (n = 4, 36.4%)[27](#r27),[28](#r28),[33](#r33),[37](#r37) as domains that should be assessed. Within the papers recommending dynamic balance, all 5[29](#r29),[30](#r30),[32](#r32),[35](#r35),[37](#r37) recommended the Star Excursion Balance Test be used. Consistency among listed thresholds (if provided) for these domains did not exist.

## Discussion

The purpose of this investigation was to determine if consensus existed among published expert opinions related to RTS criteria for LAS. Our primary findings demonstrated consensus for the need to assess sport-specific movement when determining an athlete’s readiness for RTS. Our findings also demonstrated partial agreement for the need to assess static balance, patient-reported outcomes, strength, and range of motion. Finally, partial agreement existed on using hop testing as an appropriate technique to assess the sport-specific movement domain. These findings support our a priori hypothesis that consensus among published expert opinions would be minimal.

The agreed upon domains are consistent with the domains most commonly targeted in rehabilitation protocols for LAS.[17](#r17) However, the lack of prospective data related to RTS following LAS makes it impossible to determine if assessing these domains can provide meaningful information about an individual’s risk for reinjury following RTS. Furthermore, few objective thresholds against which a RTS decision could be made were provided. This is problematic, in that practitioners can only rely on their subjective feeling of a patient’s readiness when determining RTS. Unfortunately, relying on subjective feelings alone can allow RTS decision making to be influenced by pressures from various stakeholders.

However, some inferences about objective criteria can be drawn based on how the agreed upon domains relate to known modifiable risk factors for LAS. For example, hop testing,[38](#r38) limited dorsiflexion range of motion,[39](#r39),[40](#r40) poor strength/strength asymmetries,[40](#r40)–[42](#r42) and poor static,[40](#r40),[43](#r43)–[46](#r46) and dynamic postural control[38](#r38),[47](#r47),[48](#r48) have all been identified as modifiable risk factors for LAS. These risk factors significantly overlap with the recommended domains found in the current investigation. However, it is important to note that (1) the previously mentioned risk factors are for LAS broadly and are not specific to recurrent LAS; (2) few objective thresholds (ie, cutoff scores) were calculated; and (3) additional risk factors, outside of the agreed upon domains (eg, body mass index, reaction time, coordination, running speed, etc), were identified in these investigations as well as in a more comprehensive review.[17](#r17)

The alignment of known modifiable risk factors provides face validity to the domains agreed upon within published expert opinions. These same domains represent areas of deficiency in those with CAI providing further face validity to the results.[13](#r13)–[15](#r15) However, no agreement on testable thresholds either in this study or previous investigations has been established. More importantly, there is no evidence that any of the suggested thresholds opined from the current investigation are effective indicators of risk/no risk of recurrent injury following RTS after a LAS.

It is also important to note that injury rates for LAS are higher at the end of a game[49](#r49) suggesting that fatigue may be a risk factor. Those with a history of a LAS appear to be more sensitive to the effects of fatigue than their uninjured counterparts.[50](#r50),[51](#r51) However, evidence suggests that although comprehensive treatment programs improve a wide variety of dependent variables in those with CAI in a nonfatigued state, such treatment programs do not reduce fatigue sensitivity.[52](#r52) Further, only one of the included expert opinions[37](#r37) mentioned the importance of assessing domains under a fatigued state to determine RTS readiness in athletes. Thus, future research should further investigate how to reduce fatigue sensitivity following LAS and determine if and how fatigue sensitivity should be evaluated as it relates to determining RTS post LAS.

Although there remains much work to be done in developing objective RTS criteria for LAS, no expert suggested time from injury as a criterion for determining RTS readiness. Historically, LAS severity has been graded based on a variety of scales that were associated with estimated times until RTS.[53](#r53)–[55](#r55) From a RTS perspective, scales based on anatomical damage are not practical because diagnostic imaging is needed to confirm the number of ligaments damaged or level of trauma (ie, micro vs macro) and such imaging is rarely ordered.[53](#r53),[54](#r54) Grading LAS based on functional limitations is also not helpful from a RTS perspective. First, functional limitations are not associated with time until RTS,[56](#r56) and functional deficiencies have been noted in patients who were cleared for RTS.[23](#r23) Thus, like others, we recommend that grading LAS and providing time to RTS estimates to stakeholders be avoided as they place artificial constraints on the provider.[37](#r37) Finally, providers must consider how to best phase an athlete back to full participation. Although many providers already take a phased RTS approach, there is no evidence to support how to safely progress an athlete from phase to phase. However, recently published guidelines provide an excellent review of how a continuum of RTS across musculoskeletal injuries can be structured to help providers throughout the rehabilitation process broadly[57](#r57) and have been applied preliminarily to LAS RTS scenarios.[37](#r37) These guidelines for transitioning from phase to phase of a rehabilitation process can be easily implemented and facilitate an evidence-based approach to LAS RTS procedures.

## Conclusion

Based on the expert consensus obtained, practitioners should assess sport-specific movement when determining athlete RTS following a LAS. Based on the partial agreement noted, practitioners should use a hop test to assess sport-specific movement. Self-reported function, strength, range of motion, and balance should also be assessed when determining athlete RTS readiness following LAS. Finally, prospective research is needed to quantify a broad range of outcomes at RTS and determine how those outcomes influence LAS reinjury rates (ie, establish an evidence-based RTS assessment battery and thresholds).
