Introduction Chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) is one of the most frequent complications following ankle sprain injuries [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B1-jcm-14-06046),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B2-jcm-14-06046),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B3-jcm-14-06046),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B4-jcm-14-06046)]. With continuous modification using recent emerging techniques, the Broström repair procedure provides restoration of reliable stability and satisfactory clinical outcomes, as a gold-standard anatomical ligament repair surgery for CLAI [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B1-jcm-14-06046),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B3-jcm-14-06046),[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B5-jcm-14-06046),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B6-jcm-14-06046)]. However, even after an extended period following the modified Broström procedure (MBP), a substantial proportion of patients appear to reduce their sports participation and cease sports activities prematurely. Maffulli et al. reported that a large proportion (42%) of patients experienced reduced sports activity during long-term follow-up after the MBP [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B7-jcm-14-06046)]. There is currently no consensus regarding the factors contributing to failure to resume the previous level of sports activity after surgical treatment. Return to sports (RTS) may be affected by several variables apart from patient motivation (intention to RTS), such as persistent pain or swelling, insufficient restoration of mechanical stability, weakness of peroneal strength, deficiencies in postural or neuromuscular control, and impaired proprioception [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B8-jcm-14-06046),[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B9-jcm-14-06046),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B10-jcm-14-06046),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B11-jcm-14-06046),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B12-jcm-14-06046)]. The RTS rate serves as a meaningful indicator of functional outcome following operative treatment and provides a useful reference during patient counseling for CLAI. Successful return to preinjury level of sports participation represents a key determinant of patient satisfaction after surgical intervention for CLAI. This consideration is pertinent both for professional athletes and for those engaged in recreational sports. We hypothesized that there would be specific factors that make the difference between patients with and without RTS after the MBP. This comparative study was designed to identify the factors affecting the return to sports activity after anatomical ligament repair for CLAI. ## 2. Materials and Methods ### 2.1. Study Design and Subjects This research was conducted as a single-center longitudinal cohort study employing time series analysis. All the data were collected prospectively and analyzed retrospectively. The study protocol and related investigations received approval from the Institutional Review Board. Patients were recruited for eligibility after electing to undergo surgical treatment (MBP) with a diagnosis of CLAI. All eligible patients received informed consent regarding the postoperative visit schedule and the nature of examinations. The informed consent also stated that refusal or withdrawal from the study would not result in any disadvantages for participants. Between January 2020 and December 2021, a total of 76 patients (80 ankles) consecutively underwent the MBP for CLAI after experiencing at least 3 months of unsuccessful rehabilitation. Of these patients, 64 patients (64 ankles) who met the inclusion criteria were enrolled in this study. Ultimately, 62 patients (62 ankles) with a minimum follow-up period of 3 years postoperatively were included in the analysis ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#fig_body_display_jcm-14-06046-f001)). The inclusion criteria for this study were as followings: (1) patients under 35 years of age with intention to return to sports, (2) unilateral ankle instability, (3) no previous ankle ligament or fracture surgery history, (4) absence of advanced osteochondral pathology requiring bone marrow stimulation or cartilage transplantation, (5) no hindfoot varus or equinus deformity requiring additional corrective procedures, and (6) no visual, vestibular, or neuromuscular impairments. The scheduled postoperative follow-up intervals were 1 month prior to surgery, and then 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years postoperatively. Patients were considered compliant with the follow-up schedule if they presented within 1 month before or after the designated time point. Regardless of the timing of return to sports activity, all the participants were classified as either in the return group or non-return group based on whether they achieved preinjury sports performance. Because this study included patients with various previous levels of sports activity, we thought there was clear heterogeneity on capability levels needed for sports activity. A return to preinjury level of sports activity was determined dependent on patient self-report instead of standardized tools or objective performance metrics. Among the 62 patients analyzed, 51 patients (82.3%) successfully resumed their preinjury level of sports activity (return group), while 11 (17.7%) continued to experience partial or substantial limitations (non-return group). ![Image 12: Jcm 14 06046 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/jcm/jcm-14-06046/article_deploy/html/images/jcm-14-06046-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#fig_body_display_jcm-14-06046-f001) **Figure 1.** Consort flowchart diagram of this study. The mean age of the study population was 27.1 years (range: 18 to 35 years), and the mean duration of symptoms was 33.8 months (range: 10 to 64 months). There were 38 male and 24 female patients in the cohort. Initial injuries were attributed to sports-related incidents in 36 cases, slip and fall during walking in 24 cases, and traffic accidents in 2 cases. Eleven of the 62 patients were professional or junior level athletes, and others were participants in recreational or amateur levels of sports activities. ### 2.2. Rehabilitation Protocol Following Surgery Initially, all the patients underwent arthroscopic examination and simple procedures, including synovectomy, chondral debridement, and loose body removal. The MBP was performed in a standard fashion by a single senior surgeon. Both the anterior talofibular (ATF) and calcaneofibular (CF) ligaments were repaired using suture anchors, and the inferior extensor retinaculum was imbricated over the repaired lateral ligaments. A short-leg cast was applied, and partial weight-bearing ambulation with crutches was maintained for 3 weeks after surgery. Subsequently, active range-of-motion (ROM) exercises for the ankle joint were initiated and gradually advanced to gentle passive ROM exercises, including inversion. Patients were encouraged to perform weight-bearing ambulation with an elastic ankle bandage as tolerated, and full weight-bearing gait was allowed 4 weeks after surgery. It was recommended that regular rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physiotherapist be conducted twice weekly for at least 8 weeks postoperatively. The rehabilitation regimen included peroneal muscle strengthening (eccentric–contraction eversion exercises), tandem stance, single-limb stance, single-limb stance with ball toss, wobble board exercise, quadrant hop drills, and treadmill running. Return to sport was made in accordance with the clinical guideline suggested by Song et al. [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B13-jcm-14-06046)] and was permitted no sooner than 8 weeks postoperatively. At each follow-up visit, proprioceptive-oriented exercises aimed at reducing postural sway and enhancing postural control ability were continuously encouraged. The full duration of proprioceptive-oriented rehabilitation was closely monitored using the modified Romberg test (single-leg stance test with eyes closed). All the patients were encouraged to improve their balance retention time, from when they placed their non-stance leg on the floor to when they had a feeling of being unable to maintain a one-leg standing position, and reported the best record at follow-up visit. ### 2.3. Assessment of Patient-Reported Clinical Outcomes The changes of clinical outcomes before and after surgery were periodically evaluated using the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS) [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B14-jcm-14-06046)] and the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B15-jcm-14-06046)]. The reliability of these patient-reported outcome measures has been validated for patients with lateral ankle instability [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B14-jcm-14-06046),[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B15-jcm-14-06046)]. The FAOS questionnaire contains 5 distinct subscales evaluating pain (9 questions), other symptoms (7 questions), function in daily living (17 questions), function in sport and recreation (5 questions), and foot- and ankle-related quality of life (4 questions). The FAAM questionnaire consists of 2 subscales, evaluating activities of daily living (21 questions) and sports activities (8 questions). The total subscale scores were calculated and normalized to a 100-point scale. A score of 100 reflects optimal clinical status without symptoms, while a score of 0 signifies the poorest function and severe symptoms. ### 2.4. Assessment of Mechanical Ankle Stability Mechanical ankle stability was periodically assessed before and after surgery using both physical examination and stress radiography. A senior surgeon consistently performed the manual varus and anterior drawer stress tests, comparing results to the contralateral (unaffected) ankle. Varus and anterior drawer stress radiographs of the ankle were obtained with a Telos device (Telos GmbH, Marburg, Germany), utilizing a standardized load of 150 Newton. Three independent researchers measured the talar tilt angle and the degree of anterior talar translation on a digital PACS imaging system. Each measurement task was carried out twice, and the average value was used for analysis. ### 2.5. Assessment of Peroneal Strength Concentric and eccentric muscle strengths for eversion were periodically measured using the Biodex-II isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex Medical Systems, Shirley, NY, USA). Peak torque normalized to body weight, as well as total work were measured at an angular velocity of 60°/s. All assessments were administered by the same physical therapist following a standardized examination protocol. Each evaluation was conducted two times with a 5 min interval between tests, and the results were averaged. Peak torque represented the highest force generated at any point during five consecutive repetitions at 60°/s, serving as an indicator of muscle strength. Total work indicated the average amount of force produced during repetitive motions and represented muscle endurance. ### 2.6. Assessment of Static and Dynamic Postural Control Ability Static and dynamic postural control abilities were periodically evaluated using Biodex posturography (Biodex Medical Systems, Shirley, NY, USA), which is recognized for its reliability in balance assessment [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B16-jcm-14-06046)]. Patients received real-time visual biofeedback on a monitor displaying shifts in their center of gravity as they maintained a one-leg standing posture with eyes open. This task was performed during automated changes in platform tilt and rotation, progressing from level 8 (most stable) to level 1 (most unstable) over 20 s ([Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#fig_body_display_jcm-14-06046-f002)). The balance platform moved up to 20° of planar slope in a 360° range of motion. Under the supervision of the same researcher, both the static (on a fixed platform) and dynamic (on a mobile platform) stability tests were repeated two times with an interval of 3 min, and the measurements were averaged. The anterior–posterior stability index (APSI), medial–lateral (MLSI) stability index, and overall stability index (OSI) were recorded as quantitative measures related to postural stability. Each index reflected the horizontal deviation (fluctuation) from the center of pressure (COP), with higher index values indicating increased movement away from the individual’s center of gravity (poor balance). ![Image 13: Jcm 14 06046 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/jcm/jcm-14-06046/article_deploy/html/images/jcm-14-06046-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#fig_body_display_jcm-14-06046-f002) **Figure 2.** Photographs show the quantitative evaluation of (**A**) static and (**B**) dynamic postural control ability using Biodex posturography. Participants stand barefoot with one leg on the platform. ### 2.7. Statistical Analysis The statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 23.0 (SPSS Inc., IBM Company, Chicago, IL, USA), and a p value ≤ 0.05 with a confidence interval of 95% was set to the statistical level of significance. A normal distribution of all the collected data was confirmed with Shapiro–Wilks and Kolmogorov–Smirnov normality tests. The Mann–Whitney U test was used to compare the patient-reported clinical outcomes, mechanical ankle stability, peroneal strength, and static and dynamic postural control ability between the return group and non-return group. Categorical data, such as patient demographics and complication rates, were compared using the Fisher exact test. The changes between before and after surgery in the same individuals were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to assess which variables are independent predictors of failure to return to sports activity. On power analysis to determine the appropriate sample size, we calculated that allocation of 11 patients into each group would provide 80% power to compare the validated functional outcome measure (FAOS). The 95% confidence interval (a type-I error rate of 0.05) was used to analyze whether the difference in sports activity subscale of the FAOS at 3 years postoperative was within a margin of noninferiority. The set margin of noninferiority was −10 points (a delta of 10 points in the FAOS), and the estimated dropout rate was 5%. The margin of noninferiority and the dropout rate were determined on the basis of the clinical data of previous studies. Eventually, the sample size required to make statistically significant results was 11~12 patients in each group. ## 3. Results ### 3.1. Comparison of Demographic and Clinical Characteristics No statistically significant differences were observed in the demographic and clinical characteristics between the return and non-return groups ([Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t001)). **Table 1.** Comparison of demographic and clinical characteristics (Mann–Whitney U test and Fisher exact test). ![Image 14](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t001) ### 3.2. Comparison of Patient-Reported Clinical Outcomes Both the return and non-return groups showed significant improvements in FAOS and FAAM scores compared to their preoperative values ([Table 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t002)). When examining each subscale, there were significant differences in FAOS pain (94.7 points in the return group vs. 85.1 points in the non-return group; p = 0.004) and FAOS sports (91.2 vs. 78.8 points; p< 0.001) subscales. In addition, the FAAM sports activity subscale showed a significant difference between the groups (90.5 vs. 77.4 points; p< 0.001). **Table 2.** Comparison of the patient-reported clinical outcomes (Mann–Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test). ![Image 15](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t002) ### 3.3. Comparison of Postoperative Complications With the exception of the recurrence rate of ankle instability, the postoperative complication rates did not differ significantly between the return and non-return groups ([Table 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t003)). The recurrence rate of mechanical ankle instability was significantly higher in the non-return group (36.4%) compared to the return group (3.9%) (p< 0.001). **Table 3.** Comparison of postoperative complications (Fisher exact tests). ![Image 16](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t003) ### 3.4. Comparison of Mechanical Ankle Stability Postoperative periodic physical examinations (stress test) revealed mechanical ankle instability as unstable as that prior to surgery in 2 patients in the return group and 4 patients in the non-return group. Periodic stress radiographic examinations demonstrated significant improvements in both talar tilt angle and anterior talar translation in both groups compared to preoperative values ([Table 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t004)). No significant differences were detected between the return and non-return groups in stress radiographic measurements. **Table 4.** Comparison of mechanical ankle stability evaluated with stress radiographs (Mann–Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test). ![Image 17](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t004) ### 3.5. Comparison of Isokinetic Peroneal Strength Both the return and non-return groups showed significant improvements in concentric and eccentric muscle strength for eversion compared to prior to surgery ([Table 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t005)). There were no significant differences in concentric and eccentric peroneal strength between the return and non-return groups. **Table 5.** Comparison of peroneal strength evaluated with isokinetic dynamometer (Mann–Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test). ![Image 18](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t005) ### 3.6. Comparison of Static and Dynamic Postural Control Ability Static postural control abilities did not show significant improvement in either the return or non-return group when compared to preoperative assessments ([Table 6](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t006)). Additionally, no significant differences were identified in APSI, MLSI, and OSI between the two groups. **Table 6.** Comparison of static postural control ability (Mann–Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test). ![Image 19](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t006) The return group demonstrated a significant improvement in dynamic postural control ability compared to prior to surgery, whereas the non-return group demonstrated no significant improvement ([Table 7](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t007)). An analysis of individual stability indices revealed significant differences in APSI (0.94 in the return group vs. 1.95 in the non-return group; p< 0.001), MLSI (0.73 vs. 1.58; p = 0.041), and OSI (1.41 vs. 2.33; p = 0.002). **Table 7.** Comparison of dynamic postural control ability (Mann–Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed rank test). ![Image 20](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t007) ### 3.7. Comparison Between Professional Athletes and Amateur (Recreational Level) Participants All (11 patients) professional or junior-level athletes were able to return to their preinjury level of sports activity, whereas 11 (21.6%) out of a total of 51 patients with a recreational or amateur level of sports activity failed to return to preinjury level of sports activity (p< 0.001). Statistically significant differences were observed in FAOS sports (95.1 in the professional group vs. 84.6 points in the amateur group; p = 0.001) and FAAM sports subscales (94.2 vs. 83.8 points; p = 0.004). Recurrence of mechanical instability occurred in 1 patient (9.1%) in the professional group and in 5 patients (9.8%) in the amateur group, showing no significant difference. No significant differences were detected in measurements of stress radiography or peroneal strength. A posturography assessment revealed significant differences in static postural control ability (overall stability index: 0.92 in the professional group vs. 1.37 in the amateur group; p = 0.039) and dynamic postural control ability (1.13 vs. 1.98; p = 0.001). ### 3.8. The Risk Factors Associated with Failure to Return to the Preinjury Level of Sports Activity Multivariate logistic regression analyses of variables were significantly different between the return and non-return groups and identified several risk factors associated with a failure to return to the preinjury level of sports activity. Patients with an FAOS pain score < 90 demonstrated a higher risk of failure to RTS compared to those with an FAOS pain ≥ 90 (odds ratio 8.66; p< 0.001) ([Table 8](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t008)). Patients with recurrence of mechanical instability were at a greater risk of failure to RTS than those without recurrent instability (odds ratio 13.99; p< 0.001). Additionally, patients with inadequate dynamic postural control ability > overall stability index 1.8 had a greater risk of failure to RTS than those with OSI ≤ 1.8 (odds ratio 4.21; p = 0.012). **Table 8.** The risk factors associated with the failure to the return to preinjury level of sports activity (multivariate logistic regression analysis). ![Image 21](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#table_body_display_jcm-14-06046-t008) ## 4. Discussion This comparative study reports specific factors that make the difference between patients with and without return to preinjury level of sports activity in 62 patients with a periodic follow-up of 3 years after anatomical ligament repair for CLAI. The most critical finding is that residual pain, recurrence of mechanical instability, and insufficient recovery of dynamic postural control ability are associated with the return to preinjury level of sports activity after the MBP. These findings provide valuable information to guide the functional rehabilitation process aimed at facilitating a return to sports activity following surgery. Successful return to sports activity is a key factor for evaluating functional outcomes and influences patient satisfaction following operative treatment for CLAI. However, there is limited literature addressing the underlying reasons for delayed or unsuccessful recovery to the previous level of sports activity. The reduction in return to sports activity after operative treatment for CLAI is widely believed to result from multiple factors, many of which are challenging to measure objectively [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B11-jcm-14-06046),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B12-jcm-14-06046),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B17-jcm-14-06046),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B18-jcm-14-06046)]. Sigonney et al. have suggested that increased patient perception and fear of re-injury is a critical cause of decreased RTS [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B19-jcm-14-06046)]. Substantial agreement exists that intra- or extraarticular lesions associated with acute lateral ligament injury or CLAI are among the leading causes [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B5-jcm-14-06046),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B10-jcm-14-06046),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B12-jcm-14-06046),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B18-jcm-14-06046)]. In the present study, we excluded patients exhibiting concomitant advanced osteochondral lesions that required microfracture or osteochondral transplantation. Our operative experience indicates that such advanced osteochondral lesions are frequently associated with more persistent symptoms and diminished functional activity. Postoperative recurrence of instability is recognized as an additional contributing factor. A long-term follow-up study after the MBP found that around 26% of patients had ceased active sports participation and 16% transitioned to sports activities at a lower level [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B7-jcm-14-06046)]. In that study, the most critical cause leading to failure to RTS was recurrence of mechanical and functional ankle instability. Similarly, Bridgman et al. documented that patients with recurrent ankle instability were more likely to discontinue sports participation [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B20-jcm-14-06046)]. Our results show a markedly lower rate of recurrent mechanical instability in the RTS group (3.9%) compared with the non-return group (36.4%), underscoring the impact of instability recurrence on RTS. With respect to lateral ligament repair for acute grade-III injuries (characterized by complete rupture of the ATFL and the CFL with substantial instability), a meta-analysis by Kerkhoffs et al. found that surgical treatment was superior to conservative treatment in terms of return to preinjury level of activities, rate of recurrence, chronic pain, and subjective or functional instability [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B21-jcm-14-06046)]. Hong et al. reported that the median time to return to preinjury level of sports was 69 days in elite athletes [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B10-jcm-14-06046)]. White et al. reported that the median time for RTS was 11 weeks in professional athletes [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B8-jcm-14-06046)]. Their study identified that the major contributors to delayed return to training and competition were concomitant injuries, such as osteochondral lesions or deltoid ligament involvement. Goru et al. further indicated that associated intra-articular or extra-articular lesions were a primary reason for delayed recovery after surgical management [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B18-jcm-14-06046)]. Patients with CLAI are also predisposed to a variety of intra-articular pathologies secondary to repeated sprain episodes [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B1-jcm-14-06046),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B3-jcm-14-06046),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B22-jcm-14-06046)]. Even when appropriate interventions for these concurrent pathologies are implemented, such patients may still experience ongoing symptoms and obstacles in resuming sports participation. Raja et al. reported that postoperative residual pain did not account for diminished RTS rates [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B23-jcm-14-06046)]. Conversely, the present study identified residual pain as one of the determinants affecting RTS after anatomical ligament repair for CLAI. Patients who returned to preinjury level of sports activity (return group) exhibited significantly superior pain scores compared to the non-return group. Therefore, more comprehensive diagnostic approaches and tailored treatments are recommended for individuals unable to RTS due to persistent, long-term postoperative pain. Postural control ability is understood to depend on visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive inputs [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B24-jcm-14-06046)]. Multiple individual factors, such as proprioception, nerve conduction velocity, postural reflex, joint range of motion, and muscle strength, contribute to postural control ability of the ankle joint [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B25-jcm-14-06046)]. The mechanoreceptors in the ligaments and capsule of the ankle joint serve as crucial sources of afferent proprioceptive information. Patients with CLAI frequently report deficient postural control attributable to damage to proprioceptors resulting from repeated sprains [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B17-jcm-14-06046),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B25-jcm-14-06046)]. A systematic review reported that a deficit of postural control ability was associated with increased risk of ankle sprain [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/14/17/6046#B26-jcm-14-06046)]. In this study, inadequate recovery of dynamic postural control ability was among the factors influencing RTS following the MBP for CLAI. args.summary: This is an open-access scientific article published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine (2025, Volume 14, Issue 17, Article 6046) titled "Predictors of Return to Sports Following the Modified Broström Procedure for Chronic Ankle Instability" by Kim, Choi, and Cho. The study investigated factors influencing return to sports (RTS) after the modified Broström procedure (MBP) for chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). Sixty-two patients under 35 years old were followed for up to 3 years post-surgery, with 51 (82.3%) returning to preinjury sports levels (return group) and 11 (17.7%) not (non-return group). Key findings: Significant differences were found in FAOS pain scores (94.7 vs. 85.1 points, p=0.004), FAOS sports scores (91.2 vs. 78.8, p<0.001), and FAAM sports subscale scores (90.5 vs. 77.4, p<0.001) between groups. Mechanical instability recurrence was significantly higher in the non-return group (36.4% vs. 3.9%, p<0.001). Dynamic postural control ability differed substantially (OSI 1.41 vs. 2.33, p=0.002), while static postural control and peroneal strength showed no significant differences. Multivariate logistic regression identified three risk factors for failure to RTS: FAOS pain score <90 (OR 8.66, p<0.001), recurrence of mechanical instability (OR 13.99, p<0.001), and inadequate dynamic postural control (OSI >1.8) (OR 4.21, p=0.012). The study concludes that comprehensive rehabilitation protocols should address residual pain, mechanical stability, and dynamic postural control to facilitate optimal postoperative sports participation.

# Does suture tape aid return to play after lateral ankle ligament reconstruction?

Chronic lateral ankle instability represents a significant burden for athletes. An estimated 20%-40% of individuals who experience an acute lateral ankle sprain will develop chronic ankle instability, characterized by recurrent sprains and persistent pain that can limit athletic performance.

For competitive athletes, prolonged recovery times can profoundly impact their season and career trajectory. Consequently, return-to-play timing has become a critical postoperative outcome measure. Suture tape augmentation of the modified Brostrom procedure has emerged as a promising adjunct that may facilitate accelerated rehabilitation and earlier return to competition.

![](/globalassets/now/article-images/2026/march/research05_figure1.jpg)
![](/globalassets/now/article-images/2026/march/research05_figure2.jpg)

**The evolution of suture tape augmentation**

Suture tape augmentation was popularized in the 2010s as a method to reinforce traditional Brostrom or modified Brostrom-Gould lateral ankle ligament reconstruction. The technique involves placing a high-strength, nonabsorbable suture tape secured with knotless anchors that parallel the reconstructed anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) (Figure 1).

The biomechanical findings are compelling: Cadaveric studies have demonstrated that suture tape augmentation provides ultimate load-to-failure strength of 250-315 N, exceeding the native ATFL strength of approximately 154 N. Similarly, construct stiffness with augmentation (21-31 N/mm) matches or exceeds native ligament stiffness (14.5 N/mm). This enhanced mechanical strength theoretically protects the biological repair during the vulnerable early postoperative period, permitting more aggressive rehabilitation protocols and functional loading.

**Clinical evidence on return to play**

The clinical literature on return to play after suture tape augmentation has expanded recently, although it remains dominated by retrospective cohort studies, case series, and systematic reviews. Prospective randomized controlled trials are scarce, limiting the strength of current evidence. Nevertheless, emerging data suggest a consistent trend toward accelerated recovery.

In a multicenter randomized trial involving 119 patients, Kulwin et al. demonstrated that suture tape augmentation enabled return to preinjury level of activity at 13.3 weeks compared to 17.5 weeks for traditional modified Brostrom (*P* = 0.001). Similarly, systematic reviews report athletes undergoing augmented repairs often return to sport at eight to 12 weeks when following aggressive rehabilitation protocols, compared to the historical time frame of 12 to 24 (or more) weeks for nonaugmented repairs. These studies define return to play as return to the same or higher level of sport and typically use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) to assess readiness, including the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM), Tegner Activity Scale, and Ankle Ligament Reconstruction-Return to Sport After Injury scale.

Multiple studies have confirmed that both augmented and nonaugmented techniques produce excellent functional outcomes at intermediate and long-term follow-up. PROMs, including the FAAM and American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) scores, improve significantly with both techniques. Importantly, when differences exist, they typically favor augmentation primarily in the early postoperative period (three to six months), with outcomes converging beyond 12 to 24 months. This finding suggests the primary benefit of augmentation lies in facilitating earlier functional recovery.

The available randomized controlled trial (RCT) data, while limited, generally support the safety and efficacy of augmentation. Porter et al. conducted a five-year RCT comparing ligament augmentation reconstruction system (LARS) augmentation to modified Brostrom- Gould repair, finding superior Foot and Ankle Outcome Scores and higher Tegner Activity Scale scores in the augmented group, with zero failures compared to two in the traditional repair group. A systematic review of three randomized trials, involving 235 patients, found higher postoperative sports activity scores in suture tape groups, with comparable overall functional outcomes.

**Complications and safety profile**

Regarding safety, systematic reviews report no major differences in overall complication rates between augmented and nonaugmented repairs. However, the complication profiles differ slightly. Recurrence of instability and revision surgeries tend to occur more frequently after traditional Brostrom repair, while peroneal nerve and tendon irritation appear more often with suture tape constructs. In the largest randomized trial, complication rates were 8.5% for modified Brostrom versus 1.7% for suture tape augmentation, though this difference did not reach statistical significance (*P* = 0.12). These findings suggest that when performed properly, augmentation does not introduce prohibitive risks.

**Practical implications**

For orthopaedic surgeons counseling athletes about surgical options, suture tape augmentation offers several potential advantages: The enhanced biomechanical strength permits accelerated rehabilitation protocols, including earlier weight-bearing and functional exercises. Studies using aggressive postoperative protocols after surgical fixation with suture tape augmentation report excellent outcomes, with patients achieving single-leg hop and heel-raise capacity at six weeks postoperatively. This type of outcome is particularly valuable for high-level athletes with time-sensitive competition schedules or professional obligations.

However, decision-making should remain holistic and patient specific. Important factors to consider include competitive level, tissue quality, body mass index, history of prior ankle surgery, and presence of generalized ligamentous laxity. Suture tape augmentation may be especially beneficial in revision cases as well as in patients with relative contraindications to traditional repair, including those with generalized ligamentous laxity, elite athletes requiring rapid return, or patients with poor tissue quality.

Surgeons should also counsel patients about the limitations of current evidence. Despite promising early results, the long-term superiority of augmentation over traditional repair remains uncertain. Furthermore, the existing literature suffers from significant heterogeneity in surgical technique, rehabilitation protocols, and outcome definitions, making direct comparisons challenging.

**Need for standardized research and future directions**

Moving forward, the field would benefit from standardized return-to-play definitions that distinguish between return to training, return to competition, and return to preinjury performance level. Additionally, large randomized controlled studies and research incorporating sport-specific outcome measures would provide more granular insights into recovery trajectories across different athletic endeavors.

Furthermore, given that the augmented construct is stiffer than the native ligament, data-driven guidance on intraoperative tensioning is important to avoid soft tissue imbalance and range-of- motion restrictions.

Novel biomaterials, including a synthetic, degradable matrix woven from wet-spun fibers of polycaprolactone base-polyurethane urea, are now commercially available and provide a biological scaffold for integration and remodeling while also having an elastic modulus closer to the native ligament (Figure 2). This may better mimic the native tissue mechanics while reducing the potential for stress shielding. While early results are promising, further studies are needed to determine the clinical benefit of these newer materials.

**Conclusion**

Suture tape augmentation of the modified Brostrom procedure represents a valuable addition to the surgical armamentarium for chronic lateral ankle instability. The technique appears to facilitate accelerated rehabilitation and earlier return to play. For athletes, suture tape augmentation offers a promising option supported by growing evidence. Orthopaedic surgeons should engage in shared decision making that considers individual patient factors. While early results are encouraging, definitive evidence of superiority in return-to-competition rates or long-term outcomes requires completion of large, prospective comparative trials with standardized protocols. Until then, surgeons can counsel patients augmentation represents a safe, effective technique that may expedite recovery without compromising long-term stability or function.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Abstract

### Background

Returning to sport (RTS) from lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is multifaceted and interdisciplinary. This systematic review aimed to investigate the factors involved in RTS and further establish a standard paradigm of RTS to treat and rehabilitate the LAS.

### Methods

Four electronic databases, including PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, Science Direct, and Scopus, were searched until March 1, 2024. The literature was identified, screened, evaluated, managed and data was extracted by developing inclusion criteria based on the PICO model for systematic reviews. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Downs and Black checklist and the measurement parameters were summarised.

### Results

This systematic review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Participant’s information, research content, purpose, methods, and interventions were extracted and summarized. The included articles were divided into four categories for further discussion, including (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS of LAS, (3) performance assessment after RTS of LAS, and (4) the relationship between criteria and time of RTS for LAS.

### Conclusion

RTS for LAS is a continuous process, which is influenced by complex factors, such as the injury extent, injury causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The standard paradigms of RTS rehabilitation for LAS is still lacking in the literature. Current study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS. Findings may provide theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance for the RTS of LAS patients.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Background

1.
Lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is one of the most frequently occurring musculoskeletal injuries in general and athletic populations engaged in recreational and competitive sports [[1–8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0001)]. The precise etiology of LAS is complex [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0009)] and often presents as a mechanical laxity and proprioception deficit [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0005)]. Clinically, lateral ankle sprains are categorized into grade I injury as mild, grade II injury as moderate, and grade III injury as severe [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0001),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0005)]. Although LAS is typically believed to be a one-off injury, the evidence from hospital emergency department records shows that up to 74% of patients with LAS continue to have persistent symptoms [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0010),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0011)]. Studies reported that LAS patients have the most significant risk of re-injury in all lower-extremity musculoskeletal injuries [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0012)]. In specific sports populations, the re-injured population could be as high as 70% [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0013)], and nearly 40% of LAS patients would experience chronic ankle instability within a year of the initial injury due to the re-injury [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0013),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0014)]. The high rate of re-injury might be brought on by either premature return to sport (RTS) or inadequate rehabilitation [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0015),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0016)].

RTS is considered safe for an injured athlete to return to training or competition [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0017)]. This also results from the anticipated evaluation, medical intervention, and rehabilitation procedure [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0017),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0018)] RTS should be viewed as a continuous process rather than finished in a single step. Thus, each stage is seen as a tiny step toward the RTS [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0019)]. Ardern et al. [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0020),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021)] defined the RTS continuum as the three process parts of “return to performance”, “return to sport”, and “return to participation” [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0019),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0022)]. These three processes are influenced by the injury grade, rehabilitation strategies, pre and post RTS foot function tests, the amount of time spent in RTS, psychosocial elements of RTS, emotional values, and self-perceptions [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021),[23–25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0023)]. All these factors could be combined to assess whether the injured athlete satisfied the criteria for RTS and gauged the performance level after RTS.

Even though the criteria for RTS in patients with LAS have not been clarified in the current literature, the components of RTS decision-making (i.e. pain, ankle perception, including proprioception, ankle injuries, muscle activation, sensorimotor control systems, and motor testing) were previously described in narrative reviews, with consensus among clinical experts [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0010),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0026),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0027)]. Furthermore, it has been shown that the decision-making factors for RTS in patients with LAS consider using quantitative methods, which is a crucial criterion for RTS [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0021),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0028)]. Similarly, these quantitative parameters should be incorporated into self-reporting and assessing ability after RTS decision-making in patients with LAS [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0029)]. The evidence-based clinical guidelines [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0016),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0025),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0027)] recently included exercise-based rehabilitation programs for various treatment options for LAS patients [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0030)]. In addition, some studies have shown that kinesio taping may facilitate RTS by improving muscle contraction [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0031)], although this is not without debate[[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0032)]. This treatment can help LAS to have a good supporting effect during exercise performance, but it may also have a negative impact on the active stability of the lateral muscles [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0033)]. In addition, there are many other therapies, such as (acupuncture [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0034)], laser [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0035)], manual [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0036)], etc.), which can help LAS to RTS [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0037)]. However, the clinical experience typically dictates how best to treat patients with LAS and when sports activities may be resumed [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0038),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0039)]. In such cases, the time of RTS is used to measure and quantify the rehabilitation success [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0018),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0040)]. However, the isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive, as evidenced by the significant recurrent rate of LAS injuries. Therefore, it’s essential to build a methodical decision-making process for patients with LAS regarding RTS, considering various factors.

The process of RTS from LAS is multifactorial, and there has yet to be a published systematic review that evaluates this complex process over time. Therefore, this systematic review aims to investigate the process factors of RTS for LAS, including the timing of RTS for LAS, the rehabilitation program, the outcome indicators, and the assessment of the performance recovery after decision-making, to provide further guidance and clinical implications for LAS patients to develop RTS program.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124)Methods

2.
### Protocol registration

2.1.
The PRISMA 2020 Guidelines Reporting Items checklist [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0041)] was strictly followed to conduct the current systematic review, with protocol in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluations (PRISMA) statement. The study protocol was registered on the International Register of Prospective Systematic Evaluations (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024522798).

### Search strategy

2.2.
Four online electronic literature databases, including Web of Science, MEDLINE (_via_ PubMed), Scopus, and ScienceDirect, were searched up to March 1, 2024. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) developed the search strategy, filtered by term-level search, to identify possible studies. Two sets of terms combined with the Boolean indicator “AND” were used, including Lateral Ankle Sprain (e.g. “Lateral Ankle Coper”, “Lateral Ankle Injury”) and Return To Sport (e.g. “Return To Play”). The terms used were either MESH or non-MESH terms, and the Boolean indicator separated the words in each term, “OR”. This technique was restricted to the use of the English language. All screened documents were imported into reference management software (Endnote®version X9, Thomson Reuters, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and duplicate references were removed. A third researcher (Q.M.) would be referred to discuss solutions if any discrepancies were found during the search.

### Eligibility criteria

2.3.
This study covered prospective studies, surveys, and randomized controlled trials (RCT) published in peer-reviewed scientific articles written in English before March 1, 2024. Firstly, the titles and abstracts were screened by two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) using a glossary of terms. Then, the full text was reviewed using the following inclusion and exclusion criteria: the third researcher (Q.M.) was referred to decide the eligibility of the final study if an agreement could not be reached during the screening process. Finally, we conducted a manual search after completing the full-text search to find any studies that had been overlooked the first time.

#### Inclusion criteria

2.3.1.
These articles were included in this review if, (1) the subjects are human and were not restricted by sex or race; (2) RTS is the article’s primary outcome; (3) the article should report the biomechanical parameters covering the lower extremity kinematics, kinetics, muscle activity, joint range of motion, functional assessment, or dynamic postural control; (4) the articles should concentrate solely on LAS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment at least 50% were included in this review [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042)].

#### Exclusion criteria

2.3.2.
The following criteria were followed to exclude articles, (1) conferences, dissertations, reviews, abstracts, and meta-analyses; (2) study subjects were non-human; (3) LAS requires ligament reconstruction surgery; (4) the results of the article were not relevant to RTS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment less than 50% were excluded in this review [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042)].

#### Outcome of RTS

2.3.3.
The result indicators in the article should be pertinent to RTS. We concluded that due to the multifactorial nature of the RTS process, the following outcome indicators should be used to screen articles, the evaluation of LAS, the duration from the time of the sprain until RTS, rehabilitation measures, decision-making indicators (pre- and post-functional tests, pre- and post-pain tests, self-perceptions, mood determinations, and quantitative parameters) and post-decision-making tests (ratings of athleticism and observations of athletic performance).

### Quality assessment and risk of bias assessment

2.4.
The quality and risk of bias of the included articles were assessed using an improved quality indicator checklist [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0028),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0043),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0044)]. Fourteen (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22) out of the 27 items on the list were used in the previous review study on chronic ankle instability and LAS [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0042),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0045),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124#CIT0046)]. This prior research could assign multiple quality labels according to quality scores. Consequently, 14 items from the list were adopted in this study to examine the confounding bias, reporting, external validity, and internal validity of all the papers. Half of the 14 item types in the list were assessments of data descriptions. According to the purpose of this study, studies with a score of > 50% were included in this review; otherwise, they were excluded. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently scored each article in this review, yielding a maximum quality score of 15.

### Data extraction and manager

2.5.
Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently employed standardized and pre-programmed data modules for extraction tables. For each article that met the requirements of this review, modules were selected and data removed according to the study: (1) authors, (2) publication year, (3) country, (4) sample size (gender and age), (5) duration (time from intervention initiation), (6) frequency of interventions (number and intervals), (7) level of LAS, (8) treatment (measures of rehabilitation interventions), (9) outcome variables (10) main result, (12) evaluator, (13) research type, (14) criteria for RTS, (15) RTS time, and (16) RTS tests.

### Statistical analyses

2.6.
Due to the large number of direct variables and lack of indirect comparative variables in the randomized controlled trials (RCT) and prospective studies included in this study, the present work failed to satisfy the meta-analysis standards. Therefore, the resultant data was presented in the Tables of this study.

args.summary:
This is a systematic review published in Annals of Medicine (2025) titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The study investigates factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard rehabilitation paradigm.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries, with up to 74% of patients experiencing persistent symptoms. Re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports populations, and nearly 40% develop chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may result from premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Studies were categorized into: (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and time of RTS.

**Key Findings:**
- 20 studies included: 3 questionnaires, 11 randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective studies
- Rehabilitation interventions included cryo-ultrasound therapy, neuromuscular training, balance exercises, bandaging, hyaluronic acid injections, neurostimulation, and electrical muscle stimulation
- RTS criteria identified include pain, swelling, ankle range of motion, muscle strength, functional instability, proprioception, and ability to perform practical tasks
- Many patients showed deficits at RTS: 65.1% had pain, 86.2% had function deficits, 35.8% had disability
- Side-to-side differences in ankle range of motion significantly correlated with time to RTS

**Conclusion:** RTS for LAS is a continuous process influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The study identified current procedures and timelines for RTS of LAS, providing theoretical basis and clinical guidance for LAS patient rehabilitation.

## Abstract

Objective The aim of this systematic review was to identify prospective studies that used a criteria-based return to sport (RTS) decision-making process for patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS) injury. Design Systematic review and narrative synthesis. Data sources The PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, PEDro, Cochrane Library, SPORTDiscus (EBSCO), ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases were searched to 23 November 2018. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies Studies were included if they prospectively applied a criteria-based RTS decisionmaking process for patients with LAS injury, but were excluded if they merely gathered outcome measures at the RTS time point. Studies were also excluded if patients were recovering from ankle fracture, high ankle sprain, medial ankle sprain, chronic ankle instability or complex ankle injury. Results No studies were identified that used a criteria-based RTS decision-making process for patients with LAS injury. We were unable to conduct a quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis, therefore we provide a narrative synthesis of relevant questionnaires, as well as clinical and functional assessments commonly used in studies retrieved in the search. Conclusion There are currently no published evidence-based criteria to inform RTS decisions for patients with an LAS injury. Based on our narrative synthesis, we propose a number of variables that could be used to develop a criteria-based RTS decision paradigm. Future research should aim to reach consensus on these variables and apply them to actual RTS decisions within prospective study designs. Furthermore, we suggest that complex systems theory and the RTS continuum could be used to inform the development of an RTS decision-making paradigm for athletes with LAS injury.

Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 1998

The minimum amount of change which represents clinical improvement following ankle sprains is unknown. This study considers the usefulness of physiological and behavioral measures commonly employed for this purpose in sports rehabilitation settings. Thirteen collegiate athletes of both genders were measured at approximately 3 and 10 days post-grade I or II ankle sprain. Volumetric displacement and sagittal plane ankle range of motion measures were used as impairment indicators. Motor ability scores (activity count) and a perceived athletic ability measure (visual analog scale) were used to indicate functional limitations. Volumetric displacement and both functional limitation measures demonstrated responsiveness to change between two occasions of measurement separated by 1 week. Observed changes in range of motion deficits could not be distinguished from measurement error. The results of this study suggest that behavioral measures of motor activity and perceived athletic ability may be at least as useful as physical measures of organic dysfunction for assessing clinical improvement following acute ankle sprains among athletes.

args.key_excerpts: No studies were identified that used a criteria-based return to sport (RTS) decision-making process for patients with LAS injury., Athletes face a 9.8 risk ratio for re-injury within 6 months post-first-time LAS., Complex systems theory should inform dynamic RTS decision-making for LAS injuries., Rehabilitation must shift from time-based to evidence-based criteria for LAS recovery., There are currently no published evidence-based criteria to inform RTS decisions for patients with an LAS injury.
args.summary:
This is a webpage from Academia.edu hosting a 2019 systematic review published in *Sports Medicine* by Jo Verschueren, titled "Criteria-Based Return to Sport Decision-Making Following Lateral Ankle Sprain Injury: a Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis."

**Objective & Methods:** The systematic review aimed to identify prospective studies that used a criteria-based return to sport (RTS) decision-making process for patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS) injury. Databases searched (PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro, Cochrane Library, SPORTDiscus, ScienceDirect, Scopus) up to November 23, 2018. Studies were included if they prospectively applied a criteria-based RTS process for LAS patients and excluded if they only gathered outcome measures at RTS time point, or involved ankle fracture, high ankle sprain, medial ankle sprain, chronic ankle instability, or complex ankle injury.

**Key Finding:** No studies were identified that used a criteria-based RTS decision-making process for LAS injury. A quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was not possible, so a narrative synthesis of relevant questionnaires and clinical/functional assessments was provided instead.

**Key Takeaways & Conclusions:**
- Athletes face a 9.8 risk ratio for re-injury within 6 months post-first-time LAS.
- There are currently no published evidence-based criteria to inform RTS decisions for LAS patients.
- The authors propose variables that could be used to develop a criteria-based RTS decision paradigm.
- Future research should aim to reach consensus on these variables and apply them within prospective study designs.
- Complex systems theory and the RTS continuum (return to participation, return to sport, return to performance) should inform dynamic RTS decision-making for LAS injuries.
- Rehabilitation must shift from time-based to evidence-based criteria for LAS recovery.
- The authors suggest a phenomenological framework and components for a dynamic RTS decision-making paradigm, using control theory as a metaphor with four requirements: (1) goal condition (RTPf), (2) observability condition (biopsychosocial assessment), (3) action condition (the athlete/patient), and (4) model condition (RTS clearance profile).

The page also includes related research papers, 218 references, and figure descriptions illustrating a dynamic RTS profile and a "road to recovery" along the RTS continuum.

## Abstract

### Background

Returning to sport (RTS) from lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is multifaceted and interdisciplinary. This systematic review aimed to investigate the factors involved in RTS and further establish a standard paradigm of RTS to treat and rehabilitate the LAS.

### Methods

Four electronic databases, including PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, Science Direct, and Scopus, were searched until March 1, 2024. The literature was identified, screened, evaluated, managed and data was extracted by developing inclusion criteria based on the PICO model for systematic reviews. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Downs and Black checklist and the measurement parameters were summarised.

### Results

This systematic review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Participant’s information, research content, purpose, methods, and interventions were extracted and summarized. The included articles were divided into four categories for further discussion, including (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS of LAS, (3) performance assessment after RTS of LAS, and (4) the relationship between criteria and time of RTS for LAS.

### Conclusion

RTS for LAS is a continuous process, which is influenced by complex factors, such as the injury extent, injury causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The standard paradigms of RTS rehabilitation for LAS is still lacking in the literature. Current study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS. Findings may provide theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance for the RTS of LAS patients.

## 1. Background

Lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is one of the most frequently occurring musculoskeletal injuries in general and athletic populations engaged in recreational and competitive sports [[Citation 1–8](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The precise etiology of LAS is complex [[Citation 9](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] and often presents as a mechanical laxity and proprioception deficit [[Citation 5](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Clinically, lateral ankle sprains are categorized into grade I injury as mild, grade II injury as moderate, and grade III injury as severe [[Citation 1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 5](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Although LAS is typically believed to be a one-off injury, the evidence from hospital emergency department records shows that up to 74% of patients with LAS continue to have persistent symptoms [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 11](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Studies reported that LAS patients have the most significant risk of re-injury in all lower-extremity musculoskeletal injuries [[Citation 12](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In specific sports populations, the re-injured population could be as high as 70% [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], and nearly 40% of LAS patients would experience chronic ankle instability within a year of the initial injury due to the re-injury [[Citation 13](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 14](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The high rate of re-injury might be brought on by either premature return to sport (RTS) or inadequate rehabilitation [[Citation 15](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 16](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

RTS is considered safe for an injured athlete to return to training or competition [[Citation 17](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This also results from the anticipated evaluation, medical intervention, and rehabilitation procedure [[Citation 17](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] RTS should be viewed as a continuous process rather than finished in a single step. Thus, each stage is seen as a tiny step toward the RTS [[Citation 19](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Ardern et al. [[Citation 20](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] defined the RTS continuum as the three process parts of “return to performance”, “return to sport”, and “return to participation” [[Citation 19](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 22](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. These three processes are influenced by the injury grade, rehabilitation strategies, pre and post RTS foot function tests, the amount of time spent in RTS, psychosocial elements of RTS, emotional values, and self-perceptions [[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 23–25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. All these factors could be combined to assess whether the injured athlete satisfied the criteria for RTS and gauged the performance level after RTS.

Even though the criteria for RTS in patients with LAS have not been clarified in the current literature, the components of RTS decision-making (i.e. pain, ankle perception, including proprioception, ankle injuries, muscle activation, sensorimotor control systems, and motor testing) were previously described in narrative reviews, with consensus among clinical experts [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 26](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Furthermore, it has been shown that the decision-making factors for RTS in patients with LAS consider using quantitative methods, which is a crucial criterion for RTS [[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 28](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Similarly, these quantitative parameters should be incorporated into self-reporting and assessing ability after RTS decision-making in patients with LAS [[Citation 29](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. The evidence-based clinical guidelines [[Citation 16](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] recently included exercise-based rehabilitation programs for various treatment options for LAS patients [[Citation 30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In addition, some studies have shown that kinesio taping may facilitate RTS by improving muscle contraction [[Citation 31](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], although this is not without debate[[Citation 32](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This treatment can help LAS to have a good supporting effect during exercise performance, but it may also have a negative impact on the active stability of the lateral muscles [[Citation 33](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In addition, there are many other therapies, such as (acupuncture [[Citation 34](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], laser [[Citation 35](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], manual [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)], etc.), which can help LAS to RTS [[Citation 37](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. However, the clinical experience typically dictates how best to treat patients with LAS and when sports activities may be resumed [[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 39](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. In such cases, the time of RTS is used to measure and quantify the rehabilitation success [[Citation 18](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 40](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. However, the isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive, as evidenced by the significant recurrent rate of LAS injuries. Therefore, it’s essential to build a methodical decision-making process for patients with LAS regarding RTS, considering various factors.

The process of RTS from LAS is multifactorial, and there has yet to be a published systematic review that evaluates this complex process over time. Therefore, this systematic review aims to investigate the process factors of RTS for LAS, including the timing of RTS for LAS, the rehabilitation program, the outcome indicators, and the assessment of the performance recovery after decision-making, to provide further guidance and clinical implications for LAS patients to develop RTS program.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1. Protocol registration

The PRISMA 2020 Guidelines Reporting Items checklist [[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)] was strictly followed to conduct the current systematic review, with protocol in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluations (PRISMA) statement. The study protocol was registered on the International Register of Prospective Systematic Evaluations (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42024522798).

### 2.2. Search strategy

Four online electronic literature databases, including Web of Science, MEDLINE (_via_ PubMed), Scopus, and ScienceDirect, were searched up to March 1, 2024. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) developed the search strategy, filtered by term-level search, to identify possible studies. Two sets of terms combined with the Boolean indicator “AND” were used, including Lateral Ankle Sprain (e.g. “Lateral Ankle Coper”, “Lateral Ankle Injury”) and Return To Sport (e.g. “Return To Play”). The terms used were either MESH or non-MESH terms, and the Boolean indicator separated the words in each term, “OR”. This technique was restricted to the use of the English language. All screened documents were imported into reference management software (Endnote®version X9, Thomson Reuters, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and duplicate references were removed. A third researcher (Q.M.) would be referred to discuss solutions if any discrepancies were found during the search.

### 2.3. Eligibility criteria

This study covered prospective studies, surveys, and randomized controlled trials (RCT) published in peer-reviewed scientific articles written in English before March 1, 2024. Firstly, the titles and abstracts were screened by two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) using a glossary of terms. Then, the full text was reviewed using the following inclusion and exclusion criteria: the third researcher (Q.M.) was referred to decide the eligibility of the final study if an agreement could not be reached during the screening process. Finally, we conducted a manual search after completing the full-text search to find any studies that had been overlooked the first time.

#### 2.3.1. Inclusion criteria

These articles were included in this review if, (1) the subjects are human and were not restricted by sex or race; (2) RTS is the article’s primary outcome; (3) the article should report the biomechanical parameters covering the lower extremity kinematics, kinetics, muscle activity, joint range of motion, functional assessment, or dynamic postural control; (4) the articles should concentrate solely on LAS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment at least 50% were included in this review [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

#### 2.3.2. Exclusion criteria

The following criteria were followed to exclude articles, (1) conferences, dissertations, reviews, abstracts, and meta-analyses; (2) study subjects were non-human; (3) LAS requires ligament reconstruction surgery; (4) the results of the article were not relevant to RTS; (5) studies that obtained a score of quality assessment less than 50% were excluded in this review [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)].

#### 2.3.3. Outcome of RTS

The result indicators in the article should be pertinent to RTS. We concluded that due to the multifactorial nature of the RTS process, the following outcome indicators should be used to screen articles, the evaluation of LAS, the duration from the time of the sprain until RTS, rehabilitation measures, decision-making indicators (pre- and post-functional tests, pre- and post-pain tests, self-perceptions, mood determinations, and quantitative parameters) and post-decision-making tests (ratings of athleticism and observations of athletic performance).

### 2.4. Quality assessment and risk of bias assessment

The quality and risk of bias of the included articles were assessed using an improved quality indicator checklist [[Citation 28](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 44](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. Fourteen (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22) out of the 27 items on the list were used in the previous review study on chronic ankle instability and LAS [[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#),[Citation 46](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334#)]. This prior research could assign multiple quality labels according to quality scores. Consequently, 14 items from the list were adopted in this study to examine the confounding bias, reporting, external validity, and internal validity of all the papers. Half of the 14 item types in the list were assessments of data descriptions. According to the purpose of this study, studies with a score of > 50% were included in this review; otherwise, they were excluded. Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently scored each article in this review, yielding a maximum quality score of 15.

### 2.5. Data extraction and manager

Two researchers (H.J. and Y.W.) independently employed standardized and pre-programmed data modules for extraction tables. For each article that met the requirements of this review, modules were selected and data removed according to the study: (1) authors, (2) publication year, (3) country, (4) sample size (gender and age), (5) duration (time from intervention initiation), (6) frequency of interventions (number and intervals), (7) level of LAS, (8) treatment (measures of rehabilitation interventions), (9) outcome variables (10) main result, (12) evaluator, (13) research type, (14) criteria for RTS, (15) RTS time, and (16) RTS tests.

### 2.6. Statistical analyses

Due to the large number of direct variables and lack of indirect comparative variables in the randomized controlled trials (RCT) and prospective studies included in this study, the present work failed to satisfy the meta-analysis standards. Therefore, the resultant data was presented in the Tables of this study.

## 3. Result

### 3.1. Search results

In the beginning, 1081 records were found. After removing all duplicates, 690 records were retained. Three hundred eighteen records were included based on title and abstract screening for a full-text review of inclusion and exclusion criteria. A total of 18 articles satisfied the inclusion criteria. After another manual search for studies missed during the initial search, two articles fulfilled the inclusion criteria. In the end, all 20 articles achieved more than 50% scores of quality. This review divided the 20 studies into four categories based on the topic and content of the included studies, which were the rehabilitation measures for patients with LAS to RTS (Table 2), the criteria for RTS in LAS patients (Table 3), the performance assessment after RTS in LAS patients (Table 4), and the relationship between test assessment and time of RTS in LAS patients (Table 5).
