### **Ankle mobility (Figure 1)**

From the standing position, the player places one foot on a box the top of which is level with the top third of the shinbone of the other leg. The distance of the elastic band is fixed in a position to generate sufficient tension to pull the ankle joint. This distance may vary depending on the player. The elastic band is placed at floor height and may be in line with the ankle or slightly displaced medially or laterally (up to 30º-45º). The elastic band should be placed just below the peroneal and tibial malleolus, the objective being to secure it to the neck of the astragalus. From this position, the player performs an active dorsiflexion, without moving their foot, and the heel must remain in contact with the ground at all times. Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed.

### **Working the peroneal muscles in CKC (Figure 2) and the tibialis posterior (Figure 3)**

Place two platforms between 3 and 5 cm high on the floor. From the standing position, the player places each foot on one surface so that one half of the foot is in contact with the surface and the other half is not. From this position, the player touches the floor with the side of the foot that is free or not in contact with the surface (eccentric contraction). This is followed by a movement to return to the initial position (concentric contraction). This exercise focuses on the peroneus muscle (Figure 2). Same exercise idea is realized for posterior tibialis but placing the other half part of foot on platform and performing counter movement (Figure 3). Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed.

### **Working plantar flexion in CKC with one-leg flexion of the knee on an Airex (Figure 4)**

The player places one leg on an Airex. From this position, the player performs a (concentric) plantar flexion and an (eccentric) dorsiflexion in the full range of motion. The knee should be bent to between 30º and 70°. The player should use their hands to stabilize themselves if necessary. Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed.

### **Single-foot active functional exercise 1 (Figure 5)**

The player takes up position on one foot on an unstable platform with degrees of hip and knee flexion that allow them to attain a comfortable and stable position. From this position, the objective is to reach a static single-leg balance position on the Pielaster. Once this has been achieved, the next objective is to perform rotations with a soft medicine ball following diagonal patterns in different combinations. Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed. The repetitions will always be different, no more than 2-3 consecutive repetitions performing the same diagonal.

### **Single-foot active functional exercise 2 (Figure 6)**

The player takes up position with one foot on a Pielaster-platform with degrees of ankle, knee and hip flexion that provide a comfortable position to perform an exercise while remaining stable. From this position, the first objective is to reach a static balance position. Once this has been achieved, the next goal will be to perform a hip and upper body flexion of up to 90 degrees with the other leg raised in extension. Players can place Mini Band-type elastic bands between their knees to increase exercise difficulty. Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed.

### **Lateral movement exercise (Figure 7)**

From the standing position, the player attaches an elastic band to their hip and secures it to a stable surface that allows them to generate tension. The player should take up a position so that when they perform a lateral movement in one direction the elastic band will pull in the opposite direction. The exercise has to be performed taking two lateral steps at high speed. Two sets of between 6 and 8 repetitions should be performed. The repetitions should not always be performed in the same direction on one plane, but should be executed in different directions.

### **Footwork with competitive movement (Figure 8)**

This exercise seeks to simulate “coordination ladders” by placing marks and using the lines of the field of play or court. Two players take up position, one on each side, ready to perform the same exercise identically, 4.9 m away from each other. From this position, they perform the footwork as quickly as possible and then run as speedily as possible to a 1.5 m-space marked out on the free-throw line. Each player should perform 2 sets of 3 repetitions. This work should always be done in pairs, it is a competitive exercise.

## **Conclusions**

This proposal provides an example of ankle joint neuromuscular exercises to be performed during pre-basketball practice warm-up. The main practical application for physiotherapists and strength conditioning professional is to show examples of exercises and how to organise this idea during a competitive week in an elite professional basketball schedule. Moreover, this idea would help medical staff to improve their injury prevention strategies.

**Article Title:** A specific neuromuscular warm-up focusing on ankle sprain injuries in elite basketball  
**Authors:** Javier Ruiz, Jairo Vázquez, David Urbano, Carlos Martín, Eduard Torrent, Fernando Rupérez, Mindaugas Gudelis  
**Journal:** Apunts Educación Física y Deportes, Issue 145 (3rd Quarter, July-September 2021)  
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.5672/apunts.2014-0983.es.(2021/3).145.08

**Background & Rationale:**  
Basketball involves explosive actions (accelerations, jumps, changes of direction) placing high demands on the ankle joint. The ankle is the most commonly injured area in athletes. Nearly 80% of athletes with an ankle sprain may sustain repetitive sprains, and ~72% may develop chronic instability. Basketball players are five times more likely to sustain an ankle injury after a previous one, with a 73% recurrence rate. Players with less lower-limb strength and fewer neuromuscular/proprioception abilities are at greater risk.

**Objective:**  
To propose a weekly ankle-specific neuromuscular warm-up program for elite basketball teams, integrated into pre-training warm-up sessions.

**Key Epidemiological Data:**  
- Ankle joint injuries in sports account for 11%–17% of all injuries.  
- Elite players cover ~73 m·min⁻¹, ~3 m·min⁻¹ at high-speed running (>18 km/h), with ~4 accelerations/decelerations >2 m/s² per minute, ~0.2 jumps >3Gs per minute, and ~1.3 impacts >8Gs per minute.

**Proposed Exercises (9 exercises, performed as a circuit in pairs):**  
1. **Ankle Mobility (Figure 1):** Standing, one foot on a box with elastic band at floor height below the malleoli; active dorsiflexion, heel grounded. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
2. **Peroneal Muscles in CKC (Figure 2):** Foot half-on platform; touch floor with free side of foot (eccentric → concentric eversion). 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
3. **Tibialis Posterior in CKC (Figure 3):** Same setup but performing inversion movement. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
4. **Plantar Flexion in CKC on Airex (Figure 4):** One leg on Airex, knee bent 30°–70°, perform concentric plantar flexion and eccentric dorsiflexion. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
5. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 1 (Figure 5):** Stand on one foot on unstable platform (Pielaster); perform diagonal rotational patterns with a soft medicine ball. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
6. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 2 (Figure 6):** One foot on Pielaster; perform hip and upper body flexion to 90° with opposite leg extended (single-leg deadlift). Optional Mini Band between knees. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
7. **Lateral Movement (Figure 7):** Elastic band on hip secured to stable surface; perform two lateral steps at high speed against band resistance. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
8. **Footwork with Competitive Movement (Figure 8):** Two players 4.9 m apart; perform footwork on coordination ladder then sprint to a marked space (1.5 m on free-throw line). 2 sets of 3 reps, competitive.  
9. **Progression:** Include perturbations (teammate unbalancing) and simple decision-making.

**Practical Application:**  
The program is designed to be integrated into a typical competition week schedule as part of the regular team warm-up. A holistic approach is recommended, with coaches, strength coaches, medical staff, and players sharing responsibility.

**Conclusions:**  
This proposal provides an example of ankle joint neuromuscular exercises for pre-basketball warm-up. It offers physiotherapists and strength/conditioning professionals practical exercises and a weekly organization framework for elite professional basketball, aiding injury prevention strategies.

<webpage_content>
Central Bringing Excellence in Open Access   JSM Foot and Ankle Cite this article: Dabadghav R (2016) Treating Lateral Ankle Sprain in Basketball Players-A physiotherapists’ Prospective. JSM Foot Ankle 1(1): 1002.
*Corresponding author Rachana Dabadghav, Department of Physiotherapy, Sancheti Institute College of Phyiotherapy, Thube Park, Shivajinagar, Pune-411005, India, Tel: 91-9923173525; Submitted: 20 April 2016 Accepted: 16 May 2016 Published: 18 May 2016 Copyright © 2016 Dabadghav OPEN ACCESS Prospective Treating Lateral Ankle Sprain in Basketball Players-A physiotherapists’ Prospective Rachana Dabadghav* Department of Physiotherapy, Sancheti Institute College of Physiotherapy, India INTRODUCTION Basketball is a team game and a non- contact sport. It is a fast moving and aggressive game which requires lot of vertical jumps and multidirectional activities [1]. Taylor, 2004 found out that on an average a basketball player performs 1050 ± 51 movements in a game out of which 46±12 are vertical jumps [2]. As the game includes lot of vertical jumps and multidirectional activities, the injury rate is quite high [3]. The injury rate is as high as 7.9 injuries per 1000 athlete exposures (AEs) in females and 7.1 injuries per 1000 AEs in males [4]. Amongst all the injuries, ankle sprains are most common. The incidence of ankle sprains is greater than 80% in basketball players because of the nature of the game [5]. More than 90% of elite athletes reported a history of at least one ankle injury in their athletic career [6]. The common mechanism of injury is excessive supination of the rear foot on an externally rotated lower leg soon after the initial contact of the rear foot during gait or landing from a jump [7]. Lateral ankle sprains are based on grades 1-3. Grade 1 is microscopic tearing of ATFL, grade 2- microscopic tearing of larger cross sectional portion of ATFL and grade 3- complete rupture of the ATFL [8].
As the injury rate and demands of the game are high, a rehabilitation programme should include exercises which will train the athlete as a whole and reduce the risk of further injuries. Rehabilitation Goals of rehabilitation [9] • Reduce pain and swelling • Increase pain free range.
• Increase strength.
• Improve joint proprioception • Improve overall conditioning and endurance.
• Return to participation.
• Prevent recurrence Reduce pain and inflammation- Immediate post- injury phase: (injury- 2 days) In most cases of lateral ankle sprains, grade 1, 2 and 3, nonsurgical management plan has proven to be effective [10]. The best treatment for grade 1, 2 and 3 in the early stage rehabilitation or the acute stage is to follow the PRICE protocol i.e. protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation as there is swelling and pain at rest immediately after the injury. Application of ice and compression with crepe bandage within 36 hours of injury has found to limit the effusion and has been demonstrated to be effective in minimizing the amount of exudates [11]. For grade 1 and 2 gentle strengthening exercises and weight bearing with support should be started as early as possible [10]. Whereas, for grade 3 ankle sprains a more careful approach should be taken, if the athlete is unable to bear weight, the ankle should be put in functional walking orthosis and instructed to ambulate with crutches in a non weight bearing gait at least for 4 days [9].
For grade 1, 2 and 3- For grade 1 and 2 the rehabilitation protocol is generally faster than grade 3. For grade 3 lateral ankle sprains also mobilization should be started as soon as the pain permits [10].
Increase pain free range- Initial stage rehabilitation (2 – 5 days) It is found that after ankle sprain, there is restriction of dorsiflexion which is very important during gait. Also there is excessive anterior displacement of talus which leads to laxity of anterior talo fibular ligament (ATFL). At least 10° of dorsiflexion is required for walking, whereas 20° to 30° is required for running [12]. Mulligan (1993), reported rapid restoration of pain free dorsiflexion movement with mobilisation with movement (MWM) technique [13]. Weight-bearing treatment techniques are believed to be superior to non-weight-bearing techniques, as they replicate aspects of functional activities [14]. It is found from the previous studies that mobilisation produces more of a mechanical effect than a direct hypoalgesic effect. Hence to restore the dorsiflexion range MWM technique is used as it reduces any residual anterior displacement of talus [15]. Stretching exercises can also be given to improve the range of motion [10]. Strengthening exercises should also be incorporated to avoid muscle wasting [11].
Improve muscle strength and joint proprioception- Intermediate stage rehabilitation: (2- 6 weeks) After an ankle sprain there is peroneal muscle weakness. Evertor muscles have suggested playing an important role in Central Bringing Excellence in Open Access   Dabadghav (2016) Email: JSM Foot Ankle 1(1): 1002 (2016) 2/3 preventing ligamentous injuries. The strength of the peroneus longus and brevis muscles is supposed to provide support to the lateral ligaments [9]. It has been hypothesised that, reduced evertor muscle strength would decrease the ability of evertors to resist inversion and hence will be unable to return the foot to a neutral position thus leading to an inversion ankle sprain [16]. Hence it is important to strengthen the muscles around the ankle joint to avoid chronic ankle instability which can lead to recurrent ankle sprains. Strengthening can be done with the use of elastic bands and tubes. Isokinetic strengthening should also be given as it has been found that the functional capacity of injured ankle reached as the same level of injured ankle [17]. Strengthening should be done both concentrically and eccentrically. Along with strengthening of ankle muscles, hip muscle strengthening is also important as deficiencies in hip muscle strength have shown to increase the risk of lateral ankle sprains [18]. There are proprioception deficits after an ankle sprain as there is trauma to the mechanoreceptors present in the ligament tissues which can lead to partial differentiation [19]. Mechanoreceptors are sensitive to joint pressure and tension caused by movement and static position. This disturbance of the afferent input from mechanoreceptors affects not only the sense of movement and position but also the subsequent proprioceptive reflex to control posture and coordination is affected, resulting in ankle sprains [20]. A sports specific balance training program like dribbling with 1 leg stance, dribbling while standing on wobble board, etc reduces proprioceptive deficits in lateral ankle sprains in basketball players [21]. Strengthening muscles can enhance proprioceptive abilities by stimulating the muscle spindle and golgi tendon organ receptors. The muscle spindles receive stimuli from static and dynamic gamma efferent nerves, and strength training increases the gamma efferent activity, thereby resulting in greater acuity in sensing joint position [17].
Return to sport- (4- 6 weeks) This phase should be more sport specific. Concentration should be on improving power, speed, agility and coordination as these are the components required for maximal strength levels in the shortest period of time in basketball. Plyometric exercises with weights or resistance have found to improve jumping skills in basketball players [22]. Jumping forward, backward, laterally; box drills, etc should be incorporated as these are effective methods for improving movement performance [9]. Plyometric exercises have shown to improve eccentric control of the muscles [23]. This improves stability of the joint while jumping thus supporting the joint while landing. Multidirectional sports specific exercises like catch and throw close to the body progressing to away from the body on a wobble board improves proprioception and co-ordination [9]. The athlete must be able to demonstrate proficiency in stopping, changing direction, jumping, and landing before returning to practice as all these skills are required for playing basketball. These exercises should be maintained throughout the season and also in off- season as they help in maintaining strength and improves proprioception thus, reducing the chances of recurrence. Also to avoid recurrence prevention strategies should be taken into consideration.
Prevention Sastinopoulos D 2004 reported that ankle bracing reduced the incidence, severity, and long-term complications of ankle sprains, and thus this resulted in less time lost from athletic performance [24]. Ankle taping has also been found to prevent injuries. It is also believed to improve proprioception [18]. But taping has been criticized of loosening and after one hour of physical activity taping offers no useful support as there is loss of 40% to 50% of original support. Hence semi rigid ankle support was found to be more effective as it helps in reloading and maintains anatomical alignment of the ankle. Shoes play an important role in prevention of ankle sprains as high top shoes provide an extra support in addition to taping or bracing [25]. Criteria for Returning To Sport [26] Time should be given for tissue healing • There should be pain free full range of motion.
• There should be no persistent swelling.
• There should be adequate muscle strength i.e. at least 90% of the contra lateral limb.
• Flexibility equal bilaterally.
• Joint stability is maintained by muscle control and/ or a brace or tape.
• There should be good proprioception.
• Cardiovascular fitness should be equal to or better than the requirements of the game.
• Skills must have been regained.
• There should be no biomechanical dysfunction.
• The athlete should be ready psychologically.
CONCLUSION While rehabilitating a player a holistic approach towards his/ her injury is required. While considering this, the athlete’s capacity and requirement of the game should also be considered. A precise approach will benefit the athlete and help in early and complete recovery.

This article by Rachana Dabadghav (2016) from JSM Foot and Ankle presents a physiotherapist's perspective on treating lateral ankle sprains in basketball players. The paper highlights that ankle sprains account for over 80% of basketball injuries, with injury rates of 7.9 per 1000 athlete exposures in females and 7.1 in males. The article outlines a phased rehabilitation protocol:

**Acute Phase (0-2 days):** PRICE protocol (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). For grade 1-2 sprains, early gentle strengthening and weight-bearing are recommended. For grade 3, functional walking orthosis with non-weight-bearing gait for at least 4 days.

**Initial Stage (2-5 days):** Focus on restoring dorsiflexion range (minimum 10° needed for walking, 20-30° for running) using Mulligan's Mobilisation with Movement (MWM) technique. Stretching and strengthening exercises to prevent muscle wasting.

**Intermediate Stage (2-6 weeks):** Address peroneal muscle weakness through strengthening (elastic bands, isokinetic, concentric/eccentric exercises). Hip muscle strengthening also important. Proprioception training using sports-specific balance exercises (dribbling on one leg, wobble board work).

**Return to Sport (4-6 weeks):** Sport-specific training including plyometrics, multidirectional exercises, and agility drills. Criteria for return include: pain-free full ROM, no persistent swelling, strength at least 90% of contralateral limb, good proprioception, equal flexibility, cardiovascular fitness meeting game requirements, and psychological readiness.

**Prevention:** Ankle bracing reduces incidence and severity. Semi-rigid ankle supports are more effective than taping (which loses 40-50% support after 1 hour). High-top shoes provide additional support. Prevention strategies should be maintained throughout the season and off-season.

# Ankle Sprain Management

## Recovery and Prevention

An ankle sprain occurs when the ligaments that support the ankle are stretched or torn due to a sudden twist, fall, or misstep. This common injury affects people of all ages and activity levels, from athletes to individuals walking on uneven surfaces. Proper management is crucial to ensure a full recovery and prevent recurrent sprains.

Ankle sprains range from mild to severe, depending on the degree of ligament damage. With the right treatment, most sprains heal well, allowing individuals to regain full mobility and strength.

## Causes & Risk Factors of Ankle Sprains

* **Sudden Twisting Movements** – Common during sports, running, or walking on uneven ground.
* **Weak Ankles or Previous Injuries** – A history of ankle sprains increases the risk of recurrence.
* **Inadequate Footwear** – Wearing unsupportive shoes can lead to instability.
* **Poor Balance or Coordination** – Increases the likelihood of rolling the ankle.
* **High-Impact Activities** – Sports that involve jumping, cutting, or rapid direction changes put extra stress on the ankles.

## Signs & Symptoms of an Ankle Sprain

* Pain, swelling, and bruising around the ankle
* Difficulty bearing weight or walking
* Stiffness and reduced range of motion
* A popping or tearing sensation at the time of injury
* Tenderness when touching the affected area

## Diagnosis of Ankle Sprains

* **Physical Examination** – Assessing swelling, pain, and ligament stability.
* **Range of Motion Tests** – Checking mobility and strength.
* **Imaging Tests** – X-rays may be performed to rule out fractures, while MRI or ultrasound may be used for severe ligament injuries.

## Treatment Options for Ankle Sprains

### Immediate Care (R.I.C.E. Protocol)

* **Rest** – Avoid activities that put stress on the ankle.
* **Ice** – Apply ice packs for 15-20 minutes every few hours to reduce swelling.
* **Compression** – Use an elastic bandage or ankle brace to provide support.
* **Elevation** – Keep the ankle raised above heart level to minimise swelling.

### Non-Surgical Treatment

* **Bracing & Support** – A stabilising brace or taping can protect the ankle during recovery.
* **Pain Management** – Anti-inflammatory medication helps reduce pain and swelling.
* **Physiotherapy & Rehabilitation** – Strengthening and balance exercises restore stability and prevent future sprains.

### Surgical Treatment (For Severe Cases)

* **Ligament Repair or Reconstruction** – In cases of chronic instability or severe ligament tears, surgery may be necessary to restore function.
* **Arthroscopic Surgery** – Used to assess and repair damage within the ankle joint.

## Preventing Ankle Sprains

* **Strength & Stability Training** – Strengthening the muscles around the ankle improves support.
* **Proper Footwear** – Supportive shoes reduce the risk of rolling the ankle.
* **Balance Exercises** – Activities like single-leg stands or wobble board training help prevent sprains.
* **Taping or Bracing** – Provides additional support during high-risk activities.
* **Gradual Return to Activity** – Avoid rushing back to sports or strenuous exercise too soon after an injury.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle Sprain: a systematic review ---
URL: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in *Annals of Medicine* (2025, Volume 57, Issue 1) by Jiang et al. from Ningbo University, University of Auckland, and University of Essex, titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The review investigates the factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries in athletic populations. Up to 74% of patients have persistent symptoms, and re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports, with nearly 40% developing chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may be due to premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024522798). Quality assessment used the Downs and Black checklist. Inclusion criteria required human subjects, RTS as a primary outcome, biomechanical parameters, and quality scores ≥50%.

**Results:** Twenty papers were included (mean quality score 75.36±10.40%; 11 RCTs, 7 prospective studies, 3 questionnaires). Studies were divided into four categories: (1) rehabilitation measures, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and RTS time.

**Rehabilitation interventions identified:** Electrotherapy (high-voltage pulsed current, noninvasive interactive nerve stimulation), balanced intervention approach (active video gaming), joint injection (hyaluronic acid), functional movement approach (neuromuscular training, exercise therapy), ligament fixation/protection (immobilization 4-12 weeks), and combination approaches (ultrasound + cold therapy, electrical muscle stimulation + isometric exercise).

**Key findings:** The RTS process is multifactorial, influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. No standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation currently exists. The review identified that RTS should be viewed as a continuous process (not a single event), with the RTS continuum comprising "return to participation," "return to sport," and "return to performance." Outcome indicators were classified according to PAASS guidelines: pain severity, ankle impairments, athlete perception, sensorimotor control, and sport/functional performance.

**Conclusion:** The study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS, providing theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance. The authors emphasize that isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive given the high recurrence rate, and a methodical decision-making process considering multiple factors is essential.
</summary>

"Lateral ankle sprain (LAS) is one of the most frequently occurring musculoskeletal injuries in general and athletic populations engaged in recreational and competitive sports", "Up to 74% of patients with LAS continue to have persistent symptoms", "The re-injured population could be as high as 70%", "Nearly 40% of LAS patients would experience chronic ankle instability within a year of the initial injury due to the re-injury", "RTS for LAS is a continuous process, which is influenced by complex factors, such as the injury extent, injury causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The standard paradigms of RTS rehabilitation for LAS is still lacking in the literature."
</key_excerpts>

This is a systematic review published in Annals of Medicine (2025) titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review" by Jiang, Mei, Wang, Yang, Liew, Fernandez, and Gu from Ningbo University, University of Auckland, and University of Essex. The review investigates factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Scopus) were searched up to March 1, 2024. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024522798). Quality assessment used the Downs and Black checklist (14 items).

**Results:** 20 papers were included with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. The studies were categorized into four areas: (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and time of RTS. The 20 studies included 3 questionnaires, 11 randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective studies, and 1 study that qualified as both.

**Key Findings:**
- LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries; up to 74% of patients have persistent symptoms, and re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports populations
- Nearly 40% of LAS patients develop chronic ankle instability within a year
- RTS should be viewed as a continuous process with three stages: "return to participation," "return to sport," and "return to performance"
- Rehabilitation measures included cryo-ultrasound, neuromuscular training, balance exercises, electrical stimulation, bracing, hyaluronic acid injections, and various therapeutic modalities
- RTS criteria included pain, swelling, range of motion, muscle strength, proprioception, functional stability, and functional tests
- Standard paradigms for RTS rehabilitation for LAS are still lacking in the literature

**Conclusion:** RTS for LAS is a continuous process influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The findings provide theoretical basis and clinical guidance for RTS decision-making in LAS patients.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This systematic review and meta-analysis published in the American Journal of Sports Medicine (February 2024) examined return to sport (RTS) outcomes after anatomic lateral ankle stabilization (ALAS) surgery for chronic ankle instability. The review analyzed 25 publications with 1,384 participants from databases searched through August 2021.

Key findings: 95% of patients returned to any sport, 83% returned to their preinjury level, and 87% returned to competitive sport. Mean time to RTS was 12.45 weeks (95% CI, 10.8-14.1 weeks). Risk factors for RTS failure included age (6% increased risk per decade) and BMI (4% increased risk per 5 kg/m² increase). Professional/competitive athletes had higher RTS rates (93%) than recreational athletes (83%). No significant differences were found between arthroscopic vs. open surgery, repair vs. reconstruction, or early vs. late weightbearing.

<summary>
This is a systematic review published in the Journal of Sport Rehabilitation examining whether consensus exists among published expert opinions on return-to-sport (RTS) criteria following lateral ankle sprains (LAS). LAS are among the most common sports injuries with one of the highest recurrence rates of all musculoskeletal injuries, yet no standardized objective RTS criteria exist.

**Methods:** The authors searched PubMed, CINHL, and SPORTDiscus from inception to March 2019. Eleven expert opinion papers (Level 5 evidence) were included. Consensus was defined as ≥75% agreement, partial agreement as 50-75%.

**Key Findings:**
- **Consensus reached (90.9%):** Sport-specific movement should be assessed when determining RTS readiness.
- **Partial agreement (63.6%):** Static balance should be assessed.
- **Partial agreement (54.5%):** Pain/swelling, patient-reported outcomes, range of motion, and strength should be assessed.
- **No agreement:** No consensus was reached on specific assessment techniques or cutoff thresholds for any domain.

**Important Context:** Among intercollegiate athletes, 44.4% return to sport in less than 24 hours after LAS. The average RTS time for high school athletes is 3 days. Residual deficits in ligamentous laxity, dorsiflexion range of motion, and dynamic postural control have been documented in patients cleared for RTS (average 12.7 ± 10.0 days post-injury). No expert recommended using time from injury as a criterion for RTS readiness.

**Conclusion:** Practitioners should assess sport-specific movement (using hop tests), static balance, patient-reported outcomes, range of motion, and strength when determining RTS after LAS. However, prospective research is needed to establish evidence-based assessment batteries and threshold values that minimize recurrent LAS risk.

The review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, PEDro, and Cochrane databases. **Interventions studied:** Balance training (BT), plyometric training, CrossFit, neuromuscular training (NMT), and remodeled bicycle pedal training. Intervention durations ranged from 4–12 weeks. --- SOURCE 1: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Risk Factors for Lateral Ankle Sprain: A Literature Review ---
URL: https://scholars.direct/Articles/sports-medicine/aspm-3-026.php?jid=sports-medicine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a 2019 literature review by Correia and Torres (published in Archives of Sports Medicine, ISSN: 2578-6334) examining intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors for lateral ankle sprains. The authors searched MEDLINE on September 24, 2018, and included 42 studies in their review.

**Key Intrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Gender**: Women at higher risk (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures per Doherty et al. meta-analysis)
- **Age**: Higher risk in children compared to adolescents (2.84 vs. 1.94 per 1000 exposures), and adolescents compared to adults (1.94 vs. 0.72 per 1000 exposures)
- **BMI**: Greater BMI significantly related to ankle sprain, though height and weight individually are not clearly defined risk factors
- **Muscle Strength**: Decreased slow eccentric inversion strength increases incidence; lower pronator-to-supinator ratio is a risk factor; peroneus longus weakness increases risk; hip and core strength may reduce incidence
- **Previous Ankle Sprain**: Identified as one of the strongest risk factors for re-injury, both ipsilateral and contralateral
- **Balance/Proprioception**: Proprioceptive training and balance training reduce incidence of primary and recurrent ankle sprains
- **Limb Dominance**: Inconclusive results
- **Foot Type/Anatomy**: No clear correlation found between foot type, joint laxity, anatomic alignment, or range of motion and ankle sprains

**Key Extrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Ankle Bracing/Taping**: Effective in reducing ankle sprain risk (64-69% reduction); braces and tapes are equally effective; bracing protects both mechanically and by improving proprioception
- **Shoe Type**: High top shoes reduce risk in basketball and football; specially designed swivel shoes may help
- **Sport Category**: Higher incidence in indoor, court, and team sports
- **Player Position**: May be a risk factor depending on sport-specific demands (e.g., blockers in volleyball)

**Conclusion**: Previous ankle sprain and external ankle support are the most clearly defined factors. Younger female athletes with high BMI may be at increased risk. The review found no correlation between muscle reaction time or anatomic foot type and ankle sprains. Further prospective studies are needed to reduce bias and uncertainty.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability

This systematic review (published in the Journal of Athletic Training, 2008) examined whether balance and coordination training is clinically effective for preventing and treating lateral ankle sprains. The review addressed three clinical questions:

--- SOURCE 1: Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle Sprain ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in Annals of Medicine (2025) titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The study investigates factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard rehabilitation paradigm.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries, with up to 74% of patients experiencing persistent symptoms. Re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports populations, and nearly 40% develop chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may result from premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Studies were categorized into: (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and time of RTS.

**Key Findings:**
- 20 studies included: 3 questionnaires, 11 randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective studies
- Rehabilitation interventions included cryo-ultrasound therapy, neuromuscular training, balance exercises, bandaging, hyaluronic acid injections, neurostimulation, and electrical muscle stimulation
- RTS criteria identified include pain, swelling, ankle range of motion, muscle strength, functional instability, proprioception, and ability to perform practical tasks
- Many patients showed deficits at RTS: 65.1% had pain, 86.2% had function deficits, 35.8% had disability
- Side-to-side differences in ankle range of motion significantly correlated with time to RTS

**Conclusion:** RTS for LAS is a continuous process influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The study identified current procedures and timelines for RTS of LAS, providing theoretical basis and clinical guidance for LAS patient rehabilitation.
</summary>

- Rehabilitation must shift from time-based to evidence-based criteria for LAS recovery.

URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2022.902886/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review and expert opinion published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (May 26, 2022) that identifies the most relevant functional performance tests and self-reported questionnaires to help clinicians make valid return to sport (RTS) decisions in patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI). 

**Key Background:** Lateral ankle sprain is the most common sports injury, with up to 40% of patients developing CAI. Premature RTS may contribute to high recurrence rates. Currently, there are no specific, objectively validated criteria with cut-off scores to guide RTS decisions in this population.

**Methods:** An exhaustive literature review was conducted across PubMed, PEDro, Cochrane Library, and ScienceDirect. Tests and questionnaires were selected based on their ability to differentiate CAI patients from copers or healthy individuals, reliability, clinical relevance, and practicality for daily use.

**Key Findings and Recommended Tests:**

1. **Single Leg Stance Test (firm surface):** Assesses static postural control. Proposed cut-off: <3 errors. Interrater ICC = 0.93, MDC = 0.6 errors.

2. **Foot Lift Test:** Similar to SLS but 30s duration focusing on foot displacements. Proposed cut-off: <5 lifts. ICC = 0.73-0.97.

3. **Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT):** Assesses dynamic postural control. Proposed cut-off scores: Composite score >90%, Anterior asymmetry <4.5% or <4cm, Posteromedial >91%, Posterolateral >91%.

4. **Side Hop Test:** 10 lateral/medial hops over 30cm. Proposed cut-off: <10 seconds. ICC = 0.84, MDC = 5.82s.

5. **Figure-of-8 Hop Test:** 20m figure-8 pattern. Proposed cut-off: <12 seconds. ICC = 0.95, MDC = 4.59s.

6. **Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM):** Self-reported function. Proposed cut-off: 95% for both ADL and Sport subscales. ICC = 0.89 (ADL), 0.87 (Sport). MCID = 8 (ADL), 9 (Sport).

7. **Ankle Ligament Reconstruction-Return to Sport after Injury (ALR-RSI):** Psychological readiness. Proposed cut-off: 55/120. ICC = 0.92, MDC = 10 points.

**Conclusions:** A combination of the SEBT and Side Hop Test has the greatest clinical value. The authors recommend combining FAAM and ALR-RSI questionnaires with functional tests. However, objective scientific criteria with cut-off scores are still lacking. Additional considerations include ankle evertor strength testing, neurocognitive functional testing, and sport-specific testing. The proposed test cluster should be used within the broader RTS continuum (return to participation → return to sport → return to performance).
</summary>

<summary>
This is the National Athletic Trainers' Association (NATA) Position Statement on conservative management and prevention of ankle sprains in athletes, published in the Journal of Athletic Training (2013;48(4):528-545). The document provides evidence-based recommendations for athletic trainers and allied health professionals.

Key background: An estimated 28,000 ankle injuries occur daily in the US, with ankle sprains accounting for up to 45% of all athletic injuries. The highest incidence rates are in field hockey, volleyball, football, and basketball. The only consistent risk factor identified across studies is a previous history of ankle sprain.

The position statement includes 37 graded recommendations across several categories:

**Diagnosis (Recommendations 1-13):** Patient history, mechanism of injury, and palpation provide insights into injured structures. Special tests (anterior drawer, inversion talar tilt) have better diagnostic accuracy 5 days post-injury than at 2 days. The Ottawa Ankle Rules are a valid clinical tool (Evidence A) for determining need for radiographs. MRI is reliable for detecting acute ligament tears (Evidence B). Stress radiography is unreliable for detecting acute ligamentous disruption.

**Treatment and Rehabilitation (Recommendations 14-25):** Cryotherapy, compression, and elevation are recommended for acute management (Evidence C). NSAIDs (oral or topical) reduce pain and improve short-term function (Evidence A). Functional rehabilitation is more effective than immobilization for grade I and II sprains (Evidence A). Grade III sprains should be immobilized for at least 10 days (Evidence B). Balance training reduces reinjury rates (Evidence A). Electrical stimulation may help minimize swelling. Thermotherapy should be avoided during acute/subacute phases.

**Return-to-Play (Recommendations 26-28):** Patient perception of function and functional performance testing should guide RTP decisions. The injured limb should achieve at least 80% of the uninjured limb's function. Athletes with prior ankle sprains should wear prophylactic supports (taping or bracing) for all practices and games (Evidence B).

**Prevention (Recommendations 29-31):** Multi-intervention programs focusing on balance and neuromuscular control lasting at least 3 months reduce ankle injury risk (Evidence A). Addressing leg muscle and hip strength may be preventive (Evidence C). Limited dorsiflexion ROM should be assessed and addressed.

**Special Considerations (Recommendations 32-37):** Syndesmotic ("high") ankle sprains require more conservative treatment than lateral sprains. Surgical fixation is indicated for mortise widening >2mm. Chronic ankle instability (CAI) involves mechanical and functional deficits that should be identified and addressed with specific interventions.

The literature review section provides detailed evidence on physical examination, imaging (including OARs, MRI, CT, ultrasound), management of lateral ankle sprains (RICE, cryotherapy, compression, electrical stimulation, NSAIDs, functional rehabilitation, therapeutic exercise, ROM exercises, and joint mobilization techniques).

To propose a weekly ankle-specific neuromuscular warm-up program for elite basketball teams, integrated into pre-training warm-up sessions.

**Key Epidemiological Data:**  
- Ankle joint injuries in sports account for 11%–17% of all injuries.  
- Elite players cover ~73 m·min⁻¹, ~3 m·min⁻¹ at high-speed running (>18 km/h), with ~4 accelerations/decelerations >2 m/s² per minute, ~0.2 jumps >3Gs per minute, and ~1.3 impacts >8Gs per minute.

**Proposed Exercises (9 exercises, performed as a circuit in pairs):**  
1. **Ankle Mobility (Figure 1):** Standing, one foot on a box with elastic band at floor height below the malleoli; active dorsiflexion, heel grounded. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
2. **Peroneal Muscles in CKC (Figure 2):** Foot half-on platform; touch floor with free side of foot (eccentric → concentric eversion). 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
3. **Tibialis Posterior in CKC (Figure 3):** Same setup but performing inversion movement. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
4. **Plantar Flexion in CKC on Airex (Figure 4):** One leg on Airex, knee bent 30°–70°, perform concentric plantar flexion and eccentric dorsiflexion. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
5. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 1 (Figure 5):** Stand on one foot on unstable platform (Pielaster); perform diagonal rotational patterns with a soft medicine ball. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
6. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 2 (Figure 6):** One foot on Pielaster; perform hip and upper body flexion to 90° with opposite leg extended (single-leg deadlift). Optional Mini Band between knees. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
7. **Lateral Movement (Figure 7):** Elastic band on hip secured to stable surface; perform two lateral steps at high speed against band resistance. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
8. **Footwork with Competitive Movement (Figure 8):** Two players 4.9 m apart; perform footwork on coordination ladder then sprint to a marked space (1.5 m on free-throw line). 2 sets of 3 reps, competitive.  
9. **Progression:** Include perturbations (teammate unbalancing) and simple decision-making.

**Practical Application:**  
The program is designed to be integrated into a typical competition week schedule as part of the regular team warm-up. A holistic approach is recommended, with coaches, strength coaches, medical staff, and players sharing responsibility.

**Conclusions:**  
This proposal provides an example of ankle joint neuromuscular exercises for pre-basketball warm-up. It offers physiotherapists and strength/conditioning professionals practical exercises and a weekly organization framework for elite professional basketball, aiding injury prevention strategies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Risk Factors for Lateral Ankle Sprain: A Literature Review ---
URL: https://scholars.direct/Articles/sports-medicine/aspm-3-026.php?jid=sports-medicine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a 2019 literature review by Correia and Torres (published in Archives of Sports Medicine, ISSN: 2578-6334) examining intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors for lateral ankle sprains. The authors searched MEDLINE on September 24, 2018, and included 42 studies in their review.

**Key Intrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Gender**: Women at higher risk (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures per Doherty et al. meta-analysis)
- **Age**: Higher risk in children compared to adolescents (2.84 vs. 1.94 per 1000 exposures), and adolescents compared to adults (1.94 vs. 0.72 per 1000 exposures)
- **BMI**: Greater BMI significantly related to ankle sprain, though height and weight individually are not clearly defined risk factors
- **Muscle Strength**: Decreased slow eccentric inversion strength increases incidence; lower pronator-to-supinator ratio is a risk factor; peroneus longus weakness increases risk; hip and core strength may reduce incidence
- **Previous Ankle Sprain**: Identified as one of the strongest risk factors for re-injury, both ipsilateral and contralateral
- **Balance/Proprioception**: Proprioceptive training and balance training reduce incidence of primary and recurrent ankle sprains
- **Limb Dominance**: Inconclusive results
- **Foot Type/Anatomy**: No clear correlation found between foot type, joint laxity, anatomic alignment, or range of motion and ankle sprains

**Key Extrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Ankle Bracing/Taping**: Effective in reducing ankle sprain risk (64-69% reduction); braces and tapes are equally effective; bracing protects both mechanically and by improving proprioception
- **Shoe Type**: High top shoes reduce risk in basketball and football; specially designed swivel shoes may help
- **Sport Category**: Higher incidence in indoor, court, and team sports
- **Player Position**: May be a risk factor depending on sport-specific demands (e.g., blockers in volleyball)

**Conclusion**: Previous ankle sprain and external ankle support are the most clearly defined factors. Younger female athletes with high BMI may be at increased risk. The review found no correlation between muscle reaction time or anatomic foot type and ankle sprains. Further prospective studies are needed to reduce bias and uncertainty.
</summary>

This is a scientific article (a systematic review and meta-analysis) published in the journal *Sports* (MDPI) on March 28, 2025, titled "Risk Factors of Ankle Sprain in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." The study was conducted by Hoveidaei et al., involving researchers from multiple institutions in the US and Iran. 

**Purpose:** To identify and synthesize risk factors for ankle sprain injuries (ASIs) in soccer players, including gender, age, BMI, history of ASIs, and other factors.

**Methods:** A systematic literature search was conducted in October 2023 across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ProQuest. The review included 26 studies (randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies). Data were analyzed using Stata 17.

**Key Findings:**
- A history of previous ankle sprain is the most significant risk factor for future ASIs.
- BMI was identified as a risk factor in 3 out of 7 studies.
- Age and height were significant in only 1 out of 6 studies each.
- Gender and weight were not found to significantly affect ASI occurrence.
- Other factors identified (but not meta-analyzed due to heterogeneity) included playing surface, joint laxity, muscle weakness, match congestion, strength asymmetries, ground reaction forces, balance maintenance, skill level, and playing position.
- Soccer is associated with 13 to 35 injuries per 1000 player-hours, with approximately 77% of ankle injuries attributed to ASIs.
- Neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up routines can lower acute lower extremity injury incidence by 29-60%.

**Conclusions:** The research highlights the importance of previous ankle sprains and playing surface quality as key risk factors, providing insights for prevention strategies.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article titled "The epidemiology, evaluation, and assessment of lateral ankle sprains in athletes" by Cavazos GJ Jr. and Harkless LB, published May 26, 2021 in the Journal of Sports Medicine and Therapy.

**Key Findings on Epidemiology:**
- Approximately 30,000 ankle injuries occur daily in the US, with over 3 million annually at a rate of 2.15/1,000 persons
- Ankle sprains account for 50% of all sports injuries; 45% of all sports-related injuries involve the ankle
- 85% of ankle sprains are inversion type; the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is affected 65% of the time
- True incidence is underestimated as fewer than half of individuals seek medical attention
- Economic burden is close to $4 billion annually
- 40% of ankle sprains are misdiagnosed or poorly treated, leading to chronic pain and disability
- Up to 80% of LAS are inversion type; 75% lead to recurrence and instability
- Highest incidence in ages 15-19 (7.2 per 1000 person-years)
- Most common in basketball (41.1%), football (9.3%), and soccer (7.9%)
- Re-injury rates range from 3% to 73% depending on sport
- 40% develop chronic ankle instability after first-time sprain; 55-72% have residual symptoms after 6 months
- Over 50% of adults with ankle osteoarthritis report history of sport-related ankle injury

**Anatomy & Mechanism:**
The lateral collateral ligaments include the ATFL, calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), and posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL). Inversion injury occurs with supination (plantarflexion, inversion, internal rotation) coupled with external rotation of the lower leg. The ATFL is the weakest and first ligament injured. Isolated ATFL injury occurs in 66% of LAS; ATFL and CFL rupture simultaneously 20% of the time.

**Grading Systems:**
Multiple classification systems exist (Karlsson, O'Donahue, Leach, AMA), ranging from Grade I (microscopic stretch/microtear) to Grade III (complete rupture). Recovery timelines range from 1-2 weeks (Grade I) to 6-10 weeks (Grade III).

**Clinical Evaluation:**
Emphasizes thorough history, physical examination, Ottawa Ankle Rules for radiography indication, and special tests (anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, cotton test, squeeze test). Alternative imaging includes diagnostic ultrasonography (sensitivity 92%, specificity 64%) and MRI (gold standard, sensitivity 92-100%, specificity 100%).

**Prevention & Treatment:**
POLICE protocol (Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation) preferred over traditional RICE. Emphasizes early mobilization, functional rehabilitation, proprioceptive training, and external supportive devices. Return to sport averages 12 days, with 44% of intercollegiate athletes returning in less than 24 hours. The article advocates for an interprofessional team approach and cautions against premature return to sport.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability

**Key Results:**

This systematic review (published in the Journal of Athletic Training, 2008) examined whether balance and coordination training is clinically effective for preventing and treating lateral ankle sprains. The review addressed three clinical questions:

# Treatment of acute lateral ankle ligament rupture in the athlete: Conservative versus surgical treatment

* [Scott A. Lynch](https://pure.psu.edu/en/persons/scott-lynch/)
* , Per A.F.H. Renström

* [Department of Orthopaedics and Therapy Services](https://pure.psu.edu/en/organisations/department-of-orthopaedics-and-therapy-services/)
* [Division of Sports Medicine](https://pure.psu.edu/en/organisations/division-of-sports-medicine/)

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › peer-review

[190   Link opens in a new tab](https://www.scopus.com/pages/publications/0032925618#tab=citedBy)  Scopus citations

## Abstract

Acute lateral ankle ligament sprains are common in young athletes (15 to 35 years of age). Diagnostic and treatment protocols vary. Therapies range from cast immobilisation or acute surgical repair to functional rehabilitation. The lateral ligament complex includes 3 capsular ligaments: the anterior tibiofibular (ATFL), calcaneofibular (CFL) and posterior talofibular (PTFL) ligaments. Injuries typically occur during plantar flexion and inversion; the ATFL is most commonly torn. The CFL and the PTFL can also be injured and, after severe inversion, subtalar joint ligaments are also affected. Commonly, an athlete with a lateral ankle ligament sprain reports having 'rolled over' the outside of their ankle. The entire ankle and foot must be examined to ensure there are no other injuries. Clinical stability tests for ligamentous disruption include the anterior drawer test of ATFL function and inversion tilt test of both ATFL and CFL function. Radiographs may rule out treatable fractures in severe injuries or when pain or tenderness are not associated with lateral ligaments. Stress radiographs do not affect treatment. Ankle sprains are classified from grades I to III (mild, moderate or severe), Grade I and II injuries recover quickly with nonoperative management. A nonoperative 'functional treatment' programme includes immediate use of RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), a short period of immobilisation and protection with a tape or bandage, and early range of motion, weight-bearing and neuromuscular training exercises. Proprioceptive training on a tilt board after 3 to 4 weeks helps improve balance and neuromuscular control of the ankle. Treatment for grade III injuries is more controversial. A comprehensive literature evaluation and meta-analysis showed that early functional treatment provided the fastest recovery of ankle mobility and earliest return to work and physical activity without affecting late mechanical stability. Functional treatment was complication-free, whereas surgery had serious, though infrequent, complications. Functional treatment produced no more sequelae than casting with or without surgical repair. Secondary surgical repair, even years after an injury, has results comparable to those of primary repair, so even competitive athletes can receive initial conservative treatment. Sequelae of lateral ligament injuries are common. After conservative or surgical treatment, 10 to 30% of patients have chronic symptoms, including persistent synovitis or tendinitis, ankle stiffness, swelling, pain, muscle weakness and 'giving-way'. Well-designed physical therapy programmes usually reduce instability. For individuals with chronic instability refractory to conservative measures, surgery may be needed. Subtalar instability should be carefully evaluated when considering surgery.

args.summary:
This 1999 article from Sports Medicine (Vol. 27, Issue 1, pp. 61-71) by Scott A. Lynch and Per A.F.H. Renström reviews treatment approaches for acute lateral ankle ligament ruptures in athletes aged 15-35. The lateral ligament complex includes three ligaments (ATFL, CFL, PTFL), with injuries typically occurring during plantar flexion and inversion. Diagnosis involves the anterior drawer test, inversion tilt test, and radiographs to rule out fractures. Ankle sprains are classified Grades I-III.

For Grade I and II injuries, nonoperative functional treatment (RICE protocol, short immobilization, early ROM and weight-bearing, neuromuscular training, proprioceptive training on a tilt board after 3-4 weeks) leads to quick recovery. For Grade III injuries, evidence from meta-analysis shows early functional treatment provides the fastest recovery and return to activity without compromising mechanical stability. Functional treatment was complication-free, while surgery carried infrequent but serious complications. Secondary surgical repair performed years after injury has comparable results to primary repair, supporting initial conservative treatment even for competitive athletes. Chronic symptoms (synovitis, tendinitis, stiffness, swelling, pain, weakness, giving-way) occur in 10-30% of patients regardless of treatment. Physical therapy typically reduces instability, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

# [Foot & Ankle](https://www.ankleinfo.net)

Current Concepts & Evidence Base



## Ankle Instability

Acute Instability

​

The ATFL, which is the weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments, is involved in the majority of lateral ankle sprains; the CFL is involved in 50% to 75% of such injuries and the PTFL in less than 10%.

Clinical assessment is based on the history of inversion and internal rotation of the foot. Examination is focussed on excluding the fracture and generally include swelling and localised tenderness on palpation.

Imaging starts from plain radiographs of the ankle in acute injuries.

​

Treatment

​

First line of treatment is conservative and includes a combination of an ankle brace (2 – 4 weeks), appropriate pain management, rest, ice, compression, elevation and activity modification.

​

After the initial acute phase, functional recovery involves ROM exercises, strengthening, proprioception, and activity-specific training.

​

Majority of patients achieve a satisfactory resolution of symptoms in about 3 to 6 months.

​

Adequately treated ankle sprains have been shown to lead to a better outcome than an untreated sprain.

An RCT by Bleakley et al. compared an accelerated intervention including early therapeutic exercise and a standard regime with protection, rest, ice, compression, and elevation and showed that an accelerated exercise protocol during the first week after an ankle sprain improved ankle function.

​

Another RCT by Petrella et al. suggested that peri-articular injections of hyaluronic acid combined with standard care in acute grade I or II sprains were associated with reduced pain, more rapid return to sports, fewer recurrent ankle sprains and fewer adverse events for up to 24 months after injury when compared with a placebo injection of normal saline solution combined with standard care.

​

An RCT by Hupperets et al. showed that the use of a proprioceptive training programme after standard care of an ankle sprain was effective in the prevention of recurrent episodes in athletes who had sustained an acute sports-related ankle sprain.

​

In a study by Lamb et al. it was found that immobilisation in a below-knee cast or an Aircast boot for 10 days resulted in faster resolution of pain than if a patient was only given a tubular compression bandage.

​

In an RCT by Cooke et al. showed that a below-knee cast and an Aircast brace offered cost-effective alternatives to a simple tubular bandage in cases of acute severe ankle sprain; however, there were no differences in long-term outcome, therefore the treating doctor should consider the likely compliance and acceptability to patients when choosing a brace.

​

Proprioceptive training, compared with no intervention, is considered an effective way to reduce the rate of ankle sprains among male soccer players In a meta-analysis of RCTs, functional management was found to be associated with a higher percentage of patients returning to sports and higher rates of patient satisfaction compared to immobilisation with functional management for acute sprains.

​

In a systematic review of nine studies on functional management by Kerkhoffs, lace-up supports were found most effective, tapes were associated with skin irritation and elastic bandages were found least effective form of management.

​

A Cochrane review comparing surgical versus non-surgical management of acute ankle sprains found that all available trials had methodological flaws and it was not possible to demonstrate a clearly superior management option based on the available pooled data.

An RCT comparing surgery with functional management, found statistically significant differences in favour of surgical intervention in respect of pain, giving way and recurrent sprains at follow-up.

​

​

​

Chronic Instability

​

Chronic ankle instability refers to repeated episodes of instability that result in recurrent ankle sprains.

About 20% of acute ankle sprain patients develop chronic ankle instability. The failure of functional rehabilitation after acute ankle sprain leads to the development of chronic ankle instability. Patients usually complain of persistent pain and recurrent episodes of ‘giving way’.

​

Chronic ankle instability can be functional or mechanical. Functional instability depends on the patient-generated reports or complaints that could be accompanied by clinical laxity while mechanical instability can be identified by physical examination.

Other co-existent deformities including hindfoot varus, plantar flexion of the first ray, midfoot cavus, and generalised laxity may also contribute. Ligamentous laxity is more easily noticeable in chronic instability because of lesser amount of pain.

​

Imaging

​

MRI is considered a useful modality to show associated pathologies, such as chondral injury, occult fractures, bone bruising, peri-articular tendon tears, degeneration, sinus tarsi injury, and impingement syndrome. The main signs of ligament injury on MRI scans are ligament swelling, discontinuity, a lax or wavy ligament, and non-visualisation.

​

Treatment

​

Differentiation between functional and anatomical ankle instability is essential to guide an appropriate treatment.

The usual indication for surgery in chronic instability is a failure of conservative management and persistent symptoms. 

Surgical techniques include anatomical and non-anatomical repairs.

Anatomical repairs aim to restore normal anatomy and joint mechanics and seek to maintain movement of the ankle and subtalar joints.

However, the injured and attenuated ligament may not permit this type of repair.

​

The most commonly performed anatomical repair is the Broström-Gould repair that implies mid-substance imbrication and suture of the ruptured ends of the ligament augmented with the mobilised lateral portion of the extensor retinaculum, attached to the fibula after imbrication of the ATFL and the CFL.

​

Augmentation by internal brace system is becoming increasingly popular especially in revision case and high risk patients for failure (hypermobility, elite sportsmen). Failure of a standard repair usually occurs at the ligament to suture interface. Internal brace significantly decreases this potential failure, and hence aids in an accelerated rehab.

Non-anatomical repairs employ various types of local tendon graft in order to restrict movement, but without repair of the injured ligaments and result in altered biomechanics.

​

Non-anatomical repairs include Evans repair and Chrisman-Snook repair. The Evans method involves a distally-attached peroneus brevis graft through an oblique posteriosuperior drill hole in the distal fibula but does not replicate the ATFL or the CFL as it lies in a position in between these two ligaments. Chrisman and Snook described a weave intended to more closely approximate the ATFL and the CFL, incorporating a split peroneus brevis tendon graft in order to maintain some function of peroneus brevis.

​

A meta-analysis of seven RCTs was unable to reach a conclusion about the best surgical option for the management of chronic ankle instability. There was insufficient statistical significance and poor methodological quality of the randomised controlled trials that were available.

In one study with a small number of patients but with 26 years follow up, anatomic repairs revealed good and excellent results in 85% of patents.

​

Arthroscopic repairs are also in use and imply the reconstruction of autogenous plantaris tendon of the CFL and ATFL by using a 3-portal arthroscopic approach. For chronic ankle instability with no ligamentous repair, arthroscopic thermal capsular shrinkage is also recommended. Arthroscopy is also routinely performed as an adjunct to Broström-Gould procedure to look for and treat associated lesions.

​

The reported incidence of wound complications is about 1.6% after anatomic repair and about 4% after nonanatomic repair. Other complications include stiffness, recurrent instability, and nerve problems. Nerve-related problems account for 3.8% for anatomic repair and 9.7% for nonanatomic repair.

Long-standing instability and ligamentous laxity in addition to a cavovarus foot are among the risk factors for failure after surgery. Stiffness is common but can usually be tolerated. The loss of tibiotalar and subtalar motion can be caused by overtightening when performing nonanatomic tenodesis reconstruction. To treat subjective failure, physiotherapy is highly recommended. Late recurrent instability may be caused by minor chronic injuries while early recurrent instability may be caused by acute injury.

​

A systematic review by So et al. for standard repair reviewed 11 studies including 669 patients with a mean follow up of 8.4 years and revealed over 85% good functional results with a revision rate of 1.2%.

​

Another systematic review by Majeed et al. reviewed 10 studies including 343 elite athletes and showed a return to sports in 89% athletes at a mean of 16 weeks after surgical repair.

​

Augmentation with internal brace has been demonstrated to be at least as strong as the native ATFL in cadaveric models.

​

A retrospective review by Coetzee et al. compared the results of  augmentation repair with standard repair and reported that the former allowed an accelerated rehabilitation protocol with immediate weight-bearing and early range of motion.

​

A multicenter, prospective, RCT  by Kulwin et al. reported an average return to pre-injury activity levels 4.2 weeks earlier with brace than standard repair (12 vs 16 weeks).

​

However, Calder et al, in their study recommended that return to sport is not allowed until individuals can demonstrate 90% of pre-injury levels of strength, proprioception, and balance.

![Accelerated Rehab](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/2c5717_ffe0a88d0e5b4d7bb87b7f5d1245bdc4~mv2.png/v1/fill/w_805,h_474,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/Accelerated%20Rehab.png)

Summary

​

Ankle instability is common among general population and athletes.

​

First line of treatment is conservative with a combination of appropriate measures and functional rehab leading to satisfactory recovery in majority of individuals in about 6 months.

​

Persistent symptoms despite functional rehab warrant surgical repair, of which anatomic repair using Brostrom Gould technique remains the gold standard and provides good to excellent results.

​

Augmentation using internal brace provides excellent results and is recommended in high risks individuals and elite sports persons.

​

Physiotherapy rehab remains the key to achieve the intended outcomes.

​

​

​

args.summary:
This webpage from Foot & Ankle (ankleinfo.net) provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of ankle instability, covering both acute and chronic forms.

**Acute Ankle Instability:**
- The ATFL is involved in most lateral ankle sprains; the CFL in 50-75% and PTFL in less than 10%.
- First-line treatment is conservative: ankle brace (2-4 weeks), pain management, RICE, activity modification, followed by functional recovery (ROM, strengthening, proprioception). Most patients achieve satisfactory resolution in 3-6 months.
- Key RCT findings: Accelerated exercise protocols improve function (Bleakley et al.); hyaluronic acid injections reduce pain and recurrence (Petrella et al.); proprioceptive training prevents recurrence in athletes (Hupperets et al.); below-knee cast or Aircast boot for 10 days resolves pain faster than tubular bandage (Lamb et al.).
- A Cochrane review found no clearly superior surgical vs. non-surgical management option due to methodological flaws.

**Chronic Ankle Instability:**
- About 20% of acute sprain patients develop chronic instability, which can be functional or mechanical.
- MRI is useful for detecting associated pathologies (chondral injury, occult fractures, tendon tears, etc.).
- Surgical treatment is indicated after failure of conservative management. The Broström-Gould anatomical repair is the gold standard.
- Augmentation with an internal brace system is increasingly popular for revision cases and high-risk patients (hypermobility, elite athletes), enabling accelerated rehabilitation.
- Non-anatomical repairs (Evans, Chrisman-Snook) alter biomechanics.
- Systematic reviews: Over 85% good functional results with standard repair (So et al., mean 8.4 years follow-up); 89% return to sports in elite athletes (Majeed et al., mean 16 weeks).
- Internal brace augmentation allows earlier return to activity (12 vs 16 weeks per Kulwin et al. RCT).
- Complications: wound issues (1.6% anatomic, 4% non-anatomic), nerve problems (3.8% anatomic, 9.7% non-anatomic).

**Summary:** Conservative treatment is first-line with satisfactory recovery in ~6 months. Broström-Gould repair with internal brace augmentation is recommended for high-risk patients. Physiotherapy rehab is key to achieving intended outcomes.
