## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240)Abstract

### Background

Single-legged hop tests are commonly used functional performance measures that can capture limb asymmetries in patients after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Hop tests hold potential as predictive factors of self-reported knee function in individuals after ACL reconstruction.

### Hypothesis

Single-legged hop tests conducted preoperatively would not and 6 months after ACL reconstruction would predict self-reported knee function (International Knee Documentation Committee [IKDC] 2000) 1 year after ACL reconstruction.

### Study Design

Cohort study (prognosis); Level of evidence, 2.

### Methods

One hundred twenty patients who were treated with ACL reconstruction performed 4 single-legged hop tests preoperatively and 6 months after ACL reconstruction. Self-reported knee function within normal ranges was defined as IKDC 2000 scores greater than or equal to the age- and sex-specific normative 15th percentile score 1 year after surgery. Logistic regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of self-reported knee function within normal ranges. The area under the curve (AUC) from receiver operating characteristic curves was used as a measure of discriminative accuracy.

### Results

Eighty-five patients completed single-legged hop tests 6 months after surgery and the 1-year follow-up with 68 patients classified as having self-reported knee function within normal ranges 1 year after reconstruction. The crossover hop and 6-m timed hop limb symmetry index (LSI) 6 months after ACL reconstruction were the strongest individual predictors of self-reported knee function (odds ratio, 1.09 and 1.10) and the only 2 tests in which the confidence intervals of the discriminatory accuracy (AUC) were above 0.5 (AUC = 0.68). Patients with knee function below normal ranges were over 5 times more likely of having a 6-m timed hop LSI lower than the 88% cutoff than those with knee function within normal ranges. Patients with knee function within normal ranges were 4 times more likely to have a crossover hop LSI greater than the 95% cutoff than those with knee function below normal ranges. No preoperative single-legged hop test predicted self-reported knee function within normal ranges 1 year after ACL reconstruction (all _P_> .353).

### Conclusion

Single-legged hop tests conducted 6 months after ACL reconstruction can predict the likelihood of successful and unsuccessful outcome 1 year after ACL reconstruction. Patients demonstrating less than the 88% cutoff score on the 6-m timed hop test at 6 months may benefit from targeted training to improve limb symmetry in an attempt to normalize function. Patients with minimal side-to-side differences on the crossover hop test at 6 months possibly will have good knee function at 1 year if they continue with their current training regimen. Preoperative single-legged hop tests are not able to predict postoperative outcomes.

**Keywords:**anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, hop testing, self-report measure, knee function

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240)METHODS

### Patients

Between October 2006 and May 2009, 160 patients with a unilateral ACL rupture (mean, 54.6 days from injury; range, 8–279 days from injury) were included in this prospective international cohort study. Eighty patients (50%) were included from site A (Oslo) and 80 patients from site B (Delaware). Patients ranged in age from 15 to 54 years (mean, 26.0) and were regular participants in level I or II activities (≥50 h/y) before ACL rupture.[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R5) Patients were excluded if they had concomitant ligamentous injury, bilateral lower limb involvement, symptomatic meniscal injury, fracture, or full-thickness articular cartilage damage. The ACL rupture was confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging and ≥3-mm side-to-side difference[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R5) with a KT-1000 arthrometer (MedMetrics, San Diego, California).

Of the 160 patients included in this study, 37 (23.1%) chose to pursue nonoperative management. Three patients were lost to follow-up, and we were not able to determine if they had undergone ACL reconstruction. One hundred twenty subjects (75.0%) underwent reconstructive surgery and compose the target population in this study. The flow diagram for subject participation in this study is presented in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#F1). All patients gave informed consent at the time of inclusion. The study was approved by the ethical/human subjects committees at the Regional Ethics Committee for South-Eastern Norway and University of Delaware.

### Testing and Rehabilitation

All patients underwent initial rehabilitation to address acute impairments. Once patients had minimal knee effusion, no limitations in knee range of motion, a quadriceps side-to-side strength deficit less than 30%, and the ability to hop on the involved limb without subsequent pain or effusion, they were enrolled in a 10-session preoperative rehabilitation program.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R12) Preoperative rehabilitation consisted of a progressive exercise training program emphasizing aggressive quadriceps strengthening and specialized perturbation training to restore muscle strength and appropriate neuromuscular responses. Muscle strength training involved the use of high loads and low repetitions as recommended by the American College of Sports Medicine position stand on progression models in resistance training for healthy adults[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R45) for nonweightbearing (open chain) and weightbearing (closed chain) quadriceps strengthening exercises.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R10),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R20) Perturbation training was administered according to the protocol outlined by Fitzgerald et al.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R12)

Upon completion of the preoperative rehabilitation phase, patients performed 4 single-legged hop tests: the single hop for distance (single hop), crossover hop for distance (crossover hop), triple hop for distance (triple hop), and 6-meter timed hop (6-m timed hop) ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#F2)).[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R40) These 4 tests have demonstrated good test-retest reliability in normal, young adults[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R49) and in patients after ACL reconstruction.[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R46) The single hop for distance was performed with the patient standing on the leg to be tested, hopping as far as possible, and landing on the same leg. For the crossover hop for distance, patients stood on 1 leg, then hopped as far as possible forward 3 times while alternately crossing over a 15-cm marked strip on the floor. The total distance hopped forward was recorded. The triple hop for distance was performed with the patient standing on 1 leg and performing 3 consecutive hops as far as possible. The single hop, the crossover hop, and the triple hop for distance were considered successful if the landing was stable. To be considered a valid trial, the landing must be on 1 limb, under complete control of the patient. If the patient landed with early touchdown of the contralateral limb, had loss of balance, touched the wall, or had additional hops after landing, the hop was repeated. Patients were instructed to begin with the uninjured leg, with their lead toe behind a marked starting line. The hop distance was measured to the nearest centimeter from the starting line to the patient’s heel with a standard tape measure. For the 6-m timed hop, patients stood on 1 leg, then hopped as fast as possible over a marked distance of 6 meters. The time was recorded with a standard stopwatch. The stopwatch was started when the patient’s heel left the floor and stopped when the patient crossed the finish line. Measurements were recorded to the nearest 100th of a second. All single-legged hop tests were conducted by physical therapists who had undergone detailed training in the test procedures. In accordance with the respective clinic guidelines, no patients wore a knee brace at site A (Oslo), whereas all patients wore a functional knee brace at site B (Delaware). All other test procedures were similar at the 2 sites.

All patients (n = 120) underwent reconstructive surgery with a semitendinosus-gracilis autograft, bone–patellar tendon–bone autograft, or soft tissue allograft. After surgery, the same ACL reconstruction rehabilitation guidelines were followed for all patients.[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R32),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R47) Patients were systematically progressed through rehabilitation based on the clinical milestones outlined in the guidelines. They underwent the same 4 single-legged hop tests 6 months after surgery and completed the IKDC 2000[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R25) one year after surgery. The IKDC 2000 is a joint-specific outcome measure pertinent to a variety of knee conditions for assessing symptoms, function, and sports activity.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R25) The form contains 18 questions, in which the total scores are expressed as a percentage from 0% to 100%, with higher scores representing better knee function and less symptoms. The IKDC 2000 is a valid and reliable self-reported outcome measure.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R25)

### Data Management and Statistics

The single-legged hop scores were calculated as the average of 2 measured trials for each limb. The limb symmetry index (LSI) was expressed as a percentage of the averaged involved limb hop distances divided by the averaged uninvolved limb hop distances for each patient and each hop distance test. For the 6-m timed hop, LSI was expressed as the percentage of the averaged uninvolved limb hop time divided by the averaged involved limb hop time.

Normative data of the IKDC 2000 for men and women with no current or previous knee problems have been previously established.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R1) We operationally defined self-reported knee function within normal ranges as IKDC 2000 scores greater than or equal to the subject-specific age- and sex-matched population 15th percentile, indicating 85% of the uninjured population would describe their knee within normal ranges. The 15th percentile from the normative data from uninjured individuals was chosen as the cutoff score to ensure that individuals who scored below the cutoff were different from what could be considered a normal variation in IKDC scores.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R16)

The LSI from preoperative and 6-month postoperative single-legged hop tests was used to predict self-reported knee function at 1 year. Comparisons between patients from each site and individuals with knee function within normal ranges and below normal ranges were made using χ 2 tests for nominal data and the Mann-Whitney _U_ test for continuous data. Univariate logistic regression was performed to evaluate if hop test LSI preoperatively and 6 months postoperatively predicted knee function within normal ranges 1 year postoperatively. The resulting odds ratios were presented, representing the increase in odds of having self-reported knee function within normal ranges for every 1-point increase in LSI. Interaction was assessed in a logistic regression model that included hop test LSI, site, and a multiplicative interaction term. No interaction of site and hop test LSI preoperatively (all _P_> .11) and 6 months postoperatively (all _P_> .13) was found in predicting knee function within normal ranges 1 year postoperatively, and therefore data from both sites were merged for further analysis. The area under the curve (AUC) from receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to determine the overall discriminative accuracy of each single-legged hop test.[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R18) Optimal cutoff scores for each single-legged hop test were determined by the hop LSI with the highest product of sensitivity and specificity. The corresponding sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio, and negative likelihood ratio were reported. Sensitivity was reported as the percentage of patients with hop LSI below the cutoff value correctly identified as having knee function below normal ranges and specificity as the percentage of patients with hop LSI above the cutoff value correctly identified as having knee function within normal ranges. A priori a level of 0.05 was set for all analyses. All analyses were conducted in PASW version 18 (SPSS, Inc, an IBM Company, Chicago, Illinois).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240)RESULTS

Of the 120 patients who underwent ACL reconstruction, 101 (84%) performed preoperative hop testing, 100 (83%) completed 6-month hop testing, and 96 (80%) participated in 1-year on-site testing, but 3 patients did not complete IKDC 2000 ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#F1)). Reasons for patients not completing hop testing were meniscal injury, poor dynamic stability, marked joint effusion, marked quadriceps weakness, soft tissue injury, pregnancy, rupture of the ACL graft, missed appointment, or relocated out of the area ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#F1)). No differences were found in IKDC 2000 scores between those who hopped and those who did not hop preoperatively (_P_ = .357) or 6 months after ACL reconstruction (_P_ = .858). Six months after ACL reconstruction, the mean (SD) IKDC 2000 score was 83.0 (12.9). One year after ACL reconstruction, the mean (SD) IKDC 2000 score was 90.8 (11.1).

Seventy-nine patients completed both preoperative single-legged hop tests and the 1-year follow-up. Sixty-one (77.2%) were classified as having self-reported knee function within normal ranges 1 year after reconstruction, meaning that their IKDC 2000 score was above the age- and sex-specific 15th percentile score of an uninjured population. The remaining 18 (22.8%) were classified as having knee function below normal ranges. There were no significant differences in preoperative hop test LSI between patients with IKDC 2000 scores within and below normal ranges ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T1)). None of the preoperative single-legged hop tests significantly predicted self-reported knee function 1 year after ACL reconstruction ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T2)).

Eighty-five (70.8%) patients completed both single-legged hop tests 6 months after surgery and the 1-year follow-up. Sixty-eight (80.0%) were classified as having self-reported knee function within normal ranges 1 year after reconstruction. No significant differences were seen in sex, preinjury activity level, or median age between patients with knee function within and below normal ranges ([Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T3)).

Patients who were classified as having self-reported knee function within normal ranges at the 1-year follow-up had significantly higher crossover hop and 6-m timed hop symmetry indexes 6 months after surgery ([Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T4)). The single hop, crossover hop, triple hop, and the 6-m timed hop 6 months after ACL reconstruction significantly predicted self-reported knee function 1 year after ACL reconstruction ([Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T5)). Of the 4 single-legged hop tests, the 6-m timed hop and the crossover hop were the strongest individual predictors of self-reported knee function (odds ratio [OR] = 1.10 for 6-m timed hop and 1.09 for crossover hop) and had the highest discriminative accuracy (AUC = 0.68 for 6-m timed hop and crossover hop). The discriminative accuracy (AUC), optimum cutoff scores, and corresponding sensitivity and specificity for the 4 individual single-legged hop tests are shown in [Tables 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T4) and [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T6). The optimal cutoff for the 6-m timed hop was 87.7% LSI with a sensitivity of 53%, specificity of 90%, and positive likelihood ratio of 5.14. The optimal cutoff for the crossover hop was 94.9% LSI with a sensitivity of 88%, specificity of 47%, and negative likelihood ratio of 0.25.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240)DISCUSSION

The purpose of this investigation was to determine if preoperative and postoperative single-legged hop tests predict self-reported knee function 1 year after ACL reconstruction. Preoperative hop tests did not significantly predict self-reported knee function 1 year after ACL reconstruction. However, hop tests conducted 6 months postoperatively statistically significantly predicted self-reported knee function (_P_< .02). Of the 4 hop tests, the 6-m timed hop and the crossover hop were the best predictors and the only 2 tests in which the confidence intervals of the discriminatory accuracy (AUC) were above 0.5. With a specificity of 90% ([Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T6)), the 6-m timed hop test was the most useful test for identifying patients with self-reported knee function below normal ranges at 1 year. The crossover hop test had a sensitivity of 88% ([Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#T6)) and was thus the test that most accurately identified patients with knee function within normal ranges. These results have significant implications for the clinical management of patients after ACL reconstruction as the ease of application of these hop tests allows for a practical method to determine the need for directed interventions to restore medium-term knee function.

In the current study, the 6-m timed hop was the strongest independent predictor and had the highest discriminatory accuracy. Patients with knee function below normal ranges were more than 5 times more likely to have 6-m timed hop LSI lower than 88% at 6 months than those with knee function within normal ranges. Previous work by Fitzgerald et al[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R11) has shown that the 6-m timed hop along with other variables can identify those with poor dynamic knee stability from those with good knee stability early after ACL injury. In those individuals with good dynamic knee stability, this test can also discriminate between those who did not successfully return to high-level sports from those who did.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R11) The 6-m timed hop, the least demanding hop,[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R23),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R46) can effectively challenge neuromuscular control in patients who have deficits in limb-to-limb differences. These asymmetries strongly predict those who will have knee function below normal ranges at 1 year. Limb asymmetries may be the result of underlying impairments, such as quadriceps weakness,[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R26),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R53) that may contribute to low hop performance and should be identified and corrected. In addition, limb asymmetries in athletes may result in suboptimal performance on the playing field and are linked with an increased risk of a second ACL injury.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R22),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R38),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R43) Sports-specific activities are more challenging than landing from a planned hop in a controlled environment, and thus the deficits seen in single-legged hop performance may be magnified in sports-specific activities, potentially predisposing the ipsilateral or contralateral knee to injury. Our data suggest that patients demonstrating an LSI less than 88% on a 6-m timed hop test may benefit from continued rehabilitation to address impairments and functional performance in an attempt to normalize function.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R35),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R42) Restoration of symmetrical function between limbs remains an important goal of postoperative rehabilitation, and limb asymmetry for all patients remains a risk for poor knee function.

The crossover hop predicted knee function within normal ranges, with similar predictive ability and discriminatory accuracy as the 6-m timed hop. Patients with knee function within normal ranges were 4 times more likely to have crossover hop LSI greater than 95% than those with knee function below normal ranges. The crossover hop is the most demanding hop test as it imposes forces in frontal and transverse planes, combined with multiple hops in the sagittal plane. Side-to-side differences are minimized in these patients, likely indicating superior neuromuscular control, therefore increasing the probability of knee function within normal ranges at 1 year. These patients appear to have improved their ability to generate and attenuate forces on the involved limb.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R35),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R37) Furthermore, patients with high limb symmetry after ACL reconstruction favor the involved limb less during functional activities, are more confident in its function, move more symmetrically, and are more likely to attempt full competition sports.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R3),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R31) Patients with minimal side-to-side differences on the crossover hop test at 6 months possibly will have good knee function at 1 year if they continue with their current training regimen.

The timing of hop testing affects prediction models. Conducting hop tests 6 months after ACL reconstruction is appropriate for predictive purposes. The ability to predict knee function is better after a period of rehabilitation than acutely after injury or surgery.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R9),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R19) Six months after surgery is a typical time point in which patients begin to transition to sports or preinjury activities,[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R30) so administering hop testing at this time point provides clinicians valuable information relevant to patients’ current function, their progress during rehabilitation and the necessity for additional rehabilitation, and their readiness to return to sporting activities.

Self-reported measures are frequently used as an outcome variable for knee function.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R8),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R29),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R51) Patient demographics, health behaviors, concomitant injuries, meniscal surgery, and knee extension range-of-motion loss have been identified as predictors of self-reported knee function.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R21),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R29),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R44) Lower knee function based on self-report outcomes after ACL reconstruction has been associated with lower patient satisfaction and fear of reinjury.[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R28),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R31) Impaired medium-term self-reported knee function was predictive of symptomatic radiographic knee osteoarthritis 10 to 15 years after reconstruction.[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R41) Being able to ascertain after ACL surgery those patients who will more likely have knee function below normal ranges highlights the importance of identifying modifiable predictive factors, such as the 6-m timed hop LSI, that can be readily administered by clinicians to develop targeted interventions to potentially improve knee function, increase patient satisfaction, and reduce the risk of symptomatic arthritis.

Preoperative hop testing was not predictive of postoperative knee function. Eitzen et al[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R8) found that neither the preoperative triple nor the stair hop test was predictive of knee function 2 years after reconstruction. The LSI after preoperative rehabilitation does not delineate between those who will have IKDC 2000 scores within normal ranges compared with those with scores below normal ranges 1 year after surgery. The median LSI for all hop tests preoperatively was greater than 93% after preoperative neuromuscular rehabilitation, indicating as a group, patients were able to achieve adequate limb symmetry in all 4 hops. Although prediction is better after rehabilitation than before rehabilitation, the ACL reconstruction is a “game-changer,” and the passive stability it provides likely makes the preoperative functional hop performance irrelevant to outcome after ACL reconstruction.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R34),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R48) Although preoperative impairments, such as quadriceps weakness and knee extension range of motion, can influence knee function after reconstruction,[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R8),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R50) preoperative hop performance does not predict postoperative knee function.

Furthermore, in patients who are treated nonoperatively, hop tests provide a different assessment. Fitzgerald et al[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R11) found that the 6-m timed hop test along with other measures can predict return to previous activity level in the short term. In a prospective cohort study in nonoperatively treated individuals with ACL injury, Grindem et al,[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R16) using a similar design and methodology of the current study, reported that only the single-hop test significantly predicted self-reported knee after 1 year. Therefore, the effect of a stabilization procedure such as ACL reconstruction may affect which hop tests predict knee function.

### Limitations

Many factors may contribute to the failure to achieve self-reported knee function within normal ranges. Our group was young and active and may only be generalizable to this physically active age population. This study had some incomplete data. Some patients did not meet the minimal criteria for allowing hop testing (weakness, effusion, recurrent instability) at each time period. The results can only be generalized to those with isolated ACL injuries or asymptomatic concomitant injuries and cannot be generalized to individuals with symptomatic concomitant injuries. The hop test battery was administered in the same fashion each session[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R11),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R40) and may not be generalized to different hop test paradigms. A portion of patients did not complete either 6-month or 1-year testing, reducing the participants available for analysis.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240)CONCLUSION

Preoperative hop tests are not predictive of knee function after ACL reconstruction. Hop tests are clinically useful in predicting future outcomes[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3462240#R16) as individual hop tests 6 months after ACL reconstruction can predict who will have knee function within or below normal ranges in the medium term (1 year after ACL reconstruction). These tests have considerable implications on clinical decision making on future knee function as they can be used to inform the clinician and patient about the patient’s likely prognosis and the development of directed rehabilitation to address hop limb asymmetries to promote normal knee function.

args.summary:
This scientific article, published in the American Journal of Sports Medicine (2012), investigates whether single-legged hop tests can predict self-reported knee function one year after Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) reconstruction. 

**Study Design:** Cohort study (prognosis), Level of evidence 2.

**Methods:** 120 patients who underwent ACL reconstruction performed four single-legged hop tests (single hop, crossover hop, triple hop, and 6-meter timed hop) preoperatively and at 6 months post-surgery. Self-reported knee function was measured using the IKDC 2000 score at 1 year post-surgery, with "within normal ranges" defined as scores above the age- and sex-specific 15th percentile of normative data. Logistic regression and ROC curve analyses were used to identify predictors.

**Key Results:** 85 patients completed both 6-month and 1-year follow-ups. 68 (80%) were classified as having knee function within normal ranges at 1 year.

- **Preoperative hop tests:** Did NOT predict self-reported knee function at 1 year (all P > .353).
- **6-month postoperative hop tests:** Significantly predicted self-reported knee function at 1 year.
  - The **crossover hop** (odds ratio 1.09) and **6-meter timed hop** (odds ratio 1.10) were the strongest individual predictors, with the highest discriminative accuracy (AUC = 0.68 for both).
  - **6-meter timed hop cutoff (88% LSI):** Specificity of 90%. Patients with knee function below normal ranges were >5 times more likely to have a 6-m timed hop LSI below 88%.
  - **Crossover hop cutoff (95% LSI):** Sensitivity of 88%. Patients with knee function within normal ranges were 4 times more likely to have a crossover hop LSI above 95%.

**Conclusion:** Single-legged hop tests conducted 6 months after ACL reconstruction can predict the likelihood of successful or unsuccessful outcome at 1 year. The 6-m timed hop is best for identifying those at risk of poor function (high specificity), while the crossover hop is best for identifying those likely to have good function (high sensitivity). Preoperative hop tests are not predictive. These tests provide clinicians with a practical method to identify patients who may need continued rehabilitation to address limb asymmetries.

--- SOURCE 1: Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle Sprain: a systematic review ---
URL: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586334

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in *Annals of Medicine* (2025, Volume 57, Issue 1) by Jiang et al. from Ningbo University, University of Auckland, and University of Essex, titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The review investigates the factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries in athletic populations. Up to 74% of patients have persistent symptoms, and re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports, with nearly 40% developing chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may be due to premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024522798). Quality assessment used the Downs and Black checklist. Inclusion criteria required human subjects, RTS as a primary outcome, biomechanical parameters, and quality scores ≥50%.

**Results:** Twenty papers were included (mean quality score 75.36±10.40%; 11 RCTs, 7 prospective studies, 3 questionnaires). Studies were divided into four categories: (1) rehabilitation measures, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and RTS time.

**Rehabilitation interventions identified:** Electrotherapy (high-voltage pulsed current, noninvasive interactive nerve stimulation), balanced intervention approach (active video gaming), joint injection (hyaluronic acid), functional movement approach (neuromuscular training, exercise therapy), ligament fixation/protection (immobilization 4-12 weeks), and combination approaches (ultrasound + cold therapy, electrical muscle stimulation + isometric exercise).

**Key findings:** The RTS process is multifactorial, influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. No standard paradigm for RTS rehabilitation currently exists. The review identified that RTS should be viewed as a continuous process (not a single event), with the RTS continuum comprising "return to participation," "return to sport," and "return to performance." Outcome indicators were classified according to PAASS guidelines: pain severity, ankle impairments, athlete perception, sensorimotor control, and sport/functional performance.

**Conclusion:** The study identified the procedure and timeline of RTS for LAS, providing theoretical basis, clinical implications, and decision-making guidance. The authors emphasize that isolated assessment methods may be counterproductive given the high recurrence rate, and a methodical decision-making process considering multiple factors is essential.
</summary>

No expert recommended using time from injury as a criterion for RTS readiness.

**Conclusion:** Practitioners should assess sport-specific movement (using hop tests), static balance, patient-reported outcomes, range of motion, and strength when determining RTS after LAS. However, prospective research is needed to establish evidence-based assessment batteries and threshold values that minimize recurrent LAS risk.

This is a clinical guideline published in Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine (2019) by the Chinese Society of Sports Medicine, providing consensus recommendations for the surgical management of Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability (CLAI). The guideline was developed by 14 physicians through systematic literature review of databases including PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Chinese databases, covering literature since 1980. Recommendations were graded using the GRADE approach (strong 1A to weak 2D).

**Key Recommendations:**
1. **Surgical Indications (2C):** Surgery suggested when patients have CLAI symptoms after 3-6 months of nonsurgical treatment, with positive physical exam findings (anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, tenderness) and confirmation via stress radiography or MRI.
2. **Osteochondral Lesions (OCLs) (2C):** Simultaneous surgical management of CLAI and OCLs of the talus or tibia is safe and recommended.
3. **Open vs. Arthroscopic Repair (1B):** Equivalent short-term functional outcomes; both procedures are recommended.
4. **Open vs. Arthroscopic Reconstruction (1C):** Equivalent short-term outcomes.
5. **Autograft vs. Allograft (1C):** Neither type of graft shows superiority; both are promising candidates.
6. **CFL Reconstruction (2C):** When both ATFL and CFL are ruptured with subtalar joint instability, reconstructing both ligaments is recommended.
7. **Rehabilitation (1C):** Early ROM (dorsiflexion) and partial weightbearing with a brace from day 2 post-surgery are recommended. For OCL patients with microfracture, early ROM but delayed weightbearing is advised.
8. **Return to Sports (1C):** Joint stability, muscle strength (90-100% of unaffected limb), and full ROM are important indicators.
9. **Outcome Assessment (1C):** Most commonly used measures are AOFAS score (68% of studies), Karlsson score (31.4%), VAS score, FAAM scale, talus tilt test, and anterior drawer stress radiography.

The guideline targets patients aged 16-60 years and will be revised every 5 years.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Treatment of acute lateral ankle ligament rupture in the athlete: Conservative versus surgical treatment - Penn State ---
URL: https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/treatment-of-acute-lateral-ankle-ligament-rupture-in-the-athlete-

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This 1999 article from Sports Medicine (Vol. 27, Issue 1, pp. 61-71) by Scott A. Lynch and Per A.F.H. Renström reviews treatment approaches for acute lateral ankle ligament ruptures in athletes aged 15-35. The lateral ligament complex includes three ligaments (ATFL, CFL, PTFL), with injuries typically occurring during plantar flexion and inversion. Diagnosis involves the anterior drawer test, inversion tilt test, and radiographs to rule out fractures. Ankle sprains are classified Grades I-III.

For Grade I and II injuries, nonoperative functional treatment (RICE protocol, short immobilization, early ROM and weight-bearing, neuromuscular training, proprioceptive training on a tilt board after 3-4 weeks) leads to quick recovery. For Grade III injuries, evidence from meta-analysis shows early functional treatment provides the fastest recovery and return to activity without compromising mechanical stability. Functional treatment was complication-free, while surgery carried infrequent but serious complications. Secondary surgical repair performed years after injury has comparable results to primary repair, supporting initial conservative treatment even for competitive athletes. Chronic symptoms (synovitis, tendinitis, stiffness, swelling, pain, weakness, giving-way) occur in 10-30% of patients regardless of treatment. Physical therapy typically reduces instability, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Acute lateral ankle ligament sprains are common in young athletes (15 to 35 years of age)., A comprehensive literature evaluation and meta-analysis showed that early functional treatment provided the fastest recovery of ankle mobility and earliest return to work and physical activity without affecting late mechanical stability., After conservative or surgical treatment, 10 to 30% of patients have chronic symptoms, including persistent synovitis or tendinitis, ankle stiffness, swelling, pain, muscle weakness and 'giving-way'., Secondary surgical repair, even years after an injury, has results comparable to those of primary repair, so even competitive athletes can receive initial conservative treatment.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Ankle Instability ---
URL: https://www.ankleinfo.net/ankle-instability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Foot & Ankle (ankleinfo.net) provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of ankle instability, covering both acute and chronic forms.

**Acute Ankle Instability:**
- The ATFL is involved in most lateral ankle sprains; the CFL in 50-75% and PTFL in less than 10%.
- First-line treatment is conservative: ankle brace (2-4 weeks), pain management, RICE, activity modification, followed by functional recovery (ROM, strengthening, proprioception). Most patients achieve satisfactory resolution in 3-6 months.
- Key RCT findings: Accelerated exercise protocols improve function (Bleakley et al.); hyaluronic acid injections reduce pain and recurrence (Petrella et al.); proprioceptive training prevents recurrence in athletes (Hupperets et al.); below-knee cast or Aircast boot for 10 days resolves pain faster than tubular bandage (Lamb et al.).
- A Cochrane review found no clearly superior surgical vs. non-surgical management option due to methodological flaws.

**Chronic Ankle Instability:**
- About 20% of acute sprain patients develop chronic instability, which can be functional or mechanical.
- MRI is useful for detecting associated pathologies (chondral injury, occult fractures, tendon tears, etc.).
- Surgical treatment is indicated after failure of conservative management. The Broström-Gould anatomical repair is the gold standard.
- Augmentation with an internal brace system is increasingly popular for revision cases and high-risk patients (hypermobility, elite athletes), enabling accelerated rehabilitation.
- Non-anatomical repairs (Evans, Chrisman-Snook) alter biomechanics.
- Systematic reviews: Over 85% good functional results with standard repair (So et al., mean 8.4 years follow-up); 89% return to sports in elite athletes (Majeed et al., mean 16 weeks).
- Internal brace augmentation allows earlier return to activity (12 vs 16 weeks per Kulwin et al. RCT).
- Complications: wound issues (1.6% anatomic, 4% non-anatomic), nerve problems (3.8% anatomic, 9.7% non-anatomic).

**Summary:** Conservative treatment is first-line with satisfactory recovery in ~6 months. Broström-Gould repair with internal brace augmentation is recommended for high-risk patients. Physiotherapy rehab is key to achieving intended outcomes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The ATFL, which is the weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments, is involved in the majority of lateral ankle sprains; the CFL is involved in 50% to 75% of such injuries and the PTFL in less than 10%.", "Adequately treated ankle sprains have been shown to lead to a better outcome than an untreated sprain.", "About 20% of acute ankle sprain patients develop chronic ankle instability.", "The most commonly performed anatomical repair is the Broström-Gould repair that implies mid-substance imbrication and suture of the ruptured ends of the ligament augmented with the mobilised lateral portion of the extensor retinaculum.", "Physiotherapy rehab remains the key to achieve the intended outcomes."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://advancedortho.org/selecting-the-right-treatment-option-for-ankle-instability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from OCC Advanced Orthopedics provides an educational overview of ankle instability, covering its causes, diagnosis, conservative treatments, and surgical options. Ankle instability often results from repeated ankle sprains or incomplete rehabilitation, leading to lengthened ligaments. Diagnosis involves physical examination and imaging showing excess range of motion, with an unstable ankle tilting 15-20 degrees (3-4 times that of a healthy ankle). Conservative treatments focus on strengthening outer ankle muscles, with braces, taping, and muscle development being effective for recreational patients. For competitive athletes or those unresponsive to conservative care, surgical options include anatomic reconstruction (shortening/tightening stretched ligaments, which preserves mobility and has a high success rate with shorter recovery) or non-anatomic ligament repair (using a tendon/graft for severely damaged ligaments, requiring larger incisions and longer recovery). Recovery involves immobilization for 2 weeks, a cast/boot for 2-4 weeks, physical therapy starting at 6 weeks, and transition to normal activities around 10 weeks. The page also features foot and ankle specialists Dr. Keith Jacobson, Dr. Alan Ng, and Dr. Scott Resig, and promotes related articles on foot and ankle conditions.
</summary>

"Pain, swelling, and tenderness in the joint – both during movement and while stationary – can be signs of possible ankle instability," says Dr. Alan Ng, Advanced Orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon. "If your ankle slips or turns frequently in athletic movements or while walking on uneven surfaces, it's a good idea to seek medical evaluation and treatment.", "Surgical treatments for ankle instability focus on the repair or replacement of damaged ankle ligaments," says foot and ankle surgeon Dr. Keith Jacobson. "The degree of damage within the ankle, the patient's weight and activity level, and the patient's ankle injury history all influence which surgical procedure is best suited for each patient.", An unstable ankle will tilt as much as 15-20 degrees (3-4 times the tilt of a healthy ankle)., Anatomic reconstruction is the shortening and tightening of a stretched ligament. Generally, anatomic reconstruction is the preferred method of correcting ankle instability. It is a simple procedure that preserves complete joint mobility, has a shorter recovery window, and a very high success rate.

SUMMARY:

This is a scientific review article titled "Chronic lateral ankle instability: current concepts and management," published in Arthroscopy and Orthopedic Sports Medicine (2025;12:54-63). The article, authored by Lim, Chun, Kim, and Lee from Korean medical institutions, provides a comprehensive overview of chronic ankle instability (CAI) as a common sequela of ankle sprains in physically active individuals and athletes. 

Key points covered include:
- **Etiology**: CAI is caused by mechanical laxity and functional deficits, leading to recurrent sprains and a "giving way" sensation.
- **Diagnosis**: Requires thorough history-taking, physical examination, and imaging, including evaluation for associated pathologies like subtalar instability and rotational ankle instability.
- **Conservative treatment**: Primary approach focusing on neuromuscular training, proprioceptive exercises, and functional rehabilitation to restore dynamic stability.
- **Surgical intervention**: Recommended for patients with persistent instability or significant mechanical laxity unresponsive to nonoperative management. Recent advances include arthroscopic repair and internal brace augmentation, providing improved stability and potential for earlier return to sports.
- **Athlete considerations**: Presents unique challenges due to high physical demands and need for timely return to play. Risk factor assessment, tailored rehabilitation, and surgical planning are crucial.
- **Future directions**: More studies needed on biologic augmentation, minimally invasive techniques, and return-to-sport protocols to further improve CAI management and long-term joint health.

The article includes 81 references covering epidemiology, biomechanics, diagnostics, conservative management, open and arthroscopic surgical techniques (including Broström-Gould procedure variants), suture tape augmentation, rehabilitation protocols, and prevention strategies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Recent advances in the management of chronic ankle instability ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11840320

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article from the Chinese Journal of Traumatology (2024) titled "Recent advances in the management of chronic ankle instability" by Yang, Wu, and Zhu from the Department of Sports Medicine, Huashan Hospital, Shanghai. The review provides a comprehensive overview of chronic ankle instability (CAI), covering its pathophysiology, epidemiology, clinical assessment, treatment, and rehabilitation.

**Key points:**

- **Definition & Classification:** CAI develops after acute ankle injury when the ankle fails to regain normal functional and mechanical stability, primarily due to inadequate healing of the ATFL and/or CFL. It is broadly classified as mechanical or functional instability, with the ATFL's superior fascicle (found to reside within the joint) playing a key role in microinstability.

- **Epidemiology:** Ankle sprains occur at ~7‰ in the general population, rising to 10%–30% in sports injuries. Overall CAI prevalence is ~25% after an ankle sprain. Peak incidence occurs in males aged 15–19 and females aged 10–14.

- **Mechanism:** Inversion ankle sprain is most common. The ATFL is the first ligament to rupture in >75% of acute sprains. Roughly 65%–80% of cases involve isolated ATFL injury, while 20% involve combined ATFL and CFL tears.

- **Diagnosis:** Physical examination (anterior drawer test, talar tilt test) combined with patient history is recommended. Stress ultrasound shows high sensitivity. MRI has diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of 1.0 and 0.9 for ATFL lesions. Ultrasound achieves 93.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity for ATFL tears.

- **Management:** Conservative treatment (NSAIDs, bracing, physiotherapy, proprioceptive training) is first-line for 2 months. About 20%–30% of patients fail conservative treatment and require surgery. Surgical options include anatomic repair (Broström technique, success rates 87%–95%) and non-anatomic reconstruction. Anatomic repair shows superior functional outcomes and reduced risk of secondary osteoarthritis. Arthroscopic techniques have demonstrated favorable outcomes with improved AOFAS scores.

- **Risk factors:** Include ligamentous laxity (ATFL/CFL), reduced ankle dorsiflexion, neuromuscular control deficits, altered gait patterns, strength deficits (especially evertor muscles), increased BMI, youth, and sports activity.

- **Complications:** Nerve damage (6.2% rate), recurrent instability, stiffness. Postoperative rehabilitation emphasizes early mobilization, peroneal muscle strengthening, and proprioceptive training.

- **Medial ankle instability:** The deltoid ligament is involved in ~5% of ankle sprains, though 40% prevalence reported in arthroscopic surgery for lateral instability. Surgical repair is considered when conservative management fails.

The review concludes that accurate diagnosis requires combined assessment of history, examination, and imaging, and that treatment of CAI requires a multifaceted algorithm.
</summary>

URL: https://isakos.com/GlobalLink/Abstract/5705

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an ISAKOS 2023 Congress ePoster presentation titled "Outcomes Following Broström Repair with InternalBrace Ligament Augmentation vs. Broström Repair Alone for the Treatment of Anterior Talofibular Ligament Injury of the Lateral Ankle." 

**Background:** The Broström procedure is indicated for lateral ankle instability with ATFL injury. An augmented repair using nonabsorbable suture tape (InternalBrace, Arthrex) has demonstrated similar strength/stiffness to native ATFL, but clinical outcome comparisons are lacking.

**Methods:** Retrospective cohort study (January 2009-December 2017) of 104 patients aged 18-75 who underwent either Broström repair alone (Cohort A, n=55) or augmented Broström repair with suture tape (Cohort B, n=49) with minimum 2-year follow-up. Outcomes measured included FAAM (ADL and Sport), SF-12, Tegner activity scale, and patient satisfaction.

**Results:** Cohort A: median age 32, 95% follow-up at median 6 years (range 2-12). Cohort B: median age 34, 82% follow-up at median 4.5 years (range 2-8). No significant differences in age, sex, or baseline outcomes between cohorts. At follow-up, no significant differences in FAAM ADL (96% vs 98%, p=0.641), FAAM Sport (88% vs 92%, p=0.396), SF-12 PCS (55 vs 54, p=0.982), Tegner score (5 vs 5, p=0.683), or patient satisfaction (9 vs 9, p=0.938). SF-12 MCS was significantly higher in Cohort B (55.7 vs 57.3, p=0.03). Patient age was a significant independent predictor of lower postoperative FAAM ADL (p=0.009).

**Conclusion:** Both procedures demonstrated similar clinical outcomes. The suture tape augmentation offers advantages in strength and stiffness and allows earlier return to full weightbearing and quicker rehabilitation, so it should be considered for lateral ankle instability treatment.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from Sports Health (2012) by Thomas O. Clanton et al. reviewing evidence-based guidelines for return to play (RTP) in athletes following ankle injuries. The ankle is the most common injury site in 24 of 70 sports, with ankle sprains accounting for 76.7% of injuries and fractures 16.3%. Once an ankle sprain occurs, up to 80% suffer recurrent sprains, and up to 72% develop chronic instability. Recurrence most strongly correlates with premature return to sport and prior ankle injury.

The article documents four functional tests for assessing RTP readiness:

1. **Dorsiflexion Lunge Test** (Range of Motion): A weightbearing test where the foot is placed perpendicular to a wall and the knee lunges toward the wall. Less than 9-10 cm distance or less than 35°-38° tibial angle is considered restricted. Predictive of future injury in cricket and soccer.

2. **Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT)** (Balance and Proprioception): Determines unilateral balance and dynamic neuromuscular control by reaching maximally in defined directions with the contralateral leg. The Y Balance Test is an instrumented version testing anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral components. The SEBT is a predictive measure of lower extremity injury in high school basketball players.

3. **Agility T-Test** (Agility): Measures movement in multiple directions via a T-shaped course (10 yd each arm). Typical times for athletic adults: 8.9 to 13.5 seconds. High reliability demonstrated.

4. **Sargent/Vertical Jump Test** (Strength): Evaluates explosive power of the lower limb. The athlete squats and jumps upward into full extension. Efficiency index = weight (lb) × jump (in) / height (in).

Psychological factors are also highlighted: 5%-19% of athletes experience psychological distress following injury. Stress, loss of confidence, fear, and anxiety increase reinjury risk. Scoring systems include the Trait Sport Confidence Inventory, State Sport Confidence Inventory, and Injury-Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport Scale (I-PRRS).

--- SOURCE 1: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Risk Factors for Lateral Ankle Sprain: A Literature Review ---
URL: https://scholars.direct/Articles/sports-medicine/aspm-3-026.php?jid=sports-medicine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a 2019 literature review by Correia and Torres (published in Archives of Sports Medicine, ISSN: 2578-6334) examining intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors for lateral ankle sprains. The authors searched MEDLINE on September 24, 2018, and included 42 studies in their review.

**Key Intrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Gender**: Women at higher risk (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures per Doherty et al. meta-analysis)
- **Age**: Higher risk in children compared to adolescents (2.84 vs. 1.94 per 1000 exposures), and adolescents compared to adults (1.94 vs. 0.72 per 1000 exposures)
- **BMI**: Greater BMI significantly related to ankle sprain, though height and weight individually are not clearly defined risk factors
- **Muscle Strength**: Decreased slow eccentric inversion strength increases incidence; lower pronator-to-supinator ratio is a risk factor; peroneus longus weakness increases risk; hip and core strength may reduce incidence
- **Previous Ankle Sprain**: Identified as one of the strongest risk factors for re-injury, both ipsilateral and contralateral
- **Balance/Proprioception**: Proprioceptive training and balance training reduce incidence of primary and recurrent ankle sprains
- **Limb Dominance**: Inconclusive results
- **Foot Type/Anatomy**: No clear correlation found between foot type, joint laxity, anatomic alignment, or range of motion and ankle sprains

**Key Extrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Ankle Bracing/Taping**: Effective in reducing ankle sprain risk (64-69% reduction); braces and tapes are equally effective; bracing protects both mechanically and by improving proprioception
- **Shoe Type**: High top shoes reduce risk in basketball and football; specially designed swivel shoes may help
- **Sport Category**: Higher incidence in indoor, court, and team sports
- **Player Position**: May be a risk factor depending on sport-specific demands (e.g., blockers in volleyball)

**Conclusion**: Previous ankle sprain and external ankle support are the most clearly defined factors. Younger female athletes with high BMI may be at increased risk. The review found no correlation between muscle reaction time or anatomic foot type and ankle sprains. Further prospective studies are needed to reduce bias and uncertainty.
</summary>

"Most of the studies didn't show any significant difference in ankle sprain incidence between male and female. Nonetheless Doherty, et al. reviewed and meta-analyzed 181 prospective studies and found that women were at a higher risk of sustaining an ankle sprain, compared to men (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures).", "Recent studies reported previous ankle sprain as a risk factor for ipsilateral and contralateral future lateral ankle injury. Moreover, a systematic review identified and reviewed 26 articles... their results showed that previous ankle sprain is the most common injury resulting in a secondary sprain of the ipsilateral or contralateral ankle, which may be explained by neuromuscular factors.", "A recent systematic review concluded that athletes who wore braces had fewer ankle sprains (p < 0.05) and reduced the risk of sprains by 64%, either if they had or hadn't a previous sprain history.", "Most professionals working with athletes would rather prevent an injury than treat one. However, solid scientific evidence is needed to build structured and efficient prevention programs.", "Even though there are a few clearly defined risk factors for ankle sprain, further prospective studies are needed to properly evaluate each suggested risk factor for this injury, reducing the actual bias and uncertainty."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article (a systematic review and meta-analysis) published in the journal *Sports* (MDPI) on March 28, 2025, titled "Risk Factors of Ankle Sprain in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." The study was conducted by Hoveidaei et al., involving researchers from multiple institutions in the US and Iran. 

**Purpose:** To identify and synthesize risk factors for ankle sprain injuries (ASIs) in soccer players, including gender, age, BMI, history of ASIs, and other factors.

**Methods:** A systematic literature search was conducted in October 2023 across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ProQuest. The review included 26 studies (randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies). Data were analyzed using Stata 17.

**Key Findings:**
- A history of previous ankle sprain is the most significant risk factor for future ASIs.
- BMI was identified as a risk factor in 3 out of 7 studies.
- Age and height were significant in only 1 out of 6 studies each.
- Gender and weight were not found to significantly affect ASI occurrence.
- Other factors identified (but not meta-analyzed due to heterogeneity) included playing surface, joint laxity, muscle weakness, match congestion, strength asymmetries, ground reaction forces, balance maintenance, skill level, and playing position.
- Soccer is associated with 13 to 35 injuries per 1000 player-hours, with approximately 77% of ankle injuries attributed to ASIs.
- Neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up routines can lower acute lower extremity injury incidence by 29-60%.

**Conclusions:** The research highlights the importance of previous ankle sprains and playing surface quality as key risk factors, providing insights for prevention strategies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Lower Extremity Review (LER) Magazine, originally published in April 2011, provides a comprehensive analysis of the epidemiology and risk factors for ankle sprain. Authored by military medical professionals including CPT Brian R. Waterman, MD, and LTC Brett D. Owens, MD, the article notes that ankle sprain is one of the most common athletic injuries, accounting for 10% to 30% of single sport injuries and resulting in nearly 1.2 million healthcare visits annually, with costs up to $3.8 billion.

The article categorizes risk factors into two groups:

**Non-modifiable risk factors:**
- **Gender:** Female military cadets had an incidence rate 83% higher than males (96.4 vs. 52.7 per 1000 person-years), though results vary across studies. Female service members overall had 21% higher rates than males.
- **Age:** Peak incidence occurs during the second decade of life (ages 15-19 for males, 10-14 for females), with rates generally declining with age.
- **Previous ankle sprain:** Prior sprain significantly increases re-injury risk due to scar tissue formation (60% reduction in energy absorbing capacity) and persistent proprioceptive impairment.

**Modifiable risk factors:**
- **Weight and BMI:** Higher BMI is associated with increased ankle sprain risk, particularly in high school football players and military cadets.
- **Neuromuscular control/postural stability:** Pre-injury postural sway is a predictor of ankle sprain risk.
- **Sport:** Basketball (41.1%), football (9.3%), and soccer (7.9%) account for over half of all sports-related ankle sprains. Rugby has the highest incidence per 1000 person-hours (4.20).
- **Level of competition:** Games produce more injuries than practices (55% to 66% occur during games).

**Prevention interventions:** Prophylactic bracing can reduce risk by up to 50%, and neuromuscular/balance training programs yield 20% to 60% relative risk reduction, especially for those with prior ankle sprain history.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability

The trial was conducted in Turkey by Medipol University, running from April 1, 2024 to December 16, 2024, with the last update on March 25, 2025.

**Background:** Chronic ankle instability results from recurrent ankle sprains, with 58.5% of professional basketball and football athletes experiencing ankle sprains. Approximately three-quarters of patients have persistent symptoms 1.5-4 years post-injury. Both functional instability (proprioceptive/neuromuscular deficiencies) and mechanical instability (structural changes) contribute to CAI.

**Hypotheses:** 
- H0: Balance and DNS training do not positively affect functionality, balance, stabilization, proprioception, and performance.
- H1: Both positively affect outcomes; balance training is superior.
- H2: Both positively affect outcomes; DNS training is superior.

**Eligibility:** 36 participants aged 18-25, amateur athletes, non-smokers, with CAIT score ≤25, at least one ankle inversion sprain ≥12 months prior, and ≥2 episodes of giving way in the last 6 months. Exclusions include neurological diseases, vestibular dysfunction, recent lower extremity surgery/trauma, and head trauma.

**Interventions (3 arms):**
1. DNS Training: Exercises based on developmental kinesiology (supine, prone, oblique sitting, tripod, high kneeling, bear, squat, etc.), progressing from 1 set of 3 reps to 1 set of 20 reps, barefoot.
2. Balance Training: Multi-plane single limb challenges, jumping/landing, proprioceptive, and perturbation exercises, progressing from 1 set of 10 reps to 3 sets of 15 reps, barefoot.
3. Conventional Training: Education, electrotherapy, soft tissue massage, stretching, ROM, strengthening, and postural control exercises, same progression as balance training.

**Primary Outcomes:** Star Excursion Balance Test (dynamic balance/postural stability) and Balance Error Scoring System (BESS, static balance).

**Secondary Outcomes:** Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM), Cumberland Ankle Instability Questionnaire (CAIT), International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form, Manual Muscle Strength Test (hand dynamometer), Single Heel Lift Test, Joint Position Sense Test, Foot Lift Test, Blazepod Reaction Time, and Side Hop Test.
</summary>

DNS training aims to stimulate the natural movement control system in the brain to activate the body's stabilization system.

URL: https://www.clinmedjournals.org/articles/ijfa/international-journal-of-foot-and-ankle-ijfa-4-048.php?jid=ijfa

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Subtle Cavovarus Foot: A Missed Risk Factor for Chronic Foot and Ankle Pathologies

**Source:** Green B, Anne-Laure M, Leduc S, Marie-Lyne N (2020) Int J Foot Ankle 4:048. doi.org/10.23937/2643-3885/1710048

**Type:** Literature Review | Level of Evidence: Level IV | SORT: B

## Overview
The subtle cavovarus foot is a mild, often undiagnosed form of cavovarus deformity characterized by a high medial plantar arch and hindfoot varus. It is estimated to affect up to 25% of the population and is most commonly idiopathic. The condition alters foot biomechanics, leading to lateral foot overload, instability, and increased injury risk.

## Key Biomechanics
- Hyperactivity of peroneus longus induces plantarflexion of the first metatarsal (forefoot-driven deformity)
- Hindfoot cannot evert, leading to decreased mobility and increased rigidity
- Pressure concentrates on the lateral aspect of the foot, predisposing to chronic pathologies

## Clinical Evaluation
Three key physical exam tests:
1. **Peek-a-boo heel sign** – heel pad visible from anterior view
2. **Coleman block test** – determines if hindfoot varus is forefoot-driven (flexible, correctable)
3. **Silfverskiold test** – assesses for equinus/gastrocnemius tightness

Radiographic evaluation (secondary importance) includes Meary's angle, calcaneal pitch angle, Hibbs' angle, and medial arch height on lateral weight-bearing views.

## Plantar Pressure Measurement
Dynamic pedobarography is the ideal method for evaluation. Subtle cavovarus feet show:
- Decreased midfoot pressure in static stance
- Increased lateral foot and heel pressure during gait
- Lateral shift of center of pressure

## Associated Pathologies/Injuries
- **Lateral ankle sprains** – increased risk due to inadequate pronation and peroneal dysfunction
- **Chronic ankle instability** – altered gait with lateral shift of center of pressure; cavovarus deformity is predictive of operative failure if not corrected
- **Peroneal tendon pathologies** – tendinopathy and tears due to stretching of lateral soft tissues
- **Stress fractures** – especially 4th and 5th metatarsals and cuboid
- Other associations: plantar fasciitis, ankle arthritis, Morton's neuroma, hallux valgus, Achilles tendon pathology

## Treatment
**Conservative:** Flexible or semi-rigid orthotics to laterally offload the foot; posting of lateral forefoot with recession under the first ray; physiotherapy and gastrocnemius stretching.

**Surgical (for rigid/refractory cases):** Lateral displacement calcaneal osteotomy, plantar fascia release, dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal, peroneal tendon surgery, Achilles tendon lengthening. Return to athletics within 12 weeks post-operatively.

## Key Conclusion
Subtle cavovarus foot is a significant risk factor for chronic foot and ankle pathologies. Early identification and conservative management with appropriate foot orthotics favor safer return to sports and help prevent recurrence.
</summary>

This scientific article from Yonsei Medical Journal (2020) examines the diagnosis and surgical treatment of chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) in patients with subtle cavovarus foot deformity and a positive "peek-a-boo heel sign." The study retrospectively reviewed 15 patients (all male, mean age 25.7) who underwent a modified Broström procedure (MBP) combined with additional corrective osteotomies between August 2009 and April 2015, with a mean follow-up of 58.5 months.

Key findings: Cavovarus deformity is an anatomical risk factor for CLAI, but subtle deformity is often difficult to detect. The "peek-a-boo heel sign" (visible heel pad from the front when standing) helps identify subtle cavus deformity. Additional procedures performed included: calcaneal lateral closing wedge osteotomy (7 patients for fixed hindfoot varus), first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy (11 patients for plantarflexed first ray), and gastrocnemius recession (2 patients). Three patients underwent both calcaneal and metatarsal osteotomies.

Clinical outcomes improved significantly: VAS pain score improved from 5.5 to 1.7 (p=0.002), AOFAS ankle-hindfoot score improved from 61.0 to 85.3 (p<0.001), and Karlsson-Peterson score improved from 56.8 to 83.1 (p<0.001). No patient experienced recurrent ankle instability. Radiographically, talar tilt angle decreased from 12.3° to 5.6° (p=0.001), and talar anterior translation decreased from 7.9mm to 4.8mm (p=0.007). The Meary angle, arch height, and hindfoot alignment all improved significantly.

The authors conclude that simultaneous correction of cavovarus deformity with MBP for CLAI improves clinical outcomes and prevents recurrent instability, recommending comprehensive evaluation for subtle cavovarus deformity when treating CLAI patients.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from PM&R KnowledgeNow provides a comprehensive clinical overview of **Pes Cavus**, an orthopedic foot deformity characterized by an elevated longitudinal medial plantar arch (also known as "claw foot," "hollow foot," or "cavovarus foot"). It is authored by Mooyeon Oh-Park, MD, et al., originally published September 15, 2015, and last updated December 17, 2025.

**Key Points:**

- **Etiology & Epidemiology:** Pes cavus has four primary causes: neuromuscular, traumatic, congenital, and idiopathic. It occurs in approximately 8-15% of the general population. Severe cases are idiopathic (30%) or secondary to neurological causes (70%), most commonly Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease.
- **Pathoanatomy:** The deformity results from muscle imbalances (e.g., weak tibialis anterior overpowered by peroneus longus), leading to forefoot valgus, hindfoot varus, and clawing of the toes. In neuromuscular cases, the foot is initially flexible but becomes more rigid over time.
- **Associated Conditions:** Common complications include lateral foot pain/calluses, stress fractures (5th metatarsal, sesamoids), peroneal tendinitis, lateral ankle sprains, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, and knee pain.
- **Assessment:** Diagnosis involves history (family history, recurrent lateral ankle sprains), physical exam (inspection for "peek-a-boo heel sign," hindfoot varus, forefoot valgus), range of motion, strength testing, the Coleman Block Test, neurologic exam, and imaging (weight-bearing radiographs with specific angles: Meary's Angle >5°, Hibb's Angle >45°).
- **Rehabilitation Management:** Treatment varies by etiology and stage. For idiopathic cases, conservative management includes physical therapy (gastrocnemius stretching, subtalar eversion), custom orthoses (lateral wedge, heel lift, lateral forefoot wedge), and proper footwear. For neurologic cases (e.g., CMT), ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) are often needed, along with contracture prevention and gait training. Surgical indications include recurrent plantar ulceration and lateral ankle instability, with procedures including osteotomies, tendon transfers, and soft tissue releases.
- **Cutting Edge/Emerging:** New techniques include extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT), PRP, prolotherapy, percutaneous needle tenotomy, 3D-printed surgical guides, and Ilizarov external frame for severe rigid deformities. Deep learning AI tools are being developed to assist in diagnosis from radiographs.
- **Gaps in Evidence:** Robust classification systems for adult neurological cavus feet are lacking. More research is needed on PRP, botulinum toxin, stem cells, and comparison-outcome trials for surgical vs. conservative approaches.
</summary>

URL: https://www.physio-pedia.com/Talar_tilt

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Talar Tilt Test Summary

## Purpose
The talar tilt test is a clinical examination technique used to assess the ankle for injury to the **Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL)** and the **Calcaneofibular Ligament (CFL)** — the lateral collateral ligaments of the ankle.

## Technique
- **Patient position:** Seated with foot and ankle unsupported.
- **Foot positioning:** 10-20 degrees of plantarflexion.
- **Examiner action:** One hand stabilizes the distal lower leg just proximal to the malleoli; the other hand inverts the hindfoot.
- **Assessment:** The lateral aspect of the talus is palpated to determine if tilting occurs. Laxity is compared to the contralateral (uninjured) side.

## Evidence & Key Findings
1. **Prospective study (244 patients with ankle lesions):**
   - Ligament lesions not identified by talar tilt may be diagnosed by the anterior drawer sign.
   - The two methods are **complementary** — one cannot replace the other.
   - It is not possible to differentiate between an isolated ATFL lesion and a combined ATFL + CFL lesion using these methods alone.

2. **Reliability study using MRI (112 athletes with lateral ankle ligament injuries):**
   - Athletes with a talar tilt of ≥15° were treated operatively.
   - The talar tilt test cannot evaluate specific pathology of lateral ankle ligaments but was **reliable in indicating complete double-ligament ruptures** (ATFL + CFL) when talar tilt was ≥15° compared to the uninjured side.
   - **Diagnostic accuracy:** Sensitivity 67%, Specificity 75%, LR+ 2.7, LR- 0.44.

3. **Recent cross-sectional diagnostic study:** Found the talar tilt test to be a valuable method for identifying **mechanical ankle instabilities**.

## Additional Notes
- A positive test result is typically **5° to 10° of increased inversion** as compared with the uninjured ankle, indicating a CFL injury.
- The test is also known as the **inversion stress test**.
- The patient should be positioned in sitting or supine lying with the knee in full extension for optimal performance. It is important to hold the talus and calcaneus as one unit to prevent excessive subtalar movement.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: Lateral Ankle Instability - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf ---
URL: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538215

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This StatPearls article (last updated May 23, 2023) covers lateral ankle instability, a condition involving the talocrural, subtalar, and tibiofibular syndesmosis joints. The lateral ankle ligaments include the ATFL (resists inversion in plantarflexion), CFL (resists inversion in neutral/dorsiflexion), and PTFL (the strongest but supplementary ligament).

Etiology: Can result from mechanical instability (acute injury or chronic stress) or functional instability (proprioceptive deficits). The most common mechanism is a plantar-flexory force on an inverted ankle.

Epidemiology: 40% of all athletic injuries are ankle sprains. Over 50% of basketball injuries and ~30% of soccer injuries are ankle-related. 30,000 ankle sprains occur daily in the US, with 75% involving the lateral ankle. 90% involve the ATFL, 50-75% the CFL, and 10% the PTFL. 55-72% of patients have residual symptoms.

Diagnosis: History of recurrent sprains or ankle "giving way." Physical exam includes alignment assessment, range of motion, strength, and stress tests (anterior drawer test >8mm shift is pathological; talar tilt >10 degrees or >5 degrees difference from contralateral is pathological). MRI is useful for evaluating concomitant pathologies.

Treatment: Conservative management includes RICE, progressive weight-bearing, and physical therapy. 10-40% of patients develop chronic instability despite conservative treatment. Over 70 surgical techniques exist, categorized as anatomic (Brostrom procedure), non-anatomic (Evans and Christman-Snook), and anatomic augmented tenodesis reconstruction. Anatomic repairs yield 85-95% good-to-excellent results; 94% of high-demand athletes return to sports after surgery.

URL: https://www.physio-pedia.com/Anterior_Drawer_of_the_Ankle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Anterior Drawer of the Ankle test is a physical examination used to assess mechanical instability or hypermobility in the sagittal plane of the talocrural joint (upper ankle joint). The technique involves the patient lying supine with the ankle in 20° of flexion while the examiner stabilizes the tibia and fibula and draws the calcaneus anteriorly, observing the amount of anterior translation and end feel change. Anterior translation greater than 1 cm compared to the healthy contralateral ankle, along with a weakened end feel from hard ligamentous to weak elastic, indicates a partial or complete rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). The test is graded on a 4-point scale (0 = no laxity, 3 = gross laxity).

**Evidence:** The anterior drawer test has a sensitivity of 86% and specificity of 74% when compared to arthrogram (van Dijk et al., 1996). A more recent study (Croy et al., 2013) using ultrasound imaging found sensitivity of 0.74–0.83 and specificity of 0.38–0.40, with positive likelihood ratios of 1.2–1.4 and negative likelihood ratios of 0.41–0.66. The test was found beneficial when comparing side-to-side in patients. A systematic review (Beynon et al., 2022) found mixed reliability, validity, and sensitivity, but high specificity when used alongside other tests (anteriolateral drawer test, reverse anterior lateral drawer test, proximal fibula tenderness, and squeeze test). Murahashi et al. (2023) found that examiner experience affects translation measurements, but a modified technique (patient's tibia on an elevated surface with hip near 90°) improved inter-rater reliability across clinicians with varying experience levels.
</summary>

This perspective article published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (October 22, 2025) presents a clinical decision-making system for restoring ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (ROM) in athletes. **Background:** Ankle dorsiflexion ROM is critical for lower limb biomechanics, injury prevention, and athletic performance.
