**The 3-Step Clinical Decision-Making Framework:**

1. **Quantitative and qualitative assessment using the Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT):** Four standardized rules are provided for reliable measurement. Clinically relevant impairments are defined as asymmetries >1.5 cm toe-to-wall distance or >4.7° tibial inclination. Normative values are >9-10 cm and >40-42°. Qualitative assessment identifies pain/blocking zones: anterior (talocrural/transversal tarsal joints), anterolateral (inferior tibiofibular joint), medial retromalleolar (FHL tendon/subtalar joint), lateral retromalleolar (fibularis tendon/inferior tibiofibular joint), and posterior (triceps surae/tibial nerve).

2. **Confirmatory diagnostic testing:** Specific tests are described for each pain zone, including the posterior talar glide test, modified WBLT positions for FHL and fibularis tendons, and modified straight leg raise for tibial nerve mechanosensitivity.

3. **Targeted interventions:** Based on individual findings, interventions include joint mobilizations (antero-posterior talar gliding, MWM, transversal tarsal, subtalar, and inferior tibiofibular joint mobilizations), chronic stretching protocols for the triceps surae, FHL, and fibularis tendons (≥1,200 seconds/week under stretch, 5-7 sessions/week), and tibial nerve neurodynamics.

**Dosage recommendations:** Joint mobilizations: 60-120 glides per session, 2-3 sessions/week. Stretching: high-intensity, low-rest intervals (e.g., 3 sets of 75s with 30s rest, 5-7 days/week). Neurodynamics: 80-100s total tension time per session, 3 sessions/week.

<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle Sprain ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704124

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in Annals of Medicine (2025) titled "Towards the strategies of return to sport after lateral ankle sprain: a systematic review." The study investigates factors involved in returning to sport (RTS) after lateral ankle sprain (LAS) and aims to establish a standard rehabilitation paradigm.

**Background:** LAS is one of the most common musculoskeletal injuries, with up to 74% of patients experiencing persistent symptoms. Re-injury rates can reach 70% in specific sports populations, and nearly 40% develop chronic ankle instability within a year. High re-injury rates may result from premature RTS or inadequate rehabilitation.

**Methods:** Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, Scopus) were searched until March 1, 2024. The review included 20 papers with a mean quality score of 75.36±10.40%. Studies were categorized into: (1) rehabilitation measures for LAS, (2) criteria for RTS, (3) performance assessment after RTS, and (4) relationship between criteria and time of RTS.

**Key Findings:**
- 20 studies included: 3 questionnaires, 11 randomized controlled trials, 7 prospective studies
- Rehabilitation interventions included cryo-ultrasound therapy, neuromuscular training, balance exercises, bandaging, hyaluronic acid injections, neurostimulation, and electrical muscle stimulation
- RTS criteria identified include pain, swelling, ankle range of motion, muscle strength, functional instability, proprioception, and ability to perform practical tasks
- Many patients showed deficits at RTS: 65.1% had pain, 86.2% had function deficits, 35.8% had disability
- Side-to-side differences in ankle range of motion significantly correlated with time to RTS

**Conclusion:** RTS for LAS is a continuous process influenced by injury extent, causation, treatment protocols, and recovery criteria. The study identified current procedures and timelines for RTS of LAS, providing theoretical basis and clinical guidance for LAS patient rehabilitation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: A specific neuromuscular warm-up focusing on ankle sprain injuries in elite basketball - INEFC ---
URL: https://revista-apunts.com/en/a-specific-neuromuscular-warm-up-focusing-on-ankle-sprain-injuries-in-elite-basketball

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Article Title:** A specific neuromuscular warm-up focusing on ankle sprain injuries in elite basketball  
**Authors:** Javier Ruiz, Jairo Vázquez, David Urbano, Carlos Martín, Eduard Torrent, Fernando Rupérez, Mindaugas Gudelis  
**Journal:** Apunts Educación Física y Deportes, Issue 145 (3rd Quarter, July-September 2021)  
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.5672/apunts.2014-0983.es.(2021/3).145.08

**Background & Rationale:**  
Basketball involves explosive actions (accelerations, jumps, changes of direction) placing high demands on the ankle joint. The ankle is the most commonly injured area in athletes. Nearly 80% of athletes with an ankle sprain may sustain repetitive sprains, and ~72% may develop chronic instability. Basketball players are five times more likely to sustain an ankle injury after a previous one, with a 73% recurrence rate. Players with less lower-limb strength and fewer neuromuscular/proprioception abilities are at greater risk.

**Objective:**  
To propose a weekly ankle-specific neuromuscular warm-up program for elite basketball teams, integrated into pre-training warm-up sessions.

**Key Epidemiological Data:**  
- Ankle joint injuries in sports account for 11%–17% of all injuries.  
- Elite players cover ~73 m·min⁻¹, ~3 m·min⁻¹ at high-speed running (>18 km/h), with ~4 accelerations/decelerations >2 m/s² per minute, ~0.2 jumps >3Gs per minute, and ~1.3 impacts >8Gs per minute.

**Proposed Exercises (9 exercises, performed as a circuit in pairs):**  
1. **Ankle Mobility (Figure 1):** Standing, one foot on a box with elastic band at floor height below the malleoli; active dorsiflexion, heel grounded. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
2. **Peroneal Muscles in CKC (Figure 2):** Foot half-on platform; touch floor with free side of foot (eccentric → concentric eversion). 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
3. **Tibialis Posterior in CKC (Figure 3):** Same setup but performing inversion movement. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
4. **Plantar Flexion in CKC on Airex (Figure 4):** One leg on Airex, knee bent 30°–70°, perform concentric plantar flexion and eccentric dorsiflexion. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
5. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 1 (Figure 5):** Stand on one foot on unstable platform (Pielaster); perform diagonal rotational patterns with a soft medicine ball. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
6. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 2 (Figure 6):** One foot on Pielaster; perform hip and upper body flexion to 90° with opposite leg extended (single-leg deadlift). Optional Mini Band between knees. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
7. **Lateral Movement (Figure 7):** Elastic band on hip secured to stable surface; perform two lateral steps at high speed against band resistance. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
8. **Footwork with Competitive Movement (Figure 8):** Two players 4.9 m apart; perform footwork on coordination ladder then sprint to a marked space (1.5 m on free-throw line). 2 sets of 3 reps, competitive.  
9. **Progression:** Include perturbations (teammate unbalancing) and simple decision-making.

**Practical Application:**  
The program is designed to be integrated into a typical competition week schedule as part of the regular team warm-up. A holistic approach is recommended, with coaches, strength coaches, medical staff, and players sharing responsibility.

**Conclusions:**  
This proposal provides an example of ankle joint neuromuscular exercises for pre-basketball warm-up. It offers physiotherapists and strength/conditioning professionals practical exercises and a weekly organization framework for elite professional basketball, aiding injury prevention strategies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Rachana Dabadghav (2016) from JSM Foot and Ankle presents a physiotherapist's perspective on treating lateral ankle sprains in basketball players. The paper highlights that ankle sprains account for over 80% of basketball injuries, with injury rates of 7.9 per 1000 athlete exposures in females and 7.1 in males. The article outlines a phased rehabilitation protocol:

**Acute Phase (0-2 days):** PRICE protocol (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). For grade 1-2 sprains, early gentle strengthening and weight-bearing are recommended. For grade 3, functional walking orthosis with non-weight-bearing gait for at least 4 days.

**Initial Stage (2-5 days):** Focus on restoring dorsiflexion range (minimum 10° needed for walking, 20-30° for running) using Mulligan's Mobilisation with Movement (MWM) technique. Stretching and strengthening exercises to prevent muscle wasting.

**Intermediate Stage (2-6 weeks):** Address peroneal muscle weakness through strengthening (elastic bands, isokinetic, concentric/eccentric exercises). Hip muscle strengthening also important. Proprioception training using sports-specific balance exercises (dribbling on one leg, wobble board work).

**Return to Sport (4-6 weeks):** Sport-specific training including plyometrics, multidirectional exercises, and agility drills. Criteria for return include: pain-free full ROM, no persistent swelling, strength at least 90% of contralateral limb, good proprioception, equal flexibility, cardiovascular fitness meeting game requirements, and psychological readiness.

**Prevention:** Ankle bracing reduces incidence and severity. Semi-rigid ankle supports are more effective than taping (which loses 40-50% support after 1 hour). High-top shoes provide additional support. Prevention strategies should be maintained throughout the season and off-season.

# Ankle Sprain Management – Recovery and Prevention

This webpage from **The Centre for Advanced Orthopaedics (Singapore)** provides comprehensive information on ankle sprain management, led by **Dr Sarbjit Singh**, Senior Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon.

**Causes & Risk Factors:** Sudden twisting movements, weak ankles or prior injuries, inadequate footwear, poor balance/coordination, and high-impact activities.

**Signs & Symptoms:** Pain, swelling, bruising, difficulty bearing weight, stiffness, reduced range of motion, popping/tearing sensation at injury, tenderness.

**Diagnosis:** Physical examination, range of motion tests, and imaging (X-rays to rule out fractures; MRI/ultrasound for severe ligament injuries).

**Treatment Options:**
- **Immediate Care (R.I.C.E. Protocol):** Rest, Ice (15–20 min every few hours), Compression (elastic bandage/brace), Elevation (above heart level).
- **Non-Surgical Treatment:** Bracing & support, pain management (anti-inflammatory medication), physiotherapy & rehabilitation (strengthening and balance exercises).
- **Surgical Treatment (severe cases):** Ligament repair/reconstruction for chronic instability or severe tears; arthroscopic surgery to assess and repair joint damage.

**Prevention:** Strength & stability training, proper footwear, balance exercises (single-leg stands, wobble board), taping or bracing, gradual return to activity.

--- SOURCE 1: Comparison of the Effect of Resistance and Balance Training on Isokinetic Eversion Strength, Dynamic Balance, Hop Test, and Ankle Score in Ankle Sprain ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/11/4/307

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in the journal *Life* (2021, Volume 11, Issue 4, Article 307) titled "Comparison of the Effect of Resistance and Balance Training on Isokinetic Eversion Strength, Dynamic Balance, Hop Test, and Ankle Score in Ankle Sprain" by Haifang Wang, Hailong Yu, Yong Hwan Kim, and Wencong Kan.

**Purpose:** To compare the rehabilitation effects of resistance training (RT) versus balance training (BT) in patients with recurrent ankle sprain who are non-professional athletes.

**Methods:** 54 patients with recurrent lateral ankle sprain were assigned to either RT (n=27) or BT (n=27). RT consisted of exercises using elastic tube bands (Therabands) of progressive resistance. BT consisted of exercises on unstable surfaces (TOGU DYNAAIR, BOSU, or pillows). Both programs were home-based, performed for 6 weeks, twice daily for 20 minutes, 5 days per week. Outcome measures included: isokinetic eversion strength (30°/s and 120°/s), Y-Balance Test (YBT), four hop tests (single, triple, crossover, 6-m timed), and the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS) questionnaire.

**Key Results:**
- Both RT and BT significantly improved isokinetic eversion strength (absolute and relative) and dynamic balance (p < 0.05).
- BT showed significantly greater improvement in the crossover hop test compared to RT (p = 0.008).
- BT demonstrated significantly greater improvement in YBT total score (p = 0.002) and posterior medial (p < 0.001) and posterior lateral (p < 0.001) directions.
- FAOS scores showed significantly greater improvements in the BT group for pain (p = 0.022), sports function (p = 0.027), and quality of life (p = 0.033).
- Both groups improved significantly across most measures from pre- to post-training.

**Conclusions:** Six weeks of home-based RT and BT both improved eversion strength, lower extremity hop function, and subjective ankle assessment. However, BT was more effective than RT in improving dynamic balance, crossover hop test performance, pain relief, and return to sporting activities. The authors recommend BT for patients who need to return to sports or who experience pain and reduced quality of life due to recurrent ankle sprain, while RT may be safer for fall-prone patients.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a cross-sectional study published in World Journal of Orthopedics (2025) that establishes normative isokinetic ankle strength values for healthy, physically active adults. The study evaluated 200 ankles (100 participants: 69 males, 31 females; mean age 38.5 ± 13.5 years; mean BMI 25.8 ± 4.2) using the Biodex 3 System, assessing eversion, inversion, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion at 30°/s (torque) and 120°/s (power).

**Key Findings:**
- **Mean maximum torque (N/m) by gender:** Eversion: 22.3 (F) / 33.4 (M); Inversion: 30.0 (F) / 37.0 (M); Dorsiflexion: 37.4 (F) / 53.6 (M); Plantar Flexion: 100.4 (F) / 158.1 (M). All gender differences were statistically significant (P < 0.001).
- **Agonist/antagonist ratios:** Evertors/invertors = 88.8%; Dorsiflexors/plantar flexors = 36.1%.
- **Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) and Muscular Deficiency Index (MDI):** Both were balanced between sides (>90%) for all movements, with average global differences <10%.
- No significant correlation between age or BMI and maximum torque was found.
- The non-dominant side was consistently stronger for eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion.

**Clinical Significance:** The study fills a gap in ankle normative data, providing gender-specific reference values. The authors propose that LSI and MDI thresholds above 90%—similar to established knee criteria—can serve as objective benchmarks for rehabilitation planning and return-to-activity assessment after ankle injuries. The MDI is introduced as a novel composite index considering torque, power, and work across movements.

# Ankle Eversion Strength Test Summary

This webpage from MAT Assessment provides a comprehensive guide to the Ankle Eversion Strength Test, an isometric force assessment measuring how much force a client can produce when turning the sole of the foot outward (eversion) against resistance using the Muscle Meter dynamometer.

## Key Details

**Purpose:** Measures eversion force output from lateral ankle muscles (fibularis longus and brevis) in a controlled isometric setup. Useful for side-to-side ankle strength comparison, lateral ankle capacity, balance, running, cutting, landing assessment, and progress tracking.

**Primary Metric:** Peak force is the main routine metric. Force as percentage of body weight can be used if directly calculated. Rate of force development and time to peak are relevant for rapid ankle control tasks (cutting, landing, change-of-direction). Impulse is relevant for sustained force; fatigue index for repeated efforts.

**Step-by-Step Protocol:**
1. Prepare client with explanation and submaximal practice trial
2. Set client position (seated with hip/knee flexed, ankle near neutral is common)
3. Set up device or straps (handheld or strap-stabilised)
4. Place device against lateral forefoot near fifth metatarsal
5. Stabilise lower leg to prevent compensation
6. Give consistent instructions (e.g., "Turn your foot outward into the device as hard as you can")
7. Record 1-2 practice trials, then 2-3 maximal trials of 3-5 seconds with 30-60 second rest
8. Identify invalid trials (hip rotation, knee movement, device slip, compensation)
9. Record symptoms (pain, cramping, paraesthesia, apprehension)

**Reference Values:** Published comparison values for chronic ankle instability: approximately **141.2–175.5 N** (roughly 14-18 kg). Manual testing may be less consistent above ~120 N due to tester strength limitations. A side-to-side difference of ~10% or more warrants closer review.

**Key Limitations:** The test does not diagnose ankle instability, tendon injury, nerve involvement, pain, balance risk, or readiness for sport/work on its own. Results are setup-dependent and should be interpreted alongside symptoms, functional tasks, and clinical context.

**Reliability:** Repeatability improves with standardised setup. Belt-stabilised dynamometry has shown reliable results for ankle inversion/eversion in healthy adults.

## Practical Interpretation Priorities
1. Compare with client's own baseline
2. Compare right and left sides
3. Compare eversion with inversion
4. Consider symptoms during/after testing
5. Consider confidence and effort quality
6. Review compensations
7. Compare with related strength/mobility tests
8. Relate to client's sport/work/daily demands
9. Retest under same conditions
10. Do not use reference values as pass/fail criteria
</summary>

## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter (YBT-LQ)

**Published:** October 01, 2021, in *IJSPT* (Vol. 16, Issue 5, pp. 1190-1209)
**Authors:** Plisky P, Schwartkopf-Phifer K, Huebner B, Garner MB, Bullock G
**DOI:** 10.26603/001c.27634 | **PMCID:** PMC8486397 | **PMID:** 34631241

### Purpose
To review the reliability of the YBT-LQ, determine if performance varies among populations (sex, sport/activity, competition level), and determine injury risk identification validity based on asymmetry, individual reach direction performance, or composite score.

### Methods
- Systematic review of 10 databases from inception to October 30, 2019
- 57 studies included: 9 assessing reliability, 36 assessing population differences, 16 assessing injury prediction
- Quality assessed using modified Downs and Black scale and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale

### Key Results

**Reliability:**
- Intra-rater reliability: 0.85-0.91 in adult populations; 0.57-0.82 in adolescents
- Inter-rater reliability ICCs: 0.81-1.00
- Test-retest reliability ICCs: 0.63-0.93

**Sex Differences:**
- Posteromedial reach: Males 109.6 (95%CI 107.4-111.8) vs Females 102.3 (95%CI 97.2-107.4); p=0.01
- Posterolateral reach: Males 107.0 (95%CI 105.0-109.1) vs Females 102.0 (95%CI 97.8-106.2); p=0.036
- No significant sex differences in anterior reach or composite score

**Sport Differences:**
- Soccer vs Basketball: Significant differences in all reach directions and composite score (Soccer composite: 97.6; Basketball: 92.8; p<0.01)
- Baseball vs Basketball: Significant differences in posteromedial, posterolateral, and composite score (Baseball composite: 97.4; Basketball: 92.8; p=0.02)

**Competition Level:** No significant differences observed when competition level was considered alone (middle school, high school, college, professional).

**Injury Prediction:**
- Anterior reach asymmetry (≥4cm): OR of 2.20 (95%CI 1.09-4.46) in one study (Smith et al.)
- Posteromedial asymmetry (≥4cm): OR of 3.86 (95%CI 1.46-10.95) in male soccer players (Gonell et al.)
- Composite score: Only 1 of 13 studies found a relationship (Butler et al., OR 3.5 using cutoff of 89.6%)
- Due to heterogeneity, meta-analysis of injury prediction data was not possible

### Conclusions
The YBT-LQ is a reliable dynamic neuromuscular control test with moderate to high quality evidence. Significant differences in performance exist by sex and sport. If general cut points are used (not population-specific), the YBT-LQ may not be predictive of injury. Clinical population-specific requirements (age, sex, sport/activity) should be considered when interpreting YBT-LQ performance, particularly for injury risk identification.

<summary>
# Lower Quarter Y-Balance Test (LQYBT) - Summary

## Overview
The Y Balance Test (YBT) is a component of the Functional Movement Systems screen used to evaluate dynamic balance and functional symmetry for injury risk assessment and return-to-sport readiness. It was developed from the Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) and assesses single-leg balance while reaching in three directions: anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral. The YBT follows a specific protocol using standardized instrumentation requiring online training certification.

**Acronym:** LQYBT  
**Cost:** $269.95 (Not Free)  
**Time to Administer:** 10-15 minutes  
**Required Training:** Training Course  
**Age Ranges:** Adolescent (13-17), Adult (18-64)  
**Equipment:** Y Balance Testing Kit  
**ICF Domain:** Body Function | **Measurement Domain:** Motor

## Key Administration Protocol
- Subject stands barefoot on foot plate center with toes behind red starting line
- While maintaining single-leg stance, subject reaches with free leg in anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral directions
- Testing order: Right anterior → Left anterior → Right posteromedial → Left posteromedial → Right posterolateral → Left posterolateral
- Maximal reach (or average of 3 trials) is measured to nearest half centimeter
- Composite score = (Sum of 3 reach directions) / (3 × limb length) × 100
- Subject cannot touch down or place foot on top of reach indicator

## Psychometric Properties

### Reliability
- **Interrater Reliability:** Excellent (ICC 0.80-1.0) across multiple populations including service members, athletes, healthy adults, and older adults
- **Intrarater Reliability:** Excellent (ICC 0.82-0.89) for athletes
- **Test-Retest Reliability:** Excellent (ICC 0.89-0.93) for high school basketball players; Acceptable to Excellent for older adults (ICC 0.75-0.97)

### Validity
- **Predictive Validity:** Anterior reach asymmetry ≥4cm associated with 2.7x increased injury risk (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.4-5.3); Composite score ≤94% associated with 3x increased risk (OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.5-6.1)
- **Concurrent Validity:** Adequate to Excellent correlation between YBT-LQ anterior reach and ankle dorsiflexion measured by Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (r = 0.74 inclinometer, r = 0.64 tape measurement)
- **Construct Validity:** Adequate to Excellent correlations with TUG, 8UG, CST, ABCS, and single-leg stance in older adults

### Cut-Off Scores
- **Athletes (collegiate football):** Composite score < 89% (100% sensitivity, 71.7% specificity)
- **Firefighters:** Posteromedial asymmetry > 2cm predicted ankle sprain (AUC = 0.902, 100% sensitivity, 80% specificity)

### Normative Data
Extensive normative data provided for:
- Service members (21-29 years)
- Healthy adults (19-25 years)
- High school basketball players
- Collegiate athletes (by sport and sex)
- Healthy women aged 50-79 (by decade: 50-59, 60-69, 70-79)
- College students with flexible flatfoot
- Professional baseball players (by position)

### Key Considerations
- Significant reach differences exist between YBT and SEBT in the anterior direction; clinicians should not use these tests interchangeably
- Performance differences between genders should be accounted for when analyzing data
- Injury and surgery history did not significantly influence YBT performance in collegiate athletes
- Considerable normative data exists across multiple populations for clinical comparison

- **Sleep & Recovery**: Adolescent athletes sleeping less than 8 hours nightly had a 1.7-fold increased injury risk. Partial sleep deprivation reduces endurance, strength, and speed.
- **Individual Factors**: Biomechanics, sex, age, injury history, and fitness level critically shape injury risk. Female athletes have higher ACL injury rates; youth athletes need age-appropriate training limits.

**Purpose:** The study examined the relationship between patient-reported psychological readiness (ACL-RSI scores) and limb symmetry index (LSI) for five hop tests (single hop for distance [SHD], triple hop for distance [THD], crossover hop for distance [CHD], timed 6-meter hop [T6H], and single leg vertical hop [SLVH]) in NCAA Division 1 collegiate athletes after ACL reconstruction.

**Methods:** 21 athletes (7 males, 14 females; mean age 20.38 ± 1.67 years) at 6.62 ± 1.69 months post-ACLR were included in this retrospective cross-sectional study. All had primary ACLR with bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft. Correlation analysis and stepwise linear regression were used.

**Conclusions:** Physical function can influence psychological status after ACLR. **Level of Evidence:** Level 3

**Methods:** A cross-sectional study was conducted with 275 healthy adults (143 men, 132 women; mean age ~20 years), including recreational athletes, NCAA Division I athletes, and Army ROTC cadets. <summary>
This scientific article, published in the American Journal of Sports Medicine (2012), investigates whether single-legged hop tests can predict self-reported knee function one year after Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) reconstruction. 

**Study Design:** Cohort study (prognosis), Level of evidence 2.

**Methods:** 120 patients who underwent ACL reconstruction performed four single-legged hop tests (single hop, crossover hop, triple hop, and 6-meter timed hop) preoperatively and at 6 months post-surgery. **Conclusion:** Single-legged hop tests conducted 6 months after ACL reconstruction can predict the likelihood of successful or unsuccessful outcome at 1 year. The 6-m timed hop is best for identifying those at risk of poor function (high specificity), while the crossover hop is best for identifying those likely to have good function (high sensitivity). --- SOURCE 1: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Risk Factors for Lateral Ankle Sprain: A Literature Review ---
URL: https://scholars.direct/Articles/sports-medicine/aspm-3-026.php?jid=sports-medicine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a 2019 literature review by Correia and Torres (published in Archives of Sports Medicine, ISSN: 2578-6334) examining intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors for lateral ankle sprains. The authors searched MEDLINE on September 24, 2018, and included 42 studies in their review.

**Key Intrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Gender**: Women at higher risk (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures per Doherty et al. meta-analysis)
- **Age**: Higher risk in children compared to adolescents (2.84 vs. 1.94 per 1000 exposures), and adolescents compared to adults (1.94 vs. 0.72 per 1000 exposures)
- **BMI**: Greater BMI significantly related to ankle sprain, though height and weight individually are not clearly defined risk factors
- **Muscle Strength**: Decreased slow eccentric inversion strength increases incidence; lower pronator-to-supinator ratio is a risk factor; peroneus longus weakness increases risk; hip and core strength may reduce incidence
- **Previous Ankle Sprain**: Identified as one of the strongest risk factors for re-injury, both ipsilateral and contralateral
- **Balance/Proprioception**: Proprioceptive training and balance training reduce incidence of primary and recurrent ankle sprains
- **Limb Dominance**: Inconclusive results
- **Foot Type/Anatomy**: No clear correlation found between foot type, joint laxity, anatomic alignment, or range of motion and ankle sprains

**Key Extrinsic Risk Factors:**
- **Ankle Bracing/Taping**: Effective in reducing ankle sprain risk (64-69% reduction); braces and tapes are equally effective; bracing protects both mechanically and by improving proprioception
- **Shoe Type**: High top shoes reduce risk in basketball and football; specially designed swivel shoes may help
- **Sport Category**: Higher incidence in indoor, court, and team sports
- **Player Position**: May be a risk factor depending on sport-specific demands (e.g., blockers in volleyball)

**Conclusion**: Previous ankle sprain and external ankle support are the most clearly defined factors. Younger female athletes with high BMI may be at increased risk. The review found no correlation between muscle reaction time or anatomic foot type and ankle sprains. Further prospective studies are needed to reduce bias and uncertainty.
</summary>

Nonetheless Doherty, et al. reviewed and meta-analyzed 181 prospective studies and found that women were at a higher risk of sustaining an ankle sprain, compared to men (13.6 vs. 6.94 sprains per 1000 exposures).", "Recent studies reported previous ankle sprain as a risk factor for ipsilateral and contralateral future lateral ankle injury. Moreover, a systematic review identified and reviewed 26 articles... their results showed that previous ankle sprain is the most common injury resulting in a secondary sprain of the ipsilateral or contralateral ankle, which may be explained by neuromuscular factors.", "A recent systematic review concluded that athletes who wore braces had fewer ankle sprains (p < 0.05) and reduced the risk of sprains by 64%, either if they had or hadn't a previous sprain history.", "Most professionals working with athletes would rather prevent an injury than treat one. However, solid scientific evidence is needed to build structured and efficient prevention programs.", "Even though there are a few clearly defined risk factors for ankle sprain, further prospective studies are needed to properly evaluate each suggested risk factor for this injury, reducing the actual bias and uncertainty."

<summary>
This is a scientific article (a systematic review and meta-analysis) published in the journal *Sports* (MDPI) on March 28, 2025, titled "Risk Factors of Ankle Sprain in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." The study was conducted by Hoveidaei et al., involving researchers from multiple institutions in the US and Iran. 

**Purpose:** To identify and synthesize risk factors for ankle sprain injuries (ASIs) in soccer players, including gender, age, BMI, history of ASIs, and other factors.

**Methods:** A systematic literature search was conducted in October 2023 across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ProQuest. The review included 26 studies (randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies). Data were analyzed using Stata 17.

**Key Findings:**
- A history of previous ankle sprain is the most significant risk factor for future ASIs.
- BMI was identified as a risk factor in 3 out of 7 studies.
- Age and height were significant in only 1 out of 6 studies each.
- Gender and weight were not found to significantly affect ASI occurrence.
- Other factors identified (but not meta-analyzed due to heterogeneity) included playing surface, joint laxity, muscle weakness, match congestion, strength asymmetries, ground reaction forces, balance maintenance, skill level, and playing position.
- Soccer is associated with 13 to 35 injuries per 1000 player-hours, with approximately 77% of ankle injuries attributed to ASIs.
- Neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up routines can lower acute lower extremity injury incidence by 29-60%.

**Conclusions:** The research highlights the importance of previous ankle sprains and playing surface quality as key risk factors, providing insights for prevention strategies.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability

URL: https://www.clinmedjournals.org/articles/ijfa/international-journal-of-foot-and-ankle-ijfa-4-048.php?jid=ijfa

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Subtle Cavovarus Foot: A Missed Risk Factor for Chronic Foot and Ankle Pathologies

**Source:** Green B, Anne-Laure M, Leduc S, Marie-Lyne N (2020) Int J Foot Ankle 4:048. doi.org/10.23937/2643-3885/1710048

**Type:** Literature Review | Level of Evidence: Level IV | SORT: B

## Overview
The subtle cavovarus foot is a mild, often undiagnosed form of cavovarus deformity characterized by a high medial plantar arch and hindfoot varus. It is estimated to affect up to 25% of the population and is most commonly idiopathic. The condition alters foot biomechanics, leading to lateral foot overload, instability, and increased injury risk.

## Key Biomechanics
- Hyperactivity of peroneus longus induces plantarflexion of the first metatarsal (forefoot-driven deformity)
- Hindfoot cannot evert, leading to decreased mobility and increased rigidity
- Pressure concentrates on the lateral aspect of the foot, predisposing to chronic pathologies

## Clinical Evaluation
Three key physical exam tests:
1. **Peek-a-boo heel sign** – heel pad visible from anterior view
2. **Coleman block test** – determines if hindfoot varus is forefoot-driven (flexible, correctable)
3. **Silfverskiold test** – assesses for equinus/gastrocnemius tightness

Radiographic evaluation (secondary importance) includes Meary's angle, calcaneal pitch angle, Hibbs' angle, and medial arch height on lateral weight-bearing views.

## Plantar Pressure Measurement
Dynamic pedobarography is the ideal method for evaluation. Subtle cavovarus feet show:
- Decreased midfoot pressure in static stance
- Increased lateral foot and heel pressure during gait
- Lateral shift of center of pressure

## Associated Pathologies/Injuries
- **Lateral ankle sprains** – increased risk due to inadequate pronation and peroneal dysfunction
- **Chronic ankle instability** – altered gait with lateral shift of center of pressure; cavovarus deformity is predictive of operative failure if not corrected
- **Peroneal tendon pathologies** – tendinopathy and tears due to stretching of lateral soft tissues
- **Stress fractures** – especially 4th and 5th metatarsals and cuboid
- Other associations: plantar fasciitis, ankle arthritis, Morton's neuroma, hallux valgus, Achilles tendon pathology

## Treatment
**Conservative:** Flexible or semi-rigid orthotics to laterally offload the foot; posting of lateral forefoot with recession under the first ray; physiotherapy and gastrocnemius stretching.

**Surgical (for rigid/refractory cases):** Lateral displacement calcaneal osteotomy, plantar fascia release, dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal, peroneal tendon surgery, Achilles tendon lengthening. Return to athletics within 12 weeks post-operatively.

## Key Conclusion
Subtle cavovarus foot is a significant risk factor for chronic foot and ankle pathologies. Early identification and conservative management with appropriate foot orthotics favor safer return to sports and help prevent recurrence.
</summary>

The study retrospectively reviewed 15 patients (all male, mean age 25.7) who underwent a modified Broström procedure (MBP) combined with additional corrective osteotomies between August 2009 and April 2015, with a mean follow-up of 58.5 months.

Key findings: Cavovarus deformity is an anatomical risk factor for CLAI, but subtle deformity is often difficult to detect. The "peek-a-boo heel sign" (visible heel pad from the front when standing) helps identify subtle cavus deformity. Additional procedures performed included: calcaneal lateral closing wedge osteotomy (7 patients for fixed hindfoot varus), first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy (11 patients for plantarflexed first ray), and gastrocnemius recession (2 patients). Three patients underwent both calcaneal and metatarsal osteotomies.

Clinical outcomes improved significantly: VAS pain score improved from 5.5 to 1.7 (p=0.002), AOFAS ankle-hindfoot score improved from 61.0 to 85.3 (p<0.001), and Karlsson-Peterson score improved from 56.8 to 83.1 (p<0.001). No patient experienced recurrent ankle instability. Radiographically, talar tilt angle decreased from 12.3° to 5.6° (p=0.001), and talar anterior translation decreased from 7.9mm to 4.8mm (p=0.007). The Meary angle, arch height, and hindfoot alignment all improved significantly.

The authors conclude that simultaneous correction of cavovarus deformity with MBP for CLAI improves clinical outcomes and prevents recurrent instability, recommending comprehensive evaluation for subtle cavovarus deformity when treating CLAI patients.

<summary>
This webpage from PM&R KnowledgeNow provides a comprehensive clinical overview of **Pes Cavus**, an orthopedic foot deformity characterized by an elevated longitudinal medial plantar arch (also known as "claw foot," "hollow foot," or "cavovarus foot"). It is authored by Mooyeon Oh-Park, MD, et al., originally published September 15, 2015, and last updated December 17, 2025.

**Key Points:**

- **Etiology & Epidemiology:** Pes cavus has four primary causes: neuromuscular, traumatic, congenital, and idiopathic. It occurs in approximately 8-15% of the general population. Severe cases are idiopathic (30%) or secondary to neurological causes (70%), most commonly Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease.
- **Pathoanatomy:** The deformity results from muscle imbalances (e.g., weak tibialis anterior overpowered by peroneus longus), leading to forefoot valgus, hindfoot varus, and clawing of the toes. In neuromuscular cases, the foot is initially flexible but becomes more rigid over time.
- **Associated Conditions:** Common complications include lateral foot pain/calluses, stress fractures (5th metatarsal, sesamoids), peroneal tendinitis, lateral ankle sprains, plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, and knee pain.
- **Assessment:** Diagnosis involves history (family history, recurrent lateral ankle sprains), physical exam (inspection for "peek-a-boo heel sign," hindfoot varus, forefoot valgus), range of motion, strength testing, the Coleman Block Test, neurologic exam, and imaging (weight-bearing radiographs with specific angles: Meary's Angle >5°, Hibb's Angle >45°).
- **Rehabilitation Management:** Treatment varies by etiology and stage. For idiopathic cases, conservative management includes physical therapy (gastrocnemius stretching, subtalar eversion), custom orthoses (lateral wedge, heel lift, lateral forefoot wedge), and proper footwear. For neurologic cases (e.g., CMT), ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) are often needed, along with contracture prevention and gait training. Surgical indications include recurrent plantar ulceration and lateral ankle instability, with procedures including osteotomies, tendon transfers, and soft tissue releases.
- **Cutting Edge/Emerging:** New techniques include extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT), PRP, prolotherapy, percutaneous needle tenotomy, 3D-printed surgical guides, and Ilizarov external frame for severe rigid deformities. Deep learning AI tools are being developed to assist in diagnosis from radiographs.
- **Gaps in Evidence:** Robust classification systems for adult neurological cavus feet are lacking. More research is needed on PRP, botulinum toxin, stem cells, and comparison-outcome trials for surgical vs. conservative approaches.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Talar Tilt Test Summary

## Purpose
The talar tilt test is a clinical examination technique used to assess the ankle for injury to the **Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATFL)** and the **Calcaneofibular Ligament (CFL)** — the lateral collateral ligaments of the ankle.

## Technique
- **Patient position:** Seated with foot and ankle unsupported.
- **Foot positioning:** 10-20 degrees of plantarflexion.
- **Examiner action:** One hand stabilizes the distal lower leg just proximal to the malleoli; the other hand inverts the hindfoot.
- **Assessment:** The lateral aspect of the talus is palpated to determine if tilting occurs. Laxity is compared to the contralateral (uninjured) side.

## Evidence & Key Findings
1. **Prospective study (244 patients with ankle lesions):**
   - Ligament lesions not identified by talar tilt may be diagnosed by the anterior drawer sign.
   - The two methods are **complementary** — one cannot replace the other.
   - It is not possible to differentiate between an isolated ATFL lesion and a combined ATFL + CFL lesion using these methods alone.

2. **Reliability study using MRI (112 athletes with lateral ankle ligament injuries):**
   - Athletes with a talar tilt of ≥15° were treated operatively.
   - The talar tilt test cannot evaluate specific pathology of lateral ankle ligaments but was **reliable in indicating complete double-ligament ruptures** (ATFL + CFL) when talar tilt was ≥15° compared to the uninjured side.
   - **Diagnostic accuracy:** Sensitivity 67%, Specificity 75%, LR+ 2.7, LR- 0.44.

3. **Recent cross-sectional diagnostic study:** Found the talar tilt test to be a valuable method for identifying **mechanical ankle instabilities**.

## Additional Notes
- A positive test result is typically **5° to 10° of increased inversion** as compared with the uninjured ankle, indicating a CFL injury.
- The test is also known as the **inversion stress test**.
- The patient should be positioned in sitting or supine lying with the knee in full extension for optimal performance. It is important to hold the talus and calcaneus as one unit to prevent excessive subtalar movement.
</summary>

This StatPearls article (last updated May 23, 2023) covers lateral ankle instability, a condition involving the talocrural, subtalar, and tibiofibular syndesmosis joints. The lateral ankle ligaments include the ATFL (resists inversion in plantarflexion), CFL (resists inversion in neutral/dorsiflexion), and PTFL (the strongest but supplementary ligament).

Etiology: Can result from mechanical instability (acute injury or chronic stress) or functional instability (proprioceptive deficits). The most common mechanism is a plantar-flexory force on an inverted ankle.

Epidemiology: 40% of all athletic injuries are ankle sprains. Over 50% of basketball injuries and ~30% of soccer injuries are ankle-related. 30,000 ankle sprains occur daily in the US, with 75% involving the lateral ankle. 90% involve the ATFL, 50-75% the CFL, and 10% the PTFL. 55-72% of patients have residual symptoms.

Diagnosis: History of recurrent sprains or ankle "giving way." Physical exam includes alignment assessment, range of motion, strength, and stress tests (anterior drawer test >8mm shift is pathological; talar tilt >10 degrees or >5 degrees difference from contralateral is pathological). MRI is useful for evaluating concomitant pathologies.

Treatment: Conservative management includes RICE, progressive weight-bearing, and physical therapy. 10-40% of patients develop chronic instability despite conservative treatment. Over 70 surgical techniques exist, categorized as anatomic (Brostrom procedure), non-anatomic (Evans and Christman-Snook), and anatomic augmented tenodesis reconstruction. Anatomic repairs yield 85-95% good-to-excellent results; 94% of high-demand athletes return to sports after surgery.

Complications include nerve injury (3.8-9.7%), wound healing issues (4%), stiffness, and potential early-onset degenerative joint disease without intervention.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Anterior Drawer of the Ankle ---
URL: https://www.physio-pedia.com/Anterior_Drawer_of_the_Ankle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Anterior Drawer of the Ankle test is a physical examination used to assess mechanical instability or hypermobility in the sagittal plane of the talocrural joint (upper ankle joint). The technique involves the patient lying supine with the ankle in 20° of flexion while the examiner stabilizes the tibia and fibula and draws the calcaneus anteriorly, observing the amount of anterior translation and end feel change. Anterior translation greater than 1 cm compared to the healthy contralateral ankle, along with a weakened end feel from hard ligamentous to weak elastic, indicates a partial or complete rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). The test is graded on a 4-point scale (0 = no laxity, 3 = gross laxity).

**Evidence:** The anterior drawer test has a sensitivity of 86% and specificity of 74% when compared to arthrogram (van Dijk et al., 1996). A more recent study (Croy et al., 2013) using ultrasound imaging found sensitivity of 0.74–0.83 and specificity of 0.38–0.40, with positive likelihood ratios of 1.2–1.4 and negative likelihood ratios of 0.41–0.66. The test was found beneficial when comparing side-to-side in patients. A systematic review (Beynon et al., 2022) found mixed reliability, validity, and sensitivity, but high specificity when used alongside other tests (anteriolateral drawer test, reverse anterior lateral drawer test, proximal fibula tenderness, and squeeze test). Murahashi et al. (2023) found that examiner experience affects translation measurements, but a modified technique (patient's tibia on an elevated surface with hip near 90°) improved inter-rater reliability across clinicians with varying experience levels.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The purpose of this test was to determine whether ankle mechanical instability or hypermobility in the sagittal plane of the talocrural joint (or upper ankle joint) is present., An anterior translation greater than 1 cm compared to the healthy contralateral ankle and an evident weakening of the end feel are most indicative of a partial rupture or complete rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament., Anterior drawer has sensitivity of 86 percent and specificity of 74 percent for a diagnostic test of 160 patients with an inversion ankle sprain when compared to an arthrogram., Sensitivity of the anterior drawer test was 0.74 (95% CI: 0.58, 0.86) and 0.83 (95% CI: 0.64, 0.93) at the 2.3 mm or greater and 3.7 mm or greater reference standards, respectively., A systematic review did find that the anterior drawer had mixed reliability, validity and sensitivity but the specificity was high when used with the anteriolateral drawer test, the reverse anterior lateral drawer test, tenderness to palpation of the proximal fibula and the squeeze test.

--- SOURCE 16: Frontiers | Restoring ankle dorsiflexion range of motion in athletes: an individualized clinical decision-making system ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2025.1677383/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This perspective article published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (October 22, 2025) presents a clinical decision-making system for restoring ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (ROM) in athletes. Authored by Tourillon, M'Baye, and Smith, the article addresses the gap in practical guidance for diagnosing and treating ankle dorsiflexion restriction.

**Background:** Ankle dorsiflexion ROM is critical for lower limb biomechanics, injury prevention, and athletic performance. Restricted dorsiflexion is a risk factor for lateral ankle sprain, chronic ankle instability, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar heel pain, patellar tendinopathy, and metatarsal stress fractures. It also impacts deceleration capacity and force absorption during athletic movements.

**The 3-Step Clinical Decision-Making Framework:**

1. **Quantitative and qualitative assessment using the Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT):** Four standardized rules are provided for reliable measurement. Clinically relevant impairments are defined as asymmetries >1.5 cm toe-to-wall distance or >4.7° tibial inclination. Normative values are >9-10 cm and >40-42°. Qualitative assessment identifies pain/blocking zones: anterior (talocrural/transversal tarsal joints), anterolateral (inferior tibiofibular joint), medial retromalleolar (FHL tendon/subtalar joint), lateral retromalleolar (fibularis tendon/inferior tibiofibular joint), and posterior (triceps surae/tibial nerve).

2. **Confirmatory diagnostic testing:** Specific tests are described for each pain zone, including the posterior talar glide test, modified WBLT positions for FHL and fibularis tendons, and modified straight leg raise for tibial nerve mechanosensitivity.

3. **Targeted interventions:** Based on individual findings, interventions include joint mobilizations (antero-posterior talar gliding, MWM, transversal tarsal, subtalar, and inferior tibiofibular joint mobilizations), chronic stretching protocols for the triceps surae, FHL, and fibularis tendons (≥1,200 seconds/week under stretch, 5-7 sessions/week), and tibial nerve neurodynamics.

**Dosage recommendations:** Joint mobilizations: 60-120 glides per session, 2-3 sessions/week. Stretching: high-intensity, low-rest intervals (e.g., 3 sets of 75s with 30s rest, 5-7 days/week). Neurodynamics: 80-100s total tension time per session, 3 sessions/week.

**Caution noted:** No interventional data yet demonstrate that this individualized system produces superior ROM gains compared to generalized protocols.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This study published in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (2013) investigated the relationship between ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (ROM) and dynamic balance in 45 individuals (mean age 23.2 years) with chronic ankle instability (CAI). Ankle dorsiflexion ROM was measured in a weight-bearing position using a digital inclinometer, and dynamic balance was assessed using the Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) in anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral directions.

Key findings: There was a fair positive correlation between dorsiflexion ROM and the anterior reach direction (r = .55, r² = .31, p < .001), explaining 31% of the variance. Weaker correlations were found for the posterolateral reach direction (r = .29, r² = .09, p = .03) and composite SEBT scores (r = .30, r² = .09, p = .02). No significant relationship was found between ankle dorsiflexion and the posteromedial reach direction (r = .01, p = .47).

The authors conclude that ankle dorsiflexion ROM, particularly for the anterior reach component of the SEBT, influences dynamic balance in individuals with CAI. Clinicians should consider addressing dorsiflexion ROM deficits in rehabilitation programs for individuals with CAI who demonstrate difficulty with dynamic balance tasks. The study was supported by a grant from the Sports Section of the American Physical Therapy Association and registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01423513).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from LER Magazine (2020) examines chronic ankle instability (CAI) as a serious long-term consequence of ankle sprains, emphasizing that it is not "just an ankle sprain" but a condition with significant physical and quality-of-life impacts.

**Key Epidemiology:** An estimated 2 million individuals seek ED treatment annually for ankle sprains, with actual incidence possibly 5.5 times higher. Nearly half of sprains are non-sport related. Incidence is higher in females (13.6 vs 6.9/1000 exposures) and decreases with age (children: 2.85, adolescents: 1.94, adults: 0.72/1000 exposures). Ankle sprains account for 80% of ED visits, with 85% being lateral ligament injuries (primarily anterior talofibular ligament).

**Grades of Injury:** Grade I (ATFL/CFL injury without rupture), Grade II (complete ATFL rupture, CFL intact), Grade III (complete ATFL and CFL rupture).

**Functional vs Mechanical Instability:** The article distinguishes between functional ankle instability (FAI) and mechanical ankle instability (MAI). FAI involves sensorimotor and postural control deficits best treated conservatively. MAI involves structural ligamentous laxity requiring mechanical stabilization (taping, orthoses, or surgery). The article heavily features a 2020 study by Wenning et al examining 43 patients with chronic, unilateral MAI who had failed conservative treatment.

**Key Findings from Wenning et al:** 
- Plantarflexion, supination, and pronation strength significantly reduced in MAI ankles
- Peak pronation torque reached earlier in non-MAI ankles (20° vs 14° of supination)
- Active range of motion reduced in dorsiflexion and supination
- Increased postural sway in injured ankles
- During gait, increased external rotation in MAI ankles (8.7° vs 6.8°)
- The novel finding was that end-range pronation strength deficits (especially in the early phase of pronation) may limit ability to actively prevent excessive supination, suggesting these patients may benefit from mechanical treatment like operative ligament reconstruction

**Conclusions:** Severe mechanical instability may not be compensable through functional training alone. A certain degree of mechanical instability will eventually require operative stabilization. Future research should focus on quantifying mechanical ankle instability to establish cutoff values for when functional treatment is likely to fail and early operative stabilization should be recommended.
</summary>

URL: https://www.physio-pedia.com/Chronic_Ankle_Instability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
About 20% of acute ankle sprain patients develop chronic ankle instability, Two million lateral ankle sprains occur annually in the United States, CAI includes mechanical instability (motion exceeds normal physiological limits) and functional instability (objectively stable with subjective feelings of instability related to sensorimotor or neuromuscular deficits), The main causes of chronic ankle instability that have been found are: decreased proprioceptive abilities because of a loss of mechanoreceptors and decreased muscle strength of invertor and evertor muscles, The combination of the SEBT as a predictor of dynamic balance in combination with the Foot and Ankle Ability measure as a patient self reported outcome can predict the likelihood of CAI

## Abstract

Context:There is minimal patient-oriented evidence regarding the effectiveness of interventions targeted to reduce symptoms associated with chronic ankle instability (CAI). In addition, clinicians aiming to prioritize care by implementing only the most effective components of a rehabilitative program have very little evidence on comparative efficacy.Objective:To assess the comparative efficacy of 2 common ankle rehabilitation techniques (wobble-board [WB] balance training and ankle strengthening using resistance tubing [RT]) using patient-oriented outcomes.Design:Randomized controlled trial.Setting:Laboratory.Patients:40 patients with CAI randomized into 2 treatment groups: RT and WB. CAI inclusion criteria included a history of an ankle sprain, recurrent “giving way,” and a Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) score ≤25.Interventions:Participants completed 5 clinician-oriented tests (foot-lift test, time-in-balance, Star Excursion Balance Test, figure-of-8 hop, and side-hop) an...

## Key takeaways

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

1.   Wobble-board (WB) training shows greater patient-oriented efficacy than resistance tubing (RT) for chronic ankle instability (CAI).
2.   Both interventions improved clinical outcomes, but only WB significantly enhanced FAAM-ADL scores post-intervention.
3.   40 participants with CAI were randomized into two treatment groups to assess rehabilitation efficacy.
4.   The study provides practical evidence for clinicians on effective rehabilitation techniques for CAI.
5.   Patient-oriented outcomes should prioritize functional improvements over laboratory measures in CAI rehabilitation.

Objective: To examine the effects of a four-week balance training programme on ankle kinematics during walking and jogging in those with chronic ankle instability. A secondary objective was to evaluate the effect of balance training on the mechanical properties of the lateral ligaments in those with chronic ankle instability. Design: Randomized controlled trial. Setting: Laboratory. Subjects/patients: Twenty-nine participants (12 males, 17 females) with selfreported chronic ankle instability were randomly assigned to a balance training group or a control group. Intervention: Four weeks of supervised rehabilitation that emphasized dynamic balance stabilization in single-limb stance. The control group received no intervention. Main outcome measures: Kinematic measures of rearfoot inversion/eversion, shank rotation, and the coupling relationship between these two segments throughout the gait cycle during walking and jogging on a treadmill. Instrumented ankle arthrometer measures were taken to assess anterior drawer and inversion talar tilt laxity and stiffness. Results: No significant alterations in the inversion/eversion or shank rotation kinematics were found during walking and jogging after balance training. There was, however, a significant decrease in the shank/rearfoot coupling variability during walking as measured by deviation phase after balance training (balance training posttest: 13.1 AE 6.2 , balance training pretest: 16.2 AE 3.3 , P ¼ 0.03), indicating improved shank/rearfoot coupling stability. The control group did not significantly change. (posttest: 16.30 AE 4.4 , pretest: 18.6 AE 7.1 , P40.05) There were no significant changes in laxity measures for either group. Conclusions: Balance training significantly altered the relationship between shank rotation and rearfoot inversion/eversion in those with chronic ankle instability.

Background: Lateral ankle sprain results in positional faults in the fibula which are thought to limit accessory motion in the ankle, leading to hypomobility and negatively influencing sensorimotor function and postural control. Although it has been shown that fibular reposition taping (FRT) is effective in the prevention of recurrent lateral ankle sprain, its ability to produce significant changes in balance measures in patients with chronic ankle instability is inconclusive. Objective: This study aimed to determine whether a FRT intervention affects balance performance in patients with chronic ankle instability. Design: Randomized controlled trial. Methods: Sixty individuals with chronic ankle instability were randomly allocated to three groups: FRT, sham taping, or no intervention (control group). Kinesiotape was applied and then reapplied on 3 occasions per week for 2 weeks. Static and dynamic balance were measured with three functional tests before and 1 day after the last session of intervention with the tape removed: single-leg stance test, single-leg hop test for distance, and modified Star Excursion Balance Test (mSEBT). Results: The results of ANCOVA showed that there were no significant differences between the three groups except for mSEBT reach distance in the posterolateral direction, which was significantly greater in the FRT group than the control group (p ¼ 0.03). Conclusion: Applying FRT for 2 weeks did not significantly affect static or dynamic balance measures in individuals with chronic ankle instability, hence its clinical efficacy to influence balance remains uncertain in this population. Journal of Athletic Training, 2008

To answer the following clinical questions: (1) Is poor postural control associated with increased risk of a lateral ankle sprain? (2) Is postural control adversely affected after acute lateral ankle sprain? (3) Is postural control adversely affected in those with chronic ankle instability? PubMed and CINAHL entries from 1966 through October 2006 were searched using the terms ankle sprain, ankle instability, balance, chronic ankle instability, functional ankle instability, postural control, and postural sway. Only studies assessing postural control measures in participants on a stable force plate performing the modified Romberg test were included. To be included, a study had to address at least 1 of the 3 clinical questions stated above and provide adequate results for calculation of effect sizes or odds ratios where applicable. We calculated odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for studies assessing postural control as a risk factor for lateral ankle sprains. Effect sizes were estimated with the Cohen d and associated 95% confidence intervals for comparisons of postural control performance between healthy and injured groups, or healthy and injured limbs, respectively. Poor postural control is most likely associated with an increased risk of sustaining an acute ankle sprain. Postural control is impaired after acute lateral ankle sprain, with deficits identified in both the injured and uninjured sides compared with controls. Although chronic ankle instability has been purported to be associated with altered postural control, these impairments have not been detected consistently with the use of traditional instrumented measures. Instrumented postural control testing on stable force plates is better at identifying deficits that are associated with an increased risk of ankle sprain and that occur after acute ankle sprains than at detecting deficits related to chronic ankle instability.

args.key_excerpts: Wobble-board (WB) training shows greater patient-oriented efficacy than resistance tubing (RT) for chronic ankle instability (CAI)., Both interventions improved clinical outcomes, but only WB significantly enhanced FAAM-ADL scores post-intervention., The study found that wobble board training significantly improved patient-oriented outcomes, with a 6.1% increase in FAAM-ADL scores (Hedge's g=0.928) post-intervention., 40 participants with CAI were randomized into two treatment groups to assess rehabilitation efficacy., Context: There is minimal patient-oriented evidence regarding the effectiveness of interventions targeted to reduce symptoms associated with chronic ankle instability (CAI).
args.summary: This is an Academia.edu page for a 2017 randomized controlled trial published in the Journal of Sport Rehabilitation by Shelley Linens, titled "A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Rehabilitation Efficacy in Chronic Ankle Instability." The study compared the patient-oriented efficacy of two common ankle rehabilitation techniques: wobble-board (WB) balance training and resistance tubing (RT) ankle strengthening for chronic ankle instability (CAI). Forty participants with CAI (history of ankle sprain, recurrent "giving way," and CAIT score ≤25) were randomized into two treatment groups. The study found that wobble-board training showed greater patient-oriented efficacy, with a 6.1% increase in FAAM-ADL scores (Hedge's g=0.928) post-intervention, while resistance tubing did not significantly affect FAAM-ADL scores. Both interventions improved clinical outcomes on five clinician-oriented tests (foot-lift test, time-in-balance, Star Excursion Balance Test, figure-of-8 hop, and side-hop). Participants were recruited from September 2012 to April 2014, with all 40 completing the full program. The DOI is 10.1123/JSR.2015-0189. The page also includes references (48 citations), related papers, and an AI-generated FAQ section.

## Abstract

The goal of this meta‐analysis was to explore the overall safety and efficacy of surgical therapy vs conservative therapy for acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament based on eligible studies. Eligible studies were identified by searching PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase databases using appropriate updated index words to January 2018. We also searched relevant publication sources. Eligible studies included randomised controlled trials and comparative studies. Mean difference or relative risk (RR), along with 95% confidence interval (CI), was used to analyse the main outcomes. A total of 13 studies were eligible for this meta‐analysis, with 834 patients in the surgical therapy group and 930 patients in the conservative therapy group. Compared with patients receiving conservative treatment, patients undergoing surgical treatment had a significant higher American Orthopedic Foot And Ankle Society (AOFAS) score (weighted mean difference(WMD): 10.33, 95% CI: 6.83‐13.83) and an effective rate (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04‐1.28). No significant differences were observed in the incidence of recurrent ankle injury (RR: 1.01, 95% CI: 0.62‐1.65), limited range of motion (RR: 1.44, 95% CI: 0.83‐2.50), deep vein thrombosis (RR: 1.33, 95% CI: 0.73‐2.41), and wound infection or necrosis (RR: 3.99, 95% CI: 0.45‐35.34). However, compared with patients receiving conservative treatment, patients undergoing surgical therapy had significantly increased rates of complications (RR: 3.31, 95% CI: 2.55‐4.28), ankylosis (RR: 3.63, 95% CI: 2.16‐6.08), scare tenderness (RR: 10.16, 95% CI: 3.89‐26.52) and sensory loss (RR: 5.66, 95% CI: 2.76‐11.59). The results demonstrated that surgical treatment increased the AOFAS score and effective rate compared with conservative treatment. Besides, surgical treatment increased the rate of complications. Nevertheless, more high‐quality randomised controlled trials with a larger sample size conducted at multiple centres with a long‐term follow up are needed to confirm our conclusions.

**Keywords:** conservative treatment, lateral ankle ligament, meta‐analysis, surgical

## 1. INTRODUCTION

Acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament is one of the most common injuries related to the musculoskeletal system, accounting for nearly 25% of all injuries.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0001), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0002), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0003) If not handled correctly in the early stage, lateral ankle laxity may ensue, leading to chronic ankle instability, recurrent ankle sprain, and chronic pain, which consequently influence ankle activity and increase the risks of ankle degeneration and osteoarthritis.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0004), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0005) The overall number of ankle injuries each day in the United States and United Kingdom is about 23 000 and 5000, respectively. It has been reported that 600 000 patients suffer from ankle injury with each passing day, of whom approximately 120 000 patients present with sporting injuries. Moreover, nearly 43 000 patients present for medical care.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0006), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0007), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0008), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0009) About 125 000 patients in the Netherlands with a ankle sprain seek treatment by general practitioners every year, with an incidence of 8 per 1000 patients annually. For acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament, the treatment methods include suture, plaster fixation, elastic bandage, ankle support, ligament reconstruction, functional treatment, anchor repair, and so on. In this meta‐analysis, moderate to strong evidence was collected to explore the safety and efficacy of surgical treatment vs conservative treatment for acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament based on eligible studies.

## 2. METHODS

### 2.1. Search strategy

The following electronic databases were searched to identify eligible studies updated to January 2018 on conservative therapy vs surgical therapy for acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament: PubMed, The Cochrane Library, and Embase. In addition, literature or publications that were related to this meta‐analysis were identified as well. The literature research process was performed by two reviewers independently. Any differences were settled by discussion with a third reviewer to reach consensus.

### 2.2. Study selection

The inclusion criteria were as follows: (a) randomised controlled trials or comparative studies; (b) the study patients had no other serious concurrent disease; (c) the surgery group was treated using ligament repair or reconstruction; and (d) the conservative therapy group were treated using plaster fixation, bandage fixation, ankle support, and functional treatment.

The exclusion criteria were as follows: (a) duplicate publications or duplicate contents and results; (b) meta‐analysis, conference report, theoretical research, economic analysis, expert comment, systematic review, and case report; and (c) irrelevant outcomes.

### 2.3. Data extraction and quality assessment

The search process for all the included studies was performed to determine the above‐mentioned criteria by two reviewers independently. Any differences were settled by discussion with a third reviewer. Data were extracted from all the included studies in two parts: the main outcomes and basic information. The name of the first author, year of publication, study design, country, details of therapy, sample size, and Jadad score were included in the first part. The following clinical outcomes were obtained from the second part: recurrent ankle injury, limited range of motion, ankylosis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), scar tenderness, sensory loss, necrosis or wound infection, complications, the AOFAS score, and effective rate. The Jadad score checklist was used to appraise the quality of the included studies. We evaluated all the randomised controlled trial (RCTs) in five aspects: appropriateness of generating randomised sequence, randomisation statement, use of double blind, description of double‐blinding methods, and details of withdrawals and dropouts. Studies with a score of less than 3 represented low quality and high bias risks, studies with a score > 3 were indicated to be a high‐quality trial. The above‐mentioned process for all the included studies was performed by two reviewers independently. Any differences were settled by discussion with a third reviewer to reach an agreement.

### 2.4. Statistics Analysis

Statistical analysis of all the included studies was performed using STATA 10.0 (StataCorp, College Station, Texas). The heterogeneity of clinical trial results was assessed by _χ_ 2 and _I_ 2 tests to determine the model of analysis (the random‐effects model or the fixed‐effects model). Heterogeneity was considered to be high if the _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value was less than 0.05 and _I_ 2 test value was larger than 50%, and the random‐effects model was used. Heterogeneity data were considered to be acceptable if the _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value was larger than 0.05 and _I_ 2 test value was less than 50%, and the fixed‐effects model was used. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± SD and analysed by mean difference (MD). Categorical data were presented as percentages and analysed by relative risk (RR) or odds ratio (OR). Recurrent ankle injury, limited range of motion, ankylosis, DVT, scar tenderness, wound infection or necrosis, sensory loss, complications, and effective rate were analysed by RR and 95% confidence interval (CI). The AOFAS score was analysed by MD and 95% CI.

## 3. RESULTS

### 3.1. Study characteristics

A total of 819 articles were identified through search using the indexes. During a brief screening of abstracts and titles, 761 articles were excluded from the current study, leaving 58 articles to be further evaluated. During full‐text screening, 45 articles failed to meet the following criteria: no eligible groups (8), nonblack of clinical outcomes (19), or theoretical research (18). Finally, 13 studies[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0010), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0011), [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0012), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0013), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0014), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0015), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0016), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0017), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0018), [19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0019), [20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0020), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0021), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-bib-0022) were included in this meta‐analysis, with 834 patients in the surgery group and 930 patients in the conservative therapy group. ### 3.2. Recurrent ankle injury

Six studies with six case‐control groups provided data on recurrent ankle injury. Based on the _I_ 2 test value (_I_ 2 = 61.8%) and _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value (_P_ = 0.022), we chose the random‐effects model to analyse recurrent ankle injury. The pooled results showed no significant difference in the incidence of recurrent ankle injury between the two study groups (RR: 1.01, 95% CI: 0.62‐1.65, Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-fig-0002)).

### 3.3. Complications

Twelve studies with 15 case‐control groups provided data on complications. Based on the _I_ 2 test value (_I_ 2 = 0.0%) and _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value (_P_ = 0.969), we chose the fixed effects model to analyse the complications. The pooled results showed significantly higher rates of complications in the surgery group than the conservative treatment group (RR: 3.31, 95% CI: 2.55‐4.28, Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-fig-0003)).

### 3.4. AOFAS score

Three studies with six case‐control groups provided data on AOFAS scores. Based on the _I_ 2 test value (_I_ 2 = 97.8%) and _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value (_P_ = 0.000), we chose the random‐effects model to analyse AOFAS scores. The pooled results showed that, compared with the conservative treatment, surgical treatment significantly increased the AOFAS score (weighted mean difference: 10.33, 95% CI: 6.83‐13.83, Figure [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-fig-0005)).

### 3.5. Effective rate

Three studies with six case‐control groups provided data on the effective rate. Based on the _I_ 2 test value (_I_ 2 = 65.0%) and _χ_ 2 test _P_‐value (_P_ = 0.014), we chose the random‐effects model to analyse the effective rate. The pooled results showed that the effective rate was significantly higher in the surgery group in comparison with the conservative therapy group (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04‐1.28, Figure [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7948700#iwj13120-fig-0006)).
