## Background

Acute lateral ankle ligament injury is one of the most common problems in foot and ankle medicine [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR1 "Guillo S, Bauer T, Lee JW, Takao M, Kong SW, Stone JW, Mangone PG, Molloy A, Perera A, Pearce CJ, et al. Consensus in chronic ankle instability: aetiology, assessment, surgical indications and place for arthroscopy. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res. 2013;99:S411–9.")]. The lateral ankle ligament complex consists of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL). The weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments is the ATFL, which is the most frequently injured in ankle sprains, whereas the CFL is involved in 50~75% of such injuries, and the PTFL in < 10% [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR2 "Ferran NA, Maffulli N. Epidemiology of sprains of the lateral ankle ligament complex. Foot Ankle Clin. 2006;11:659–62.")]. The ATFL rupture is evaluated by the anterior drawer test, which is generally classified as mild, moderate, and severe degree. The CFL is rarely injured alone, but is associated with ATFL tears in more severe injuries. The CFL rupture is evaluated by the talar tilt test and is corroborated with a stressed anteroposterior radiograph. The PTFL is the strongest ligament of the lateral ligament complex and is rarely injured [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR3 "Hertel J. Functional anatomy, pathomechanics, and pathophysiology of lateral ankle instability. J Athl Train. 2002;37:364–75.")]. After injury, initial treatment is usually conservative, such as functional rehabilitation. An incidence of 10–30% of patients will fail conservative treatment, result in chronic ankle instability (CAI), and require surgical management [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR4 "Peters JW, Trevino SG, Renstrom PA. Chronic lateral ankle instability. Foot Ankle. 1991;12:182–91.")].

To date, many surgical procedures have been described to manage chronic ankle instability, indicating the complexity of the current status. These procedures and their modifications fall into the following three categories: non-anatomic reconstruction, anatomic repairment, and anatomic reconstruction [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR1 "Guillo S, Bauer T, Lee JW, Takao M, Kong SW, Stone JW, Mangone PG, Molloy A, Perera A, Pearce CJ, et al. Consensus in chronic ankle instability: aetiology, assessment, surgical indications and place for arthroscopy. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res. 2013;99:S411–9.")].

Non-anatomic reconstruction procedures use various configurations of local tendon grafts to accomplish the restriction function of the ligament without repair of the ligament remnants. Several techniques have been described, including partial or complete tenodesis from the Achilles tendon or peroneal tendon [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR5 "Gerstner Garces JB. Chronic ankle instability. Foot Ankle Clin. 2012;17:389–98.")] or allografts mimicking the function of the lateral ankle ligaments such as the Chrisman-Snook (CS) procedure, the Watson-Jones procedure, and the modified Evans procedure [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR6 "Chrisman OD, Snook GA. Reconstruction of lateral ligament tears of the ankle: an experimental study and clinical evaluation of seven patients treated by a new modification of the Elmslie procedure. J Bone Joint Surg Ser A. 1969;51:904–12."),[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR7 "Evans DL. Recurrent instability of the ankle; a method of surgical treatment. Proc R Soc Med. 1953;46:343–4."),[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR8 "Watson-Jones R. Recurrent forward dislocation of the ankle joint. J Bone Joint Surg B. 1952;34:519.")].

Anatomic repairment is to restore normal anatomy and joint mechanics by in situ repair of the injured ligament. Anatomic repairment includes repair ligaments by either shortening and fixing them to the bone surfaces or augmenting them with local structures to enhance the repairment. A typical example is the Brostrom-Gould procedure [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR9 "Gould N, Seligson D, Gassman J. Early and late repair of lateral ligament of the ankle. Foot Ankle. 1980;1:84–9.")], which enhances the original ligaments with the extensor retinaculum and has proved to be a strong procedure without sacrificing other normal structures [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR5 "Gerstner Garces JB. Chronic ankle instability. Foot Ankle Clin. 2012;17:389–98.")].

Anatomic reconstruction procedures use tendon grafts to recreate joint biomechanics anatomically by replicating the anatomic positions of the ATFL and CFL origin and insertion sites. They vary in the means by which they attain that positioning, including the number and angle of tunnels in the fibula and the fixation techniques selected in each bone tunnel location [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR1 "Guillo S, Bauer T, Lee JW, Takao M, Kong SW, Stone JW, Mangone PG, Molloy A, Perera A, Pearce CJ, et al. Consensus in chronic ankle instability: aetiology, assessment, surgical indications and place for arthroscopy. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res. 2013;99:S411–9."), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR10 "Coughlin MJ, Schenck RC Jr, Grebing BR, Treme G. Comprehensive reconstruction of the lateral ankle for chronic instability using a free gracilis graft. Foot Ankle Int. 2004;25:231–41."),[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR11 "Boyer DS, Younger AS. Anatomic reconstruction of the lateral ligament complex of the ankle using a gracilis autograft. Foot Ankle Clin. 2006;11:585–95."),[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR12 "Paterson R, Cohen B, Taylor D, Bourne A, Black J. Reconstruction of the lateral ligaments of the ankle using semi-tendinosis graft. Foot Ankle Int. 2000;21:413–9."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR13 "Xu X, Hu M, Liu J, Zhu Y, Wang B. Minimally invasive reconstruction of the lateral ankle ligaments using semitendinosus autograft or tendon allograft. Foot Ankle Int. 2014;35:1015–21.")].

A key point to surgical treatment of chronic lateral ankle instability is choosing a suitable surgical procedure, which is a complex question that has many arguments in the theory and clinical practice. The biggest limiting factor is that there are few high-quality controlled trials available to assist foot and ankle surgeons in making an informed decision.

The purpose of this meta-analysis was to perform an extensive review of the literature systematically and to attempt to compare different surgical techniques for management of chronic lateral ankle instability.

## Methods

This meta-analysis was reported according to the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis guidelines. All analyses were based on previous published studies; thus, no ethical approval and patient consent are required.

### Criteria for considering studies for this review

#### Eligible trial design

Any randomized and quasi-randomized (methods of allocating participants to a treatment which is not strictly random, e.g., by date of birth, hospital record number, alternation) controlled clinical trial evaluating any surgical treatments for chronic lateral ankle instability in adults was considered for inclusion. Chronic lateral ankle instability was defined as symptoms of lateral ankle instability, giving way or recurrent sprains, persisting for more than 6 months.

#### Patient characteristics

Studies including adult participants with chronic lateral ankle instability who underwent a surgical intervention were included. Trials containing adults and children were included if separate data for adults could be obtained. Studies evaluating exclusively with people with congenital deformities or children or degenerative conditions were excluded. Studies dealing exclusively with the prevention of ankle sprains in healthy individuals or conservative intervention of acute injury to the lateral ankle ligaments were also excluded.

#### Intervention-comparator characteristics

Trials comparing different types of surgical treatment used for treating chronic lateral ankle instability were included. We planned to include all three major types of surgical interventions (non-anatomic reconstruction, anatomic repairment, and anatomic reconstruction) and compare the clinical effect of different operative approaches. In this article, we define anatomic repairment as the primary or secondary suturing of the torn lateral ligaments at their anatomic position. The Brostrom procedure is a true repairment of the lateral ligaments. The classic Brostrom procedure is rarely performed as an operative technique alone. It is usually augmented with the mobilized lateral portion of the extensor retinaculum or periosteal flap. This kind of procedure is considered as a modified Brostrom procedure (MB). The procedure may be performed in the traditional manner through drill holes or with bone anchors [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR9 "Gould N, Seligson D, Gassman J. Early and late repair of lateral ligament of the ankle. Foot Ankle. 1980;1:84–9."), [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR14 "Hamilton WG, Thompson FM, Snow SW. The modified Brostrom procedure for lateral ankle instability. Foot Ankle. 1993;14:1–7."),[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR15 "Paden MH, Stone PA, McGarry JJ. Modified Brostrom lateral ankle stabilization utilizing an implantable anchoring system. J Foot Ankle Surg. 1994;33:617–22."),[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR16 "Angirasa AK, Barrett MJ. Talar anchor placement for modified Brostrom lateral ankle stabilization procedure. J Am Podiatr Med Assoc. 2008;98:473–6.")]. We define reconstruction as the replacement of the chronically deficient lateral ligaments with local tissues or with autograft or allograft tissue. Anatomic reconstruction is placement of the transferred tendon grafts in such a way as to replicate the anatomic positions of the ATFL and CFL origin sites. These procedures vary in the means of the fixation techniques selected in each bone tunnel location. The position, number, and angle of tunnels are varied, too. Non-anatomic reconstruction stabilizes the ankle using tendon grafts placed non-anatomically, such as the CS, Evans, and Watson-Jones procedure. In reconstruction procedures, there are many different ways the ligament graft can be secured in the bone including anchors, bone tunnels with interference screws, and endobutton-type devices [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR10 "Coughlin MJ, Schenck RC Jr, Grebing BR, Treme G. Comprehensive reconstruction of the lateral ankle for chronic instability using a free gracilis graft. Foot Ankle Int. 2004;25:231–41."),[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR11 "Boyer DS, Younger AS. Anatomic reconstruction of the lateral ligament complex of the ankle using a gracilis autograft. Foot Ankle Clin. 2006;11:585–95."),[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR12 "Paterson R, Cohen B, Taylor D, Bourne A, Black J. Reconstruction of the lateral ligaments of the ankle using semi-tendinosis graft. Foot Ankle Int. 2000;21:413–9."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR13 "Xu X, Hu M, Liu J, Zhu Y, Wang B. Minimally invasive reconstruction of the lateral ankle ligaments using semitendinosus autograft or tendon allograft. Foot Ankle Int. 2014;35:1015–21.")].

#### Clinical state

### Subjective evaluation of symptoms

1.   (1)
Satisfaction after operation: For the assessment of clinical outcomes post-operation, the Karlsson score and/or FAOS (foot and ankle outcome score) and/or the Sefton grading system were used. The Karlsson score and FAOS are methods of evaluating improvement in postoperative function and outcome by examining the stability of the ankle joint, pain, swelling, range of motion, activities at work or during sports, activities of daily living, the ability to climb stairs, running ability, and the use of ankle support aids. The Sefton grade was measured postoperatively at the follow-up visit and was classified as excellent, good, fair, or poor. Grades greater than good were considered as satisfactory treatment results.

2.   (2)
Subjective instability, pain, and swelling: Some studies did not use the grading system to assess the functional outcomes, but instead provide the number of patients with subjective instability, pain, swelling, and so on.

### Clinical measurements

For clinical assessment, the anterior drawer and varus stress radiography were measured preoperatively and at the follow-up visit in most studies. We collected preoperative and postoperative data of anterior talar translation and the talar tilt angle for comparison.

### Complications

We collected data for intraoperative complications (drill hole fracture, breakage of the anchor, etc.) and postoperative ones (wound complications, nerve damage, stiffness, subsequent sprains, deep vein thrombosis, revision, etc.)

### Search methods for identification of studies

We searched the Cochrane Library (to December 2016), MEDLINE (1990 to December 2016), and EMBASE (1990 to December 2016). We did not apply any language restrictions. In MEDLINE (PubMed online), a subject-specific strategy was combined with the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy for identifying randomized trials. Search strategies for Cochrane, MEDLINE, and EMBASE can be found in Additional file[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM1). We looked for reference lists of articles deemed eligible in the field to identify further studies or additional data. We also attempted to locate unpublished material or contact researchers for unpublished studies.

### Data collection

The titles and abstracts of all downloaded documents from the electronic searches were screened by CYX, who discarded clearly irrelevant reports. The remaining citations were then screened independently by CYX and HY to establish the need for obtaining full-text articles. Full-text articles were also obtained where there was any uncertainty about the relevance of the study. Subsequently, CYX and HY independently selected studies according to the inclusion criteria of the review. Disagreements were resolved by consultation and discussion with another review author (ZY).

Two review authors (CYX and HY) independently extracted data from each trial using a data extraction form and entered data into Review Manager 5.3 [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR17 "Review Manager (RevMan). [Computer program]. Version 5.3. Copenhagen: The Nordic Cochrane Centre TCC; 2014.")]. We recorded qualitative details and data regarding the study groups, interventions, and outcomes. Where necessary, we contacted trial authors for further details. Any differences in the data extraction between the review authors were resolved by discussion with a third review author (ZY).

### Evaluation of trial quality

Two review authors (CYX and HY) independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Any differences were resolved by a consensus procedure, followed, if required, by scrutiny from a third review author (ZY). We used The Cochrane Collaboration’s “Risk of bias tool” [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR18 "Higgins JP, Altman DG, Gotzsche PC, Juni P, Moher D, Oxman AD, Savovic J, Schulz KF, Weeks L, Sterne JA, et al. The Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials. BMJ. 2011;343:d5928.")]. Each study was graded for risk of bias in each of the following domains: adequate sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data addressed, free of selective outcome reporting, and free of other bias. Due to the nature of the interventions, assessors blinding was evaluated too.

### Data analysis

Treatment effect was measured using risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals for dichotomous data. Mean differences (MD), standardized mean differences (SMD), and 95% confidence intervals were calculated for continuous outcomes. When the measurement method or unit of the same intervention effect is exactly the same, MD was chosen. When different measurement methods or units are used for the same intervention effect, SMD was chosen.

Trail investigators were contacted for missing data if necessary. No studies with missing information on the variance measure were found. Where appropriate, we performed intention-to-treat analyses and were alert to the possibility of unreported loss to follow-up.

We combined trial results only where the participant groups, interventions, and outcome measures were sufficiently similar, as judged by clinical criteria and consideration of the statistical heterogeneity. Between-study variance was estimated using the DerSimonian and Laired estimator.

The data available from the included trials were insufficient to carry out our preplanned subgroup analyses (isolated ATFL repair versus ATFL and CFL repair; open versus mini-invasive approach) as well as a set of sensitivity analyses to examine the impact of the inclusion of trials with a high risk of bias, and also the effects of missing data on trial results.

## Results

### Description of studies

We identified and screened a total 1231 records from the following databases: Cochrane Library (327), MEDLINE (593), and EMBASE (311). Another 312 articles were identified through screening the reference list of included studies. After removing duplicates, 836 titles and abstracts were reviewed. We identified no relevant trials from searching conference proceedings or the reference lists of the included studies. A total of 77 potentially trials were identified. We excluded a total of 16 studies on acute or sub-acute ankle injury [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR19 "Best R, Bohle C, Schiffer T, Petersen W, Ellermann A, Brueggemann GP, Liebau C. Early functional outcome of two different orthotic concepts in ankle sprains: a randomized controlled trial. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2015;135:993–1001."),[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR20 "Beynnon BD, Renstrom PA, Haugh L, Uh BS, Barker H. A prospective, randomized clinical investigation of the treatment of first-time ankle sprains. All studies were published in English between 1990 and 2016 and identified in the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, or EMBASE. All studies evaluated patients with CAI. They are summarized below, with a full summary for each trial detailed in the characteristics of included studies (Additional files[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM2), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM3), [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM4), [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM5), [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM6), [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM7), and [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM8)).

As expected, the unit of randomization was the individual patient in the included studies. There were no trials with a cluster-randomized design. None of the seven studies evaluated exactly the same criteria. Larsen [[67](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR67 "Larsen E. Static or dynamic repair of chronic lateral ankle instability. A prospective randomized study. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1990;257:184–92.")] compared a dynamic tenodesis with a static tenodesis. Both procedures were non-anatomic reconstruction. The main outcome measures were a self-designed evaluation scheme and postoperative complications. Two studies compared an anatomic repairment with non-anatomic reconstruction [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR65 "Hennrikus WL, Mapes RC, Lyons PM, Lapoint JM. Outcomes of the Chrisman-Snook and modified-Brostrom procedures for chronic lateral ankle instability: a prospective, randomized comparison. Am J Sports Med. 1996;24:400–4."), [69](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR69 "Rosenbaum D, Engelhardt M, Becker HP, Claes L, Gerngross H. Clinical and functional outcome after anatomic and nonanatomic ankle ligament reconstruction: Evans tenodesis versus periosteal flap. Foot Ankle Int. 1999;20:636–9.")]. Hennrikus et al. [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR65 "Hennrikus WL, Mapes RC, Lyons PM, Lapoint JM. Outcomes of the Chrisman-Snook and modified-Brostrom procedures for chronic lateral ankle instability: a prospective, randomized comparison. Am J Sports Med. 1996;24:400–4.")] compared the outcome after a MB procedure with the CS procedure in 42 ankles. The main outcome measure was the Sefton ankle score, radiographic stability, and postoperative complications. Rosenbaum et al. [[69](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR69 "Rosenbaum D, Engelhardt M, Becker HP, Claes L, Gerngross H. Clinical and functional outcome after anatomic and nonanatomic ankle ligament reconstruction: Evans tenodesis versus periosteal flap. Foot Ankle Int. 1999;20:636–9.")] compared the outcome after a MB procedure with the Evans procedure in 20 participants. The main outcome measures were manual evaluation of joint mobility and radiographic stability. The other two studies compared a transosseous anatomic repairment procedure with an imbrication procedure [[63](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR63 "Cho BK, Kim YM, Kim DS, Choi ES, Shon HC, Park KJ. Comparison between suture anchor and transosseous suture for the modified-Brostrom procedure. Foot Ankle Int. 2012;33:462–8."), [66](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR66 "Karlsson J, Eriksson BI, Bergsten T, Rudholm O, Swärd L. Comparison of two anatomic reconstructions for chronic lateral instability of the ankle joint. Am J Sports Med. 1997;25:48–53.")]. Cho et al. [[63](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR63 "Cho BK, Kim YM, Kim DS, Choi ES, Shon HC, Park KJ. Comparison between suture anchor and transosseous suture for the modified-Brostrom procedure. Foot Ankle Int. 2012;33:462–8.")] compared a MB procedure with a transosseous suture procedure. The main outcome measure was Karlsson score, radiographic stability, and complications. Karlsson et al. [[66](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR66 "Karlsson J, Eriksson BI, Bergsten T, Rudholm O, Swärd L. Comparison of two anatomic reconstructions for chronic lateral instability of the ankle joint. Am J Sports Med. 1997;25:48–53.")] compared two different anatomic repairment in 60 patients. The lateral ankle ligaments were shortened by transosseous suture in one group. In the other group, the lateral ligaments were imbricated and reinforced by the inferior extensor retinaculum, a MB procedure. The main outcome measure was the Karlsson score, radiographic stability, and postoperative complications. Cho et al. [[64](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR64 "Cho BK, Kim YM, Kim DS, Choi ES, Shon HC, Park KJ. Outcomes of the modified Brostrom procedure using suture anchors for chronic lateral ankle instability—a prospective, randomized comparison between single and double suture anchors. J Foot Ankle Surg. 2013;52:9–15.")] compared single anchor MB procedure with double anchor MB procedure in 50 patients. The main outcome measures were Karlsson score, radiographic stability, and complications. Porter et al. [[68](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR68 "Porter M, Shadbolt B, Stuart R. Primary ankle ligament augmentation versus modified Brostrom-Gould procedure: a 2-year randomized controlled trial. ANZ J Surg. 2015;85:44–8.")] compared a MB procedure with an anatomic reconstruction procedure with ligament advanced reinforcement system (LARS). The main outcome measures of Porter et al. [[68](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#ref-CR68 "Porter M, Shadbolt B, Stuart R. Primary ankle ligament augmentation versus modified Brostrom-Gould procedure: a 2-year randomized controlled trial. ANZ J Surg. 2015;85:44–8.")] were FAOS and complications.

We excluded a total of 26 studies. Detailed reasons for exclusion can be found in the characteristics of excluded studies (Additional file[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6#MOESM9)).

args.summary:
This is a meta-analysis published on June 25, 2018, in the Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research (Volume 13, article 159), comparing different surgical techniques for managing chronic lateral ankle instability (CAI). The article is an open-access review by Yongxing Cao, Yuan Hong, Yang Xu, Yuan Zhu, and Xiangyang Xu.

**Background:** Acute lateral ankle ligament injury is common, with 10-30% of patients failing conservative treatment and requiring surgery. Surgical procedures fall into three categories: non-anatomic reconstruction, anatomic repairment, and anatomic reconstruction.

**Methods:** The authors searched Cochrane Library (through December 2016), MEDLINE, and EMBASE for randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Collaboration's "Risk of bias tool."

**Results:** Seven randomized controlled trials were included, falling into five groups:
1. One study compared dynamic vs. static tenodesis (both non-anatomic reconstruction), finding static tenodesis yielded better clinical satisfaction and fewer subsequent sprains.
2. Two studies compared non-anatomic reconstruction vs. anatomic repairment—one found more nerve damage in the non-anatomic group; the other found non-anatomic reconstruction provided higher reduction of talar tilt angle.
3. Two studies comparing transosseous suture vs. imbrication (anatomic repairment techniques) found no significant difference in clinical outcomes except operation time.
4. One study found the double anchor technique was superior to single anchor in reducing talar tilt.
5. One study found anatomic reconstruction with ligament advanced reinforcement system (LARS) resulted in better patient-scored outcomes at 2 years post-surgery than the modified Brostrom technique.

**Search results:** 1231 records were screened (Cochrane: 327, MEDLINE: 593, EMBASE: 311), plus 312 from reference lists. After removing duplicates, 836 titles/abstracts were reviewed, with 77 potentially relevant trials identified. Ultimately, 7 studies were included, all published in English between 1990 and 2016 (Cho 2012, Cho 2013, Hennrikus 1996, Karlsson 1997, Larsen 1990, Porter 2015, Rosenbaum 1999).

**Conclusions:** There is limited evidence supporting any one surgical technique over another. Key conclusions: (1) dynamic tenodesis has limitations with poor clinical satisfaction and more subsequent sprains; (2) non-anatomic reconstruction abnormally increased inversion stiffness at the subtalar level compared to anatomic repairment; (3) multiple types of modified Brostrom procedures can achieve good clinical results; (4) anatomic reconstruction is a better procedure for some specific patients.

Review Article

# Current concepts in arthroscopic treatment for chronic lateral ankle instability: a clinical practice review

Shohei Sano [![ORCID logo](https://info.orcid.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/orcid_16x16.png)](https://orcid.org/0009-0003-5195-6045), Yuichi Hoshino, Tetsuya Yamamoto, Noriyuki Kanzaki, Ryosuke Kuroda

Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine, Kobe, Japan

*Contributions:* (I) Conception and design: S Sano, Y Hoshino, N Kanzaki; (II) Administrative support: Y Hoshino, R Kuroda; (III) Provision of study materials or patients: S Sano; (IV) Collection and assembly of data: S Sano, T Yamamoto, N Kanzaki; (V) Data analysis and interpretation: S Sano, Y Hoshino; (VI) Manuscript writing: All authors; (VII) Final approval of manuscript: All authors.

*Correspondence to:* Yuichi Hoshino, MD, PhD. Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine, 7-5-1 Kusunoki-cho, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo 650-0017, Japan. Email: u1ho4no@med.kobe-u.ac.jp.

---

**Abstract:** Chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) is a frequent sequela of acute lateral ligament injury, causing recurrent sprains, persistent pain, and functional limitations, particularly among athletes and active individuals. While most acute ankle sprains respond well to conservative treatment, approximately 20–30% of patients experience persistent mechanical or functional instability requiring surgical intervention. In recent years, arthroscopic techniques have grown in popularity due to their minimally invasive nature, ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology, and favorable recovery profiles compared to open surgery. This clinical practice review integrates recent evidence from randomized controlled trials, comparative cohort studies, and technical reports with expert clinical experience to provide practical guidance on the arthroscopic management of CLAI. For patients with adequate ligament tissue quality, arthroscopic Broström repair remains the preferred first-line option, offering high return to sport (RTS) rates and low complication rates. For cases involving revision, poor-quality tissue, or generalized ligamentous laxity, arthroscopic ligament reconstruction using autografts or allografts is recommended. Concomitant procedures such as synovectomy, loose body removal, and cartilage debridement or microfracture can be performed during the same operation. A structured postoperative rehabilitation program is essential for achieving optimal outcomes. Early protected mobilization is followed by progressive range of motion (ROM) and strengthening phases, with sport-specific training typically initiated at about 3 months postoperatively. Current evidence suggests that arthroscopic management yields comparable clinical results to open procedures, while enabling the simultaneous treatment of associated joint pathologies and potentially facilitating faster recovery. Arthroscopic management of CLAI should be regarded not merely as a surgical alternative, but as a comprehensive clinical approach that integrates diagnosis, surgical decision-making, and rehabilitation for optimized patient outcomes. This review aims to provide an evidence-informed framework to guide orthopedic surgeons and sports medicine clinicians in the individualized, evidence-based management of CLAI.

**Keywords:** Chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI); arthroscopic Broström repair; lateral ankle ligament reconstruction; return to sport (RTS); ankle instability surgery

---

Received: 17 January 2026; Accepted: 20 April 2026; Published online: 17 July 2026.

doi: 10.21037/aoj-2026-1-0008

---

## Introduction

### Background

Chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI) commonly follows inadequately healed injuries of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and manifests as recurrent sprains, pain, and functional limitations in athletes and active individuals ([1](#B1),[2](#B2)). Although most acute sprains improve with nonoperative management, approximately 20–30% of patients develop persistent mechanical or functional instability that may ultimately require surgical treatment ([3](#B3),[4](#B4)).

The traditional open Broström or Broström-Gould repair has long been considered the gold standard surgical approach. It reliably restores ankle stability and enables a return to sport (RTS). Long-term follow-up studies have demonstrated that both augmented direct anatomical repair and lateral ligament reconstruction provide durable restoration of ligament laxity and functional stability for up to 15 years after surgery ([5](#B5)). However, arthroscopic techniques provide a minimally invasive approach that allows for the management of concomitant intra-articular findings, including synovitis and periarticular soft-tissue adhesions ([6](#B6)), and achieve clinical outcomes comparable to those of open procedures ([1](#B1),[7](#B7)-[9](#B9)). Recent comparative reviews and meta-analyses have reported similar stability and complication profiles between arthroscopic and open Broström-Gould repairs ([1](#B1),[7](#B7)), with some data suggesting faster RTS after arthroscopy ([3](#B3),[8](#B8),[10](#B10)).

Additionally, advancements in arthroscopic instrumentation and suture anchor technology have made possible various modified techniques possible, such as all-inside repairs, double-row constructs, and anatomic reconstructions using autografts or allografts under arthroscopic guidance ([11](#B11),[12](#B12)). These innovations have broadened the scope of arthroscopic procedures, allowing them to be tailored to each patient’s specific pathology and functional demands. Consequently, arthroscopy is now viewed not only as a minimally invasive alternative, but also as a versatile platform for repair and reconstruction strategies in CLAI.

### Rationale and knowledge gap

Despite the expanding evidence base, important practice questions remain. Meta-analyses show broadly equivalent functional outcomes between arthroscopic and open repair ([1](#B1),[7](#B7)), but considerable variation remains regarding surgical indications ([13](#B13)), rehabilitation protocols ([14](#B14)), and reporting of RTS timelines ([3](#B3)). Recent cohort studies suggest that arthroscopy may facilitate earlier RTS in selected patients ([3](#B3)), but consistent superiority over open repair remains inconclusive ([1](#B1),[7](#B7)).

Furthermore, there are no clear recommendations for cases with poor remnant tissue, generalized ligamentous laxity, or revision surgery—settings in which anatomic reconstruction with an autograft or allograft may be preferable ([12](#B12),[15](#B15)). In these contexts, the optimal surgical strategy is often left to the surgeon’s discretion, underscoring the importance of reaching a consensus and establishing standardized treatment frameworks. Similarly, although arthroscopy allows for the treatment of intra-articular lesions at the same time, the prognostic significance of these lesions and how they influence outcomes remains understudied ([16](#B16),[17](#B17)).

Diagnostic pathways continue to evolve as well. History and physical examination remain central, but stress radiography, ultrasonography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are increasingly employed as adjunctive modalities to refine patient selection and preoperative planning ([18](#B18),[19](#B19)). However, there is no universally accepted diagnostic framework, and the lack of a clear distinction of mechanical versus functional instability complicates clinical practice and research comparisons.

Finally, postoperative rehabilitation remains an area of persistent variability, and further research is needed to improve postoperative outcomes. Although early mobilization, weight-bearing progression, and sport-specific retraining are recognized as key factors in functional recovery, there is limited high-level evidence defining optimal timelines ([14](#B14),[20](#B20),[21](#B21)). Therefore, clinicians would benefit from a pragmatic, stepwise framework that integrates diagnosis, patient selection, surgical technique, and rehabilitation milestones into a single cohesive continuum of care ([2](#B2),[19](#B19)).

### Objective

This clinical practice review summarizes the latest evidence and expert recommendations on the arthroscopic management of CLAI to inform daily decision-making. We aim to: (I) outline a practical diagnostic strategy and patient selection criteria; (II) summarize indications, key steps, and expected outcomes for arthroscopic Broström repair versus anatomic ligament reconstruction; and (III) present rehabilitation principles and RTS expectations that are most relevant to orthopedic surgeons and sports medicine clinicians.

---

## Diagnosis and patient selection

An accurate diagnosis of CLAI requires a combination of medical history, physical examination, and imaging studies. Patients typically present with recurrent ankle sprains, lateral ankle pain, swelling, and a subjective feeling of instability ([18](#B18),[22](#B22)). In addition to symptom assessment, functional performance tests have been proposed to objectively evaluate neuromuscular control and postural stability. Jump battery tests may help detect functional deficits not identifiable on imaging studies and assist in distinguishing patients with CLAI from healthy individuals ([23](#B23)). Anterior drawer and talar tilt tests confirm mechanical instability by demonstrating excessive translation or tilt compared to the contralateral side ([24](#B24),[25](#B25)). Stress radiography typically demonstrates increased anterior talar translation and talar tilt compared with the contralateral side, providing objective quantification of mechanical instability ([26](#B26),[27](#B27)). Pathological thresholds have been reported as ≥10 or ≥3 mm side-to-side difference for anterior talar translation and ≥10° or ≥6° side-to-side difference for talar tilt ([18](#B18)). Dynamic ultrasound enables real-time visualization of ATFL elongation, discontinuity, and increased anterior talar translation under stress, allowing functional assessment of ligament laxity ([28](#B28),[29](#B29)). However, unlike stress radiography, no universally accepted cutoff values have been established for ultrasonographic diagnosis of CLAI. Although increased ATFL length under stress and higher ATFL stress-to-rest ratios have been reported in unstable ankles, consensus thresholds have not yet been clearly defined ([18](#B18)). MRI provides detailed assessment of the ATFL, CFL, and associated intra-articular pathology such as osteochondral lesions or synovitis ([30](#B30)-[32](#B32)). In patients with CLAI, MRI commonly demonstrates ligament attenuation and wavy or irregular morphology of the ATFL and CFL rather than complete discontinuity. Attenuated appearance is the most frequent finding. ([32](#B32))

Surgical intervention is generally recommended when CLAI persists for 3 to 6 months despite structured rehabilitation programs focusing on proprioceptive training, strengthening, and bracing support ([13](#B13),[22](#B22),[33](#B33)). High-demand athletes and patients with recurrent injuries despite optimized nonoperative management are prime candidates for surgical treatment, as persistent instability can impair performance and predispose to progressive chondral and osteochondral damage ([19](#B19),[34](#B34)). [*Figure 1*](#figure1) illustrates the diagnostic workflow and patient selection process for CLAI, summarizing the integration of clinical findings, imaging assessments, and indications for surgical treatment. Patients with persistent instability after appropriate rehabilitation, or those with high functional demands and recurrent injuries, are considered surgical candidates.

[![](//cdn.amegroups.cn/journals/aoj/files/journals/28/articles/9878/public/9878-PB5-8078-R1.jpg/w300 "Click on image to zoom")](//cdn.amegroups.cn/static/magazine_modules/imgRender/dist/index.html?imgSource=https://cdn.amegroups.cn/journals/aoj/files/journals/28/articles/9878/public/9878-PB5-8078-R1.jpg)

**Figure 1** Surgical decision flow for arthroscopic management of CLAI. Flowchart illustrating the diagnostic and patient selection process for CLAI. The algorithm integrates clinical history, physical examination, and imaging evaluation to determine surgical indications. Patients with persistent instability despite rehabilitation or high athletic demands are considered candidates for surgical intervention. CLAI, chronic lateral ankle instability.

The preoperative evaluation should also consider factors specific to the patient that influence the choice of surgery. Generalized ligamentous laxity and comorbidities such as collagen disorders may compromise the outcomes of direct repair and should be considered during surgical planning ([35](#B35)-[37](#B37)). In selected patients, augmentation techniques such as suture tape augmentation (internal brace) may provide additional mechanical stability ([38](#B38)). In addition, patients with poor-quality ligament remnants after multiple sprains or revision cases may not be ideal candidates for arthroscopic Broström repair and may benefit from graft-based reconstruction ([39](#B39),[40](#B40)). Therefore, careful intraoperative assessment of ligament tissue quality is essential for selecting the appropriate surgical strategy, as poor remnant quality may necessitate ligament reconstruction rather than direct repair.

In terms of procedure selection, isolated ATFL repair is generally considered in patients with predominant ATFL insufficiency and preserved CFL integrity ([13](#B13),[15](#B15)). Combined ATFL and CFL repair is recommended when severe CLAI is accompanied by a CFL injury or when intraoperative findings suggest combined ligament insufficiency ([41](#B41)-[43](#B43)). Anatomic reconstruction using autografts or allografts may be preferred in patients with generalized ligamentous laxity, poor ligament tissue quality, or revision cases ([12](#B12),[40](#B40)). In selected patients, augmentation techniques such as suture tape augmentation (internal brace) may be considered to provide additional mechanical stability and facilitate early rehabilitation ([38](#B38)).

---

## Arthroscopic surgical techniques

### Arthroscopic Broström repair (with knotted suture anchors)

The arthroscopic Broström repair using knotted suture anchors has become a well-established, minimally invasive alternative to the open Broström-Gould procedure. Standard anteromedial and anterolateral portals are created to allow direct visualization of the ATFL footprint and any concomitant intra-articular pathology. The lateral gutter is debrided to expose the bleeding bone at the origin of the fibula, which promotes ligament healing. One or two knotted suture anchors are placed at the origin of the ATFL on the fibula. Sutures are subsequently passed through the ligament remnant using a suture passer. Knots are tied securely to anatomically reattach and tension the ligament.

Clinical outcomes have shown that this technique provides reliable stability and favorable functional results. Corte-Real *et al.* ([44](#B44)) reported that arthroscopic repair of CLAI provided good clinical results and high patient satisfaction. Similarly, Kim *et al.* ([45](#B45)) demonstrated favorable clinical results using a suture anchor technique for arthroscopic ATFL repair in chronic ankle instability, supporting the reliability of this procedure.

Clinically, this technique offers a reproducible and anatomically precise method for restoring lateral ankle stability while minimizing surgical morbidity, making it an effective option for patients seeking a balance between minimal invasiveness and durable functional recovery.

### Arthroscopic Broström repair (with knotless suture anchors for capsuloligamentous complex fixation)

Recent advances in implant design have led to the use of knotless suture anchors for the arthroscopic Broström procedure, aiming to simplify the repair and eliminate complications related to knot prominence, irritation, or impingement. After creating the standard anteromedial and anterolateral portals, the ATFL’s fibular footprint is prepared through debridement. A knotless anchor is then inserted at the fibular origin, and the suture is passed through the ATFL remnant and capsule, after which it is cinched within the anchor to complete fixation—without extracapsular knot tying. This approach minimizes soft tissue dissection and the amount of implanted material, which can reduce postoperative pain, swelling, and nerve irritation.

Kanzaki *et al.* ([46](#B46)) investigated the clinical outcomes of arthroscopic Broström repair using knotless suture anchors in patients with CLAI. They reported a significant improvement in Japanese Society for Surgery of the Foot (JSSF) ankle-hindfoot scores and a marked increase in all Self-Administered Foot Evaluation Questionnaire (SAFE-Q) subscales, with no recurrent instability observed. The authors emphasized that the use of knotless fixation reduced knot-related complications, enabled early rehabilitation, and allowed a safe RTS activities. Similarly, Shimabukuro *et al.* ([47](#B47)) reported favorable mid-term outcomes following arthroscopic lateral ligament repair using a knotless suture anchor, with significant improvements in JSSF and SAFE-Q scores and no major complications or recurrent instability. Building on this, Teramoto *et al.* ([48](#B48)) reported that an accelerated rehabilitation protocol following arthroscopic ankle lateral ligament repair using knotless anchors enable early weight-bearing and jogging, with 75% of patients returning to sports within 8 weeks maintaining improved mechanical stability.

Collectively, these findings establish the arthroscopic Broström repair with knotless suture anchors as a safe, efficient, and minimally invasive alternative to conventional knotted techniques, providing strong fixation, reduced soft-tissue irritation, and the potential for accelerated rehabilitation and early RTS.

Clinically, this technique offers a simplified surgical procedure that minimizes soft-tissue irritation and provides stable anatomic fixation, thereby promoting early mobilization, accelerating functional recovery, and enabling a safe, timely RTS for active patients.

### All-inside arthroscopic repair

The all-inside arthroscopic Broström repair is a minimally invasive, fully intra-articular evolution of lateral ankle ligament repair that eliminates the need for extracapsular knot-tying because the entire procedure is performed from within the joint. Isolated all-inside arthroscopic ATFL repair is generally indicated in patients with predominant ATFL insufficiency and preserved CFL function. Zhou *et al.* ([49](#B49)) compared their all-inside arthroscopic modified Broström technique, in which both the ATFL and inferior extensor retinaculum are sutured under direct visualization, with the conventional open Broström-Gould procedure. At a minimum follow-up of 2 years, both techniques achieved comparable improvements in pain visual analog scale (VAS), American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS), and Karlsson scores, as well as similar anterior drawer test results. The arthroscopic procedure significantly reduced operative time without increasing complications, demonstrating that it is a safe, reproducible, and minimally invasive alternative to the open approach. Pereira *et al.* ([50](#B50)) described an all-soft, all-knotless arthroscopic Broström repair using suture-based anchors, which reduce hardware prominence and foreign-body reaction risk while providing reliable fixation and favorable functional recovery. Won *et al.* ([51](#B51)) reported that arthroscopic all-inside ATFL repair resulted in significant improvements in clinical outcomes at a minimum 24-month follow-up. Postoperative VAS, foot and ankle outcome score (FAOS), and Karlsson scores improved significantly, indicating favorable outcomes for patients with chronic ankle instability.

### Combined ATFL and CFL repair

CFL repair should be considered in patients with severe CLAI accompanied by a CFL injury, particularly when intraoperative assessment—such as stress radiography after ATFL repair or hook palpation demonstrating loss of mechanical resistance of the ATFL—suggests combined ATFL and CFL insufficiency ([52](#B52),[53](#B53)). Recent clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes after combined ATFL and CFL repair in patients with chronic ankle instability involving both ligaments. Yoshimoto *et al.* ([42](#B42)) demonstrated that combined ATFL and CFL repair significantly reduced the incidence of recurrent ankle instability compared with ATFL-only repair in patients with severe CLAI accompanied by a CFL injury. Similarly, Mao *et al.* ([43](#B43)) reported superior functional outcomes and improved ankle stability after combined ligament repair compared with isolated ATFL repair. In addition, Vega *et al.* ([41](#B41)) showed that arthroscopic all-inside repair of the ATFL and CFL provided excellent functional outcomes and reliable restoration of ankle stability with a low complication rate. Clinically, this technique offers a safe and effective method for restoring lateral ankle stability in patients with combined ligament insufficiency and may reduce the risk of recurrent instability.

Clinically, this technique offers a safe, fully intra-articular, and minimally invasive alternative to open repair, enabling precise anatomic restoration with reduced soft-tissue trauma, fewer complications, and faster functional recovery that facilitates an early RTS.

### Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction

Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction has been developed as an alternative to Broström repair techniques for patients with generalized ligamentous laxity, poor ATFL tissue quality, or failure after primary repair. Reconstruction procedures typically utilize autografts or allografts to restore ankle stability, and recent advances in arthroscopic instrumentation have enabled minimally invasive graft passage and fixation.

Several techniques have been described in the literature. Alayane *et al.* ([40](#B40)) described arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle reconstruction using an extensor hallucis longus (EHL) allograft, which enables precise graft tension control safe anatomic reconstruction of both the ATFL and CFL. Similarly, Pettit *et al.* ([54](#B54)) reported that arthroscopic-assisted reconstruction using suture tape augmentation and knotless all-suture anchors may enhance fixation stability while reducing soft-tissue irritation. Feng *et al.* ([55](#B55)) reported that arthroscopic lateral ligament reconstruction using a semitendinosus autograft demonstrated favorable mid-term functional outcomes, including improvements in AOFAS and Karlsson scores, suggesting reliable mechanical stability.

Taken together, these studies suggest that arthroscopic ligament reconstruction is a safe and effective option in cases unsuitable for direct ligament repair, providing reliable stability and favorable clinical outcomes while minimizing soft-tissue dissection.

From a clinical perspective, this technique offers a valuable solution for complex or revision cases, enabling anatomic restoration of both the ATFL and CFL through a minimally invasive approach that preserves soft tissue, reduces donor-site morbidity, and promotes early functional recovery.

[*Table 1*](#table1) summarizes the arthroscopic surgical techniques for CLAI, comparing key procedural features, fixation methods, and reported clinical outcomes. This overview illustrates the evolution from knotted to knotless and fully arthroscopic all-inside techniques, as well as the role of anatomic ligament reconstruction for revision or complex cases.

### **Table 1**

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

---

## Postoperative rehabilitation

Postoperative rehabilitation is essential for achieving optimal outcomes after surgical treatment for CLAI. Most programs follow a structured, phased approach that progresses from management of swelling and pain to restoring function and performing sport-specific training. Although considerable heterogeneity exists among published protocols, many studies have described progression based on functional criteria rather than fixed timelines, allowing each phase to begin once specific recovery goals are achieved ([14](#B14),[56](#B56),[57](#B57)).

---

## Deltoid ligament (DL) involvement in CLAI

In addition to lateral ligament insufficiency, concomitant injury to the DL has recently gained increasing attention in patients with CLAI ([19](#B19),[58](#B58)). Recent imaging and arthroscopic studies suggest that DL abnormalities may be present in a substantial proportion of patients with CLAI ([59](#B59)), indicating that medial ligament pathology may contribute to persistent instability in some cases. However, the optimal management of these injuries remains controversial ([58](#B58)). While most surgical procedures focus primarily on lateral ligament repair, careful evaluation of the medial structures is recommended, and DL repair or reconstruction may be considered in selected patients with persistent medial instability ([58](#B58)).

---

## Rationale and key considerations

The overarching goals are to (I) protect the surgical construct during the early healing phase, (II) restore range of motion (ROM), (III) regain peroneal and global ankle strength, (IV) enhance proprioception and neuromuscular control, and (V) facilitate a safe and efficient RTS. Early protected mobilization and progressive weightbearing have been shown to promote functional recovery, though excessive acceleration may increase the risk of laxity or complications ([14](#B14),[56](#B56),[60](#B60)).

---

## Evidence summary and rationale

### Immobilization and early protection

Most studies recommend cast, boot or splint immobilization for 10–14 days to promote wound healing and minimize edema ([14](#B14),[56](#B56)). Pearce *et al.* ([56](#B56)) emphasized that a brief immobilization period followed by early mechanical stimulation supports tendon-to-bone healing without increasing complications. However, several studies have reported favorable outcomes with immediate or early full weight-bearing when protected with functional bracing after ligament repair ([20](#B20)). Therefore, postoperative weight-bearing protocols should be individualized depending on fixation strength, concomitant procedures, and patient-specific factors.

### Controlled mobilization

Early mobilization beginning 2–3 weeks postoperatively has been associated with improved AOFAS and Karlsson scores compared with delayed protocols, though at the expense of slightly increased laxity ([60](#B60)). Therefore, gradual dorsiflexion–plantarflexion exercises under protective support are recommended beginning after the initial immobilization period, while inversion-eversion movements should be limited to a restricted ROM (approximately 10–15°) and avoided without protection until 6 weeks postoperatively ([56](#B56)).

### Strengthening and neuromuscular recovery

From 6 weeks postoperatively, progressive closed-chain strengthening and proprioceptive training—including standing heel-rise and foot intrinsic (‘short-foot’) exercises—are recommended to enhance postural control and restore functional stability ([56](#B56),[57](#B57)).

---

## RTS

RTS represents the final phase of postoperative rehabilitation following surgical treatment for CLAI. The optimal timing and criteria for RTS remain subjects of debate; however, most evidence supports a criterion-based progression rather than a strictly time-based schedule. Meta-analyses and cohort studies have demonstrated that RTS is typically achieved between 12 and 16 weeks after anatomic repair, while reconstruction protocols extended up to 20 weeks ([14](#B14),[56](#B56),[57](#B57)). In contrast, several protocols incorporating suture-tape augmentation recommended RTS at 12–16 weeks postoperatively ([14](#B14)).

[*Table 2*](#table2) summarizes the phase-based rehabilitation protocol after surgical treatment for CLAI. This table integrates evidence-based recommendations across each phase—from immobilization to sport-specific retraining—and highlights progression criteria that facilitate safe and effective return to function and sport.

### **Table 2**

**Phase-based postoperative rehabilitation protocol following arthroscopic treatment for CLAI**

  

| Rehabilitation focus | Typical time frame | Key recommendations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immobilization and early protection | 0–2 weeks | Immobilization with cast, boot, or splint for 10–14 days |
| Non-weightbearing or limited partial weightbearing |
| Controlled mobilization | 2–6 weeks | Gradual transition to partial → full weightbearing as tolerated (usually after 2 weeks) |

| Limit inversion-eversion to 10–15° and avoid unprotected movement until 6 weeks |

| Progress to functional unilateral fully weight-bearing exercises, including plyometrics and jogging |

| Sport-specific drills and functional testing |

---

## Current recommendations

Based on current evidence, anatomic direct repair (Broström or modified Broström-Gould procedure) remains the first-line surgical treatment for CLAI. Arthroscopic Broström-Gould repair provides clinical outcomes comparable to those of the open approach while offering the advantages of minimal invasiveness and the ability to simultaneously address concomitant intra-articular pathology. Therefore, it is widely supported as a preferred alternative in appropriately selected patients ([1](#B1),[15](#B15)). Treatment strategies should be individualized according to ligament tissue quality, patient activity level, and associated intra-articular findings. Optimal outcomes depend on accurate diagnosis, meticulous surgical technique, and adherence to a structured postoperative rehabilitation protocol.

---

## Future perspectives

Although arthroscopic management of CLAI has advanced considerably, several important areas warrant further investigation. First, high-quality multicenter randomized controlled trials directly comparing arthroscopic repair, anatomic reconstruction, and augmentation techniques are needed to clarify optimal surgical indications and long-term durability. Standardization of outcome reporting—particularly with regard to RTS criteria, objective functional performance testing, and patient-reported outcome measures—would enhance comparability across studies and strengthen the evidence base. Second, refinement of patient selection remains a priority. Future research should aim to integrate structural imaging findings with dynamic functional assessments, including neuromuscular control, postural stability, and biomechanical analysis. A clearer distinction between mechanical and functional instability would improve diagnostic consistency and treatment algorithms.

Third, emerging biologic and augmentation strategies—such as suture-tape reinforcement, biologic scaffolds, and combined intra-articular procedures—require long-term validation in larger prospective cohorts. While early outcomes appear promising, robust data are necessary to determine their true added value over conventional repair or reconstruction. Finally, rehabilitation protocols should move toward more individualized, criterion-based progression models supported by objective monitoring tools. Advances in wearable technology, motion analysis systems, and performance metrics may enable data-driven rehabilitation and more precise RTS decision-making.

Continued collaborative research efforts will be essential to establish standardized treatment frameworks and optimize patient-specific management strategies in arthroscopic CLAI surgery.

---

## Conclusions

Arthroscopic treatment for CLAI has evolved into a reliable and versatile surgical approach, offering the advantages of minimally invasive access, the ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology, and functional outcomes comparable to those achieved with traditional open techniques. For patients with good-quality ligament tissue, arthroscopic Broström repair is widely used as one of the standard treatment options, demonstrating high rates of RTS and low complication rates. For more complex cases, such as revision surgery, generalized ligamentous laxity, or poor-quality ligament remnants, arthroscopic anatomic reconstruction using autografts or allografts may represent an alternative that shows favorable mid-term results. Achieving optimal outcomes likely depend on careful patient selection, meticulous surgical technique, and adherence to evidence-based rehabilitation protocols. Future high-quality studies with long-term follow-up are necessary to evaluate emerging techniques, such as suture-tape augmentation, biologic scaffolds, and combined procedures, and to develop standardized rehabilitation guidelines.

Arthroscopic management of CLAI should be regarded not merely as a surgical option, but as a comprehensive clinical approach that integrates diagnostic assessment, procedure selection, and postoperative rehabilitation. This review provides a practical, evidence-based framework that connects diagnostic evaluation, surgical decision-making, and postoperative rehabilitation, aiming to support individualized management of CLAI.

Ultimately, individualized treatment strategies grounded in current evidence and tailored to each patient’s specific functional demands may help support and promote durable ankle stability.

args.summary:
This is a clinical practice review article published in the Annals of Joint (Vol 11, July 30, 2026) on the arthroscopic treatment of chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). Authors: Shohei Sano, Yuichi Hoshino, Tetsuya Yamamoto, Noriyuki Kanzaki, and Ryosuke Kuroda from the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine, Japan. Received 17 January 2026, accepted 20 April 2026, published online 17 July 2026. DOI: 10.21037/aoj-2026-1-0008.

BACKGROUND: CLAI is a frequent sequela of acute lateral ligament injury (ATFL and CFL), causing recurrent sprains, pain, and functional limitations, particularly in athletes. While most acute sprains respond to conservative care, approximately 20-30% of patients develop persistent mechanical or functional instability requiring surgery. Open Broström/Broström-Gould repair has been the gold standard with durable results for up to 15 years, but arthroscopic techniques are increasingly popular due to minimally invasive access, ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology (synovitis, loose bodies, cartilage lesions), and comparable outcomes with potentially faster recovery.

DIAGNOSIS AND PATIENT SELECTION: Diagnosis combines history, physical exam (anterior drawer and talar tilt tests), stress radiography (pathological thresholds: ≥10 or ≥3 mm side-to-side difference for anterior talar translation; ≥10° or ≥6° for talar tilt), dynamic ultrasound (no established cutoffs), and MRI (commonly shows ATFL/CFL attenuation rather than complete discontinuity). Surgery is recommended when CLAI persists 3-6 months despite structured rehab. Candidates include high-demand athletes and those with recurrent injuries. Poor tissue quality, generalized ligamentous laxity, collagen disorders, or revision cases may require graft-based reconstruction rather than direct repair.

SURGICAL TECHNIQUES (Table 1 comparison):
1. Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotted suture anchors - reliable stability, high satisfaction (Corte-Real, Kim studies).
2. Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotless anchors - reduces knot irritation/complications, enables early rehab and faster RTS (Kanzaki, Shimabukuro, Teramoto studies; 75% returned to sports within 8 weeks in Teramoto's accelerated protocol).
3. All-inside arthroscopic repair - fully intra-articular, no extracapsular knot-tying; comparable outcomes to open (Zhou study), reduced operative time, significant improvements in VAS, AOFAS, FAOS, and Karlsson scores (Won study).
4. Combined ATFL and CFL repair - indicated in severe CLAI with CFL injury; reduces recurrent instability vs. ATFL-only repair (Yoshimoto, Mao, Vega studies).
5. Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction - for revision, poor tissue, or generalized laxity using autografts/allografts (e.g., EHL, semitendinosus); favorable mid-term outcomes (Alayane, Pettit, Feng studies).

REHABILITATION (Table 2 phase-based protocol): 
- 0-2 weeks: immobilization (cast/boot/splint for 10-14 days).
- 2-6 weeks: controlled mobilization, partial to full weightbearing, gentle dorsiflexion-plantarflexion ROM; limit inversion-eversion to 10-15° until 6 weeks.
- 6-10 weeks: strengthening, proprioception, balance, gait training, plyometrics/jogging.
- 10-16 weeks (repair) or up to 20 weeks (reconstruction): sport-specific drills, RTS typically 12-16 weeks after anatomic repair; 8-12 weeks with suture-tape augmentation.

KEY CONSIDERATIONS: Deltoid ligament involvement is gaining attention in CLAI, though optimal management remains controversial. Current recommendations favor arthroscopic Broström repair as first-line for good-quality tissue, with reconstruction for complex cases. Future research needs multicenter RCTs, standardized outcome reporting, better patient selection integrating structural and functional imaging, and data-driven rehabilitation. The review concludes that arthroscopic CLAI management should be viewed as a comprehensive clinical approach integrating diagnosis, surgical decision-making, and rehabilitation, with individualized, evidence-based treatment strategies.

# Emerging Insights On Surgical Options For Chronic Ankle Instability

[![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment1_1.png)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment1_1.png "Here one can see sutures placed through anchors in the lateral ankle and fibula prior to fixation of the ligaments.")Lateral ankle sprains are very common injuries that foot and ankle specialists frequently treat. An estimated 2 million ankle sprains occur in the United States each year.1 Lateral ankle sprains are common among recreational and competitive athletes.

![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment1_1.png)

The majority of lateral ankle injuries or sprains resolve with conservative therapy. Conservative therapy includes immobilization, rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medication and rehabilitation or physical therapy. However, up to 20 to 40 percent of injuries can lead to prolonged disability and/or recurrent injuries.2 Increased recovery time and recurrent injuries can be frustrating to patients who are eager to return to their physical activity level.

When evaluating a patient with chronic lateral ankle instability, it is important to differentiate whether the patient is suffering from functional or mechanical ankle instability. The typical definition of functional instability is the patient having a feeling of the ankle “giving out” during activity or walking on uneven ground. Patients who present with functional instability typically do not have a true disruption of the ligamentous structure. For these patients, it is normal for anterior drawer and talar tilt stress testing to be negative. Mechanical instability, on the other hand, results from a true disruption of one or more of the lateral ankle ligaments. Patients presenting with mechanical instability will have a positive anterior drawer test with or without talar tilt.

Whether the patient is suffering from functional or mechanical instability, it is also imperative to assess for any other associated pathology. Common associated injuries include peroneal injury, synovitis, arthrofibrosis and the presence of loose bodies or chondral lesions.3 If conservative treatment fails, there are several surgical options that have proven to be very successful with excellent postoperative outcomes.

**A Closer Look At The Broström-Gould Procedure**  
A modified Broström-Gould procedure has become the most routine procedure for primary lateral ankle ligament stabilization. The popularity of the procedure is due to its excellent and reproducible surgical outcomes. The procedure also uses native tissue to stabilize the ankle, which aids in maintaining anatomic foot and ankle mechanics.

At the University Foot and Ankle Institute, our surgical technique involves a curvilinear incision along the distal aspect of the fibula. When there is concomitant peroneal tendon injury, one can extend the incision along the posterior aspect of the fibula, which facilitates examination and repair of peroneal tendons as necessary. Then identify the peroneal sheath and incise it to retract the peroneals inferiorly in order to gain access to the calcaneofibular ligament. Proceed to identify the extensor retinaculum and incise it in order to visualize the anterior talofibular ligament. Reflect the ligament off the distal tip of the fibula and take a small section as needed.

At this time, insert two suture anchors into the fibula and repair the ligaments in a pants-over-vest fashion with FiberWire Suture (Arthrex). We then augment the repair by passing the sutures through an additional PushLock Anchor (Arthrex), which we secure proximally into the fibula. We have found this technique to be advantageous because it provides additional stability.

Cho and coworkers compared the postoperative success of the modified Broström procedure using single versus two suture anchors.4 Their results showed that both techniques provided an effective repair. There was no significant difference in clinical or subjective outcomes. However, the study did reveal slightly more reduction in the talar tilt test postoperatively in the double anchor group.

**Keys To Augmenting The Lateral Ankle Stabilization**

The modified Broström procedure has had excellent results when the native tissue is healthy enough to provide the necessary stability following the repair.3 The disadvantage of using this approach is the utilization of damaged ligamentous and capsular tissue, which may compromise the strength of the repair.

Several techniques have emerged to help augment the anatomic repair with the use of autograft, allograft and synthetic materials. Autograft procedures include the use of peroneal, semitendinosus, plantaris and gracilis tendons. The benefit of using a peroneal graft is there is no secondary operative site morbidity. However, the potential complication is sacrificing strength of the tendon. We typically reserve tendon grafting for revisional surgery when primary stabilization procedure has failed.5-8 The preferred procedure would be to utilize an allograft to perform a more anatomic stabilization procedure.

Mulhern and coworkers described an anatomic reconstruction of the anterior talofibular ligament and calcaneofibular ligament utilizing an acellular dermal matrix with interference screws.5 The authors advocate the use of biologic scaffolding to reinforce the attenuated ligament when there is insufficient soft tissue for a successful direct repair. They utilized the Graftjacket Maxstrip (Wright Medical Technology) to directly recreate the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments.

[![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment2.png)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment2.png "This photo shows a peroneal tear associated with ankle instability prior to repair. Note there is a different incision if peroneal repair is necessary.")The described surgical technique includes placing one end of the allograft in the talar neck with a lateral to medial interference screw. Then one would pull the allograft through the fibular channel and place a second interference screw from posterior to anterior to recreate the anterior talofibular ligament. Pass the allograft from lateral to medial subcutaneously along the lateral aspect of the calcaneus. Then insert a third non-absorbable interference screw under appropriate physiological tension to recreate the calcaneofibular ligament. Utilizing an allograft in the technique described by authors maintains an anatomic repair.5 This preserves physiologic kinematics and motion at the ankle joint.

![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment2.png)

Basra published a technique utilizing the InternalBrace system (Arthrex).9 The system includes #2 FiberTape (Arthrex), which is an ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene fiber blended with long chain synthetic polymers. Surgeons have used this suture tape successfully for rotator cuff and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repairs. The InternalBrace (Arthrex) system also includes BioComposite knotless anchors (Arthrex) for the attachment of suture tape to the talus and fibula. Basra indicates this technique as an alternative to allograft reconstruction in athletic and high-demand patients.

The operative technique includes performing a standard Broström procedure with the foot in a dorsiflexed and everted position. Insert two or three metallic bone anchors into the anterior lateral aspect of the fibula. Then utilize nonabsorbable sutures to imbricate the lateral ankle capsule in a pants-over-vest technique and reapproximate the anterior talofibular ligament with the tarsal and fibular flaps. At this time, utilize the FiberTape to reinforce the Broström procedure, which one would orient in line with the anterior talofibular ligament. Using fluoroscopic guidance, place the 3.4 mm drill along the lateral aspect of the talus in a posterior medial orientation. Tap the hole, load a 4.7 mm SwiveLock BioComposite anchor (Arthrex)with the #2 FiberTape and insert this into the talus.

Then direct attention approximately 1.5 cm proximal to the distal tip of the fibula and utilize a 2.7 mm drill bit in a slight proximal-superior orientation. Tap the drill hole and insert the limbs of the FiberTape with a 3.5 mm SwivelLock anchor. Basra cautions against over-tightening of the FiberTape as it can lead to postoperative stiffness.9 The postoperative protocol is a 14-day period of non-weightbearing in a slightly dorsiflexed and everted position, transitioning to a 14-day period of partial weightbearing in a removable cast boot. The author has found that on average, patients are able to begin passive range of motion exercises approximately 14 days postoperatively.

It is essential to critically evaluate the native soft tissues and augment the repair if necessary. Regardless of the material utilized for augmentation of the repair, surgeons must take care to maintain proper anatomic positioning and physiologic motion at the ankle and subtalar joint. Exercise caution when performing the repair as overtightening can result in ankle joint stiffness and a less than optimal surgical outcome. Postoperative management should include a comprehensive physical therapy and rehabilitation protocol.

**[![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment3.png)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment3.png "Here one can see a double bundle repair with anchors in the distal fibula and an adjunct anchor in the lateral fibula for two points of fixation. Note the small incision for ligament repair only.")Assessing Related Joint And Tendon Pathology**  
Patients who present with chronic ankle instability commonly have associated joint and tendon pathology. A thorough history and physical exam are essential to evaluate for any pathology that one should address during surgical intervention. Our standard evaluation includes stress testing, assessment of the peroneal tendons for any subluxation or entrapment, and preoperative MRI. It is also important to consider each patient’s physical demands and desired functional outcome. We routinely perform an ankle arthroscopy in combination with all lateral ankle stabilization procedures.

![](https://s3.amazonaws.com/HMP/hmp_ln/imported/pt0315treatment3.png)

Komenda and Ferkel found that in 52 ankles with chronic ankle instability, 93 percent of the ankles exhibited intra-articular pathology with the most common finding being synovitis followed by the presence of loose bodies.3 With arthroscopic evaluation, Lee and colleagues found that 28 patients with chronic lateral ankle instability had intra-articular pathology including synovitis, talar cartilage fibrillation, talar dome cartilage defects, loose bodies, Bassett’s lesion, anterolateral impingement and distal anterior tibial osteophytosis.10

We have found the use of ankle arthroscopy to be beneficial for the debridement of synovitis, removal of any scar tissue and adhesions, and resection of any associated osteophytes. We also advocate for visual inspection of the peroneal tendons intraoperatively to evaluate for any associated injury. If there is any peroneal damage, we primarily repair it at this time.

**In Conclusion**  
Although the majority of ankle sprains resolve with conservative therapy, a significant number of patients go on to develop chronic ankle instability. Prolonged disability and recurrent ankle sprains are frustrating for both recreational and elite athletes. Chronic lateral ankle instability is a common and complicated complaint that requires thorough evaluation and surgical planning. It is essential to critically assess for any associated intra-articular and peroneal pathology. Clinicians should ensure a thorough history and physical examination, including stress testing, peroneal evaluation and MRI. One should repair any associated pathology during surgical intervention. Advances in surgical technology and techniques have aided anatomic repair and improved surgical outcomes.

*[Dr. Baravarian](https://docsfootankle.com/dr-bob-baravarian-los-angeles-podiatrist/) is an Assistant Clinical Professor at the UCLA School of Medicine. He is the Chief of Podiatric Foot and Ankle Surgery at the Santa Monica UCLA Medical Center and Orthopedic Hospital, and is the Director of the University Foot and Ankle Institute in Los Angeles.*
