**Journal:** Apunts Educación Física y Deportes, Issue 145 (3rd Quarter, July-September 2021)  
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.5672/apunts.2014-0983.es.(2021/3).145.08

**Background & Rationale:**  
Basketball involves explosive actions (accelerations, jumps, changes of direction) placing high demands on the ankle joint. The ankle is the most commonly injured area in athletes. Nearly 80% of athletes with an ankle sprain may sustain repetitive sprains, and ~72% may develop chronic instability. Basketball players are five times more likely to sustain an ankle injury after a previous one, with a 73% recurrence rate. Players with less lower-limb strength and fewer neuromuscular/proprioception abilities are at greater risk.

**Objective:**  
To propose a weekly ankle-specific neuromuscular warm-up program for elite basketball teams, integrated into pre-training warm-up sessions.

**Key Epidemiological Data:**  
- Ankle joint injuries in sports account for 11%–17% of all injuries.  
- Elite players cover ~73 m·min⁻¹, ~3 m·min⁻¹ at high-speed running (>18 km/h), with ~4 accelerations/decelerations >2 m/s² per minute, ~0.2 jumps >3Gs per minute, and ~1.3 impacts >8Gs per minute.

**Proposed Exercises (9 exercises, performed as a circuit in pairs):**  
1. **Ankle Mobility (Figure 1):** Standing, one foot on a box with elastic band at floor height below the malleoli; active dorsiflexion, heel grounded. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
2. **Peroneal Muscles in CKC (Figure 2):** Foot half-on platform; touch floor with free side of foot (eccentric → concentric eversion). 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
3. **Tibialis Posterior in CKC (Figure 3):** Same setup but performing inversion movement. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
4. **Plantar Flexion in CKC on Airex (Figure 4):** One leg on Airex, knee bent 30°–70°, perform concentric plantar flexion and eccentric dorsiflexion. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
5. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 1 (Figure 5):** Stand on one foot on unstable platform (Pielaster); perform diagonal rotational patterns with a soft medicine ball. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
6. **Single-foot Functional Exercise 2 (Figure 6):** One foot on Pielaster; perform hip and upper body flexion to 90° with opposite leg extended (single-leg deadlift). Optional Mini Band between knees. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
7. **Lateral Movement (Figure 7):** Elastic band on hip secured to stable surface; perform two lateral steps at high speed against band resistance. 2 sets of 6–8 reps.  
8. **Footwork with Competitive Movement (Figure 8):** Two players 4.9 m apart; perform footwork on coordination ladder then sprint to a marked space (1.5 m on free-throw line). 2 sets of 3 reps, competitive.  
9. **Progression:** Include perturbations (teammate unbalancing) and simple decision-making.

**Practical Application:**  
The program is designed to be integrated into a typical competition week schedule as part of the regular team warm-up. A holistic approach is recommended, with coaches, strength coaches, medical staff, and players sharing responsibility.

**Conclusions:**  
This proposal provides an example of ankle joint neuromuscular exercises for pre-basketball warm-up. It offers physiotherapists and strength/conditioning professionals practical exercises and a weekly organization framework for elite professional basketball, aiding injury prevention strategies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Comparison of the Effect of Resistance and Balance Training on Isokinetic Eversion Strength, Dynamic Balance, Hop Test, and Ankle Score in Ankle Sprain ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/11/4/307

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in the journal *Life* (2021, Volume 11, Issue 4, Article 307) titled "Comparison of the Effect of Resistance and Balance Training on Isokinetic Eversion Strength, Dynamic Balance, Hop Test, and Ankle Score in Ankle Sprain" by Haifang Wang, Hailong Yu, Yong Hwan Kim, and Wencong Kan.

**Purpose:** To compare the rehabilitation effects of resistance training (RT) versus balance training (BT) in patients with recurrent ankle sprain who are non-professional athletes.

**Methods:** 54 patients with recurrent lateral ankle sprain were assigned to either RT (n=27) or BT (n=27). RT consisted of exercises using elastic tube bands (Therabands) of progressive resistance. BT consisted of exercises on unstable surfaces (TOGU DYNAAIR, BOSU, or pillows). Both programs were home-based, performed for 6 weeks, twice daily for 20 minutes, 5 days per week. Outcome measures included: isokinetic eversion strength (30°/s and 120°/s), Y-Balance Test (YBT), four hop tests (single, triple, crossover, 6-m timed), and the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS) questionnaire.

**Key Results:**
- Both RT and BT significantly improved isokinetic eversion strength (absolute and relative) and dynamic balance (p < 0.05).
- BT showed significantly greater improvement in the crossover hop test compared to RT (p = 0.008).
- BT demonstrated significantly greater improvement in YBT total score (p = 0.002) and posterior medial (p < 0.001) and posterior lateral (p < 0.001) directions.
- FAOS scores showed significantly greater improvements in the BT group for pain (p = 0.022), sports function (p = 0.027), and quality of life (p = 0.033).
- Both groups improved significantly across most measures from pre- to post-training.

**Conclusions:** Six weeks of home-based RT and BT both improved eversion strength, lower extremity hop function, and subjective ankle assessment. However, BT was more effective than RT in improving dynamic balance, crossover hop test performance, pain relief, and return to sporting activities. The authors recommend BT for patients who need to return to sports or who experience pain and reduced quality of life due to recurrent ankle sprain, while RT may be safer for fall-prone patients.
</summary>

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12576729

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a cross-sectional study published in World Journal of Orthopedics (2025) that establishes normative isokinetic ankle strength values for healthy, physically active adults. The study evaluated 200 ankles (100 participants: 69 males, 31 females; mean age 38.5 ± 13.5 years; mean BMI 25.8 ± 4.2) using the Biodex 3 System, assessing eversion, inversion, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion at 30°/s (torque) and 120°/s (power).

**Key Findings:**
- **Mean maximum torque (N/m) by gender:** Eversion: 22.3 (F) / 33.4 (M); Inversion: 30.0 (F) / 37.0 (M); Dorsiflexion: 37.4 (F) / 53.6 (M); Plantar Flexion: 100.4 (F) / 158.1 (M). All gender differences were statistically significant (P < 0.001).
- **Agonist/antagonist ratios:** Evertors/invertors = 88.8%; Dorsiflexors/plantar flexors = 36.1%.
- **Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) and Muscular Deficiency Index (MDI):** Both were balanced between sides (>90%) for all movements, with average global differences <10%.
- No significant correlation between age or BMI and maximum torque was found.
- The non-dominant side was consistently stronger for eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion.

**Clinical Significance:** The study fills a gap in ankle normative data, providing gender-specific reference values. The authors propose that LSI and MDI thresholds above 90%—similar to established knee criteria—can serve as objective benchmarks for rehabilitation planning and return-to-activity assessment after ankle injuries. The MDI is introduced as a novel composite index considering torque, power, and work across movements.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Ankle Eversion Strength Test Summary

This webpage from MAT Assessment provides a comprehensive guide to the Ankle Eversion Strength Test, an isometric force assessment measuring how much force a client can produce when turning the sole of the foot outward (eversion) against resistance using the Muscle Meter dynamometer.

## Key Details

**Purpose:** Measures eversion force output from lateral ankle muscles (fibularis longus and brevis) in a controlled isometric setup. Useful for side-to-side ankle strength comparison, lateral ankle capacity, balance, running, cutting, landing assessment, and progress tracking.

**Primary Metric:** Peak force is the main routine metric. Force as percentage of body weight can be used if directly calculated. Rate of force development and time to peak are relevant for rapid ankle control tasks (cutting, landing, change-of-direction). Impulse is relevant for sustained force; fatigue index for repeated efforts.

**Step-by-Step Protocol:**
1. Prepare client with explanation and submaximal practice trial
2. Set client position (seated with hip/knee flexed, ankle near neutral is common)
3. Set up device or straps (handheld or strap-stabilised)
4. Place device against lateral forefoot near fifth metatarsal
5. Stabilise lower leg to prevent compensation
6. Give consistent instructions (e.g., "Turn your foot outward into the device as hard as you can")
7. Record 1-2 practice trials, then 2-3 maximal trials of 3-5 seconds with 30-60 second rest
8. Identify invalid trials (hip rotation, knee movement, device slip, compensation)
9. Record symptoms (pain, cramping, paraesthesia, apprehension)

**Reference Values:** Published comparison values for chronic ankle instability: approximately **141.2–175.5 N** (roughly 14-18 kg). Manual testing may be less consistent above ~120 N due to tester strength limitations. A side-to-side difference of ~10% or more warrants closer review.

**Key Limitations:** The test does not diagnose ankle instability, tendon injury, nerve involvement, pain, balance risk, or readiness for sport/work on its own. Results are setup-dependent and should be interpreted alongside symptoms, functional tasks, and clinical context.

**Reliability:** Repeatability improves with standardised setup. Belt-stabilised dynamometry has shown reliable results for ankle inversion/eversion in healthy adults.

## Practical Interpretation Priorities
1. Compare with client's own baseline
2. Compare right and left sides
3. Compare eversion with inversion
4. Consider symptoms during/after testing
5. Consider confidence and effort quality
6. Review compensations
7. Compare with related strength/mobility tests
8. Relate to client's sport/work/daily demands
9. Retest under same conditions
10. Do not use reference values as pass/fail criteria
</summary>

One HHD paper noted that when forces are above about 120 N, tester strength may affect the measured value., The test should support assessment reasoning. It should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic or clearance measure.

--- SOURCE 6: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter: Reliability, Discriminant Validity, and Predictive Validity | Published in International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy ---
URL: https://ijspt.scholasticahq.com/article/27634-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis-of-the-y-balance-test-lower-quarter-reliability-discriminant-validity-and-predictive-validity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Y-Balance Test Lower Quarter (YBT-LQ)

**Published:** October 01, 2021, in *IJSPT* (Vol. 16, Issue 5, pp. 1190-1209)
**Authors:** Plisky P, Schwartkopf-Phifer K, Huebner B, Garner MB, Bullock G
**DOI:** 10.26603/001c.27634 | **PMCID:** PMC8486397 | **PMID:** 34631241

### Purpose
To review the reliability of the YBT-LQ, determine if performance varies among populations (sex, sport/activity, competition level), and determine injury risk identification validity based on asymmetry, individual reach direction performance, or composite score.

### Methods
- Systematic review of 10 databases from inception to October 30, 2019
- 57 studies included: 9 assessing reliability, 36 assessing population differences, 16 assessing injury prediction
- Quality assessed using modified Downs and Black scale and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale

### Key Results

**Reliability:**
- Intra-rater reliability: 0.85-0.91 in adult populations; 0.57-0.82 in adolescents
- Inter-rater reliability ICCs: 0.81-1.00
- Test-retest reliability ICCs: 0.63-0.93

**Sex Differences:**
- Posteromedial reach: Males 109.6 (95%CI 107.4-111.8) vs Females 102.3 (95%CI 97.2-107.4); p=0.01
- Posterolateral reach: Males 107.0 (95%CI 105.0-109.1) vs Females 102.0 (95%CI 97.8-106.2); p=0.036
- No significant sex differences in anterior reach or composite score

**Sport Differences:**
- Soccer vs Basketball: Significant differences in all reach directions and composite score (Soccer composite: 97.6; Basketball: 92.8; p<0.01)
- Baseball vs Basketball: Significant differences in posteromedial, posterolateral, and composite score (Baseball composite: 97.4; Basketball: 92.8; p=0.02)

**Competition Level:** No significant differences observed when competition level was considered alone (middle school, high school, college, professional).

**Injury Prediction:**
- Anterior reach asymmetry (≥4cm): OR of 2.20 (95%CI 1.09-4.46) in one study (Smith et al.)
- Posteromedial asymmetry (≥4cm): OR of 3.86 (95%CI 1.46-10.95) in male soccer players (Gonell et al.)
- Composite score: Only 1 of 13 studies found a relationship (Butler et al., OR 3.5 using cutoff of 89.6%)
- Due to heterogeneity, meta-analysis of injury prediction data was not possible

### Conclusions
The YBT-LQ is a reliable dynamic neuromuscular control test with moderate to high quality evidence. Significant differences in performance exist by sex and sport. If general cut points are used (not population-specific), the YBT-LQ may not be predictive of injury. Clinical population-specific requirements (age, sex, sport/activity) should be considered when interpreting YBT-LQ performance, particularly for injury risk identification.
</summary>

This prospective cohort study published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (2018) investigated whether static balance, dynamic balance, ankle range of motion, BMI, or history of ankle sprain were associated with ankle sprain injuries in collegiate athletes. Baseline measures included the Y-Balance Test (YBT), modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS), weight-bearing lunge test (WBLT), BMI, and ankle sprain history. Participants were followed for up to two years.

A total of 59 individuals (38 males, 21 females) sustained ankle sprains. For male athletes, binary logistic regression revealed that BMI (OR=3.85; 95% CI: 1.90-7.79) and anterior reach of the YBT (OR=3.64; 95% CI: 1.83-7.23) were significantly associated with ankle sprain injury. Male athletes with both elevated BMI (≥30.2) and decreased YBT anterior reach (≤54.4%) had 4.84 times greater odds of sustaining an ankle sprain. No variables were significantly associated with ankle sprain injury in female athletes. The study concludes that YBT anterior reach and BMI are useful variables for guiding ankle sprain injury prevention in male collegiate athletes, but other risk factors should be explored for female athletes.

<summary>
# Lower Quarter Y-Balance Test (LQYBT) - Summary

## Overview
The Y Balance Test (YBT) is a component of the Functional Movement Systems screen used to evaluate dynamic balance and functional symmetry for injury risk assessment and return-to-sport readiness. It was developed from the Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) and assesses single-leg balance while reaching in three directions: anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral. The YBT follows a specific protocol using standardized instrumentation requiring online training certification.

**Acronym:** LQYBT  
**Cost:** $269.95 (Not Free)

**Required Training:** Training Course

<summary>
This is a narrative review article published in the Premier Journal of Science (July 15, 2025) by Kanwal et al., examining load management for injury prevention in elite athletes. The review synthesizes evidence on key concepts including the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR), wearable technology monitoring, periodization strategies, return-to-play protocols, and recovery factors.

Key findings include:
- **ACWR Framework**: A "sweet spot" of 0.8–1.3 is proposed to minimize injury risk, with ratios below 0.8 (undertraining) or above 1.5 (danger zone) associated with elevated injury risk. However, recent evidence, including a 10-month RCT in elite youth football, found no significant injury reduction using ACWR-guided management, and the model faces criticism for mathematical coupling and methodological issues.
- **Wearable Technology**: GPS trackers and inertial measurement units enable precise external load monitoring. Metrics like PlayerLoad help identify overload risk, but athletes with higher chronic workloads demonstrate better tolerance to acute spikes.
- **Periodization**: Structured training organization (macrocycles, mesocycles, microcycles) with planned recovery phases (e.g., 3:1 loading cycles) helps prevent overuse injuries. Linear periodization improved performance without elevating injury rates in military cadets.
- **Return-to-Play**: Gradual load progression (10–30% increments) with objective criteria across four phases (rehabilitation, reconditioning, full-intensity practice, competition) is recommended to reduce reinjury risk.
- **Sleep & Recovery**: Adolescent athletes sleeping less than 8 hours nightly had a 1.7-fold increased injury risk. Partial sleep deprivation reduces endurance, strength, and speed.
- **Individual Factors**: Biomechanics, sex, age, injury history, and fitness level critically shape injury risk. Female athletes have higher ACL injury rates; youth athletes need age-appropriate training limits.

The review concludes that effective load management requires a multifactorial, individualized approach integrating training metrics, recovery strategies, and athlete characteristics. No single metric suffices; the goal is combining insights from biomechanics, psychology, nutrition, and sleep. The authors note ongoing debates about predictive injury analytics (limited by high false-positive rates) and the tension between optimizing performance versus minimizing injury risk.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)

## Overview
Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) is a condition that develops in approximately 20% of patients following an acute ankle sprain, with two million lateral ankle sprains occurring annually in the United States. It involves both mechanical instability (motion exceeding normal physiological limits) and functional instability (sensorimotor/neuromuscular deficits).

## Clinical Presentation
- History of recurrent ankle sprains and severe inversion injuries
- Decreased proprioception due to mechanoreceptor loss
- Muscle weakness, particularly eccentric evertor weakness and concentric invertor strength deficits
- Postural control deficits, altered reflex responses, and efferent motor control deficits

## Predictors of CAI
- Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT) - particularly posteromedial reach
- Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) - particularly ADL subscale
- Combined use of SEBT and FAAM can predict CAI likelihood

## Diagnostic Procedures
- Physical examination: Anterior drawer test, talar tilt test, peroneal strength testing
- Proprioception testing: Modified Romberg test
- MRI is most useful for imaging, though limited by cost and availability
- International Ankle Consortium has established updated selection criteria

## Outcome Measures
- Patient-reported: Lower Extremity Functional Scale, Foot Function Index, FAAM, Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool
- Objective tests: Star Excursion Balance Test, Y Balance Test

## Management/Interventions
- **Conservative**: Balance training, progressive loading/isokinetic strengthening, bracing for high-risk activities
- **Surgical**: Broström procedure (primary ligament repair), tendon grafts, arthroscopy when conservative management fails

## Associated Lesions
- Sinus Tarsi Syndrome
- Osteochondral Defects (talus)
- Peroneal Tendinopathy
- Subtalar Instability
</summary>

About 20% of acute ankle sprain patients develop chronic ankle instability, Two million lateral ankle sprains occur annually in the United States, CAI includes mechanical instability (motion exceeds normal physiological limits) and functional instability (objectively stable with subjective feelings of instability related to sensorimotor or neuromuscular deficits), The main causes of chronic ankle instability that have been found are: decreased proprioceptive abilities because of a loss of mechanoreceptors and decreased muscle strength of invertor and evertor muscles, The combination of the SEBT as a predictor of dynamic balance in combination with the Foot and Ankle Ability measure as a patient self reported outcome can predict the likelihood of CAI

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review and expert opinion published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (May 26, 2022) that identifies the most relevant functional performance tests and self-reported questionnaires to help clinicians make valid return to sport (RTS) decisions in patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI). 

**Key Background:** Lateral ankle sprain is the most common sports injury, with up to 40% of patients developing CAI. Premature RTS may contribute to high recurrence rates. Currently, there are no specific, objectively validated criteria with cut-off scores to guide RTS decisions in this population.

**Methods:** An exhaustive literature review was conducted across PubMed, PEDro, Cochrane Library, and ScienceDirect. Tests and questionnaires were selected based on their ability to differentiate CAI patients from copers or healthy individuals, reliability, clinical relevance, and practicality for daily use.

**Key Findings and Recommended Tests:**

1. **Single Leg Stance Test (firm surface):** Assesses static postural control. Proposed cut-off: <3 errors. Interrater ICC = 0.93, MDC = 0.6 errors.

2. **Foot Lift Test:** Similar to SLS but 30s duration focusing on foot displacements. Proposed cut-off: <5 lifts. ICC = 0.73-0.97.

3. **Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT):** Assesses dynamic postural control. Proposed cut-off scores: Composite score >90%, Anterior asymmetry <4.5% or <4cm, Posteromedial >91%, Posterolateral >91%.

4. **Side Hop Test:** 10 lateral/medial hops over 30cm. Proposed cut-off: <10 seconds. ICC = 0.84, MDC = 5.82s.

5. **Figure-of-8 Hop Test:** 20m figure-8 pattern. Proposed cut-off: <12 seconds. ICC = 0.95, MDC = 4.59s.

6. **Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM):** Self-reported function. Proposed cut-off: 95% for both ADL and Sport subscales. ICC = 0.89 (ADL), 0.87 (Sport). MCID = 8 (ADL), 9 (Sport).

7. **Ankle Ligament Reconstruction-Return to Sport after Injury (ALR-RSI):** Psychological readiness. Proposed cut-off: 55/120. ICC = 0.92, MDC = 10 points.

**Conclusions:** A combination of the SEBT and Side Hop Test has the greatest clinical value. The authors recommend combining FAAM and ALR-RSI questionnaires with functional tests. However, objective scientific criteria with cut-off scores are still lacking. Additional considerations include ankle evertor strength testing, neurocognitive functional testing, and sport-specific testing. The proposed test cluster should be used within the broader RTS continuum (return to participation → return to sport → return to performance).
</summary>

URL: https://www.physiotutors.com/return-to-sport-ankle-sprain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from Physiotutors (written by Ellen Vandyck, Research Manager, on August 2, 2021) discusses return to sport (RTS) criteria after an acute lateral ankle sprain. The article notes that lateral ankle sprains are among the most common musculoskeletal injuries in athletes with high recurrence rates, and that no clear RTS criteria had been established, which may explain high recurrence and ongoing symptoms like instability or "giving way." The decision-making process for clearing an athlete to RTS is classified into five domains: (1) Pain – pain severity during sport and over last 24 hours; (2) Ankle impairments – range of motion, muscle strength, endurance and power; (3) Athlete perception – perceived stability, confidence, psychological readiness; (4) Sensorimotor control – proprioception and dynamic postural control, including control on unstable surfaces, jumping/landing, and unpredictable situations; (5) Sport/functional performance – hopping, jumping, agility, sport-specific activities, ultimately culminating in completing a full training session as the final criterion. The clinical application section notes that no clear cutoff values have been defined. Pain can be measured with numeric rating scale or visual analog scale; ankle ROM can be evaluated via active/passive ROM assessment (with linked YouTube videos). Athlete perception measurement is more subjective, requiring good therapeutic relationship and open communication, with decisions made together with the athlete and team. Functional movement evaluation in predictable and unpredictable situations gives an idea of proprioception and postural control. The framework is based on the PAASS framework from an international multidisciplinary consensus study (Smith et al. 2021). The article references: Smith MD et al., "Return to sport decisions after an acute lateral ankle sprain injury: introducing the PAASS framework-an international multidisciplinary consensus," Br J Sports Med. 2021 Nov;55(22):1270-1276.
</summary>

**Abstract:** Ankle sprain injuries are common during sporting activities, and the risk for additional ankle sprain increases after the initial injury. Multiple studies indicate that wearing an ankle brace can reduce the incidence of ankle sprains in sports such as football, basketball, volleyball, and soccer. This reduction has been demonstrated for lace-up braces, semirigid ankle braces, and rigid braces. Two recent studies describe reduced ankle sprain incidence for individuals wearing lace-up braces with straps. While more recent studies include multiple brace types, studies examining recovery from acute ankle sprain that include ankle bracing as part of management typically use a semirigid ankle brace.

**Related papers cited on the page provide key supporting evidence on ankle sprain prevention:**
- A systematic review (Reyes, 2010) found ankle braces reduced ankle sprain by 69% (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.18-0.51) and ankle tape by 71% (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.14-0.57) among previously injured athletes; no type of support was superior.
- A three-arm RCT (Verhagen, 2014) with 384 athletes found bracing was superior to neuromuscular training in reducing recurrence of ankle sprains (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.29-0.97), though not severity.
- A systematic review (Verhagen, 2010) found taping, bracing, and neuromuscular training were all effective for prevention of ankle sprain recurrences (RRs 0.2-0.5 vs. controls), with effects largely driven by previously injured athletes; recommended combining external prophylactic measures with neuromuscular training.
- A systematic review (Branche/Gilchrist, AJSM) recommended athletes with moderate/severe sprains wear an appropriate orthosis for at least 6 months.
- Studies on performance effects (Kimura 1994, McMorrow 1995) found ankle braces did not significantly impair speed, agility, or vertical jump performance.
- A systematic review (Evans, 2012) identified bracing as the best and cheapest intervention to prevent ankle sprains.
- A 2019 study (Ihmels) compared a novel Ankle Roll Guard against existing prophylactics.

**Cited-by paper:** A 2023 study (Gulick, Foot and Ankle Specialist) examined anterior ankle translation with braces, finding both TayCo and Aircast braces significantly constrained anterior talus translation vs. control; TayCo (permitting 51-52% of control translation) was significantly better than Aircast (58-59%).

**References (17)** include key studies on ankle sprain incidence, brace effectiveness in various sports, and treatment/recovery studies.

The paper is categorized under Medicine and Health Sciences / Physical Therapy, Sports Therapy and Rehabilitation, with related topics including Medicine, Ankle Sprain, and Sports and Health.

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044595

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review with meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (June 2018, Vol 13, Issue 3, pp. 379-388; PMID: 30038824; PMCID: PMC6044595) by Rachel Bellows (PT, DPT, OCS, Stanford Health Care) and Christopher Kevin Wong (PT, PhD, OCS, Columbia University). The study compares the effectiveness of ankle bracing and balance training in reducing ankle sprain incidence and relative risk among competitive athletes.

BACKGROUND: Approximately 23,000-25,000 ankle sprains occur daily in the US, costing $2 billion annually in healthcare. Inversion sprains comprise 80% of cases. Basketball accounts for 41% of emergency department ankle sprain visits, football 9.3%, and soccer 7.9%. Prior ankle sprains increase subsequent risk by 70%.

METHODS: The review searched four databases (Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro) for English-language RCTs published from 2005-2016. Inclusion criteria required PEDro scores ≥5 (moderate quality), competitive high school or higher-level athletes, one-year and/or post-season follow-up, and non-treatment control groups. From 1,832 citations screened, 71 full-text articles were reviewed, and 8 were included.

KEY RESULTS: The 8 included studies covered 7,195 athletes (36% female, 64% male; median age 20 years) across basketball (36%), football (29%), volleyball (16%), and soccer (1%).

- BRACING: Based on 3,581 subjects, athletes wearing braces had significantly fewer ankle sprains (p=0.0037) and a 64% reduced risk (RR=0.36) compared to controls. Braces used included McDavid Ultralight, Don-Joy Ankle Stabilizing, and Sports Stirrup braces.
- BALANCE TRAINING: Based on 3,577 subjects, athletes performing balance training had significantly fewer sprains (p=0.0057) and a 46% reduced risk (RR=0.54) compared to controls. Five of six balance training studies showed significant reduction.

DISCUSSION: Bracing results (64% risk reduction) were consistent with a prior review showing 69% reduction; balance training results (35-38% reduction) aligned with earlier findings of 36% risk reduction. Notably, although bracing reduced ankle injury risk by 64%, overall lower extremity injury risk was only reduced by 25.5%, and basketball players who braced had an 85% increased rate of lower extremity injuries and higher knee injury rates (17.9% vs. 8.8%)—possibly due to increased knee internal rotation and compression forces during cutting tasks. The balance training incidence was 10.6% versus 24.6% for bracing, though the relative risk was lower for bracing (0.36 vs. 0.54). Only the smallest study (n=80) directly compared the two interventions, preventing firm conclusions about which is more effective.

CONCLUSION: The review provides moderate-quality evidence (Level 1a) supporting both bracing and balance training to reduce ankle sprain incidence and risk in competitive athletes. Clinicians can use this information to educate patients on prevention strategies. Limitations include study heterogeneity, lack of blinding, and inability to analyze subgroups by prior injury history or competition level.
</summary>

The tested ankle is moved gradually backwards, and the participant lunges forward so the knee touches the wall without the heel lifting off the floor. Each centimetre corresponds to approximately 3.6° of ankle dorsiflexion. **Key Movements:** The ankle is a complex of joints, not a simple hinge. Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur in the sagittal plane primarily via the talocrural joint, while inversion and eversion occur in the frontal plane via the subtalar joint. **Measurement Protocol:** The goniometer remains the gold-standard tool. For talocrural measurements, the patient should be supine or seated with the knee bent to 90 degrees (to reduce gastrocnemius influence), with the subtalar joint in neutral position. The goniometer fulcrum sits on the lateral malleolus, the stationary arm aligns with the head of the fibula, and the moving arm aligns with the fifth metatarsal shaft. The Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT) measures functional dorsiflexion and has demonstrated high reliability (ICC up to 0.99 in some studies). URL: https://mtrigger.com/blogs/latest-articles/the-value-of-hop-testing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from mTrigger (written by Kaysha Bates) discusses the value of backwards, medial, and lateral hop testing for assessing return-to-sport readiness after knee injuries, particularly ACL reconstruction. While standard single leg hop, triple hop, and cross over hop tests with the traditional 90% limb symmetry index (LSI) have been gold standards, experts argue they grossly overestimate knee function and readiness.

Background: When hop testing occurs 6+ months after knee injury, the non-operative limb has undergone deconditioning, so comparison should ideally be made against pre-surgical baselines. Even passing hop tests at 6 months present an independent risk factor for re-injury. Standard tests are criticized for being straight-plane movements that fail to evaluate multiplanar performance demands.

Expert Opinion: mTrigger co-founder and ACL expert Russ Paine advocates a backwards hop test to highlight the importance of the quadriceps muscle for deceleration. A 2021 study (Ebert et al.) found that athletes passing with >90% LSI on standard hop tests struggled to meet passing criteria for single leg medial and lateral hop tests.

Clinical Application: Using mTrigger biofeedback, the author measured limb symmetry indices for multidirectional hops: Medial Hop LSI = 50%, Lateral Hop LSI = 80.1%, and Backward Hop LSI = 88.4%. Despite passing standard hop testing, these athletes showed LSI <90%, with significantly higher peak landing activation on the uninvolved side, indicating insufficient protective quad activation and deceleration. Reduced quadriceps strength is cited as a reason only 50-65% of athletes return to pre-injury level after ACL reconstruction.

Conclusion: Standardized hop testing underestimates athlete readiness to return to play. Medial, lateral, and backwards hopping may help detect multiplanar deficiencies. Using mTrigger biofeedback, hop testing can provide information on quad muscle activation capacity and load acceptance, and biofeedback can be used during exercise to improve activation levels, accuracy, and effort to maximize outcomes.
</summary>

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

Three rounds of Tavily web searches were conducted:

**Round 1 (dimension-scoping searches):**
