URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1466853X25002056

SUMMARY:
# EFFECTS OF COMBINED KINESIOLOGY TAPING AND PROPRIOCEPTIVE TRAINING ON BALANCE AND PROPRIOCEPTION IN ATHLETES WITH CHRONIC ANKLE INSTABILITY: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL. Proprioceptive training programs that include balance, postural control, and neuromuscular exercises have consistently shown beneficial effects on balance, ankle function, and sport-related technical skills in individuals with CAI (Hall et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2025). In CAI, where proprioceptive and sensorimotor function are likely impaired, increasing cutaneous afferent input via KT during a proprioceptive training program may theoretically augment central sensorimotor integration and improve balance and joint position sense beyond the effects of exercise alone. Individually, both KT and proprioceptive training have been reported to improve proprioception balance, postural control, and ankle function in healthy adults, adults with CAI and in other lower-limb conditions (Binaei et al. 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Sarvestan et al., 2020), although results across studies are inconsistent and sometimes show minimal or no additional benefit over control conditions (Yin & Wang, 2020) Likewise, proprioceptive and multicomponent training programs have proven effective in improving balance and functional outcomes in people with CAI (Gidu et al., 2022; Harry-Leite et al., 2022; Domeika et al., 2020; Zouita et al. Despite the popularity of KT in sports and rehabilitation settings, there is still uncertainty about whether adding KT to a proprioceptive training program provides any clinically meaningful functional advantage in athletes with CAI. Therefore, the aim of this randomized controlled study was to determine whether combining these interventions leads to superior improvements in ankle joint position sense, static (assessed with the Balance Error Scoring System) and dynamic balance (assessed with the Y-Balance Test) in athletes with chronic ankle instability, compared to proprioceptive training alone. The primary objective of this study was to determine whether combining KT with a standardized proprioceptive training protocol yields greater improvements in ankle joint position sense in athletes with CAI compared to proprioceptive training alone. ### Is kinesio taping effective for sport performance and ankle function of athletes with chronic ankle instability (CAI)? ### Effect of Kinesio Tape on Proprioception, Static and Dynamic Balance in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability. ### Effects of kinesio taping on balance and proprioception in patients with chronic ankle instability: A meta-analysis.

--- SOURCE 9: Chronic Ankle Instability Treatment for Athletes ---
URL: https://www.truesportsphysicaltherapy.com/blogs/breaking-the-ankle-sprain-cycle-with-advanced-rehab-strategies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from True Sports Physical Therapy (truesportsphysicaltherapy.com) is an educational article and service page addressing chronic ankle instability (CAI) in athletes, particularly those who have experienced recurring lateral ankle sprains.

**Key Statistics & Facts:**
- Up to 40% of athletes who experience a first-time lateral ankle sprain will develop chronic ankle instability.
- A cross-sectional study found females have an estimated incidence rate of 13.6 ankle sprains per 1000 exposures (nearly double that of males), and 58.5% of professional basketball and football athletes have experienced an ankle sprain.
- Balance exercises alone cause a 42% reduction in ankle injury.
- Exercise-based rehabilitation reduces the risk of reinjury following acute ankle sprain compared to usual care alone.

**The Problem:**
When a lateral ankle sprain occurs, damage happens not only to ligaments but also to mechanoreceptors (ankle "sensors") that tell the brain where the foot is in space. This leads to damaged balance sensors, slowed muscle reaction times, decreased strength on both sides, and fear-driven movement compensation.

   - Lateral low ankle sprains: Most common (80.2% of all sprains), caused by excess inversion. Treatment: RICE protocol, nonoperative management. Return to play: 6-8 weeks.

2. **Stress Fractures:**
   - 55% of lower extremity stress injuries involve foot, 21.1% involve ankle/fibula.

**Prevention Strategies:**
- External supports (taping, bracing) proven effective at reducing injury risk.

- More research on prevention strategies is warranted.

**Methodology:** Comprehensive search of MEDLINE database for publications focused on ankle injury among athletes, using PRISMA guidelines. Articles before 1990 excluded.

This webpage presents a scientific article from the Journal of Orthopaedic Reports (Volume 5, Issue 4, August 2026) titled "Arthroscopic versus open management of chronic lateral ankle instability: A prospective randomized controlled trial" by Joseph Girgis Wahib et al. The study compares open versus arthroscopic Broström-Gould repair for chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). 

**Methods:** 40 patients with CLAI (≥6 months failed conservative management or ATFL avulsion injury) were randomized to open Broström-Gould (Group A) or arthroscopic Broström-Gould (Group B) and followed for 18 months. **Key Results:** Open repair was significantly faster (44.2±8.5 min vs. 79.5±23.11 min; p<0.001). Both techniques showed significant postoperative improvement (p<0.001). However, no significant differences were found between groups at 12 and 18 months. Complication rates were comparable with no recurrent instability or reoperations.

**Conclusion:** Both techniques provide significant clinical improvement with comparable mid-to-long-term outcomes. Arthroscopic repair offers advantages mainly in the early postoperative period. Surgical decision-making should be individualized based on patient characteristics, associated pathology, and surgeon expertise.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**IMPORTANT NOTE: This article has been retracted.**

This 2019 meta-analysis and systematic review by Liu and Diao (International Wound Journal, PMID: 30924305, PMCID: PMC7948700) compared surgical therapy versus conservative therapy for patients with acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament. 

**Methods:** The authors searched PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase databases through January 2018. A total of 13 studies (10 RCTs, 2 retrospective comparative studies) were included, comprising 834 patients in the surgical group and 930 in the conservative group.

**Results:** 
- **AOFAS Score:** Significantly higher in the surgical group (WMD: 10.33, 95% CI: 6.83-13.83)
- **Effective Rate:** Significantly higher in the surgical group (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04-1.28)
- **Complications (overall):** Significantly higher in the surgical group (RR: 3.31, 95% CI: 2.55-4.28)

- **Scar tenderness:** Significantly higher with surgery (RR: 10.16, 95% CI: 3.89-26.52)
- **Sensory loss:** Significantly higher with surgery (RR: 5.66, 95% CI: 2.76-11.59)
- **No significant differences** were found for: recurrent ankle injury, limited range of motion, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or wound infection/necrosis.

**Background:** Acute lateral ankle ligament injuries account for ~25% of all musculoskeletal injuries. In the US and UK, about 23,000 and 5,000 ankle injuries occur daily, respectively.

**Limitations acknowledged by authors:** Varied treatment types, inability to perform individual patient data analysis, and need for larger, multi-center RCTs with long-term follow-up.

**Conclusion:** Surgical treatment improved AOFAS scores and effective rates compared to conservative treatment but also significantly increased complication rates (particularly scar tenderness, sensory loss, and ankylosis).

URL: https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/podiatry/conquering-peroneal-tendinopathy-athletes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Conquering Peroneal Tendinopathy In Athletes

This article from Podiatry Today provides a comprehensive clinical guide for foot and ankle surgeons managing peroneal tendon disorders in athletic patients. It emphasizes the unique challenges of treating athletes, who are highly motivated to return to sport but may face complications from psychological stress, loss of income, or scholarship pressures.

## Key Anatomical Considerations
- Peroneus longus and brevis originate from the lateral fibula, run in a common sheath through the retromalleolar groove, and are stabilized by the superior peroneal retinaculum.
- Overcrowding from anatomic anomalies (low-lying brevis muscle belly, shallow fibular groove, peroneus quartus) can lead to subluxation, longitudinal tearing, and splitting.

## Diagnosis
- Differential includes lateral ankle ligament injury, fracture, osteochondral lesion, or sural nerve entrapment.
- Key exam findings: pain/swelling along tendon course, active eversion against resistance (brevis), plantarflexion of first ray against resistance (longus), and the compression test (Sobel et al.).
- MRI is the preferred imaging modality (sensitivity ~83%, specificity ~75%). However, reliance on MRI alone can lead to unnecessary intervention; physical exam findings must be incorporated.

## Conservative Treatment
- **Tendonitis/tendinosis:** RICE protocol, NSAIDs, activity modification, bracing, physical therapy (cryotherapy, ultrasound, iontophoresis, ROM, proprioception).
- **Peroneal tears:** Non-weightbearing followed by protected weightbearing in a walking boot for 4–6 weeks, early PT.
- **Subluxation:** Higher failure rates with conservative care; more aggressive immobilization; often defers to early surgical intervention.

## Surgical Decision Making
- Untreated subluxation can lead to tears, ruptures, and secondary injuries. Athletes with prior injury are twice as likely to be reinjured.
- Ideal timing: off-season for proper healing; consider earlier intervention for subluxation or contributing pathology.

## Surgical Technique (Step-by-Step)
1. Curvilinear incision over posterior fibula to peroneal tubercle.
2. Evaluate for subluxation via active circumduction.
3. Excise low-lying muscle belly or peroneus quartus if present.
4. Incise tendon sheath, debride inflamed synovium, and evaluate tears:
   - <50% involvement: debridement with or without tubularization.
   - >50% involvement: proximal and distal tenodesis.
5. Deepen fibular groove (intramedullary reaming per Mendicino et al.).
6. Repair superior peroneal retinaculum (advancement and pants-over-vest suturing).
7. Confirm stability with circumduction.

## Postoperative Protocol
- 10–14 days non-weightbearing in splint; then walking boot.
- PT begins at 2 weeks (early mobilization, edema control).
- Protected weightbearing at 4–6 weeks.
- Return to modified activity at 6–8 weeks (delayed if concomitant bony procedures).
- Return to sport requires meeting criteria: ankle ROM, muscle strength, proprioception, sport-specific movements.

## Conclusion
Successful outcomes require addressing both tendon pathology and underlying deformities, close collaboration with physical therapists and trainers, and understanding the athlete's psychological and functional needs.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Peroneal Tendon Syndromes Treatment & Management ---
URL: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/91344-treatment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Peroneal Tendon Syndromes Treatment & Management Summary

## Approach Considerations
- Chronic peroneal tendinopathy involves tendinosis/tearing from repetitive stress and dysfunctional mechanics. Treatment must address root causes (pelvic/lumbosacral core weakness, gluteal tendinopathy, common peroneal nerve entrapment).
- Acute peroneal injuries require aggressive conservative treatment to minimize functional loss, scarring, and atrophy. Mechanism is typically inversion ankle injury with eccentric load on peroneal muscles.

## Acute Phase
- **Initial management**: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), ± short period of no weight bearing. NSAIDs for pain/inflammation. Short-term weight-bearing immobilization (walking boot) is effective. Cast immobilization (short-leg, non-weight-bearing for 4-6 weeks with foot in plantar flexion and inversion) is an alternative for acute peroneal tendon dislocation.
- **Physical therapy**: Ankle strengthening, flexibility, and proprioception regimen. Must evaluate core biomechanics (lumbosacropelvic region) and include core exercises.
- **Surgical intervention**: Indicated for peroneus brevis tendon rupture, acute dislocation, anomalous peroneal brevis muscle hypertrophy, and peroneus longus tears with diminished function. Postoperative cast immobilization 2-6 weeks depending on procedure. A literature review found good outcomes after surgery for peroneal tendon dislocation, with faster return to sports when combining groove deepening and superior peroneal retinaculum repair.
- **Corticosteroid injections**: Not recommended for peroneal tendons (superficial, close to sural nerve; risk of fat necrosis and sural neuroma).
- **Osteopathic manipulative treatment**: Demonstrated significant pain relief in acute ankle injuries.
- **Complications**: Progression of pain/instability, possible rupture (conservative); sural nerve injury, chronic lateral ankle pain, restricted ROM, infection (surgical).

## Recovery Phase
- Physical therapy starts with light ROM progressing to stretching, then strengthening until 80-90% strength/function versus nonaffected ankle. Bracing/taping recommended for up to 6 months depending on surgical repair. Proprioceptive rehabilitation is crucial due to recurrent ankle sprains being related to poor muscle firing and balance.
- **Percutaneous ultrasonic tenotomy**: Shows promise for restoring tendon function without open surgical debridement.
- **Surgical intervention**: Chronic tears with persistent pain/instability failing conservative treatment warrant surgical evaluation. Tenosynovectomy is procedure of choice for persistent peroneal tendonitis. A systematic review/meta-analysis found surgical treatment results in excellent outcomes for chronic peroneal instability.

## Maintenance Phase
- Grounded in good pre- and post-exercise ankle stretching and strengthening. Bracing/taping not necessary if fully rehabilitated. Proprioceptive physiotaping (e.g., Kinesio Taping) can speed recovery and enhance stability. Long-term ankle stability training needed, especially for those who stress ankles repetitively.

## Return to Play
- If no surgery/casting required: return to activity in 1-2 weeks with ankle bracing/taping until 90-100% strength/function.
- If surgery performed: return to play with bracing/taping allowed once 90% strength/function achieved; bracing/taping usually not necessary once near 100%.

## Prevention

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Rebuilding Stability: Exploring the Best Rehabilitation Methods for Chronic Ankle Instability" published in *Sports* (2024, Volume 12, Issue 10, 282) by Roberto Tedeschi et al. The review evaluates the effectiveness of various rehabilitation interventions for Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI), a condition characterized by repeated ankle "giving way" and impaired balance due to sensory and motor disruptions.

**Methods:** The authors analyzed 8 randomized controlled trials (from 11 full-text assessments) identified through PubMed, Cochrane Library, PEDro, Scopus, and Web of Science (search conducted April–August 2024). Primary outcomes assessed were the Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT), Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT), and Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM). Methodological quality was assessed using PEDro and ROB-2 tools.

**Results:** All rehabilitation interventions (balance training, strength exercises, BAPS, whole-body vibration, stroboscopic vision training, neuromuscular training) demonstrated significant improvements in SEBT, CAIT, and FAAM scores. However, no single intervention was found to be consistently superior. Traditional balance training, strength exercises, BAPS, and WBV all provided meaningful functional gains. Stroboscopic vision training showed similar effectiveness to conventional approaches.

**Key findings by outcome measure:**
- **SEBT:** All interventions significantly improved dynamic balance, particularly in anterior, posteromedial, and posterolateral directions.
- **CAIT:** Subjective feelings of instability reduced across all intervention groups.
- **FAAM:** Functional ability improved significantly in all rehabilitation groups.
- Additional improvements were noted in Time-in-Balance, Side-Hop, Foot-Lift, Figure-8 Hop tests, NRS (pain), and BESS scores.

**Conclusions:** Balance and proprioceptive exercises are effective in managing CAI, with improvements in both dynamic stability and subjective outcomes. No single intervention stands out as the best, but personalized programs incorporating various methods are recommended. The evidence supports a combination of balance and strength training for optimal recovery. The authors note that innovative approaches like stroboscopic vision and WBV may engage specific patient populations but do not necessarily outperform conventional methods. Future research should explore long-term effects and potential synergies of combined interventions.

--- SOURCE 2: Surgical management of chronic lateral ankle instability: a meta-analysis ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-018-0870-6

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a meta-analysis published on June 25, 2018, in the Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research (Volume 13, article 159), comparing different surgical techniques for managing chronic lateral ankle instability (CAI). The article is an open-access review by Yongxing Cao, Yuan Hong, Yang Xu, Yuan Zhu, and Xiangyang Xu.

**Background:** Acute lateral ankle ligament injury is common, with 10-30% of patients failing conservative treatment and requiring surgery. Surgical procedures fall into three categories: non-anatomic reconstruction, anatomic repairment, and anatomic reconstruction.

**Methods:** The authors searched Cochrane Library (through December 2016), MEDLINE, and EMBASE for randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Collaboration's "Risk of bias tool."

**Results:** Seven randomized controlled trials were included, falling into five groups:
1. One study compared dynamic vs. static tenodesis (both non-anatomic reconstruction), finding static tenodesis yielded better clinical satisfaction and fewer subsequent sprains.
2. Two studies compared non-anatomic reconstruction vs. anatomic repairment—one found more nerve damage in the non-anatomic group; the other found non-anatomic reconstruction provided higher reduction of talar tilt angle.
3. Two studies comparing transosseous suture vs. imbrication (anatomic repairment techniques) found no significant difference in clinical outcomes except operation time.
4. One study found the double anchor technique was superior to single anchor in reducing talar tilt.
5. One study found anatomic reconstruction with ligament advanced reinforcement system (LARS) resulted in better patient-scored outcomes at 2 years post-surgery than the modified Brostrom technique.

**Search results:** 1231 records were screened (Cochrane: 327, MEDLINE: 593, EMBASE: 311), plus 312 from reference lists. After removing duplicates, 836 titles/abstracts were reviewed, with 77 potentially relevant trials identified. Ultimately, 7 studies were included, all published in English between 1990 and 2016 (Cho 2012, Cho 2013, Hennrikus 1996, Karlsson 1997, Larsen 1990, Porter 2015, Rosenbaum 1999).

**Conclusions:** There is limited evidence supporting any one surgical technique over another. Key conclusions: (1) dynamic tenodesis has limitations with poor clinical satisfaction and more subsequent sprains; (2) non-anatomic reconstruction abnormally increased inversion stiffness at the subtalar level compared to anatomic repairment; (3) multiple types of modified Brostrom procedures can achieve good clinical results; (4) anatomic reconstruction is a better procedure for some specific patients.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a clinical practice review article published in the Annals of Joint (Vol 11, July 30, 2026) on the arthroscopic treatment of chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). Authors: Shohei Sano, Yuichi Hoshino, Tetsuya Yamamoto, Noriyuki Kanzaki, and Ryosuke Kuroda from the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine, Japan. Received 17 January 2026, accepted 20 April 2026, published online 17 July 2026. DOI: 10.21037/aoj-2026-1-0008.

BACKGROUND: CLAI is a frequent sequela of acute lateral ligament injury (ATFL and CFL), causing recurrent sprains, pain, and functional limitations, particularly in athletes. While most acute sprains respond to conservative care, approximately 20-30% of patients develop persistent mechanical or functional instability requiring surgery. Open Broström/Broström-Gould repair has been the gold standard with durable results for up to 15 years, but arthroscopic techniques are increasingly popular due to minimally invasive access, ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology (synovitis, loose bodies, cartilage lesions), and comparable outcomes with potentially faster recovery.

DIAGNOSIS AND PATIENT SELECTION: Diagnosis combines history, physical exam (anterior drawer and talar tilt tests), stress radiography (pathological thresholds: ≥10 or ≥3 mm side-to-side difference for anterior talar translation; ≥10° or ≥6° for talar tilt), dynamic ultrasound (no established cutoffs), and MRI (commonly shows ATFL/CFL attenuation rather than complete discontinuity). Surgery is recommended when CLAI persists 3-6 months despite structured rehab. Candidates include high-demand athletes and those with recurrent injuries. Poor tissue quality, generalized ligamentous laxity, collagen disorders, or revision cases may require graft-based reconstruction rather than direct repair.

SURGICAL TECHNIQUES (Table 1 comparison):
1. Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotted suture anchors - reliable stability, high satisfaction (Corte-Real, Kim studies).
2. Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotless anchors - reduces knot irritation/complications, enables early rehab and faster RTS (Kanzaki, Shimabukuro, Teramoto studies; 75% returned to sports within 8 weeks in Teramoto's accelerated protocol).
3. All-inside arthroscopic repair - fully intra-articular, no extracapsular knot-tying; comparable outcomes to open (Zhou study), reduced operative time, significant improvements in VAS, AOFAS, FAOS, and Karlsson scores (Won study).
4. Combined ATFL and CFL repair - indicated in severe CLAI with CFL injury; reduces recurrent instability vs. ATFL-only repair (Yoshimoto, Mao, Vega studies).
5. Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction - for revision, poor tissue, or generalized laxity using autografts/allografts (e.g., EHL, semitendinosus); favorable mid-term outcomes (Alayane, Pettit, Feng studies).

REHABILITATION (Table 2 phase-based protocol): 
- 0-2 weeks: immobilization (cast/boot/splint for 10-14 days).

Current recommendations favor arthroscopic Broström repair as first-line for good-quality tissue, with reconstruction for complex cases. Future research needs multicenter RCTs, standardized outcome reporting, better patient selection integrating structural and functional imaging, and data-driven rehabilitation. --- SOURCE 15: Gould Procedure for Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability ---
URL: https://www.cureus.com/articles/337862-clinical-outcomes-after-arthroscopic-brostrm-gould-procedure-for-chronic-lateral-ankle-instability.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published March 23, 2025, in Cureus, DOI: 10.7759/cureus.81025) reports a retrospective study from Changi General Hospital, Singapore, evaluating clinical outcomes of the arthroscopic Broström-Gould procedure for chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). 

**Background:** Ankle sprains are the most common sprain type, with lateral ankle sprains comprising 85% of all ankle sprains. About 20% of ankle sprains progress to CLAI. The Broström-Gould procedure is the gold standard surgical treatment for CLAI, with arthroscopic variations gaining popularity due to comparable or superior outcomes including better pain scores, earlier weight-bearing, shorter hospital stays, and lower wound complication rates.

**Methods:** Thirty-nine patients (22 males, 17 females; 20 right/19 left ankles; mean age 36.2 years, range 19.6-64.8; mean BMI 27.4 kg/m², range 19.2-40) underwent arthroscopic Broström-Gould in 2021 at a tertiary institution. All had failed conservative treatment. The procedure involved arthroscopic debridement and anchoring the ATFL to the distal fibula with Smith & Nephew SutureFIX anchors (typically two anchors). Postoperative management included immediate weight-bearing with an ankle brace removed at six weeks. Outcomes were measured using VAS, Karlsson-Peterson (K-P), and AOFAS scoring systems, analyzed with paired t-tests (significance at p<0.05).

**Results:** All three functional scores improved significantly postoperatively:
- VAS: 5.87 ± 1.92 preop to 2.0 ± 2.16 postop (t=8.75, p<0.0001)
- K-P: 43.68 ± 13.2 preop to 69.21 ± 17.86 postop (t=-8.71, p<0.0001)
- AOFAS: 62.53 ± 16.05 preop to 83.8 ± 11.49 postop (t=-5.91, p<0.0001)

No complications or recurrent instability requiring revision surgery were noted.

**Discussion highlights:** A learning curve cutoff of 22 cases exists for arthroscopic vs. 12 for open Broström-Gould. Arthroscopic approaches allow evaluation and treatment of concomitant pathologies. Common complications include neurovascular injuries (especially superficial peroneal nerve) and wound complications. Early weight-bearing improves recovery. Return to sport is an important outcome, positively influenced by preoperative motivation and elite sport participation, negatively by high BMI and age.

**Limitations:** Small sample size, single institution, single operator, subjective patient-reported outcomes, and short-term follow-up (up to one year).

**Conclusions:** Arthroscopic Broström-Gould is an effective method for treating CLAI with significantly improved functional outcomes and good results.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Significant improvement of all three functional scores (VAS, K-P, and AOFAS scores) following arthroscopic Broström-Gould was noted. This shows that the arthroscopic Broström-Gould is an effective method to treat CLAI with good outcomes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 16: Ankle Sprains in the National Basketball Association, 2013 ... ---
URL: https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/1c18dt03v

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This peer-reviewed study (published in The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019) describes the epidemiology of ankle sprains among National Basketball Association (NBA) players during the 2013-14 through 2016-17 seasons. The study was a retrospective cohort analysis of all players on an NBA roster for at least one game, using data from the NBA electronic medical record system maintained by certified athletic trainers.

Key findings:
- There were 796 ankle sprains among 389 players across 2,341 unique NBA player-seasons over the 4-season period
- The overall single-season risk of ankle sprain was 25.8% (95% CI, 23.9%-28.0%), meaning approximately 1 in 4 NBA players experiences an ankle sprain each season
- The majority of ankle sprains occurred in games (n=565, 71.0%), were lateral sprains (n=638, 80.2%), and involved a contact mechanism of injury (n=567, 71.2%)
- The game incidence rate was 4.5 ankle sprains per 1,000 player-games, which is higher than rates reported at collegiate (1.4-2.3 per 1000) and high school (0.8 per 1000) levels
- Players under 26 years old had a 54% higher incidence rate of ankle sprains than older players (IRR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.27-1.86)
- Players with a history of ankle sprain in the past year had a 41% higher incidence rate (IRR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.13-1.74) compared to those without such history
- 56% of ankle sprains (n=443) did not result in any NBA games missed; among those that did, players missed a median of 2 games (IQR 1-4) and took a median of 8 days to return
- High ankle sprains were more severe, with a median of 5 games missed and 24 days to return to play
- A cumulative total of 1,467 NBA player-games were missed due to ankle sprains over the 4-season study period (average ~370 per season)
- 44% of ankle sprains resulted in at least one missed NBA game
- Ankle sprain incidence peaked at the start of preseason games and decreased over time
- Common mechanisms included stepping on an opponent's foot (33.3% of contact sprains) and inversion (61.6% of noncontact sprains); common activities at time of injury were general defense (18.8%), layup driving (14.5%), and rebounding (12.2%)
- Most common sprain types: lateral (80.2%), with medial and high sprains making up smaller proportions (7.8% and 4.1% respectively)

The authors concluded that ankle sprains affect approximately 26% of NBA players each season and account for a large number of missed games. They recommend integrating injury prevention programs into management of initial sprains, particularly for younger players and those with prior ankle sprain history, and call for further research on basketball- and ankle-specific prevention strategies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 17: Management of ankle injuries in professional basketball players ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8077287

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed article published in Orthopedic Reviews (2021) on the management of ankle injuries in professional basketball players. The study was conducted by researchers at Mayo Clinic, Scottsdale, AZ.

**Key Findings on Prevalence:**
- Ankle injuries are the most common injury type in basketball, occurring at 3.8-5.2 injuries per 1,000 athlete exposures.
- Ankle injuries account for approximately 21.9% of all basketball-related injuries and 14.7% of all NBA injuries.
- Over half (53.7%) of playing time missed due to injury is caused by ankle injuries.
- The most common activity at time of ankle injury is rebounding (34.4%).

**Types of Ankle Injuries Covered:**

1. **Ankle Sprains:**
   - Lateral low ankle sprains: Most common (80.2% of all sprains), caused by excess inversion. Treatment: RICE protocol, nonoperative management. Return to play: 6-8 weeks.
   - Medial ankle sprains: 7.8% of sprains, caused by excessive eversion/dorsiflexion. Return to play: 3-6+ months.
   - High ankle sprains (syndesmotic): 4.1% of sprains, most severe. Surgical repair more common. Return to play: 6-8+ weeks.

2. **Stress Fractures:**
   - 55% of lower extremity stress injuries involve foot, 21.1% involve ankle/fibula.
   - Average 25.1 games missed; ~30% of athletes unable to return to previous level.
   - Surgical treatment in elite athletes yields average return of 3.8 months vs. 5.6 months with conservative management.
   - Vitamin D supplementation important for prevention and management.

3. **Jones Fracture:**
   - Fracture of proximal fifth metatarsal; high rates among NBA players.
   - ~15% of affected players did not return to an NBA game.
   - Up to 15-30% nonunion rate. Surgical intervention common in elite athletes.

4. **Weber Type A, B, C Fractures:**
   - Relatively uncommon (0.5% of injuries). Full return to play expected in ~8 weeks.

5. **Achilles Tendon Rupture:**
   - Basketball causes 42.6% of all AT ruptures in individuals under 60 in the US.
   - Almost exclusively treated with surgical repair in athletes.
   - Full return to play: 6-9 months.

**Prevention Strategies:**
- External supports (taping, bracing) proven effective at reducing injury risk.
- Proprioceptive and kinematic training programs (tilt boards, balance beams) show similar effectiveness.
- More research on prevention strategies is warranted.

**Methodology:** Comprehensive search of MEDLINE database for publications focused on ankle injury among athletes, using PRISMA guidelines. Articles before 1990 excluded.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from BASS Medical Group (published Nov 1, 2025, updated May 11, 2026) provides an overview of common NBA injuries and their typical recovery timelines for fans and athletes.

**Key Injuries and Recovery Times:**
1. **Achilles Tendon Tears** – Complete or partial tear of the tendon connecting calf to heel bone; caused by explosive takeoffs, sudden stops, or overuse. Recovery: 9–12 months (surgery + rehab). Player examples include Damian Lillard (2025, likely out for season), Tyrese Haliburton (2025 Finals, ruptured Achilles), and Kevin Durant (2019, missed a full year).
2. **Ankle Sprains** – Ligament overstretching or tearing, common in players who cut, pivot, and land on opponents' feet. Recovery: 2–8 weeks. Examples: Stephen Curry (multiple early-career sprains leading to brace use) and LeBron James (mild high-ankle sprain in 2024, missed two weeks).
3. **Hamstring Strains** – Overstretching/tearing of back-of-thigh muscles; reduces explosiveness. Recovery: 3–8 weeks. Examples: Ja Morant (2023, missed 3 weeks) and Paul George. High recurrence rates noted.
4. **Knee Injuries (ACL, MCL, Meniscus)** – Recovery: MCL sprain 2–6 weeks; meniscus repair 6–12 weeks; ACL reconstruction 9–12 months. Examples: Derrick Rose (torn ACL in 2012, year-long recovery reshaped his career) and Lonzo Ball (multiple meniscus/cartilage surgeries).
5. **Wrist and Hand Fractures** – Recovery: 4–8 weeks (mild); 10–12 weeks (post-surgery). Examples: LaMelo Ball (2024 fractured wrist, missed final months) and Anthony Davis (finger dislocation).
6. **Concussions** – Brain injury from head impact. Recovery: 1–3 weeks. Examples: Jayson Tatum (2024 concussion protocol) and Damian Lillard. Rest and neurological clearance are mandatory.
7. **Back and Core Strains** – Common in high-minute/travel-heavy players. Recovery: 1–3 weeks (minor); 6+ weeks for disc issues. Examples: Giannis Antetokounmpo and Luka Dončić.
8. **Tendinitis and Overuse Injuries** – Inflammation from repetitive motion (knees, Achilles, shoulders). Recovery: days to months. Both Damian Lillard and Tyrese Haliburton experienced chronic tendinitis before their Achilles issues.

**FAQs:** Ankle sprains are the most common NBA injury; Achilles tears typically take 9–12 months to heal; increased games, travel, and year-round training contribute to injury frequency.

The page includes a medical disclaimer stating the content is for educational purposes only and not medical advice, and promotes BASS Medical Group's orthopedic and sports medicine services for athletes of all levels.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 19: Ankle Sprain Rehab & Return to Sport ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Ankle Sprain Rehab & Return to Sport — The Basketball Doctors

This webpage from The Basketball Doctors (TBD) focuses on ankle sprain rehabilitation for basketball players, offering both in-person services in Orange County & Los Angeles County and online coaching worldwide. The site is run by Dr. Gabe Ignacio and Dr. Marco Lopez, Doctors of Physical Therapy trained at USC with over 10 years of experience each.

### Key Facts & Statistics
- Ankle sprains are the #1 basketball injury
- Only **45%** of athletes seek proper care after an ankle sprain
- Athletes are **4X** more likely to re-sprain without proper rehab
- Players with a history of ankle injury are **4.9X** more likely to sustain another ankle injury
- Up to **40%** of athletes develop Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI) after an initial sprain

### Ankle Sprain Grades
- **Grade 1 (Mild):** Ligament stretched, return in days to 1–2 weeks
- **Grade 2 (Moderate):** Partial tear, return in 2–6 weeks
- **Grade 3 (Severe):** Complete rupture, return in 6–12+ weeks (surgery may be considered)

### The Cascade of Untreated Injury
Acute sprain → proprioceptive deficits & peroneal weakness → repeated micro-instability → mechanical laxity → CAI → compensatory movement patterns → post-traumatic osteoarthritis, ACL risk, and decreased performance

### Myth Busting
1. **"Just tape it up"** — Taping without rehab creates false security; doesn't address underlying deficits
2. **"If I can walk, I don't need PT"** — Walking tolerance ≠ basketball tolerance; the gap between "walk" and "play" is where re-injury happens
3. **"My ankle is just weak, nothing will help"** — CAI is treatable; neuromuscular training reduces re-injury rates

### Rehab Phases
1. **Acute Management:** Protect joint, manage swelling, restore ROM
2. **Early-Stage:** Full weight-bearing, restore dorsiflexion, peroneal activation
3. **Middle-Stage:** Progressive strength, dynamic balance, double-leg plyometrics
4. **Late-Stage/Return to Sport:** Single-leg loading, reactive control, sport-specific movements, hop/landing tests
5. **Performance Training & Maintenance:** Long-term habits, injury prevention

### Services Offered
- **In-Person Physical Therapy:** Hands-on evaluation, manual therapy, return-to-sport testing
- **Online Coaching & Training:** Video assessment, custom programming, app-guided workouts, coordination with surgeons

### FAQ Highlights
- No referral needed; start with a free discovery call
- Rehab can begin within 24–48 hours (even acute phase)
- Chronic/late-presenting sprains are treatable regardless of how long ago the injury occurred
- Works with post-surgical patients (e.g., Brostrom procedure)
- Minimal equipment needed for online coaching (bands, foam roller, step/box, open space)
</summary>

The joint doesn't just need rest — it needs to be retrained.", "Players with a history of ankle injury were 4.9X more likely to sustain another ankle injury.", "Chronic ankle instability is NOT a life sentence. Research consistently shows that structured neuromuscular training and progressive load rehabilitation dramatically reduces re-injury rates and restores function — even in athletes with years of repeated sprains!", "Every rehab plan at TBD is built around where you are clinically, where you need to be athletically, and the specific demands of your game."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Adam Loiacono, a physical therapist with 7 NBA seasons of experience, provides a comprehensive guide to ankle sprain rehabilitation for athletes of all levels. It begins with the example of Kevin Durant rolling his ankle during warm-ups at his 2023 Phoenix Suns home debut, illustrating that even elite athletes can suffer these injuries. The article explains ankle anatomy (tibia/fibula/talus bones, ATFL, CFL, and PTFL ligaments, and muscle compartments), and emphasizes that true recovery requires treating the whole person—not just the diagnosis—by rebuilding proprioception, neuromuscular control, strength, and coordination.

Key content includes recovery timelines by injury grade (Grade I ~7 days, Grade II ~15 days, Grade IIIA ~31 days, Grade IIIB ~55 days), factors that delay recovery (swelling >2cm via figure-8 method, pain at rest, early inability to bear weight, multiligament involvement), and two early management strategies: banded stretch traction and aquatic rehab (which offers up to 90% offloading at neck depth with hydrostatic pressure benefits). Pro tips include using whole limb compression, starting isometrics by Day 2, BFR training, and multi-angle proprioceptive training. The article debunks the myth that foam pads alone are sufficient, arguing that true proprioceptive recovery requires multi-plane, multi-speed forces. It references five clinical studies on ankle sprain treatment and return-to-play protocols.
</summary>

But we can control how we respond., By restoring not just joint integrity, but muscle, movement, and mind, we can build athletes who don't just return — they come back better., Ankle sprains can happen to anyone and recovery requires more than rest and ice

Abstract
:   Ankle lateral ligament injuries are common in everyday life and sports. Because most lateral ankle ligament injuries occur during sports, proper diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are critical to the patient’s prognosis. A physical examination is necessary for determining ankle injuries. Radiographic examinations include radiography, ultrasonography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and there are differing views on these tools. The goal of treatment for acute ankle lateral ligament injuries is to prevent chronic ankle instability. Exercise and bracing are more evidenced-based recommendations that should be incorporated into the rehabilitation process. A comprehensive and progressive exercise program should include range of motion, stretching, strengthening, neuromuscular, proprioceptive, and sport-specific exercises. Many systematic reviews have found insufficient evidence to support the clinical usefulness and necessity of primary surgical repair for acute lateral ankle sprains. Surgical treatment for acute lateral ankle sprain without concomitant pathologies is not recommended and should only be considered in cases of severe injury with large bony avulsion or frank dislocation or professional athletes with complete ligament rupture (Grade III) and severe instability.

args.key_excerpts: Ankle lateral ligament injuries are common in everyday life and sports. Because most lateral ankle ligament injuries occur during sports, proper diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are critical to the patient's prognosis.
args.summary:
This webpage is an up-to-date review article titled "Acute ankle lateral ligament injury: an up-to-date review" published in Arthrosc Orthop Sports Med (2023;10:1-9), published online May 1, 2023 (DOI: 10.14517/aosm23002). Authors: Sung Hyun Lee and Min Seok Kim (Wonkwang University Hospital and Musculoskeletal and Immune Disease Research Institute, Iksan, Korea). The article reviews the diagnosis and treatment of acute ankle lateral ligament injuries, which are common in daily life and sports.

Key points from the abstract:
- Most lateral ankle ligament injuries occur during sports, so proper diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are critical to patient prognosis.
- Physical examination is necessary for determining ankle injuries.
- Radiographic examinations include radiography, ultrasonography, and MRI, with differing views on their utility.
- The goal of treatment is to prevent chronic ankle instability.
- Exercise and bracing are evidence-based recommendations for rehabilitation.
- A comprehensive, progressive exercise program should include range of motion, stretching, strengthening, neuromuscular, proprioceptive, and sport-specific exercises.
- Multiple systematic reviews found insufficient evidence to support primary surgical repair for acute lateral ankle sprains; surgical treatment is not recommended without concomitant pathologies and should only be considered for severe injuries with large bony avulsion, frank dislocation, or in professional athletes with complete (Grade III) ligament rupture and severe instability.

Keywords: Ankle; Diagnosis; Sprain; Treatment. The article includes 43 references with PubMed/PMC/CrossRef links. The full-text PDF is available free. It is an Open Access article under the Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

- About sections covering peer review, editorial board, associate editors, academic council, careers, and email alerts

## Abstract

Ankle sprain reported among 16%-40% of all sports-related injuries and most common frequent lower limb injury among athletes. It is particularly prevalent in soccer, American football, and basketball. The most commonly injured ligament is the lateral ligaments especially anterior talofibular ligament and quite a large percentage of patients report persistent symptoms and experience recurrent injuries. To prevent injuries and instability around ankle joint, various interventions evidenced are immobilization, cryotherapy, compression, elevation, analgesics, bracing, foot orthosis, exercises, electrophysical methods, and surgical interventions. Among these therapies physical exercises and splints are highly recommended across levels of rehabilitation. PubMed was used for literature search and articles on randomized control trail, systematic reviews and meta-analysis between 2017 to 2022 were included. Articles on advanced physiotherapy management for ankle injuries were included. Results from reviewing 6 RCT reported progressive exercises training significantly improved flexibility, strength, endurance, agility and balance in the ankle complex. Exercise techniques targeting the ligaments, muscle and structures around ankle joint based on the clinical presentation can lead to improved ankle joint performance in individuals diagnosed with ankle instability.

**Keywords:** Ankle injury, Ankle sprain, Exercise, Instablity

args.summary:
This webpage presents a review article titled "Recent Advances in Exercise Intervention for Athletes with Ankle Injury" published in the Journal of Clinical and Biomedical Sciences (DOI: 10.58739/jcbs/v13i4.23.9). The article was authored by Shiji Ebin (BPT Intern) and Haridass Sarulatha (Professor), both from the Dept of Physiotherapy at Sri Devaraj Urs Academy of Higher Education and Research, Kolar, Karnataka. Published in Year 2023, Volume 13, Issue 4, pages 102-107, it was received 06 April 2023, accepted 20 June 2023, and published 28 December 2023. The work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License and is open-access.

Key content of the article:
- Ankle sprains account for 16%-40% of all sports-related injuries and are the most common lower limb injury among athletes, particularly prevalent in soccer, American football, and basketball.
- The most commonly injured ligament is the lateral ligament complex, especially the anterior talofibular ligament. A large percentage of patients report persistent symptoms and experience recurrent injuries.
- Various interventions for preventing injuries and instability around the ankle joint include immobilization, cryotherapy, compression, elevation, analgesics, bracing, foot orthosis, exercises, electrophysical methods, and surgical interventions. Among these, physical exercises and splints are highly recommended across all levels of rehabilitation.
- Methodology: PubMed literature search was used, including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2017 and 2022, focusing on advanced physiotherapy management for ankle injuries.
- Results: Reviewing 6 randomized controlled trials showed that progressive exercise training significantly improved flexibility, strength, endurance, agility, and balance in the ankle complex. Exercise techniques targeting the ligaments, muscles, and structures around the ankle joint, based on clinical presentation, can lead to improved ankle joint performance in individuals diagnosed with ankle instability.
- Keywords: Ankle injury, Ankle sprain, Exercise, Instability.

The article includes 29 references covering topics such as the epidemiology of ankle sprains, ankle instability, prevention strategies, balance training, plyometric training, and whole-body vibration training. The webpage also lists the recommended citation format for the paper and provides access to full-text PDF, ePUB, and XML versions, as well as article metrics via Plum Analytics.

Can Therapeutic Exercises Improve Proprioception in Chronic Ankle Instability? A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis

## Abstract

### Objective

To assess [exercise therapies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/kinesiotherapy) that aim to enhance [proprioception](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/proprioception) in individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI).

### Data Sources

Five databases (PubMed, [Embase](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/embase), [Cochrane Library](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/cochrane-library), Web of Science, and EBSCO) were searched in October 2021.

### Study Selection

[Randomized controlled trials](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/randomized-controlled-trial) involving exercise therapy conducted on individuals with CAI were included.

### Data Extraction

Data were extracted by 2 independent reviewers using a standardized form. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed with the [Physiotherapy Evidence Database](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/pedro) scale.

### Data Synthesis

The end trial weighted mean difference and standard deviations were analyzed, and the synthetic value for the improvement in error scores of ankle joint position sense in multiple directions was evaluated.

### Results

Eleven trials with 333 participants were eligible for inclusion in this [systematic review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/systematic-review) and were included in the network meta-analysis. Foot and ankle muscle strengthening exercise showed the highest probability of being among the best treatments (surface under the cumulative ranking [SUCRA]=74.6%). The next 2 were static balance exercise only (SUCRA=67.9%) and corrective exercise (SUCRA=56.1%). The SUCRA values of proprioceptive exercise, dynamic balance exercise only, [aquatic exercise](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/aquatic-exercise), rehabilitation exercise with brace, mixed static/dynamic balance exercise, and control were at relatively low levels and scored at 49.6%, 48.8%, 47.8%, 47.7%, 44.0%, and 13.5%, respectively.

### Conclusions

Foot and ankle muscle strengthening exercise may have a good effect when used to improve joint position sense in individuals with CAI. The more complex balance exercise intervention becomes, the less effective the proprioceptive outcome.

## Discussion

In the present systematic review, the relative efficacy of different exercise therapies for improving JPS in CAI was compared. Foot and ankle muscle strengthening exercise appears to produce the best JPS results in individuals with CAI. In addition, static balance exercise only seemed to be superior to dynamic balance exercise only in improving JPS scores. With the complexity of the balance exercise intervention increased, the improved effect decreased.

## Conclusions

Network meta-analysis showed that strengthening the muscles at the foot and ankle may have a relatively good effect on improving the proprioception of individuals with ankle instability, and that the more complex the balance exercise intervention becomes, the less effective the outcome. args.summary:
This is a systematic review and network meta-analysis published in the Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (Volume 103, Issue 11, November 2022, Pages 2232-2244) examining whether therapeutic exercises can improve proprioception in individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI).

METHODOLOGY:
- Objective: Assess exercise therapies aimed at enhancing proprioception in individuals with CAI
- Data Sources: Five databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and EBSCO) searched in October 2021, with no restriction on publication year or language
- Study Selection: Randomized controlled trials involving exercise therapy on individuals with CAI
- Data Extraction: Two independent reviewers using a standardized form; methodological quality assessed with the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale
- Analysis: End trial weighted mean difference and standard deviations analyzed; synthetic value for improvement in error scores of ankle joint position sense (JPS) in multiple directions evaluated
- Registration: PROSPERO database (Registration No. CRD42021240331)
- Funding: National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 31870936) and Ministry of Education of Humanities and Social Science Project (Grant No. 18YJA0006)

RESULTS:
- Literature search yielded 762 potentially relevant records; after removing duplicates, 468 records screened, 270 full texts evaluated, and 11 studies (with 333 participants) were eligible for inclusion in the network meta-analysis

TREATMENT RANKINGS (by Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking, SUCRA):
- Foot and ankle muscle strengthening exercise: highest probability of being among the best treatments (SUCRA=74.6%)
- Static balance exercise only: SUCRA=67.9%
- Corrective exercise: SUCRA=56.1%
- Proprioceptive exercise: 49.6%
- Dynamic balance exercise only: 48.8%
- Aquatic exercise: 47.8%
- Rehabilitation exercise with brace: 47.7%
- Mixed static/dynamic balance exercise: 44.0%
- Control: 13.5%

CONCLUSIONS:
- Foot and ankle muscle strengthening exercise may have a good effect when used to improve joint position sense in individuals with CAI
- Static balance exercise only appeared superior to dynamic balance exercise only in improving JPS scores
- Key finding: "The more complex balance exercise intervention becomes, the less effective the proprioceptive outcome." With respect to interventions for JPS in CAI, "less seems to be more."

The article has been cited by 43 subsequent works, including a 2023 study in Sports Medicine and Health Science which noted methodological limitations in this review (i.e., pooling results with heterogeneous JPS test methodology including active or passive JPS, joint position reproduction test, or sloped-surface block method).

# Recurrent Ankle Sprains & Chronic Ankle Instability: Causes, Treatment, and Prevention

Share this post:

Ankle sprains are among the most common musculoskeletal injuries, affecting people of all ages and activity levels. Whether you’re an athlete or someone who enjoys occasional physical activity, the risk of an ankle sprain can be present. A sprain occurs when the ankle rolls to either side, causing the ligaments that support the joint to stretch or tear. While many people recover from an initial sprain without long-term issues, some may experience recurrent ankle sprains, leading to a condition known as chronic ankle instability (CAI).

## Understanding Chronic Ankle Instability

Chronic ankle instability is a condition where the ankle remains unstable, even after the acute stage of the initial injury has resolved. This lingering instability can significantly impact daily life and athletic performance. CAI can be classified into two main categories: mechanical and functional instability.

* **Mechanical Instability**: This occurs when there is a laxity or tear in the ankle ligaments, leading to a physically unstable joint. The ligaments are unable to provide the necessary support, making the ankle prone to rolling or giving way.
* **Functional Instability**: This type of instability is characterised by frequent subjective symptoms of the ankle “giving way” during everyday activities, such as walking or running. It is often associated with proprioceptive deficits, where the body struggles to sense the position of the ankle, leading to a lack of coordination and balance.

## The Role of Rehabilitation in Preventing Chronic Ankle Instability

*Effective* rehabilitation is crucial in preventing chronic ankle instability following an ankle sprain. However, not everyone who suffers an ankle injury consults with a [physiotherapist](http://sportsplusphysio.com.au/services/physiotherapy-brisbane/), which can result in missed steps in the recovery process. After the initial swelling and pain subside, many individuals assume their ankle is fully healed and return to their previous activities prematurely. Unfortunately, this can lead to recurrent ankle sprains and the development of CAI.

A comprehensive rehabilitation program focuses on several key areas:

1. **Strengthening**: Building strength in the muscles surrounding the ankle joint is essential to support and stabilise the area. Exercises targeting the calf, peroneal, and intrinsic foot muscles can help create a strong foundation.
2. **Balance and Proprioception**: Restoring balance and proprioception is critical for dynamic stability. Proprioception refers to the body’s ability to sense its position in space, which is vital for preventing future injuries. Balance exercises, such as standing on one leg or using a wobble board, can help retrain the ankle to respond effectively to changes in surface and direction.
3. **Neuromuscular Control**: Improving neuromuscular control ensures that the muscles around the ankle react appropriately during movement. This involves retraining the body’s reflexes and timing to better protect the ankle during activities.
4. **Gradual Return to Activity**: A phased return to activity, beginning with low-impact exercises and gradually progressing to more demanding activities, can help prevent re-injury.

## The Effectiveness of Taping in Managing Chronic Ankle Instability

![Ankle taping by a physio to reduce ankle instability](http://sportsplusphysio.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Blog-pictures-_21_-1024x576.webp)

Sports Physio Will Thwaite Ankle Strapping

Taping is a common technique used to support the ankle during recovery and prevent further injury. Research on the effectiveness of taping for CAI is mixed, but some studies suggest that it can have a moderate impact on gait function, reducing the joint’s range of motion into inversion and eversion, and decreasing postural sway during movement.

Clinically, [ankle taping](/ankle-taping-tips-and-tricks/) has been found to be particularly beneficial during the early stages of returning to training and competitive sports. It provides additional support to the ankle, allowing athletes to regain confidence in their movements while reducing the risk of re-injury.

## When Conservative Management Isn’t Enough: Surgical Options

While conservative management is the first line of treatment for CAI, with 80-90% of ligamentous injuries responding well to this approach, some cases may require surgical intervention. If an individual experiences severe ligament damage or persistent instability symptoms despite following a structured rehabilitation protocol, surgery may be necessary to restore ankle stability.

Surgical options for chronic ankle instability typically involve repairing or reconstructing the damaged ligaments. The goal is to restore the ankle’s structural integrity and prevent future sprains. Post-surgery rehabilitation is essential to ensure a full recovery and return to activity.

## Summary

Chronic ankle instability is a significant concern for individuals who have experienced recurrent ankle sprains. Understanding the importance of proper rehabilitation, including strengthening, balance training, and neuromuscular control, is key to preventing this condition. For those who do not respond to conservative management, surgical options are available to restore stability and function to the ankle.

If you’re dealing with recurrent ankle sprains or suspect you may have chronic ankle instability, it’s crucial to consult with a physiotherapist. At SportsPlus Physiotherapy, our team of experts is dedicated to helping you regain stability, strength, and confidence in your ankle, allowing you to return to the activities you love.

# Comparison of an Adaptive Ankle Brace to Conventional Taping for Rehabilitation of Acute Ankle Injury in Young Subelite Soccer Players: A Pilot Study

Click name to view affiliation

***Context**:* Ankle sprains are a common injury in sports, for which use of external ankle support during rehabilitation has been suggested to improve clinical outcomes. ***Design**:* Cohort study. ***Methods**:* Thirteen soccer players experiencing acute lateral ankle sprain injury were provided a novel adaptive ankle brace or conventional ankle taping (control) as external ankle support throughout the injury rehabilitation process. All other clinical procedures were identical, and rehabilitation was supervised by the same team staff member. Time from injury to clearance to return to sport was tracked. Player experience with the ankle brace also was queried via electronic surveys. ***Results**:* The median time to return to sport was less for the Brace group (52.5 d) compared to the Control group (79.5 d), but the distributions of the 2 groups were not found to differ significantly (*P* = .109). Player surveys indicated they felt the brace to be comfortable or very comfortable, with better freedom of movement than other braces and the same freedom of movement as wearing no brace. All players reported wearing the brace to be the same or better experience as ankle taping. ***Discussion**:* These preliminary results indicate that the adaptive ankle brace is at least as effective as ankle taping for providing external support during the rehabilitation phase following acute lateral ankle sprain and suggest it may be a more effective ankle support solution in terms of patient compliance than conventional bracing or taping.

Ankle injuries are one of the most common injuries in both elite and amateur sports.[1](#r1)–[4](#r4) In the National Basketball Association, the single-season risk of sustaining an ankle sprain was 25.8% across the 2013–2014 to 2016–2016 seasons.[2](#r2) Among National Collegiate Athletic Association men’s soccer athletes, the ankle was the second most common injury location behind the thigh.[4](#r4) Across all National Collegiate Athletic Association athletes for the academic years 2014–2015 to 2018–2019, lateral ankle sprains, the most common type of ankle sprain, were reported at a rate of 4.61 per 10,000 athlete exposures.[3](#r3) Half of these injuries resulted in time loss from sport of >1 day, with a mean time loss of 8.5 (11.4) days in men’s sports and 9.6 (13.0) days in women’s sports.[3](#r3) For this reason, it is not only important to study ways to prevent ankle sprains in athletes but also to investigate means for reducing time loss from sport following injury.

Ankle sprains are often perceived as minor, but up to 70% of individuals who sustain an acute ankle sprain report residual symptoms or persistent functional limitations, and up to 40% develop chronic ankle instability within the first year following sprain.[2](#r2),[5](#r5) Furthermore, the loss of full ankle joint function increases the propensity for not only recurrent sprains but also other subsequent musculoskeletal injuries and reduction in quality of life.[6](#r6),[7](#r7) One study found that out of 312 amateur soccer players who sustained an ankle sprain over a 2-year period, 64% had previously sustained an ankle sprain.[8](#r8) Among National Basketball Association players, the ankle sprain incidence rate in games was 41% higher among players with a history of ankle sprain in the last year.[2](#r2) Thus, proper rehabilitation of ankle sprains is critical to restoring function and reducing the burden of subsequent injuries.[9](#r9),[10](#r10)

Early rehabilitation is believed to reduce the downstream medical costs for ankle-related issues.[11](#r11) External support of the injured ankle, via bracing or taping, has been recommended to provide immobilization and protection of healing tissues in the immediate, acute phase following injury, particularly for severe injuries, and may also be beneficial during the rehabilitation phase.[12](#r12),[13](#r13) Some data suggest bracing is superior to taping for rehabilitation outcomes, such as time to clearance to return to team sport (RTS), but results are inconclusive.[14](#r14)–[17](#r17) Despite the potential benefits of bracing over taping or use of no external support, athlete compliance with ankle bracing is a challenge due to complaints of discomfort and restriction.[18](#r18),[19](#r19) For this reason, there is a critical need for a more comfortable and less restricting brace that provides the same level of protection while improving athlete compliance.

Recently, an adaptive ankle brace was developed that selectively resists sudden, high-velocity ankle inversion motions; it allows unrestricted ankle motion at physiological movement speeds while providing similar protection performance to traditional passive braces for potentially injurious motions.[20](#r20),[21](#r21) Additionally it was found to provide better comfort and freedom of movement compared to traditional passive braces in a cohort of healthy athletes without chronic ankle instability.[21](#r21) These data suggest it may be a viable alternative to traditional bracing methods for providing ankle protection during rehabilitation from acute ankle injury without compromising athlete compliance. However, previous research on the brace has only examined athletes without acute injury, with an aim to consider prevention of lateral ankle sprain during sports participation.[20](#r20),[21](#r21) The extent to which the brace could aid individuals actively rehabilitating from an acute ankle injury prior to being ready for RTS remains unknown. Thus, the purpose of this pilot study was to obtain preliminary proof-of-concept data comparing the use of the adaptive ankle brace to conventional taping during rehabilitation following acute lateral ankle sprain in a semielite soccer cohort. The primary hypothesis was that the adaptive ankle brace reduced time to RTS compared to conventional athletic taping.

## Methods

### Study Design

The study was designed as a cohort study.

### Participants

Study participants were recruited from a convenience sample of players on the male academy squads of 2 German association soccer clubs. Inclusion criteria were male, member of the youth academy squads of the respective clubs, and experiencing an acute lateral ankle sprain. Exclusion criteria were injury requiring surgical treatment and the presence of other concomitant injuries, for example, acute fracture to the lower-extremity or syndesmotic or medial ankle sprain. Participants provided written informed consent in the spirit of the Helsinki Declaration. In the case of individuals under 18 years old, participants provided written informed assent and a parent or legal guardian provided written informed consent. Details on the injury diagnosis, whether it was initial or recurrent, mechanism, and setting, were recorded, along with the player’s height, weight, club, and playing position at time of injury.

Patients were allocated to one of 2 groups: Brace or Control. The adaptive brace became available to the football clubs on June 10, 2021. Initially, all players injured between June 10, 2021, and September 30, 2022, received the brace (Brace group). Beginning October 2022, a control group was added, after which time allocation into the Brace or the Control group was randomized. The Control group was supplemented by a historical cohort from the period immediately prior to when the brace became available (February 1, 2021–June 10, 2021).

### Procedures

#### Diagnosis and Treatment

Figure [1](#f1) summarizes the study intervention. At the time of the injury, players were assessed by the team’s physiotherapist and then were referred to the team’s physician for evaluation, imaging, and diagnosis. Each team had a different team physician and team physiotherapist. Treatment was managed by the team physician along with the team physiotherapist and a single rehabilitation coach who worked with both teams (D.K.). The rehabilitation coach holds a Master’s degree in Sports, certification as an athletic trainer in professional sports, and an athletic trainer A-License including rehabilitation. During the acute injury phase, all patients received ice, compression, elevation, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication as needed. Electric stimulation, ultrasound, and manual therapy also were applied as needed, typically 3 to 4 times per week.

#### ***Rehabilitation Protocol***

Rehabilitation exercises were initiated upon the physician’s approval, typically 2 to 4 days after the injury occurred. The Brace group was fitted with the adaptive ankle brace and required to wear it during all rehabilitation activities. Participants in the Control group did not receive a brace, but they were required to have their injured ankle taped for all rehabilitation activities. Ankle taping was applied by 1 team physiotherapist of each team using 2 layers of Leukotape and additional stabilization tape in a standardized manner. The study was not blinded to bracing/taping condition. All participants received the same rehabilitation protocol, which is provided in the [Supplementary Material](https://doi.org/10.1123/jsr.2023-0290) (available online). The same medical staff conducted all brace fitting, ankle taping, and rehabilitation exercise supervision and progression.

#### Return to Sport

The treating physician provided initial approval for clearance to return to play following completion of the rehabilitation protocol. Subsequently, the player had to successfully complete 2 days of rehabilitation training at maximum effort to be cleared to RTS. After RTS, no taping or bracing was used by the players. The rehabilitation training also discontinued after RTS, but players participated in additional biweekly stabilization and strength (balance) training for the lower-extremities over a period of 8 weeks after RTS.

#### Adaptive Ankle Brace

The adaptive ankle braces used for this study were the Betterguard and the Sportomedix Malleo Fast Protect ankle braces, both with Betterguards adaptive technology (Betterguards Technology GmbH, Patents EP3238670B1, PCT/EP2019/08385, PCT/EP2018/061933, and WO 2020/074606 Figure [2](#f2)). Two braces were used because a product update became available during the course of the study. Both braces consisted of the same materials and dimensions. The main difference between the braces was a reinvented closure system providing a more individualized fit. The braces involved a close-fitting compressive ankle sleeve with the Betterguards adaptive technology attached to it along the lateral aspect of the ankle. The Betterguards adaptive technology consists of a semiflexible mini-piston embedded in an adaptor element with a valve, which allows fluid to pass within the piston when extending at physiological movement velocities. At fast movement velocities (∼300°/s), however, the valve closes within milliseconds due to fluid dynamic drag forces and inhibits further extension of the mini-piston, resulting in a limited range of motion. Afterward, the mini-piston can be extended and lock again if needed.

### Outcome Measures

The primary outcome, time to RTS, was calculated in days from the date of injury to the date of clearance to RTS. Additionally, the patients in the Brace group were provided with an electronic survey following RTS that queried their experience with the adaptive brace, including perceptions of comfort, ease of use, freedom of movement, and confidence.

### Statistical Analysis

## Results

### Participant Demographics and Injury Information

Thirteen players participated in the study from the U16 (n = 1), U17 (n = 6), and U19 (n = 6) male squads. Details of the participants are provided in Table [1](#tab01). Seven participants received the adaptive brace, and 6 received ankle taping for rehabilitation. There were no significant differences in height (*P* = .84) or weight (*P* = .21) between the groups.

### Time to RTS

RTS time ranged from 20 to 202 days across all cases (Table [2](#tab02)). Figure [3](#f3) shows boxplots of RTS time by group. Case B7 was found to be an outlier based on the Grubbs test and excluded from subsequent analyses. The median time to RTS was less for the Brace group (52.5 d, interquartile range [IQR] = 32) compared to the Control group (79.5 d, IQR = 116), but the distributions of the 2 groups were not found to differ significantly (*P* = .11, deltaMAD = 0.94). When examining only distortion external malleolus injuries, which were 10 of the 12 included cases, the median time to RTS remained less for the Brace group (52.5 d, IQR = 32) compared to the Control group (61.0 d, IQR = 131; Figure [4](#f4)), but the distributions of the 2 groups were not found to differ significantly (*P* = .39, deltaMAD = 0.52). None of the players, neither in the Control group nor the Brace group, experienced a setback or re-injury through the end of the study monitoring period (June 30, 2023).

### User Experience (Brace Group Only)

Table [3](#tab03) summarizes the user survey results from the Brace group. All users felt that they could put the brace on properly, noted that they felt the system activate during training, and felt very confident in the brace’s protection while wearing it. All users rated the brace as comfortable (14%) or very comfortable (86%) and indicated it had very good breathability. All users felt the freedom of movement of the brace was the same as wearing no brace, and all users who had previous experience with at least 1 other brace (6 out of 7) rated the freedom of movement as better than other braces they had used. Two users (29%) indicated the experience was the same as their previous experiences with ankle taping, while the remaining users (71%) indicated it was better than previous ankle taping. During the course of the study, no adverse device effects or complications were detected.
