## PART 2: SURGICAL STABILIZATION PROCEDURES

### 2.1 General Principles and Indications

**Chinese Society of Sports Medicine Clinical Guidelines (2019) — "Clinical Guidelines for the Surgical Management of Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability: A Consensus Reached by Systematic Review of the Available Data" [8]**
- Published in Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine (2019); developed by 14 physicians; GRADE approach (strong 1A to weak 2D); targets patients aged 16–60 years; will be revised every 5 years.
- **Surgical indications (2C):** "When (1) patients exhibit symptoms of CLAI after 3 to 6 months of nonsurgical treatment; (2) physical examination reveals tenderness around the lateral ligaments or a positive anterior drawer test or talar tilt test; (3) the diagnosis of CLAI was also confirmed by stress radiography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), surgery is suggested (2C)."
- **Osteochondral lesions (OCLs) (2C):** Simultaneous surgical management of CLAI and OCLs of the talus or tibia is safe and recommended.
- **Open vs. Arthroscopic Repair (1B):** "Equivalent short-term functional outcomes; both procedures are recommended." "Patients undergoing either procedure (open vs arthroscopic) can be expected to experience equivalent short-term functional outcomes (1B)."
- **Open vs. Arthroscopic Reconstruction (1C):** Equivalent short-term outcomes.
- **Autograft vs. Allograft (1C):** "Neither type of graft (autograft vs allograft) has superiority over the other. Either can be considered a promising candidate for anatomic reconstruction (1C)."
- **CFL Reconstruction (2C):** When both ATFL and CFL are ruptured with subtalar joint instability, reconstructing both ligaments is recommended.
- **Rehabilitation (1C):** "For patients who undergo anatomic repair or reconstruction, range of motion (ROM) (mostly dorsiflexion) and partial weightbearing with a brace are encouraged from the second day after surgery." For OCL patients with microfracture: early ROM but delayed weightbearing.
- **Return to Sports (1C):** Joint stability, muscle strength (90–100% of unaffected limb), and full ROM are important indicators.
- **Outcome assessment (1C):** Most commonly used measures are AOFAS score (68% of studies), Karlsson score (31.4%), VAS score, FAAM scale, talus tilt test, and anterior drawer stress radiography.

**Surgical Management of Lateral Ankle Instability in Athletes (PMC6602388, undated) [7]:** Chronic ankle instability is initially treated nonoperatively, with surgical management reserved for those who have failed to improve after 3 to 6 months of bracing and functional rehabilitation. Anatomic repair using a modification of the Broström procedure is the preferred technique.

**Current Concepts in the Surgical Management of Chronic Ankle Lateral Ligament Instability (PMC9305620, 2022) [9]:** Conservative approaches are trialled within the first 2 months.

**A Review of Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability and Emerging Alternative Outcome Monitoring Tools (PMC10816882, 2024) [10]:** Ankle sprain represents a frequent pathology among athletes and the general population; inversion-type is the most common mechanism of injury. Patients that do not respond to conservative management may develop CLAI.

**Annals of Joint (2026) — "Current concepts in arthroscopic treatment for chronic lateral ankle instability" [18]**
- Authors: Sano, Hoshino, Yamamoto, Kanzaki, Kuroda (Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine, Japan). Published online July 17, 2026. DOI: 10.21037/aoj-2026-1-0008.
- Approximately 20–30% of patients experience persistent mechanical or functional instability requiring surgical intervention.
- Open Broström/Broström-Gould repair has been the gold standard with durable results for up to 15 years; arthroscopic techniques are increasingly popular due to minimally invasive access, ability to address concomitant intra-articular pathology (synovitis, loose bodies, cartilage lesions), and comparable outcomes with potentially faster recovery.
- Diagnosis: history, physical exam (anterior drawer and talar tilt tests), stress radiography (pathological thresholds: ≥10 mm or ≥3 mm side-to-side difference for anterior talar translation; ≥10° or ≥6° for talar tilt), dynamic ultrasound (no established cutoffs), MRI (commonly shows ATFL/CFL attenuation rather than complete discontinuity).
- Surgery recommended when CLAI persists 3–6 months despite structured rehab. Candidates include high-demand athletes and those with recurrent injuries. Poor tissue quality, generalized ligamentous laxity, collagen disorders, or revision cases may require graft-based reconstruction rather than direct repair.
- Surgical techniques compared: (1) Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotted suture anchors — reliable stability, high satisfaction; (2) Arthroscopic Broström repair with knotless anchors — reduces knot irritation/complications, enables early rehab and faster RTS (75% returned to sports within 8 weeks in Teramoto's accelerated protocol); (3) All-inside arthroscopic repair — fully intra-articular, no extracapsular knot-tying; comparable outcomes to open (Zhou study), reduced operative time, significant improvements in VAS, AOFAS, FAOS, and Karlsson scores (Won study); (4) Combined ATFL and CFL repair — indicated in severe CLAI with CFL injury; reduces recurrent instability vs. ATFL-only repair (Yoshimoto, Mao, Vega studies); (5) Arthroscopic ligament reconstruction — for revision, poor tissue, or generalized laxity using autografts/allografts (e.g., EHL, semitendinosus); favorable mid-term outcomes (Alayane, Pettit, Feng studies).
- **Rehabilitation protocol (phase-based):**
  - 0–2 weeks: immobilization (cast/boot/splint for 10–14 days)
  - 2–6 weeks: controlled mobilization, partial to full weightbearing, gentle dorsiflexion-plantarflexion ROM; limit inversion-eversion to 10–15° until 6 weeks
  - 6–10 weeks: strengthening, proprioception, balance, gait training, plyometrics/jogging
  - 10–16 weeks (repair) or up to 20 weeks (reconstruction): sport-specific drills; **RTS typically 12–16 weeks after anatomic repair; 8–12 weeks with suture-tape augmentation**

### 2.2 Return-to-Play Outcomes After Anatomic Lateral Ankle Stabilization (Meta-Analysis)

**American Journal of Sports Medicine (February 2024) — "Return to Sport After Anatomic Lateral Ankle Stabilization: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis" [3]**
- 25 publications, 1,384 participants; databases searched through August 2021.
- **95% of patients returned to any sport; 83% returned to preinjury level; 87% returned to competitive sport.**
- **Mean time to RTS: 12.45 weeks (95% CI, 10.8–14.1 weeks).**
- Risk factors for RTS failure: age (6% increased risk per decade) and BMI (4% increased risk per 5 kg/m² increase).
- Professional/competitive athletes had higher RTS rates (93%) than recreational athletes (83%).
- No significant differences between arthroscopic vs. open surgery, repair vs. reconstruction, or early vs. late weightbearing.

### 2.3 Modified Broström-Gould Repair — Open Technique Outcomes

**"Return to Play after Modified Broström Operation for Chronic Ankle Instability in Elite Athletes" (2019), Clinics in Orthopedic Surgery [11]**
- 18 elite athletes (9 male, 9 female; average age 19.3 years) who underwent MBO by a single surgeon between August and December 2013. Sports included soccer (n=8), basketball, ballet/gymnastics, martial arts.
- Procedure: ATFL imbrication with inferior extensor retinaculum reinforcement. Postoperative protocol: 4 weeks immobilization, 2 weeks ankle brace, ROM exercises at 4 weeks, strengthening/stretching at 6 weeks.
- Results:
  - Mean time to return to personal training: 1.9 months (range 1–6)
  - Mean time to return to team training: 2.9 months (range 1–6)
  - Mean time to return to competitive play (RTP): 3.9 months (range 2–7)
  - "The RTP was 83.3% at 4 months after lateral ankle ligament repair and 100% at 8 months postoperatively."
  - No reoperations, infections, or neurovascular damage.
- "There were no significant differences of any variables including age, sex, body mass index, level of sports, grade of instability, presence of os subfibulare, and preoperative functional score between the early RTP and late RTP groups."
- Three patients with delayed RTP (ballerina and two gymnasts) had high Beighton scores (7–9), suggesting generalized joint hypermobility may be associated with longer recovery.

**"Predictors of Return to Sports Following the Modified Broström Procedure for Chronic Ankle Instability" (2025), Journal of Clinical Medicine [14]**
- 62 patients under 35 years old followed up to 3 years post-surgery. 51 (82.3%) returned to preinjury sports levels (return group); 11 (17.7%) did not (non-return group).
- Significant group differences: FAOS pain (94.7 vs. 85.1 points; p=0.004), FAOS sports (91.2 vs. 78.8; p<0.001), FAAM sports subscale (90.5 vs. 77.4; p<0.001).
- Mechanical instability recurrence: 2 patients (3.9%) in return group vs. 4 (36.4%) in non-return group (p<0.001).
- Dynamic postural control differed substantially (overall stability index 1.41 vs. 2.33, p=0.002); static postural control and peroneal strength showed no significant differences.
- Multivariate logistic regression identified three risk factors for failure to RTS:
  - FAOS pain score <90 (odds ratio 8.66; p<0.001)
  - Recurrence of mechanical instability (odds ratio 13.99; p<0.001)
  - Inadequate dynamic postural control (OSI >1.8) (odds ratio 4.21; p=0.012)
- Conclusion: comprehensive rehabilitation protocols should address residual pain, mechanical stability, and dynamic postural control to facilitate optimal postoperative sports participation.

### 2.4 Lateral Ligament Reconstruction — Systematic Review in Professional Athletes

**"Outcomes and Return to Sports Following the Ankle Lateral Ligament Reconstruction in Professional Athletes: A Systematic Review of the Literature" (2022), Indian Journal of Orthopaedics [12]**
- PRISMA systematic review; MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane databases, Jan 2000–Dec 2020; 982 articles screened; 10 studies; 343 athletes.
- Combined mean age: 23 years; average follow-up: 58.4 months.
- **"After surgery 308 (89%) returned to their pre-injury level of sports, 7 (2%) patients returned to a lower-level sport while the remaining 28 (9%) never returned to play."**
- **"Lateral ligament reconstruction is a safe and effective treatment for severe ruptures providing a stable ankle with a mean time of 16 weeks to return to sports."**
- Post-operative complications occurred in 68 (19.8%) patients: superficial infections (9), numbness (24), ankle stiffness (18), instability (7), re-rupture (3), peroneal nerve complications (3), CRPS (2).
- Procedures reviewed: Modified Broström operation, Chrisman-Snook procedure, Watson-Jones technique, and variations. "Modified Brostrom procedure using a suture anchor was observed to provide satisfactory clinical outcomes in high-demand athletes with lateral ligament instability."

### 2.5 Systematic Review of Lateral Ankle Ligament Repair RTP (ISAKOS 2023)

**Civilette et al. (ISAKOS 2023) — "Return to Play Following Lateral Ankle Ligament Repair: A Systematic Review" [13]**
- 37 articles, 2,593 repairs. Level 4 evidence or higher; open and arthroscopic Broström/modified Broström-Gould repairs.
- Surgical techniques: 62% modified Brostrom-Gould, 14% Brostrom-Gould, 22% Brostrom, 8% Karlsson modification. 78% open approach; 30% arthroscopic.
- Outcome scales used: AOFAS (46%), VAS (30%), KAFS (30%).
- **Average time to RTP: 13.7 weeks (range 4–16 weeks).**
- **Overall RTP rate: 86.6%; 78.9% returned to pre-injury activity level.**
- Only 30% of articles reported any RTP criteria; only 5% described specific objective/quantitative criteria.
- "After review of all available literature that contains return to play (RTP) metrics following lateral ligament repair, it is evident that there is no standardized, evidence-based RTP criteria available for physicians to return their patients to sport."
- Conclusion: Nearly one-quarter of athletes failed to return to pre-injury activity level; standardized, evidence-based RTP criteria are needed to maximize athletic performance and minimize re-injury risk.

### 2.6 Arthroscopic (All-Inside / Arthroscopic-Assisted) vs. Open Broström — Direct Comparisons

**Wahib et al. (2026) — "Arthroscopic versus open management of chronic lateral ankle instability: A prospective randomized controlled trial," Journal of Orthopaedic Reports [16]**
- 40 patients with CLAI (≥6 months failed conservative management or ATFL avulsion injury) randomized to open Broström-Gould (Group A) or arthroscopic Broström-Gould (Group B); 18-month follow-up. Outcomes: VAS, AOFAS, Karlsson Ankle Functional scores; secondary: operative time, complications, return-to-work interval.
- **Operative time significantly shorter in open group (44.2±8.5 vs. 79.5±23.11 min; p<0.001).**
- Both techniques produced significant postoperative improvement in all outcome scores (p<0.001).
- "The AB group showed better early postoperative outcomes at 6 months, including lower VAS scores and higher functional scores; however, no significant differences were observed between groups at 12 and 18 months."
- **Return to work: 8.8±1.51 vs. 11.15±3.62 weeks (p=0.002) — earlier after arthroscopic repair.**
- Complication rates comparable; no recurrent instability or reoperations.

**Lee et al. (2024) — "All-Inside Arthroscopic and Open Techniques of the Modified Broström Procedure: Comparison of the Times to Return to Play," Medicina [23]**
- 60 patients (January 2012–July 2014), 30 per group (AMBO = arthroscopic; OMBO = open). Mean age 34.9 years; 55% male; recreational athletes 51.7%. Single surgeon. Outcomes pre-op, 6 weeks, 6 months: AOFAS, VAS, satisfaction, activity level.
- **AMBO significantly shorter time to painless walking: 7.07 ± 2.96 weeks vs. 11.03 ± 8.58 weeks (p=0.02).** No significant differences in other RTP parameters.
- 6-week VAS significantly lower in AMBO group (p<0.001); 6-week AOFAS significantly higher in AMBO group (p<0.001). No significant differences at 6 months.
- AMBO: 80% excellent subjective satisfaction vs. 27.6% for OMBO (not statistically significant).
- In recreational athletes, AMBO showed significantly shorter RTP for walking normally over 10 minutes (p=0.012) and rising up on heels without pain (p=0.003); sedentary group showed no differences.

**Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (2023), Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research — "Comparison of arthroscopic and open Brostrom-Gould surgery for chronic lateral ankle instability" [24]**
- 11 studies, 686 patients (335 arthroscopic, 351 open).
- Approximately 20% of acute ankle sprains progress to CLAI requiring surgical intervention. Open Broström-Gould has long been considered the gold standard.
- No significant differences in talar tilt, anterior talar translation, complication rates, time to return to sports, or operative time.
- At 2-year follow-up: no significant differences in AOFAS, K-P, VAS, Tegner scores.
- Arthroscopic group advantages in early outcomes: earlier weight-bearing (1.33 weeks earlier), better AOFAS, K-P, VAS scores within first postoperative year; significantly less perioperative pain (VAS difference: -1.13).
- No significant difference in nerve complications (4.6% arthroscopic vs. 2.8% open).
- "We advocate for adopting arthroscopic repair as a preferred alternative to the conventional open Broström-Gould procedure for treating chronic lateral ankle instability."

**Frontiers in Surgery (2023) — "Arthroscopic vs. open Broström-Gould for repairing anterior talofibular ligament: mid-term outcomes comparison" [26]**
- Retrospective review (June 2014–June 2018, No. 967 Hospital of PLA, Dalian, China). 99 patients computer-randomized: 49 arthroscopic Broström-Gould (AB), 50 open (OB). Both used double-loaded 4.5mm PEEK suture anchor; short-leg cast 2 weeks then ankle brace. Follow-up at 6, 12, 24, 48 months.
- Baseline comparable (mean ages ~31.7–31.9; 66 males/33 females). Operation time similar (43.58 vs. 48.45 min); hospitalization similar (6.41 vs. 6.70 days).
- Both techniques significantly improved all clinical outcomes. AB significantly higher AOFAS (83.45 vs. 79.74, P=0.01) and K-P (80.27 vs. 78.80, P=0.03) at 6 months. **At 48 months, no significant differences in ADT, VAS, AOFAS, K-P, or Tegner (all P>0.05).**
- Complication rates similar (16.3% AB vs. 14% OB, P=0.75). AB: 6 superficial peroneal nerve injuries, 2 superficial wound infections; OB: 2 nerve injuries, 5 wound infections. No secondary operations within 48 months.
- Authors note this is the first study comparing the two techniques with larger sample size and longer follow-up.

**Cureus (2025) — "Clinical Outcomes After Arthroscopic Broström-Gould Procedure for Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability" (Changi General Hospital, Singapore) [27]**
- 39 patients (22 M, 17 F; mean age 36.2 years, range 19.6–64.8; mean BMI 27.4). Procedure: arthroscopic debridement; ATFL anchored to distal fibula with Smith & Nephew SutureFIX anchors (typically two). Postoperative: immediate weight-bearing with ankle brace removed at six weeks.
- Results (all significant, p<0.0001):
  - VAS: 5.87 ± 1.92 preop → 2.0 ± 2.16 postop (t=8.75)
  - K-P: 43.68 ± 13.2 preop → 69.21 ± 17.86 postop (t=-8.71)
  - AOFAS: 62.53 ± 16.05 preop → 83.8 ± 11.49 postop (t=-5.91)
- No complications or recurrent instability requiring revision surgery.
- Learning curve: 22 cases for arthroscopic vs. 12 for open Broström-Gould.
- Return to sport positively influenced by preoperative motivation and elite sport participation; negatively by high BMI and age.
- Limitations: small sample, single institution, single operator, short-term follow-up (up to one year).

### 2.7 Suture Tape Augmentation / Internal Brace

**AAOS Now (March 2026) — "Does suture tape aid return to play after lateral ankle ligament reconstruction?" [15]**
- Chronic lateral ankle instability affects 20%–40% of individuals after acute sprains.
- Suture tape augmentation: high-strength, nonabsorbable suture tape with knotless anchors paralleling the ATFL.
- Biomechanics: ultimate load-to-failure 250–315 N (exceeding native ATFL at ~154 N); stiffness 21–31 N/mm (matching/surpassing native ligament at 14.5 N/mm).
- **Multicenter RCT (Kulwin et al., 119 patients): return to preinjury activity at 13.3 weeks vs. 17.5 weeks for traditional repair (P=0.001).**
- Systematic reviews report athletes returning to sport at 8–12 weeks with aggressive rehab vs. historical 12–24+ weeks for nonaugmented repairs.
- Functional outcomes converge beyond 12–24 months between techniques.
- **Porter et al. 5-year RCT: superior Foot and Ankle Outcome Scores and higher Tegner Activity Scale scores in augmented group with zero failures vs. two in traditional repair.**
- Safety: no major differences in overall complication rates. "Recurrence of instability and revision surgeries tend to occur more frequently after traditional Brostrom repair, while peroneal nerve and tendon irritation appear more often with suture tape constructs." Largest RCT: 8.5% complication rate for modified Brostrom vs. 1.7% for augmentation (P=0.12).
- "When differences exist, they typically favor augmentation primarily in the early postoperative period (three to six months), with outcomes converging beyond 12 to 24 months."
- Particularly beneficial for elite athletes, revision cases, generalized ligamentous laxity, and poor tissue quality.
- Emerging biomaterials: "a synthetic, degradable matrix woven from wet-spun fibers of polycaprolactone base-polyurethane urea" with elastic modulus closer to native ligament.

**ISAKOS 2023 (Murray et al.) — "Return to Sport and Daily Activities After Modification of the Broström Procedure... Utilizing One Internal Brace for Augmentation of Both the ATFL and CFL" [25]**
- Retrospective case series (Level 4); 31 patients with grade III ankle sprains and lateral ankle instability who failed ≥6 months of supervised conservative management. Modified Broström with suture anchors + internal brace augmentation of both ATFL and CFL.
- Outcomes: FAAM ADL post-op 77.49/84 (vs. pre-op 46.06, P<0.00001); FAAM Sports subscale 19.31/28 (vs. pre-op 4, P<0.00001); mean Karlsson-Peterson score 82.74/100 post-operatively.
- 14 recreational athletes; **12 of 14 resumed activity in <12 months post-op; mean time to return to sport: 5.72 months.** Mean patient age 40.70 years; mean follow-up 24.06 months.

### 2.8 Suture Anchor Configuration and Surgical Technique Details

**Cao et al. (2018) — "Surgical management of chronic lateral ankle instability: a meta-analysis," Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research [17]**
- Meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (published 1990–2016): Cho 2012, Cho 2013, Hennrikus 1996, Karlsson 1997, Larsen 1990, Porter 2015, Rosenbaum 1999.
- Acute lateral ankle ligament injury is common; 10–30% of patients fail conservative treatment and require surgery.
- Five comparison groups:
  1. Dynamic vs. static tenodesis (non-anatomic reconstruction): static tenodesis yielded better clinical satisfaction and fewer subsequent sprains.
  2. Non-anatomic reconstruction vs. anatomic repairment: one study found more nerve damage in the non-anatomic group; another found non-anatomic reconstruction provided higher reduction of talar tilt angle.
  3. Transosseous suture vs. imbrication (anatomic repair techniques): no significant difference in clinical outcomes except operation time.
  4. Double anchor technique superior to single anchor in reducing talar tilt.
  5. Anatomic reconstruction with LARS resulted in better patient-scored outcomes at 2 years than modified Brostrom technique.
- Conclusions: dynamic tenodesis has limitations (poor clinical satisfaction, more subsequent sprains); non-anatomic reconstruction abnormally increased inversion stiffness at subtalar level; multiple types of modified Brostrom procedures achieve good clinical results; anatomic reconstruction is better for some specific patients.

**Podiatry Today — Surgical technique details (University Foot and Ankle Institute) [19]**
- Modified Broström-Gould described as "the most routine procedure for primary lateral ankle ligament stabilization."
- Technique: curvilinear incision along distal fibula (extended posteriorly if peroneal repair needed); identification of peroneal sheath, CFL and ATFL; repair using two suture anchors in pants-over-vest fashion with FiberWire Suture, augmented with PushLock Anchor.
- Cho and coworkers: no significant clinical difference between single vs. double suture anchors, though double-anchor group showed slightly more reduction in talar tilt postoperatively.
- Augmentation options for damaged tissue: autograft (peroneal, semitendinosus, plantaris, gracilis tendons) and allografts. Mulhern: anatomic reconstruction with acellular dermal matrix (Graftjacket Maxstrip) with interference screws. Basra: Arthrex InternalBrace system (#2 FiberTape with BioComposite knotless anchors) — suture tape reinforcement of Broström with anchors in talus and fibula; postoperative protocol 14 days non-weightbearing + 14 days partial weightbearing. Caution against overtightening FiberTape (postoperative stiffness).
- "We typically reserve tendon grafting for revisional surgery when primary stabilization procedure has failed."
- Associated pathology: "Komenda and Ferkel found that in 52 ankles with chronic ankle instability, 93 percent of the ankles exhibited intra-articular pathology with the most common finding being synovitis followed by the presence of loose bodies." Lee et al.: synovitis, cartilage defects, loose bodies, Bassett's lesion, impingement. Authors recommend routine ankle arthroscopy with all lateral stabilization procedures, debridement of synovitis, resection of osteophytes, and visual inspection and repair of peroneal tendons.

### 2.9 Peroneal Tendon Procedures (Related Findings)

- **Podiatry Today [19]:** The curvilinear incision is "extended posteriorly if peroneal repair is needed"; authors recommend "visual inspection and repair of peroneal tendons" during lateral stabilization procedures. Autograft options include the peroneal tendon for reconstruction when native tissue is insufficient.
- **PMC6602388 [7]:** Notes that peroneal tendon pathology is a known associated injury in chronic ankle instability, though the surgical management of CLAI primarily centers on the Broström-type anatomic repair.
- No dedicated comparative studies on isolated peroneal tendon procedures for CAI outcomes were identified in the searches; this remains an area where higher-level evidence is lacking.

---

## PART 3: DIRECT COMPARISONS BETWEEN CONSERVATIVE AND SURGICAL MANAGEMENT

### 3.1 Published Evidence (with critical caveats)

**CAUTION — RETRACTED ARTICLE: Liu and Diao (2019), "Surgical therapy vs conservative therapy for patients with acute injury of the lateral ankle ligament," International Wound Journal [20]**
- **IMPORTANT: This article has been formally retracted.** It is included here only for completeness and should NOT be cited as valid evidence in a systematic review. (PMCID: PMC7948700; original PMID: 30924305.)
- Original methods: 13 studies (10 RCTs, 2 retrospective comparative studies); 834 surgical patients vs. 930 conservative patients.
- Original reported findings (before retraction):
  - AOFAS score significantly higher in surgical group (WMD: 10.33, 95% CI: 6.83–13.83)
  - Effective rate significantly higher in surgical group (RR: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04–1.28)
  - Complications significantly higher with surgery (RR: 3.31, 95% CI: 2.55–4.28), including ankylosis (RR: 3.63, 95% CI: 2.16–6.08), scar tenderness (RR: 10.16, 95% CI: 3.89–26.52), sensory loss (RR: 5.66, 95% CI: 2.76–11.59)
  - No significant differences in recurrent ankle injury, limited ROM, DVT, or wound infection/necrosis.
  - Background note: acute lateral ankle ligament injuries account for ~25% of all musculoskeletal injuries; ~23,000 ankle injuries/day in the US and ~5,000/day in the UK.

### 3.2 State of the Evidence on Conservative vs. Surgical for CAI

Based on all sources retrieved in this search, the following synthesis applies:

- **There is no high-level (RCT-level) direct comparison of structured rehabilitation alone vs. operative stabilization specifically for established CAI in athletes identified in the searches.** The only direct surgical-vs-conservative meta-analysis found (Liu & Diao) addressed **acute** injuries and has been **retracted** [20].
- The foundational clinical pathway across all surgical sources is consistent: **surgery is reserved for patients who have failed 3–6 months of non-surgical management** (bracing and functional rehabilitation):
  - Chinese Society of Sports Medicine guidelines (2C): surgery suggested when patients "exhibit symptoms of CLAI after 3 to 6 months of nonsurgical treatment" [8]
  - PMC6602388: "Chronic ankle instability is initially treated nonoperatively, with surgical management reserved for those who have failed to improve after 3 to 6 months of bracing and functional rehabilitation" [7]
  - PMC9305620: "Conservative approaches are trialled within the first 2 months" [9]
  - Annals of Joint 2026: surgery recommended when CLAI persists 3–6 months despite structured rehab [18]
  - ISAKOS 2023 internal brace study: patients failed "at least six months of supervised conservative management" before surgery [25]
  - Wahib 2026 RCT: inclusion required "≥6 months failed conservative management" [16]
- **Comparative outcome implications:** The pooled RTS data from surgical meta-analyses (95% RTS to any sport; 83% to preinjury level; mean 12.45 weeks [3]; 86.6% RTP at 13.7 weeks [13]; 89% RTP at 16 weeks in professionals [12]) provide the surgical benchmarks. For conservative management, the evidence base (Jiang 2025 [1][2]; Skwiot 2025 [6]; Linens 2017 [22]) supports functional rehabilitation (balance, NMT, plyometrics) for improving postural control, proprioception, and patient-reported outcomes, but no pooled RTS timeline benchmark equivalent to the surgical meta-analyses was identified. The Mass General Brigham protocol suggests a typical non-operative RTS pathway of 11–16 weeks for lateral ankle sprain rehabilitation [21], and The Basketball Doctors suggests 2–6 weeks (Grade 2) to 6–12+ weeks (Grade 3) for basketball players [31], while the NBA physical therapist Loiacono suggests ~7–55 days depending on grade [32].
- **Recurrence context:** High re-injury rates (up to 70–80% in high-risk sports [1][6]) and 40% CAI conversion within one year [1] underpin the rationale for more aggressive management in athletes. The 2024 AJSM meta-analysis found professional/competitive athletes have higher RTS rates after surgery (93%) than recreational athletes (83%) [3].
- **Applicability note:** Because the searches did not surface any non-retracted RCT directly randomizing established CAI patients to rehabilitation vs. stabilization, conclusions about which approach yields "superior" outcomes, faster RTP, or lower recurrence for CAI specifically must be drawn indirectly from (a) conservative rehabilitation RCTs in CAI [6][22], (b) surgical RTS meta-analyses [3][12][13], and (c) the widely accepted stepped-care paradigm (3–6 months of rehabilitation before considering surgery) [7][8][9]. This gap should be explicitly acknowledged in the systematic review.

---

## PART 4: BASKETBALL-SPECIFIC AND RELATED JUMPING/CUTTING SPORT DATA

### 4.1 NBA Epidemiology

**"Ankle Sprains in the National Basketball Association, 2013-14 through 2016-17" (2019), American Journal of Sports Medicine [28]**
- Retrospective cohort of all NBA players on a roster for ≥1 game; data from NBA electronic medical record system maintained by certified athletic trainers.
- 796 ankle sprains among 389 players across 2,341 unique NBA player-seasons.
- Overall single-season risk of ankle sprain: 25.8% (95% CI, 23.9%–28.0%) — approximately 1 in 4 NBA players each season.
- 71.0% occurred in games (n=565); 80.2% were lateral sprains (n=638); 71.2% involved contact mechanism (n=567).
- Game incidence rate: 4.5 per 1,000 player-games (higher than collegiate 1.4–2.3 and high school 0.8 per 1,000).
- Players under 26 years old: 54% higher incidence rate (IRR 1.54; 95% CI 1.27–1.86).
- History of ankle sprain in past year: 41% higher incidence (IRR 1.41; 95% CI 1.13–1.74).
- 56% of sprains (n=443) resulted in no missed NBA games; for those with missed time: median 2 games missed (IQR 1–4); median 8 days to return. High ankle sprains: median 5 games missed; 24 days to return.
- Total 1,467 player-games missed over 4 seasons (average ~370/season). 44% of sprains resulted in ≥1 missed game.
- Peak incidence at start of preseason, decreasing over time.
- Mechanisms: stepping on opponent's foot (33.3% of contact); inversion (61.6% of noncontact); activities: general defense (18.8%), layup driving (14.5%), rebounding (12.2%). Types: lateral 80.2%, medial 7.8%, high 4.1%.
- Authors recommend integrating injury prevention programs into management of initial sprains, particularly for younger players and those with prior sprain history.

**Mayo Clinic (2021) — "Management of ankle injuries in professional basketball players," Orthopedic Reviews [29]**
- Ankle injury is the most common lower extremity injury, accounting for ~21.9% of all basketball-related injuries. In the NBA, ankles are the most commonly injured joint — over 1,800 game-related ankle injuries comprise 14.7% of all injuries in an average year. Ankle injuries occur at 3.8–5.2 per 1,000 athlete exposures.
- An Australian basketball study: over half (53.7%) of playing time missed due to injury was caused by ankle injury. Most common activity at time of injury: rebounding (34.4%).
- **Lateral low ankle sprains:** most common (80.2% of all sprains), caused by excess inversion. Treatment: RICE protocol, nonoperative management. Return to play: 6–8 weeks.
- **Medial ankle sprains:** 7.8% of sprains, caused by excessive eversion/dorsiflexion. Return to play: 3–6+ months.
- **High ankle sprains (syndesmotic):** 4.1% of sprains, most severe. Surgical repair more common. Return to play: 6–8+ weeks.
- **Stress fractures:** 55% of lower extremity stress injuries involve foot, 21.1% involve ankle/fibula. Average 25.1 games missed; ~30% of athletes unable to return to previous level. Surgical treatment in elite athletes yields average return of 3.8 months vs. 5.6 months with conservative management. Vitamin D important.
- **Jones fracture:** ~15% of affected NBA players did not return to an NBA game; up to 15–30% nonunion rate; surgical intervention common in elite athletes.
- **Achilles tendon rupture:** basketball is the cause of 42.6% of all AT ruptures among individuals under age 60 in the US; almost exclusively treated with surgical repair in athletes; full return to play: 6–9 months.
- **Prevention:** external supports (taping, bracing) proven effective at reducing injury risk; proprioceptive and kinematic training programs (tilt boards, balance beams) show similar effectiveness.

### 4.2 Applicability of Non-Basketball Jumping/Cutting Sport Data

The surgical RTP data from the systematic reviews above draw substantially on soccer, volleyball, gymnastics, ballet, martial arts, and mixed athlete populations:
- The 2019 MBO elite athlete study included soccer (n=8), basketball, ballet/gymnastics, martial arts [11].
- The 2022 reconstruction systematic review (professional athletes, mean age 23) included a mix of high-demand sports [12].
- The 2024 AJSM meta-analysis pooled mixed athlete populations and found no sport-specific subgroup differences; professional/competitive athletes had higher RTS (93%) than recreational (83%) [3].
- The ISAKOS 2023 internal brace study included recreational athletes (no professionals) [25].

**Applicability note:** For basketball-specific conclusions where data are sparse (e.g., no dedicated RCT of CAI surgery vs. rehab in basketball players), the jumping/cutting demands of volleyball, soccer, and handball athletes are the closest analog. The 2024 AJSM meta-analysis finding that RTS failure risk increases with age (6% per decade) and BMI (4% per 5 kg/m²) [3], combined with the NBA data showing higher incidence in players under 26 [28], suggests young, lean basketball players are in the favorable prognostic group for surgical RTS.

---

## PART 5: CROSS-CUTTING OUTCOME MEASURES AND QUALITY ISSUES

### 5.1 Outcome Measures Commonly Used
- **AOFAS (American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society) score** — most commonly used clinician measure (68% of studies per Chinese guidelines [8]; 46% of articles per ISAKOS review [13])
- **Karlsson / Karlsson-Peterson (K-P) score** — 31.4% of studies [8]; 30% of articles [13]
- **VAS pain score** — commonly used patient measure [8][13]
- **FAAM (Foot and Ankle Ability Measure)** — ADL and Sports subscales [8][14][25]
- **FAOS (Foot and Ankle Outcome Score)** — used in MBP predictor study [14]
- **CAIT (Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool)** — used for CAI diagnosis/rehab (≤25 cutoff) [22] and in rehabilitation protocols [21]
- **Tegner Activity Scale** — used in arthroscopic vs. open comparisons [26] and suture tape RCTs [15]
- **Radiographic measures:** talar tilt, anterior drawer stress radiography [8]
- **Posturography:** Overall Stability Index (OSI) for dynamic postural control [14]
- **Psychological measures:** Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) [6]

### 5.2 Re-injury/Complication Rates — Surgical
- 2022 reconstruction systematic review: complications in 68/343 (19.8%): superficial infections (9), numbness (24), ankle stiffness (18), instability (7), re-rupture (3), peroneal nerve complications (3), CRPS (2) [12]
- 2023 arthroscopic vs. open meta-analysis: nerve complications 4.6% arthroscopic vs. 2.8% open (not significant) [24]
- Frontiers 2023: total complications 16.3% arthroscopic vs. 14% open (P=0.75) [26]
- AAOS Now 2026: recurrence/revision more common with traditional Broström; peroneal nerve/tendon irritation more common with augmentation; largest RCT complication rates 8.5% (modified Broström) vs. 1.7% (augmentation), P=0.12 [15]
- Suture tape RCT (Porter 5-year): zero failures augmented vs. two in traditional repair [15]
- MBO elite athletes 2019: no reoperations, infections, or neurovascular damage [11]

### 5.3 Quality/Evidence Gaps Identified by Sources
- **No standardized RTS paradigm exists** for LAS rehabilitation [1][2]
- **No consensus on RTS criteria** after LAS; no expert recommended time-from-injury as criterion; only 30% of surgical articles report RTP criteria, only 5% use objective/quantitative criteria [5][13]
- **Lack of direct RCTs comparing conservative vs. surgical treatment for established CAI** (identified gap in this search; the only such meta-analysis found was retracted [20])
- Need for large-scale RCTs with control groups and long-term follow-up in CAI rehabilitation [6]
- Heterogeneity of rehabilitation interventions and limited sample sizes in CAI rehab trials [6]
- Need for multicenter RCTs, standardized outcome reporting, better patient selection integrating structural and functional imaging, and data-driven rehabilitation in arthroscopic CLAI management [18]
- Need for sport-specific and injury-specific studies in professional athletes [12]

---
